Title: Effects of Overripe Banana Processing Techniques on the Chemical Composition and Attractancy to Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus
Authors: Abuelmaali, S. A.; Hui, L. W.; Sabar, S. A.; Abdul Latif, N. A. H.; Ishak, W. R. w.; Vern, N. Y.; Webb, C. E.; Abu Kassim, N.
Abstract: The rising incidence of vector-borne diseases transmitted by mosquitoes has become a significant public health concern. The increasing resistance of mosquitoes to conventional insecticides has prompted the need for alternative control strategies such as Attractive Targeted Sugar Baits (ATSBs). While fruit-based attractants have shown promise, the impact of different production methods on their attractiveness remains underexplored. This study investigates the effect of three production techniques of overripe banana (Musa acuminata) extracts: liquid extraction, syrup concentration, and freeze-drying, on the chemical composition and their attractiveness to Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus. Extracts were infused into hydrogel beads and tested in dual-choice olfactometer assays to mosquito vectors Ae. aegypti and Ae. albopictus. Chemical profiling was conducted through Gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) and enzymatic sugar analysis. Results showed that all banana extracts were significantly more attractive than the 10% sucrose control. Among the extracts, syrup concentrates showed the highest attraction (PI = 0.58 {+/-} 0.17 for Ae. aegypti; 0.58 {+/-} 0.14 for Ae. albopictus), followed by freeze-dried (PI = 0.52 {+/-} 0.20; 0.54 {+/-} 0.08) and liquid extracts (PI = -0.40 {+/-} 0.04; 0.49 {+/-} 0.18). GC-MS analysis revealed that freeze-dried powder retained the greatest diversity and abundance of volatile organic compounds (VOCs), especially esters like butyl ethanoate and isoamyl acetate, which are known to influence mosquito behaviour. Although syrup concentration resulted in VOCs degradation, it also generated Maillard reaction products, such as sulphur-containing volatiles, which may enhance olfactory cues. Sugar analysis indicated that both syrup and freeze-dried extracts contained higher levels of sucrose (0.35-0.57 g/100g), glucose (21.20-28.70 g/100g), fructose (14.64-17.89 g/100g), and maltose (9.28-15.56 g/100g), aligning with mosquito preferences. Overall, the findings demonstrate that production techniques significantly influence the chemical composition and attractant potential of overripe banana extracts, offering valuable insights for the development of fruit-based mosquito lures in vector surveillance and control strategies.

Title: Engineered microvessel networks -- Longitudinal transcriptomic profiling validates chip-grown tissues as a robust model for studying vasculature
Authors: Osorio, L. A.; Hansen, B.; Suba, K.; Yuan, Y.; Witowska, M.; Xu, X.; Noman, M.; Au, S. A.; Pantazis, P.; van Batenburg-Sherwood, J.; Ahmetaj-Shala, B.; Akerman, I.; Salem, V.
Abstract: Vascularised Organ-on-Chip (OoC) models are promising New Approach Methodologies (NAMs), but their translation requires validation for defined Contexts of Use (CoU). Here, we combine microfluidic microvessel networks (MVNs) with longitudinal bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing to determine how cell provenance influences engineered vascular phenotype. Stromal cell identity produced distinct network architectures and transcriptional trajectories, demonstrating that support cells, commonly treated as interchangeable, represent an important CoU variable. Primary human pancreatic microvascular endothelial cells failed to form stable perfusable networks, but supplementation with 10% Human Umbilical Vein Endothelial Cells (HUVECs) or Blood Outgrowth Endothelial Cells (BOECs) rescued self-assembly. Single-cell transcriptomics identified specialised endothelial populations associated with vascular morphogenesis, including tip, stalk, phalanx, endothelial to mesenchymal transition (EndMT) and pericyte-like endothelial cells. Failed networks lacked coherent endothelial specialisation, whereas rescued networks restored stabilising cell states and revealed FLRT2--UNC5B signalling within pericyte-like HUVECs, recapitulating a pathway implicated in angiogenic development in vivo. These findings establish cell provenance as a critical determinant of microvascular NAM performance and demonstrate how transcriptomic validation can define and strengthen the biological relevance of microvessel-on-chip models for specific CoUs.

Title: PROST: An Open Toolbox, Harmonised Multi-Lab Dataset, and Meta-Analysis of Ankle-Foot Roll-Over Shape
Authors: Reichsbouscher, C.; Solav, D.
Abstract: The ankle-foot roll-over shape (ROS) is the sagittal-plane path of the centre of pressure (CoP) during the stance phase of walking, expressed in a shank-based coordinate system. It describes the effective rocker geometry that emerges from both the shape and the elastic deformation of the ankle-foot system during walking, and informs prosthetic and orthotic design. Previous studies characterised ROS in small samples with differing laboratory protocols, so they have not systematically assessed inter-individual variability or its relation to anthropometrics. We developed the open-source Public ROS Toolbox (PROST) for standardised ROS computation, and used it to harmonise marker trajectories, ground reaction forces and CoP data from four public gait datasets collected in independent laboratories. For each leg, we fitted a circular arc to the pooled ROS of all its stance phases. In a one-stage individual-participant data meta-analysis, linear mixed-effects models, with dataset as a fixed effect and participant as a random intercept, related the arc radius and the horizontal coordinate of the circle centre to anthropometrics, and, in the two self-selected-speed datasets, to walking speed. The harmonised dataset comprises 249 participants and 5,667 stance phases at walking speeds of 0.7-8.5 km/h. Circular arcs fitted the ROS closely (mean RMS radial residual 1.9 mm). The radius had a median of 410.3 mm (interquartile range, IQR, 237.6 mm), and the circle centre lay posterior to the ankle (median -20.6 mm, IQR 49.5 mm). Between-participant differences, quantified by the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), accounted for 42% of the variance in log radius (95% CI 25-57%) and 47% of the variance in the horizontal coordinate of the circle centre (95% CI 24-65%). Anthropometrics explained a negligible share of this variance (radius: pseudo-R2 -0.001, 95% CI -0.03 to 0.12), and height normalisation did not reduce radius variability (robust coefficient of variation 43% with and without normalisation). Faster self-selected walking was associated with a larger radius and a more posterior circle centre. To our knowledge, this study provides the first harmonised multi-lab ROS dataset. Together with the open-source toolbox, it is publicly available to support reproducible research in gait biomechanics, rehabilitation device design and clinical gait assessment. ROS geometry was participant-specific but was not predicted by age, sex, height or mass. A device ROS scaled from anthropometrics is therefore unlikely to match an individual's ROS, motivating studies of whether matching it, through device geometry and stiffness, improves gait mechanics.

Title: MorphoANOVA: Dissecting Histology-Gene Expression Relationships in Spatial Transcriptomics
Authors: Chen, P.-W.; Yan, G.; Yu, S.; Li, J. J.
Abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) measures the expression of hundreds to thousands of genes within tissue architecture, often accompanied by histology images. However, it remains challenging to systematically characterize which genes exhibit associations with tissue morphology, whether these associations vary spatially, and which genes show additional spatial expression patterns beyond those captured by morphology. Here we introduce MorphoANOVA, a gene-wise statistical framework for characterizing morphology--expression relationships across genes measured by ST. Using nested spatially varying coefficient models and sequential ANOVA, MorphoANOVA assesses slide-wide associations with an H\&E-derived morphology feature, location-specific changes in these associations, and additional spatial variation after accounting for the selected feature. The resulting statistics enable gene prioritization and pathway enrichment analysis, while spatial component maps support the interpretation of individual genes. Simulations demonstrate MorphoANOVA's ability to distinguish the modeled components and recover their spatial patterns. Applications to human cortex and breast cancer identify biological programs associated with different morphology--expression patterns and reveal distinct relationships with cell composition. Across three HER2-positive breast cancer patients, invasive-cancer marker genes consistently exhibit stronger evidence of location-specific morphology associations. MorphoANOVA thus provides a framework for systematically interpreting spatial gene-expression patterns in relation to tissue morphology.

Title: Programmable interphyla communication for Staphylococcus aureus by transferability of homoserine lactone sensors between Bacillales bacteria
Authors: Sarker, B.; Rondthaler, S. N.; Zeng, M.; Andrews, L. B.
Abstract: Staphylococcus aureus is a Gram-positive opportunistic pathogen of the order Bacillales and a frequent member of human-associated microbiomes. Despite its clinical relevance, engineering S. aureus and the communities it inhabits remains limited by a shortage of well-characterized genetic tools for precise control of gene expression and intercellular signaling. Biosensors for homoserine lactones (HSLs) are widely used in Gram-negative bacteria, as HSLs are small, passively diffusible signaling molecules for and their sensors are tightly regulated. Here, we show that synthetically designed HSL sensors using LuxR-family regulators are highly functional in S. aureus. Notably, synthetic designs previously built for the Gram-positive model Bacillus subtilis, a distantly related Bacillales, transferred functionally and establish repurposing the genetic toolbox as an effective strategy for importing these functions into S. aureus. Sensor performance correlated strongly between the two Bacillales, and activation in S. aureus reached 55-fold, exceeding the dynamic range of reported inducible systems. We further demonstrate tightly regulated, programmable interphyla communication between Gram-negative Escherichia coli and S. aureus via HSL signaling. These results provide a new toolset for engineering interbacterial communication and open a route to extending programmable HSL signaling to other tough-to-engineer bacteria.

Title: Polyphyletic origins and lineage-specific expansion of chemosensory systems in phylum Actinomycetota
Authors: S, S. N.; Brighty, S.; Sharma, G.
Abstract: Phylum Actinomycetota (syn. Actinobacteriota or Actinobacteria), one of the largest well-studied bacterial phyla, is renowned for complex morphology, non-motility, ecological versatility, and secondary metabolite production. Chemosensory systems (CSS) are among the most sophisticated prokaryotic signal transduction architectures, yet their evolutionary distribution in this phylum remains poorly understood. Here, a comparative genomic analysis of 693 high-quality genomes spanning the phylum resolves the diversity, distribution, and evolutionary trajectories of CSS. Despite extensive genomic complexity and ecological versatility, only 6.9% of genomes encode complete CSS clusters, confined to a subset of lineages within a few classes, indicating lineage-specific retention or loss. In contrast, two-component systems (TCS) are ubiquitously abundant, with hybrid kinases enriched in CSS-deficient classes, suggesting functional compensation for the absence of dedicated chemosensory pathways. Basal lineages retain simplified CSS (F1 or F5), whereas Actinomycetes show lineage-specific expansion into multiple classes (F5, F8, F9, and ACF), often co-occurring, indicative of enhanced sensory complexity. The phylogeny of CheA homologs shows a polyphyletic distribution, supporting a mosaic evolutionary history shaped by multiple independent acquisitions, diversification, and gene loss. Collectively, our findings show that, unlike motile bacteria, members of Actinomycetota rely predominantly on TCS-driven regulatory networks, with CSS retained only in select lineages where ecological demands require enhanced environmental sensing. This work provides a phylum-wide evolutionary framework for the emergence, diversification, and functional specialization of CSS in non-motile bacteria.

Title: Hypoxic Stress Induces LARP1-Driven Stress Granules That Protect mRNAs from Decay to Sustain Mitotic Cell Cycle Progression
Authors: Lim, T.; Ramanathan, J.; Gao, H.; Songci, E.; Tuan Zea, T.; Khong, A.
Abstract: Hypoxia is a defining feature of solid tumours that elicits extensive transcriptional and post-transcriptional adaptations. Stress granules (SGs) are frequently observed under hypoxia, yet how they assemble and whether they contribute to hypoxic gene regulation remain poorly understood. Here, we show that hypoxia induces SGs through an assembly mechanism distinct from that of classical acute stresses. Hypoxia SG formation occurs independently of the integrated stress response and instead requires the HIF1-REDD1-mTORCC1-4EBP1 axis. Remarkably, hypoxia SGs assemble despite robust ongoing translation, suggesting that additional mechanisms lower the threshold for RNA condensation. We identify LARP1 as a potential determinant of this process, where it promotes G3BP-dependent SG assembly specifically during hypoxia. Despite their distinct assembly mechanism, hypoxia and arsenite SGs recruit broadly similar RNA populations, with selective differences validated by single-molecule FISH, suggesting that conserved principles govern RNA partitioning across different SG states. Functionally, sequestration into hypoxia SGs correlates with enhance protein expression whereby a subset of mRNAs are protected from decay. Transcriptomic analyses further reveal that this protection sustains a broader gene-expression program enriched for MCM complex and mitotic cell-cycle regulators. Accordingly, disruption of hypoxia SGs reduces mitotic progression and proliferative competence during prolonged hypoxia. Together, our findings establish LARP1-mediated condensation as a mechanism that enables SG assembly despite ongoing translation and reveal that SG sequestration preserves selected mRNAs from decay to sustain the gene-expression programs required for long-term adaptation to hypoxia.

Title: A Standalone PD-1 Chimeric Switch Receptor T-Cell Platform Expands the Therapeutic Window of PD-L1 Targeting in Solid Tumors
Authors: Luo, Y.; Guo, S.; Qie, Y.; Zhao, B.; Ulloa-Navas, M. J.; Brooks, M.; Jones, V.; Hundal, T.; Chavez, J. C.; Lou, Y.; Deleyrolle, L. P.; Velcheti, V.; Jakub, J. W.; Dronca, R.; Kharfan-Dabaja, M. A.; Quinones-Hinojosa, A.; Qin, H.
Abstract: Programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) is a promising therapeutic target owing to its broad expression on tumor cells and immunosuppressive myeloid cells within the tumor microenvironment (TME), providing an opportunity to target both cellular compartments. However, physiological PD-L1 expression in normal tissues poses a substantial risk of on-target/off-tumor toxicity, limiting the therapeutic window and clinical translation of PD-L1-targeted cellular therapies. Here, we developed a standalone programmed death-1 (PD-1) chimeric switch receptor (CSR) T-cell platform designed to preserve the therapeutic advantages of PD-L1 targeting while improving tumor-normal discrimination. Iterative receptor engineering, with antitumor activity and normal-cell reactivity evaluated as parallel selection criteria, identified two lead PD-1 CSR T-cell candidates. Compared with our previously developed antibody-based PD-L1 CAR T cells, the lead candidates retained potent PD-L1-specific cytotoxicity against tumor cells while exhibiting markedly reduced cytotoxicity against primary human small airway epithelial cells, astrocytes, renal epithelial cells, hepatocytes, and cardiomyocytes. They also efficiently eliminated PD-L1-positive immunosuppressive myeloid cells and mediated dual-compartment targeting of tumor and myeloid cells in three-dimensional (3D) multicellular tumor organoids. In vivo, both candidates suppressed tumor growth and prolonged survival in orthotopic breast cancer and patient-derived glioblastoma models after systemic and intracranial administration, respectively. Collectively, these findings establish PD-1 CSR T cells as a standalone therapeutic platform that expands the therapeutic window of PD-L1-targeted cellular therapy by preserving dual-compartment targeting of tumor and immunosuppressive myeloid cells while reducing normal-cell reactivity, providing a foundation for further clinical translation across solid tumors.

Title: A Human Tumor Virus Recruits HSP70 Chaperone to Remodel Its Replisome on DNA
Authors: Wan, L.; Li, X.; Vittot, P.; Brodsky, J.; Wipf, P.; Moore, P. S.; Chang, Y.
Abstract: Human Merkel cell polyomavirus (MCV) large T (LT) protein functions as a replication helicase analogous to the cellular MCM complex but requires a second MCV protein, small T (sT), for efficient LT-initiated replication. Both LT and sT encode highly-conserved DnaJ domains that bind to the cellular refolding molecule, heat shock protein 70 (HSP70). Using single-molecule imaging and FRET, we find that sT recruits dimeric HSP70 to serve as a molecular bridge between sT and LT on DNA and that this complex facilitates remodeling LT into a functional double-hexameric helicase. Disruption of LT-HSP70-HSP70-sT interaction with HSP70 inhibitors or by mutations to the LT-sT DnaJ domains collapse the LT-HSP70-HSP70-sT complex, abolishing sT-enhanced LT dodecamerization and ATP-dependent DNA unwinding. Assembly of virus-free mammalian MCM3, MCM4 and MCM6 in nuclear extracts similarly recruits HSP70 to DNA suggesting that Hsp70 remodeling is used for efficient eukaryotic assembly of the multi-protein replication machinery.

Title: Palindrome Presence, Location, and Structural Context Are Predictive of RNA Self-Association
Authors: Ahn, C.; Park, H.; Rodrigues, V. L.; Dignon, G. L.
Abstract: RNA self-association is a key elementary event behind many cellular processes from ribosome assembly, to regulation of gene expression, to assembly of biomolecular condensates. While RNAs self-interact in many ways, one direct and unambiguous sequence-encoded pattern for RNA self-recognition is a palindrome, or palindromic motif. In isolation palindromic motifs tend to fold back on themselves, favoring stable stem-loop secondary structures. However, palindromes have been implicated in some cases of RNA self-recognition, segregation and phase separation, raising the question of which palindromes in a given RNA are actually available for intermolecular engagement. Toward answering this question, we define three classes of palindromic regions based on local secondary-structure context, and degree of availability for interactions via their nucleobases, sorting into three classes. We then apply this framework across known structures of RNA chains and find that the majority of palindromic regions are bound up in secondary structures. We then designed a minimal set of short stem-loop RNA sequences to evaluate the self-interaction stability of each defined palindrome class using coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations. Overall, this work provides a residue-level, structure-aware framework that connects RNA sequence, secondary-structure context, and intermolecular self-association for two interacting RNA chains.

Title: Age-associated repression of HNF4α is a driver and potential therapeutic target in liver metabolic dysfunction
Authors: Proulx, J.; Lande, K. A.; Lei, X.; Havas, A. P.; Garcia Teneche, M.; Rajesh, A.; Tanaka, H.; LaPorta, M. A.; Evensen, G.; Mamde, S.; Wang, L.; Gandhi, A.; Arnold, R.; Davis, A.; Liou, A.; Murad, R.; Garcia, G.; Sevilla, M.; Porritt, R.; D'Alessandro, A.; Berger, S. L.; Wang, A.; Yip, K.; Kaech, S.; Han, X.; Williams, A. E.; Adams, P. D.
Abstract: Aging is a major risk factors for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). However, the mechanisms by which aging disrupts hepatocyte transcriptional networks to drive metabolic dysfunction remain poorly understood. Hepatocyte nuclear factor 4 alpha (HNF4) is a master regulator of hepatocyte identity and metabolic homeostasis, but its role in liver aging has not been defined. Here, we perform a comprehensive multi-omic profiling of young and aged mouse livers combined with targeted HNF4 functional studies to define how aging remodels HNF4-dependent gene regulation and whether HNF4 can be a target to reverse age-associated liver dysfunction. Despite preserved HNF4 expression with age, aging was associated with reduced HNF4 chromatin occupancy and transcriptional activity, accompanied by epigenetic remodeling, including changes in histone acetylation, chromatin accessibility, and DNA methylation. Integration and comparison of HNF4 CUT&RUN with hepatocyte-specific Hnf4a deletion in young and aged livers identified high-confidence overlapping but distinct young- and old- specific HNF4 target gene networks. In young hepatocytes, HNF4 coordinates two complementary transcriptional programs: activation of genes governing hepatocyte identity, lipid metabolism, and metabolic function, while simultaneously inhibiting alternative developmental, proliferative, and inflammatory programs. Spatial transcriptomic analyses further revealed zone-specific specialization of HNF4-dependent gene programs. Aging selectively disrupted these regulatory networks, resulting in compromised liver identity and metabolic gene programs, de-repression of inflammatory pathways and alternative cellular identity programs and disrupted hepatocyte zonation, consistent with age-dependent lipidomic and metabolic changes, hepatic fat accumulation, and immune infiltration. Hepatocyte-specific Hnf4a deletion in young mice recapitulated key features of liver aging, including impaired hepatocyte identity, metabolic dysfunction, steatosis, inflammatory activation and altered hepatic immune-cell composition, while deletion in aged mice further exacerbated steatosis, inflammation, and hepatic dysfunction. Conversely, hepatocyte-specific HNF4 restoration in aged mice significantly reduced hepatic steatosis and lipid accumulation, restored fatty acid metabolic programs, and partially reversed age-associated transcriptional changes. However, inflammatory and interferon-associated programs were not uniformly reversed, revealing differential responsiveness of metabolic and inflammatory pathways to HNF4 restoration. Together, these findings identify age-associated impairment of HNF4 activity as a functional contributor to liver aging, linking dysregulation of hepatocyte identity, metabolic homeostasis, and inflammatory control to age-associated hepatic dysfunction. Importantly, the selective reversibility of metabolic defects following HNF4 restoration establishes HNF4 as a promising strategy for preserving hepatocyte homeostasis and reversing age-associated hepatic metabolic dysfunction.

Title: Inference of cell division parameters in bacteria under transient growth conditions
Authors: Nieto Acuna, C. A.; Rezaee, S.; Vargas-Garcia, C. A.; Singh, A.
Abstract: Most quantitative models of bacterial cell division assume steady-state growth, yet natural environments are highly dynamic. Here, we infer division control parameters of E. coli from single-cell size trajectories under nonsteady growth. We describe growth as a continuous process interrupted by stochastic divisions, whose propensity depends on cell size and on the size added since birth. Combining an estimation of time-dependent single-cell growth rates with a maximum-likelihood estimator that we previously validated on synthetic data, we obtain time-resolved estimates of the mean added size at division, its noise, and a strategy parameter that measures how added size depends on birth size. This parameter vanishes for the adder, in which cells add, on average, a fixed size regardless of their size at birth, and is negative for sizer-adder control, in which larger-born cells add less size. We apply this approach to published single-cell data covering steady exponential growth, gradual nutrient depletion, and exit from starvation. We implement a time-resolved model selection based on the Akaike information criterion, concluding that the adder is sufficient during steady growth, whereas size dynamics during entry into and exit from stationary phase are better explained by transient deviations toward sizer-adder control. The framework provides a general method to quantify time-resolved changes in the scale, stochasticity, and strategy of division in nonsteady environments.

Title: Quantitative Head-to-Tail Analysis Reveals Heterogeneous Cellular Organization and Connexin Expression in the Porcine Sinoatrial Node
Authors: Kao, H. K. J.; Smithers, R. L.; Ramos-Rodriguez, D. H.; Van Brusselen, K.; Kaleka, R.; Cameron, D.; Nolta, J. A.; Fink, K.; Leach, J. K.; Santana, L. F.; Chiamvimonvat, N.; Lieu, D. K.
Abstract: Background: The sinoatrial node (SAN) is an integral component of the cardiac conduction system that dictates heart rhythm. Optical mapping studies have demonstrated functional differences between the superior and inferior leading pacemaking sites in the human SAN; however, the mechanistic connections between structure and function in the SAN through intra-tissue and inter-tissue current source-sink relationships have not been fully resolved. Methods: Porcine SAN longitudinal cryosections along the head-to-tail axis were immunostained and analyzed for regional cell organization and connexin (CX) isoform expression. Results: Quantification of pacemaking cardiomyocyte (PCM) density revealed >9-fold more PCMs within a SAN volume than suggested by a widely cited estimate, assuming comparable PCM densities across species. The SAN head region consisted of large PCM clusters with low aspect ratios, high PCM density, low fibroblast density, and PCMs with the highest HCN4 expression and lowest CX40 and CX43 expression. These characteristics are consistent with an electrically well-insulated, strong current-source that supports pacemaking function. Although the SAN tail also exhibited high local PCM density, its smaller PCM clusters, lower HCN4 expression, and higher CX40, CX43, and CX45 expression rendered it a weaker current source. The SAN mid-region exhibited large PCM clusters aligned in the head-to-tail axis and the highest expression of CX40 and CX45, an expression profile that suggests a fast-conducting intra-tissue pathway that electrically links the leading pacemaking sites at the head and tail. The peripheral SAN at the head and tail also exhibited higher CX expression of all isoforms than the central subregions, an organization consistent with enhanced inter-tissue coupling required for proper pacing function. Conclusions: Our data provide novel insights into the distinct regional micro-organization of the SAN along the head-to-tail axis, which through intra-tissue and inter-tissue coupling, likely modulates the balance of current source-sink relationships that supports robust pacemaking and pacing functions.

Title: The tiger shark, Galeocerdo cuvier (Peron & Lesueur, 1822), genome reveals genomic and epigenomic signatures of shark evolution and demographic history
Authors: Pearce, J. R.; Doran, A.; De Jong, E.; Kwong, S.; Jewell, O.; D'Antonio, B.; Fraser, M. W.; Corrigan, S.; Thomas, L.; Edwards, R. J.
Abstract: Cartilaginous fishes (Chondrichthyes) represent one of the oldest extant vertebrate lineages, persisting for over 450 million years, yet genomic resources remain limited for many species despite widespread conservation concern. The tiger shark, Galeocerdo cuvier (Peron & Lesueur, 1822), the sole surviving member of the family Galeocerdonidae, is a circumglobally cosmopolitan predator vital in ecosystem regulation but is experiencing population declines. Here, we generated the first chromosome-scale haplotype-phased reference genome for the tiger shark and integrated comparative and population genomics with methylomics to characterise its genome architecture and evolutionary history. This assembly presented the first evidence of male heterogamety in this species. Comparative analyses revealed lineage-specific transposable element expansions across the chondrichthyan class suggesting ongoing genome restructuring in Carcharhiniform sharks. We report the first hydroxymethylome in a chondrichthyan, higher than that of other vertebrates, hinting at novel DNA evolutionary and regulatory pathways in an early-diverging lineage of jawed vertebrates. We identified genomic signatures of prolonged population decline that correlated with historical climate fluctuations and have resulted in sustained low levels of genetic heterozygosity in this species. These findings offer new insights into shark and broader vertebrate genomic and epigenomic evolution while providing valuable resources for conservation genomics of one of the world's most widespread top-order predators in the face of accelerating environmental change.

Title: Phosphorylation-dependent conformational change in the Keratin 19 head domain: Implications for filament assembly and binding to GSK3β and 14-3-3
Authors: Ji, Y.; Jeong, M.; Kim, J.; Yeom, J.; Han, M. A.; Park, C.; Lee, S.-H.; Hong, E.; Ko, Y. H.; Coulombe, P. A.; Kim, J. H.; Lee, C.-H.
Abstract: Keratins are intermediate filament (IF) proteins expressed in various cell types, playing a crucial role in mechanical support and signaling pathways. Keratin 19 (K19) is predominantly found in gut epithelia and early embryonic ectoderm. K19 interacts with signaling proteins such as GSK3{beta} and 14-3-3 to participate in cell signaling pathways. However, details on the binding sites of these proteins on K19, and specific molecular mechanisms governing these interactions, are lacking. Additionally, the N-terminal head domains of IFs including K19 are considered intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), and their atomic-resolution structures are unavailable. Using NMR spectroscopy, we obtained the first solution structures of K19 head domain peptides. Structural models involving phosphomimetic peptides suggest a phosphorylation-dependent conformational change in the K19 head domain. The phosphomimetic S35E substitution alters the conformation of the head domain, affecting its association with keratin filaments and K19-binding partners. NMR spectral changes indicate that the S35E substitution affects the association of the K19 head domain to K8/K19 filaments and GSK3{beta}, whereas no significant binding changes were observed with 14-3-3{zeta} and 14-3-3{sigma}. Cell-based analyses further showed that the S35E mutation altered keratin filament organization and reduced the proximity between K19 and GSK3{beta} in 293T cells, whereas no significant change was observed in the proximity between K19 and 14-3-3{sigma}. Our findings provide insight into the structure-function relationship of the head domains in IF proteins with direct implications for the assembly of filaments and their role in signal modulation.

Title: The ganglioside profile of mouse brain does not respond to changes in dietary n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acid supply
Authors: MASSON, E. A. Y.; MARTINE, L.; CABARET, S.; GREGOIRE, S.; DUCROCQ, F.; TRIFILIEFF, P.; ACAR, N.; BERDEAUX, O.
Abstract: Long chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (LC-PUFAs) of the n-3 and n-6 families are major components of brain lipids, both in terms of levels and biological significance. They play crucial roles in various neurological processes. The brain is largely dependent on food supply of LC-PUFAs and its lipid composition can be modulated by changes in dietary intake. Sufficient dietary supply of the n-3 LC-PUFAs as well as a balanced n-6/n-3 ratio are required for proper brain development and function. As dietary intervention using n-3 LC-PUFAs is considered a promising therapeutic approach to prevent or treat brain disorders, it is important to understand the associated biochemical changes as well as the mechanisms underlying the biological effects. In the present study, we performed lipidomic analyses to document the effects of dietary n-3 LC-PUFA supply on the composition of two families of FA-carrying complex membrane lipids playing important roles in the nervous system: phospholipids and gangliosides. We show that an unbalanced, n-3 LC-PUFA-deficient diet, from gestation to adulthood in mice resulted in decreased levels of docosahexaenoic acid (DHA, C22:6n-3) and increased levels of docosapentaenoic acid (DPA, C22:5n-6) in brain phospholipids, while a n-3 LC-PUFA-supplemented diet was associated with the reverse phenotype. However, the composition of brain gangliosides, which carry mainly saturated and mono-unsaturated fatty acids, was unaffected by the diet, suggesting that they do not directly contribute to mediating the neurological effects of dietary n-3 LC-PUFA manipulation.

Title: Vasopressin V2 receptor phosphopeptide reshapes the conformational landscape of arrestin-2 beyond C-tail detachment
Authors: Bzowka, M.; Feser, R.; Aureli, S.; Abiko, L. A.; Gervasio, F. L.
Abstract: Binding of phosphorylated GPCR tails influences arrestin conformation, but the contribution of this interaction to the interdomain rotation associated with activation remains incompletely characterised. In particular, it remains unclear whether displacement of the arrestin C-tail is sufficient to favor larger interdomain rotations or whether the bound phosphotail exerts an additional effect on the conformational landscape. Here, we used enhanced-sampling simulations to characterise the conformational free-energy landscapes of basal (unbound) and V2Rpp-bound arrestin-2. We find that V2Rpp binding broadened the range of energetically accessible interdomain rotation angles relative to basal arrestin-2. However, the pronounced rotation observed in the experimental structures, while accessible, was not strongly favored. Strikingly, C-tail displacement alone does not reproduce this effect, as arrestin-2 retains a strong preference for small interdomain rotation angles in the absence of V2Rpp. Moreover, the C-tail-detached state is energetically unfavorable in the absence of V2Rpp. Together, these findings quantify the effects of V2Rpp binding on the interdomain rotation of arrestin-2 and disentangle the effects of phosphopeptide binding from those of C-tail detachment.

Title: Modular assembly of mitochondrial complex III from a dynamic matrix domain pool
Authors: Jimenez-Niebla, J.; Jha, R.; Wirth, C.; Busto, J. V.; Feignier, A.; Cosenza-Contreras, M.; Ruoff, K.; Dorer, M.; Babic, R.; Drepper, F.; Kraft, C.; Huesgen, P. F.; Wiedemann, N.; Kao, W.-C.; Hunte, C.
Abstract: Mitochondrial complex III is a central component of the cellular energy metabolism. It is an obligate dimer of catalytic and accessory subunits that are encoded by two genomes. How its large matrix domain, formed by the core proteins Qcr1 and Qcr2, is built and joined to the membrane part and during assembly is not known. Here we show that Qcr1 and Qcr2 preassemble independently of complex III into matrix domain modules. Cryo-EM structures from a cardiolipin-deficient yeast strain and of recombinant protein resolved single, double and triple matrix domains, which are linked by the C-terminal tail of Qcr1. In the mature complex III, the same tail binds cytochrome b and cardiolipin. The modules form a dynamic pool, in which assembly species interconvert and exchange subunits. Mutations at the module interfaces, including mimics of human disease variants, reshape this pool and deletion of the Qcr1 tail impairs respiratory growth. Substitution of a tyrosine residue linked to parkinsonism exposes a conserved cysteine residue to oxidation. A cryo-EM structure of an assembly intermediate shows a cap of two matrix domains bound to a monomeric membrane module of cytochrome b, Qcr7, Qcr8 and cytochrome c1. We propose that complex III receives its matrix domain from a dynamic pool of prebuilt modules, which organizes the dimerization of the complex.

Title: Distinct mechanical signatures of dairy and plant-based cheeses
Authors: Koosis, A. O.; Darwin, E. C.; Ellingsen, V.; Kuhl, E.
Abstract: Plant-based cheeses account for about 1% of U.S. retail cheese sales and often fail to match the texture and flavor of dairy cheese. Here we compare three commercial dairy and plant-based pairs, cheddar, feta, and mozzarella, with texture profile analysis (n = 60), tension, compression, and shear tests (n = 219), constitutive artificial neural networks, and a consumer panel (n = 306). Plant mozzarella is at least five times stiffer than dairy mozzarella at small strain, yet softer and less cohesive under 50% compression. Plant feta matches the initial stiffness of dairy feta but shows a peak in its shear response. Plant cheddar differs in both stiffness and shear response. Model discovery selects first-invariant models for all six cheeses, but no model term separates the two groups. Consumers rate 68--78% of attributes "just about right" for dairy cheeses and 29--38% for plant-based cheeses. These single-product comparisons define product-specific targets for plant-based cheese design.

Title: Benchmarking foundation models for resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging time series in cognitive aging research
Authors: Liu, Y. M.; Ai, M.; Zhao, K.; Zhang, Y.; Lin, F. V.
Abstract: Foundation models trained on large neuroimaging datasets could help smaller studies investigate cognition from brain recordings. However, whether the foundation model-derived representations improve assessment of current cognition, prediction of follow-up cognition, or characterization of cognitive change remains unclear. We evaluated nine configurations from five model families that process regional resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging time series, using 3,103 scans from 1,653 participants across two observational and five intervention aging cohorts. Primary frozen representations showed no consistent superiority over conventional functional connectivity for concurrent cognitive associations or diagnostic classification. Changing the readout improved selected concurrent cognitive associations without updating model weights, indicating that performance depended partly on how representations were extracted. Additional post-training and embedding alignment yielded gains in selected settings but did not consistently improve performance across outcomes. In the primary longitudinal analyses, imaging representations did not establish added value beyond baseline clinical measures. These findings show that readout choice influences concurrent cognitive associations, while the added value of these representations for longitudinal outcomes remains unestablished.

Title: Photomechanical engineering of immunogenic whole-cell vaccines by laser-induced vapor nanobubbles for bladder cancer prophylaxis
Authors: Sabando-Garcia, N.; G. Caelles, A.; Traba, N.; Pages, J.; Cabrera, C.; Garcia Hidalgo, A.; Punj, D.; Braeckmans, K.; F. Valledor, A.; Chomiciute, G.; Abasolo, I.; Julian, E.; Sanchez, S.; Fraire, J. C.
Abstract: Whole-cell cancer vaccines can provide broad tumor-antigen repertoires, but their efficacy depends on manufacturing methods that inactivate tumor cells while preserving immunogenic danger signals. Here we show that laser-induced vapor nanobubbles (VNB) generated from dextran-coated iron oxide nanoparticles provide a drug-free photomechanical route to engineer immunogenic whole-cell vaccines against bladder cancer. Using MB49 murine urothelial carcinoma cells, we established VNB conditions that induced rapid tumor-cell killing together with calreticulin exposure and extracellular ATP and HMGB1 release. Rapid cell killing and calreticulin exposure were also reproduced in the molecularly distinct UPPL1541 bladder cancer model, supporting the generalizability of the early photomechanical response across bladder cancer cell lines. Vaccination with VNB-killed MB49 cells reduced tumor incidence and growth after subcutaneous challenge and enhanced splenocyte-mediated antitumor activity against MB49 cells. In an orthotopic bladder cancer model, vaccination prevented MRI-detectable tumor formation and was associated with marked early bladder enrichment of CD8 T cells and inflammatory monocytes. A single administration of the VNB-generated vaccine preparation showed no evident local or systemic toxicity during seven days of follow-up. These findings provide proof of concept for an externally triggered, drug-free manufacturing approach in which short laser irradiation induces rapid photomechanical killing of tumor cells on demand, generating immunogenic whole-tumor-cell vaccine preparations for further evaluation in therapeutic, post-resection and tumor-derived settings.

Title: Circulating CD4 regulatory T cells are broadly preserved in Parkinson's disease despite altered HELIOS expression
Authors: Crooks, S. C.; Prabhu, A.; Jarvis, L. B.; Georgieva, Z. G.; Rainbow, D. B.; Williams-Gray, C. H.; Jones, J. L.
Abstract: Background Regulatory T cells (Tregs) are an important component of adaptive immune regulation and have been implicated in Parkinson's disease (PD), with previous studies suggesting altered Treg proportions, phenotype and, in some cases, function. However, existing studies have been limited by variable phenotyping approaches and a lack of detailed functional assessment. Given the growing interest in Tregs as potential therapies in PD, better understanding of their phenotype and function in the disease is important. Methods Circulating FOXP3+ Tregs were characterised in individuals with PD and age-matched healthy controls (HC) using a 24-colour spectral flow cytometry panel. Treg suppressive function was assessed by their ability to inhibit proliferation and cytokine production by polyclonally stimulated autologous T effector cells in vitro. Treg lineage stability was assessed by analysis of FOXP3 TSDR demethylation. Results The proportions and phenotypic characteristics of circulating CD4 Tregs were broadly similar between individuals with PD and HCs, as were Treg suppressive function and FOXP3 TSDR demethylation. However, naive CD4 Tregs from individuals with PD showed reduced HELIOS expression, with a similar but non-significant trend in FOXP3 expression. Reduced HELIOS expression was also observed in the CD8 naive Treg compartment. Conclusions Major quantitative or functional abnormalities in circulating Tregs do not appear to be a dominant feature PD. However, reduced HELIOS expression in naive Tregs suggests more subtle phenotypic alterations that warrant further investigation. The broadly preserved suppressive function is reassuring for therapeutic approaches aimed at increasing Treg numbers, although it will be important to establish that expanded Tregs retain a stable phenotype and suppressive function in inflammatory and tissue environments.

Title: Environmental Frass Remodels the Larval Gut Microbiome to Enable Black Soldier Fly (Hermetia illucens) Bioconversion of Livestock Manure
Authors: Pettengill, A.; Stender, R.; Thitathan, K.; Cleary, M.
Abstract: Black Soldier Fly larvae (BSFL) consume nearly any organic material and show promise for the remediation of agricultural waste, including livestock manure. BSFL feeding generates frass, a mixture of unconsumed substrate, larval feces, and microorganisms. We identified a wild population of BSFL (Yuba strain) thriving on rabbit manure, a challenging substrate due to its high lignocellulose content. We investigated if frass extract from this source was necessary and sufficient to support bioconversion of manure and if such effects are altered by captive husbandry. Larvae supplemented with domestic frass failed to grow on rabbit manure but grew well when supplemented with wild-sourced frass. Microbiome analysis revealed that wild-sourced frass contributes a cohort of lignocellulose-degrading microorganisms to the BSFL gut, particularly Rummeliibacillus bacteria and Scedosporium fungi. These growth-promoting effects extended to cattle manure. Following initial seeding with wild-sourced frass, lab-cultured frass ultimately failed to support growth on rabbit manure and the gut microbiome shifted toward bacteria commonly found in domestic BSFL. This study reveals that frass extract derived from environmental sources can improve the bioconversion ability of BSFL and that beneficial microbes are lost during captive-rearing.

Title: Polyphosphate metabolism genes are associated with hydroxyapatite biomineralization capacity in a novel hydrogenotrophic methanogen Methanobacterium AMB_03
Authors: Robin-Champgneul, F. A.; Singh, A.; Sharma, S.; Tkachenko, O.; Thyr, J.; Sidiropoulos, S.; Schnurer, A.; Zajkowski, T.; Budnyak, T.; Neubeck, A.
Abstract: Methanogenic archaea play crucial roles in sedimentary phosphorus cycling, but their capacity for phosphate biomineralization remains poorly understood. Here we demonstrate that Methanobacterium AMB_03, isolated from a serpentinizing environment, mediates extracellular precipitation of carbonate-substituted hydroxyapatite (HAp) under phosphate-enriched conditions. Comparative genomic analysis of AMB_03 versus non-mineralizing strains (Methanobacterium oryzae, Methanoculleus bourgensis MAB1) shows that AMB_03 encodes polyphosphate kinase 1 (ppk1), enabling polyphosphate synthesis from ATP. In contrast, M. oryzae and MAB1 completely lack ppk1, preventing polyphosphate accumulation. Phylogenomic analysis of 320 Methanobacteriota genomes further shows that complete polyP cycling capacity is present in only ~25% of representatives, placing AMB_03 among a minority of methanogens with this capability. Experimental cultivation across phosphate gradients (0-6 mM) showed HAp early-onset precipitation was preferential at [≥]3 mM. Precipitation was eventually observed at all phosphate concentrations (except P0) by 49 weeks and was associated with extracellular polymeric substance production and localized pH increases of up to 8.08. Raman spectroscopy confirmed carbonate-substituted HAp, with characteristic peaks at 960.5 cm-1 (PO43-) and 1070-1072 cm-1 (CO32-). These findings identify a strong genomic association between polyphosphate metabolism genes and biomineralization capacity, suggesting that methanogens with complete polyP cycling systems may create localized phosphate-rich environments that promote authigenic mineral formation in sedimentary systems.

Title: Structural and functional examination of Neisseria gonorrhoeae TfpC reveals a dynamic two-domain architecture required for type IV pilus function
Authors: Nicholson, K. R.; Baczynska, M.; Ploskon, E.; Simpson, P.; Oregioni, A.; Lorenz, C.; SEIFERT, H. S.; Garnett, J.
Abstract: The Neisseria gonorrhoeae (Gc) Type IV pilus (T4p) is a critical apparatus for colonization and virulence. This molecular machine resides at the host-pathogen interface and mediates adherence to host cells, twitching motility, natural transformation, and resistance to oxidative agents. Previously, we identified a DUF4124 family, T4p component, TfpC. TfpC is required for full T4p elaboration, and deleting the tfpC gene reduced natural transformation competence and resulted in an under-piliated colony morphology. Our earlier models suggested TfpC is composed of an N-terminal transmembrane helix and a proline-rich disordered region followed by a C-terminal coiled-coil. Here, we used targeted structural and genetic approaches to define TfpC's molecular structure. Our new data show that TfpC's N-terminal domain forms a novel, dynamic three-stranded {beta}-sheet structure. These data indicate that the flexible disordered region acts as a linker between the N- and C-terminal domains. Functionally, we illustrate TfpC requires an acidic face within the C-terminal coiled-coil domain to mediate pilus biogenesis and function. This study characterizes a unique protein fold and family and defines the contributions of TfpC's domains to its function.

Title: Seasonal H1N1 influenza A virus preferentially infects a pre-existing ciliogenesis-primed secretory cell state
Authors: von Kempis, J.; Leary, P.; Opitz, L.; Stertz, S.
Abstract: Influenza A viruses (IAV) infect secretory and ciliated cells of the human airway epithelium , but whether all cells within one cell type are equally susceptible to infection remains unresolved. Here, single-cell RNA sequencing analysis of primary human bronchial epithelial cultures from three donors identified preferential infection of a transcriptionally distinct subpopulation of secretory cells by seasonal H1N1 IAV A/Hawaii/70/2019 . Genes upregulated in this subpopulation showed enrichment for cilium-related gene ontology terms. In an ex post facto approach, this enrichment persisted after excluding genes differentially expressed between infected and mock-treated samples, including those identified in secretory cell-specific comparisons. Single-cell analysis further revealed no significant increase in ciliogenesis scores in infected secretory cells compared to mock infected cells at 6 hours post-infection , arguing against infection-induced activation of the canonical ciliogenesis programme during the initial viral replication cycle . Collectively, these results support preferential infection of ciliogenesis-primed secretory cells and refine IAV tropism beyond cell type to encompass epithelial differentiation state.

Title: MmuPV1 and HPV E6 Elevate Nuclear Accumulation of IKK? to Impair NF-κB Signaling to Promote Persistent Infection
Authors: Shepherd, P. T.; Duxbury, K. R.; Morris, Z.; Romero-Masters, J. C.
Abstract: The mouse papillomavirus (MmuPV1) E6 oncoprotein is essential for persistent infection and cancer development. Previous studies identified amino acid R130 of MmuPV1 E6 as critical for its interaction with the tumor suppressor MAML1. Mutation of this residue (R130A) disrupts MAML1 binding and prevents disease development in mice. In this study, we demonstrate that MmuPV1 E6 also disrupts NF-{kappa}B signaling through interactions with proteins in the I{kappa}B kinase (IKK) complex. Specifically, the MmuPV1 E6R130A mutant is defective in binding IKK complex proteins and fails to impair NF-{kappa}B signaling in mouse keratinocytes, suggesting that these interactions are necessary for E6-mediated disruption of this pathway. Furthermore, MmuPV1 E6 expression is associated with increased nuclear localization of IKK?, whereas cells expressing the E6R130A mutant exhibit no such increase. These findings suggest that E6-mediated nuclear localization of IKK? depends on its interaction with IKK complex proteins. Importantly, we demonstrate that the human papillomavirus HPV16 E6 oncoprotein similarly impairs NF-{kappa}B signaling and increases nuclear IKK? localization in human keratinocytes, suggesting a shared mechanism between mouse and human papillomaviruses. Additionally, analysis of previously published RNA sequencing data reveals that MmuPV1 E6 induces several transcriptional changes associated with increased nuclear IKK?. Together, these findings demonstrate that both MmuPV1 and HPV16 E6 disrupt NF-{kappa}B signaling in association with increased nuclear IKK? localization. This study provides the first evidence of an E6 oncoprotein interacting with and changing subcellular localization of IKK? to disrupt cellular homeostasis.

Title: SPARK: Systematic Profiling of Antibiotic-Phage Response Kinetics
Authors: Berryhill, B. A.; Gil-Gil, T.; Sanchez-Hevia, D. L.; Andersson, D. I.; Fatsis-Kavalopoulos, N.
Abstract: Phage therapy is, in practice, combination therapy: phage are almost always added to an ongoing antibiotic regimen, yet the combination is rarely designed to have a specific interaction pattern. Interactions can be antagonistic, additive or synergistic and cannot be inferred from either agent alone. Here we introduce SPARK, a method which quantifies phage antibiotic interaction from growth curves as the integrated deviation of observed growth from the growth expected under Bliss independence. We profiled 42 combinations spanning the ESKAPE pathogens and Escherichia coli with twelve antibiotics. We show that i) synergy and antagonism are resolvable within a single high-throughput assay, with the interaction determined by the phage antibiotic bacteria pairing; ii) 21 clinical Staphylococcus aureus isolates differ among themselves as widely as the seven species do; and, iii) interactions change between a few hours and two days, several reversing direction. Overall, SPARK needs only a plate reader and the analysis is performed with a specific openly available web tool.

Title: The role of Plasmodium falciparum acyl-coenzyme A synthetase 10 in fatty acid acquisition and lipid synthesis
Authors: Fike, K. R.; Santos, H.; Klemba, M.
Abstract: During the asexual blood stage, malaria parasites synthesize large quantities of lipids to support their rapid proliferation. Exogenous fatty acids obtained from host plasma are activated for lipid synthesis by parasite acyl-coenzyme A synthetases (ACSs). Of the twelve Plasmodium falciparum ACS homologs, ACS10 has emerged as a key blood-stage enzyme. Here, we sought to define the role of ACS10 in fatty acid acquisition and lipid synthesis during asexual development. To accomplish this, we have employed fatty acid alkyne probes of parasite lipid synthesis together with selective depletion of ACS10 in a conditional knockdown parasite line. This approach revealed that ACS10 is required for efficient incorporation of 16- to 20-carbon unsaturated fatty acid alkynes and a 20-carbon, saturated fatty acid alkyne into the major parasite phospholipids and neutral lipids. In contrast, shorter saturated fatty acid alkynes were either unaffected by ACS10 depletion or were hyper-incorporated into parasite lipids. ACS10 knockdown elicited a profound deformation of the food vacuole, which was likely caused by an imbalance of saturated and unsaturated fatty acids in parasite lipids. To promote the discovery and characterization of ACS inhibitors, we have established a fatty acid alkyne-based approach for identifying compounds that target ACS10 as their primary mode of action.

Title: Tfcp2l1 recruits Thrap3 to sustain ESC self-renewal via Jmjd1c exon-5 splicing and DNA repair choice
Authors: Lu, W.; Wang, X.; Li, Y.; Chen, P.; Zhu, Y.; Ye, S.
Abstract: How embryonic stem cells (ESCs) maintain genomic integrity while sustaining self-renewal remains poorly understood. We find that transcription factor CP2-like 1 (Tfcp2l1) recruits Thrap3 in mouse ESCs, where this complex maintains RNA polymerase II activity and promotes transcription of Tfcp2l1 target genes. In addition, Thrap3 supports mESC self-renewal. Interestingly, knockdown of either Tfcp2l1 or Thrap3 induces highly overlapping alternative-splicing changes, including reduced inclusion of exon-5 in Jmjd1c. Further studies reveal that skipping of Jmjd1c exon-5 weakens the association between Jmjd1c and Mdc1, accompanied by elevated Mdc1-associated dimethylation, leading to reduced Mdc1 and Rnf8 interaction and diminished K63-linked ubiquitin signalling. These alterations impair chromatin recruitment of the Rap80 and Brca1 repair complex and increase Rad51 foci formation, indicative of a shift in DNA repair pathway preference. Accordingly, loss of Tfcp2l1 or Thrap3 results in accumulated DNA damage, hypersensitivity to genotoxic stress, compromised ESC self-renewal and enhanced apoptosis. Similar phenotypes can be recapitulated in human ESCs. Together, our findings provide new insights into how ESCs coordinate genome maintenance with self-renewal.

Title: Quantitative trait loci mapping identifies genetic loci modifying MafAS64F-mediated dysglycemia
Authors: Maurer, M.; Johnson, L.; Lee, D.; Yandell, B. S.; Keller, M. P.; Cha, J.
Abstract: Increasing evidence has shown the role of genetic background on the penetrance of monogenic diabetes. A missense mutation of the pancreatic {beta}-cell-enriched transcription factor MafA co-segregates with diabetes (MafA-MODY) and non-syndromic insulinomatosis. We recently investigated the effects of genetic background on MafAS64F-driven dysglycemia in genetically diverse mice harboring this mutation. Here we leveraged the effects of genetic background on phenotypic penetrance to map quantitative trait loci (QTL) potentially modifying glycemia in response to this variant. We investigated MafaS64F/+ mice from an F2 intercross of the C57BL/6J and SJL/J genetic backgrounds through oral glucose tolerance testing at 4, 5, 6, and 8 weeks of age to evaluate glucose tolerance and glycemic trajectory. All F2 mice were genetically monitored for single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) between the C57BL/6J and SJL/J backgrounds, allowing us to identify modifying loci on 6 chromosomes (2, 126 Mbp; 3, 59 Mbp and 103 Mbp; 7, 47 Mbp; 11 45 Mbp; 13, 4 Mbp; and 16, 85-97 Mbp), containing 172 candidate genes. For example, known MODY genes Abcc8 (Sur1) and Kcnj11 (Kir6.2) are within the QTL region on chromosome 7 and contain polymorphisms between backgrounds that may impart combinatorial effects on the phenotypic penetrance of MafAS64F-mediated dysglycemia

Title: Overlapping enhancer activity robustly regulates rax expression during ocular development in zebrafish
Authors: Jordana, D. A.; Clark, N. L.
Abstract: Vertebrate eye development relies on the tightly regulated yet highly dynamic spatiotemporal expression of eye field transcription factors that coordinate developmental programs required for the formation of a functional eye. The gene rax is among the earliest expressed eye field transcription factors and is specifically associated with ocular-fated tissue. It encodes a transcription factor that is essential for optic vesicle evagination, the precursor to the optic cup and retina. Although the developmental functions of rax are well characterized, the cis-regulatory elements that control its expression remain poorly understood. Using zebrafish (Danio rerio), I identified five novel ocular enhancers and demonstrate that they drive similar spatiotemporal expression patterns as rax at three key stages of eye development. Furthermore, I performed an in-depth characterization of two enhancers and demonstrate that they exhibit substantial transcript-level overlap with endogenous rax expression during development. Additionally, through the generation of enhancer deletion lines, I further demonstrate that the gene regulatory network (GRN) controlling rax expression is largely robust to individual and combinatorial enhancer perturbations. However, perturbation of this regulatory network can result in rax-associated ocular abnormalities, including microphthalmia and anophthalmia. Together, these findings highlight the importance of studying developmental ocular enhancers to better understand the functions of noncoding genomic regions and provide insight into potential causes of unexplained congenital eye disease.

Title: Pseudo-observations of longevity improve detection of resilience-associated genes in the Radiation Late Effects Cohort of rhesus macaques.
Authors: Lawandos, J. H.; Paukner, M.; Schaaf, G. W.; Olson, J. D.; Raveendran, M.; Harris, R. A.; Rogers, J.; Cline, J. M.; Quillen, E. E.
Abstract: Non-human primates are an ideal model for interrogating the genetic basis of human lifespan and resilience due to their long lifespan compared to other model organisms, development of similar age-related chronic conditions, and genetic similarity. However, like humans, statistical methods for modeling survival suffer from the challenges of dealing with non-proportionality of hazards, large numbers of living individuals that must be censored, and loss-to-follow-up over studies that may last a decade or more. Here we overcome these challenges through the use of pseudo-observations of Restricted Mean Survival Time as a measure of resilience to the acute challenge of radiation exposure and chronic challenges of aging and a Western-style diet in rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) from the Wake Forest Non-Human Primate Radiation Late Effects Cohort. Our whole-exome analysis used Genome-wide Efficient Mixed Model Association (GEMMA) to identify variants associated with longevity, and a subsequent Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) highlighted the cadherin and integrin signaling pathways as central to this resilience. As dysregulation of cell adhesion and extracellular matrix signaling is central to the development of fibrosis, we tested the functional relevance of these signals using a targeted Combined Annotation Dependent Depletion (CADD) score-weighted Sequence Kernel Association Test-Optimal (SKAT-O) analysis of GSEA leading-edge genes from both the cadherin and integrin pathways. This linked variant burden in PCDHGA5, PCDHGA3, PCDHGB2, PCDHA11, and PSENEN to the severity of myocardial fibrosis, and in IBSP, PDGFD, and LAMC2 to the severity of pulmonary fibrosis observed at necropsy. Critically, we note that the genetic variants are not caused by the radiation but rather create an underlying risk for disease that is then exacerbated by the acute and persistent stressors challenging these animals' intrinsic resilience. The success of this method in identifying biologically relevant genetic variants underlying survival in animals undergoing a strong challenge to their resilience highlights not only the role of genes predisposing animals to fibrosis in lifespan, but the overall utility of pseudo-observations in overcoming the limitations of survival analyses in humans and other long-lived species.

Title: Chromosome-level genome assembly of Greenland scurvy-grass (Cochlearia groenlandica) reveals extensive centromeric satellite arrays
Authors: Torresen, O. K.; Brysting, A. K.; Danneels, B.; Sandean, R.; Kollias, S.; Ferrari, G.; Tooming-Klunderud, A.; Yant, L.; Jakobsen, K. S.
Abstract: We present a chromosome-level, haplotype-resolved genome assembly from Greenland scurvy-grass (Cochlearia groenlandica). The assembly comprises two pseudo-haplotypes of 322 Mb and 295 Mb, with 89.7% and 95.6% respectively, each scaffolded into 7 chromosomes. Assembly completeness is high (BUSCO 97.8% in each haplotype), with 34,213 and 29,684 annotated protein-coding genes for haplotypes one and two, respectively. The chromosomes contain extensive centromeric satellite arrays that cover up to half of some chromosomes. Their precise functional boundaries remain undetermined.

Title: Mutation and Recombination Rates in Free-Ranging Polar Bears
Authors: Desai, D.; Rivkin, R. L.; Newediuk, L.; Northrup, J. M.; Richardson, E. S.; Garroway, C. J.; Shafer, A. B.
Abstract: Mutation rate () and recombination rate (r) are fundamental population-genetic parameters, yet demographic and conservation inference in polar bears (Ursus maritimus) has relied on values borrowed from humans and other mammals. Known values vary by an order of magnitude across mammals, and inaccuracies in these estimates propagate into downstream analyses, such as inferences of demographic history. To address this, we used high-coverage whole-genome resequencing of eight parent-offspring trios from the Western Hudson Bay subpopulation of polar bears. We identified 329 de novo mutations and estimated a pedigree-based germline mutation rate of 1.22 x 10?? per site per generation, which is within the mammalian range and close to values previously assumed for this species. Trio-based phasing yielded 522 crossovers across 16 meioses (32.6 per meiosis), and a pedigree-inferred recombination rate of 1.50 cM/Mb. From 44 unrelated individuals sampled from the same subpopulation, we inferred a demography-aware recombination map with a length-weighted genome-wide recombination rate of 3.03 cM/Mb (median 1.28 cM/Mb). We also identified 8,515 recombination hotspot regions covering 2.10% of the genome, accounting for 43.8% of total map length, a 20.9-fold concentration. Crossovers overlapped LD-defined hotspots 5.06-fold more often than expected by chance (p < 0.001). Nucleotide diversity was low and positively rank-correlated with recombination rate, consistent with linked selection. Genomic features explained only ~3% of recombination rate variation, with GC content and SINE abundance the only significant predictors. These species-specific parameters provide an empirical foundation for future demographic reconstruction and population projection in this vulnerable, ice-obligate species.

Title: Segment-dependent phylogenetic resolution reveals geographic and host sampling gaps in Oropouche virus genomes
Authors: Siam, R.; Elbehery, A. H. A.
Abstract: Background. Oropouche virus (OROV) has been reported in areas beyond its historical Amazonian range since 2023, accompanied by rapid growth in publicly available genomic data. However, the extent to which these data provide reliable phylogenetic and epidemiological resolution, and whether that resolution differs among genome segments, has not been systematically examined. Methods. Nucleotide sequences annotated under Orthobunyavirus oropoucheense were retrieved from NCBI Virus (accessed 13 May 2025) and filtered to retain records at least 70% of the reference length for each segment, yielding 898 S, 831 M, and 832 L sequences. Segments were aligned independently with MAFFT, and maximum-likelihood phylogenies were inferred with IQ-TREE using ModelFinder and ultrafast bootstrap approximation. Trees were annotated with collection date, country, and host in iTOL. Results. Phylogenetic resolution differed among segments. Contemporary Brazilian sequences formed a largely unresolved region in the S segment tree, whereas the M and L trees resolved recent clusters to differing degrees. Resolution did not track segment length: the M tree resolved contemporary structure more strongly than the longer L tree, and total tree length was approximately 3.5 times greater in the M tree despite near-identical taxon sampling. Sequences collected before 2010 were recovered in supported clusters in all three segment trees, although their configuration differed by segment. These sequences were also predominantly non-Brazilian and non-human, preventing collection date, geographic origin, and host from being separated as explanations for the observed clustering. The species-level query also retained three reassortant viruses, which may influence segment-specific topologies; sequences annotated to the United States were Iquitos virus rather than OROV. Two Italian sequences clustered with Cuban sequences across all three trees, concordant with published travel histories. Conclusions. Publicly available sequences contain phylogenetic structure that differs among the S, M, and L segment trees, but interpretation is constrained by uneven temporal, geographic, and host sampling and by the inclusion of reassortant species in a species-level dataset. The concentration of sequences from Brazil and human hosts, together with limited representation of non-human hosts, restricts inference about OROV diversity and ecology. Broader and more balanced genomic surveillance would improve the ability to resolve OROV evolutionary and transmission patterns.

Title: Transcriptome profiling reveals gene regulatory network governing seed size in Brassica napus
Authors: Zoclanclounon, Y. A. B.; Siles, L.; Woolfenden, H.; Morris, R. J.; Kurup, S.
Abstract: Seed size is a critical trait influencing yield and quality in oilseed crops such as Brassica napus. Despite their economic importance, the genetic and molecular mechanisms regulating seed size remain unclear, particularly in polyploid species, such as B. napus. To deepen our understanding of seed size regulation, we performed a comprehensive transcriptomic analysis across four developmental stages (heart, torpedo, green, and mature) and three distinct seed organs: the seed coat, embryo, and endosperm. Differential expression analysis between B. napus var. Zhongshuang (ZS11) and B. napus cv. Ragged Jack (RJ) was performed to uncover regulatory networks involved in seed size control. Our results uncovered dynamic gene regulatory networks (GRNs) and pinpointed key regulators, including well-established factors like ABI5 and BRI1, as well as novel candidate genes such as KNAT5, ARF11, SUS2, UGT72B1, UGT89A2, and SBT1.7. The present research provides an understanding of the regulatory networks governing seed size in B. napus. These findings not only enhance our knowledge of seed biology but also offer valuable resources for future breeding strategies aimed at optimizing seed size and yield in polyploid oilseed crops.

Title: Uncertainty-Aware Personalised Gene Expression Prediction Improves Cell-Type-Specific Association Testing
Authors: Styll, P.; Di, Y.; Cai, N.
Abstract: Linking genetic variation to disease requires accurate prediction of its effects on gene expression in relevant cell types. Sequence-to-function models offer a way to predict these effects and, with training on personal genomes, have begun to capture inter-individual expression differences. However, effect sign accuracy remains limited, and predictive uncertainty is unquantified. Here we introduce ATTICUS, which combines personalised sequence representations with uncertainty-aware expression prediction. ATTICUS transfers regulatory information learned in bulk expression pretraining to cell-type-specific expression prediction without requiring genotypes paired with single-cell expression data. Across blood and brain cell types in OneK1K and ROSMAP, ATTICUS approximately doubles expression prediction correlations relative to scPrediXcan and substantially improves sign accuracy. Moreover, ATTICUS enables uncertainty-aware transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS). Applied to systemic lupus erythematosus and Alzheimer's disease, ATTICUS identifies more associations, with greater cell-type specificity and stronger directional concordance, and reduced statistical inflation. Together, our results demonstrate that personalised training makes predictions more directionally consistent, and uncertainty propagation improves the calibration of TWAS and the prioritisation of disease genes. ATTICUS provides a framework for both, enabling the use of single-cell expression datasets without matched genotypes to inform uncertainty-aware TWAS, expanding their use in prioritising disease-associated genes and cell types.

Title: Integrating bacterial genomics and host transcriptomics links Burkholderia pseudomallei variation to melioidosis mortality and neutrophil responses
Authors: Wongprommoon, A.; Boonklang, P.; Burnham, K. L.; Chomkatekaew, C.; Angchagun, K.; Wongsuvan, G.; Ngernseng, T.; Limmathurotsakul, D.; Boonchalermvichien, T.; Coston, T. D.; Phunpang, R.; Yimthin, T.; Rongkard, P.; Lee, W.; Kronsteiner, B.; Knight, J.; Corander, J.; Peacock, S. J.; Parkhill, J.; Day, N. P. J.; Dunachie, S. J.; West, T. E.; Chantratita, N.; Thomson, N. R.; Davenport, E. E.; Chewapreecha, C.
Abstract: Bacterial genetic variation contributes to the outcome of infection, but its relationship with host immune responses is rarely investigated in the same patients, limiting the biological interpretation of pathogen-associated disease severity. Here, we integrated pathogen genomics, clinical outcomes and host transcriptomics to investigate host-pathogen interactions in melioidosis, a frequently fatal infection caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei. We analysed prospective clinical data from 2,142 patients, whole-genome sequences from 2,101 infecting isolates and 646 paired host blood transcriptomes across five cohorts collected between 2012 and 2023. Infections were typically dominated by a single strain, with limited within-host diversification, supporting the use of an infecting isolate genome to investigate pathogen-associated clinical outcomes. Bacterial genome-wide association studies identified one locus associated with binary mortality at genome-wide significance. Incorporating patient age, sex, body mass index and Charlson Comorbidity Index increased this to four, while modelling time to death as a continuous phenotype identified seven loci. Integration with paired host transcriptomes linked mortality-associated bacterial genetic variation to imputed signatures of increased immature neutrophils and reduced neutrophil degranulation. An intergenic region upstream of the polyketide synthesis locus BPSS1006-BPSS1011 was additionally associated with downregulation of host genes involved in myeloid-cell signalling and cell proliferation pathways. These findings connect naturally occurring B. pseudomallei genomic variation associated with mortality to distinct host immune signatures, providing insight into pathogen-host interactions underlying severe melioidosis and a framework for investigating the contribution of pathogen genetic diversity to clinical outcomes.

Title: Population Genomics of the Bovine Sialic Acid Network Reveals Functional and Evolutionary Diversity Across European and South African Cattle Breeds
Authors: Ogun, o. J.; Aiyesa, L. V.; Idowu, P. A. P.; Becker, D. P.; Galuska, S. P.
Abstract: **Background:** Sialic acids, mainly N-acetylneuraminic acid (Neu5Ac) and N-glycolylneuraminic acid (Neu5Gc), are terminal monosaccharides of glycans involved in numerous physiological processes, such as immune and neuronal function. Their biosynthesis, transport, transfer and turnover depend on a network of genes, but genetic studies in cattle have mostly addressed individual genes or genetic associations with milk oligosaccharide concentrations, leaving variation across this network largely uncharacterized. In bovine milk, sialylated glycans that depend on this network vary among animals and change rapidly during early lactation. We therefore characterized variation in 13 selected genes of the bovine sialic acid network using whole-genome sequence data from European and South African cattle. **Results:** We analyzed 346 animals from 12 European and 4 South African breeds. Of 9,724 variants in the 13 target genes, 8,675 were intronic and 62 were predicted to alter the amino acid sequence. Integration of SIFT predictions, Rate4Site conservation and protein context, with population representation as supporting evidence, identified 15 prioritized candidates, including 7 high-priority candidates in NEU3, ST8SIA2, ST8SIA4, CMAH and ST3GAL4. The most differentiated candidates were not among the 15 prioritized variants. NEU3 Y136H showed the largest regional contrast in allele frequency (0.83 in South African and 0.34 in European cattle), whereas several prioritized candidates were represented by a single allele in the South African cohort. Genome-wide principal component analysis of 950,219 linkage-disequilibrium-pruned SNPs separated South African from European cattle along the first component, which explained about 25% of the variance. None of the 220 analyzed common pathway SNPs exceeded the corresponding genome-wide differentiation thresholds at breed, country or regional level. Within the ascertained pathway SNPs, diversity was higher in South African breeds, and Tajima's D was shifted toward positive values in European breeds and centered near zero in South African breeds. **Conclusions:** This study provides a network-wide map of predicted protein-altering variation in the bovine sialic acid pathway and identifies 15 candidates for functional investigation, most of them rare. Because the most differentiated variants were not those with the strongest functional support, population contrasts, evolutionary conservation and protein context provide complementary evidence for selecting candidates. The analyzed common pathway SNPs did not show exceptional differentiation relative to the genome-wide background. The candidates provide specific targets for genotyping, enzyme-level testing and genotype-informed milk phenotyping.

Title: Synergy-informed bilevel optimization reveals joint-specific benefits for realistic exoskeleton torque prediction
Authors: Luis, I.; Gutierrez-Farewik, E. M.; Uchida, T. K.
Abstract: Simulation-driven optimization can guide exoskeleton control design, but its utility is limited by the accuracy with which muscle coordination is predicted. Strict effort-minimization formulations predict non-physiological muscle shutdown under high exoskeleton assistance, leading to peak assistive torques that exceed values reported in human-in-the-loop experiments. We evaluated the accuracy of synergy-informed simulations at predicting assistance across four single-joint exoskeleton configurations: ankle plantarflexion, knee extension, hip flexion, and hip abduction. We implemented a bilevel optimization to predict a parameterized assistive torque that minimizes metabolic cost, with assisted muscle dynamics estimated via either effort-minimization simulations (minimizing muscle effort only) or synergy-informed simulations (minimizing muscle effort constrained to a synergy structure). We used experimental data from five unimpaired adults walking at their preferred speed and compared results descriptively between the two formulations within each subject. Assistance based on effort-minimization simulations shut down agonist muscle activations and overestimated peak assistive torque compared with experimental values. In contrast, constraining muscle controls to a synergy structure prevented non-physiological muscle shutdown and yielded assistive torques closer to those measured in human-in-the-loop experiments. This benefit was not observed equally across all assisted degrees of freedom or subjects, emerging only where no single synergy could be suppressed to unload the assisted muscles. Synergy weights can therefore be interpreted as joint-specific predictors of when simulations can reliably inform wearable robot design.

Title: Rapid generation of antibody conformational ensembles using machine learning
Authors: Rao, P. V.; Sommer, D.; Davidson, D.; Alberstein, R. G.; Ludwiczak, J.; Kleinhenz, J.; Vani, B.; Park, E.; Lee, J. H.; Izadi, S.; Kiefer, J. R.; Bonneau, R.; Mahajan, S. P.; Watkins, A. M.; Dreyer, F. A.
Abstract: We introduce Cadense, a generative framework for antibody ensemble prediction that produces diverse Fv structures from sequence, informed by conformational dynamics. While a valuable resource, static structure prediction provides only a single snapshot of dynamic proteins, whose motions influence their binding and other properties. This is particularly relevant for antibodies, an important class of molecules for drug discovery, where flexible complementarity determining region (CDR) loops are difficult to model with static approaches. Cadense addresses this gap by generating ensembles that match conformational and biophysical property distributions from molecular dynamics (MD), while reducing the computational burden from days of simulation to seconds of generation. We show Cadense ensembles can recover both apo and holo conformations of the same antibody and serve as effective input to physics-based docking, capturing the conformational flexibility important to properly model antibody antigen interactions.
