Together, these results establish Cadense as a useful tool for antibody conformational ensemble generation with the promise to enable faster, dynamics-aware antibody design.

Title: Cell cycle progression and stalked cell morphogenesis in Caulobacter crescentus are regulated independently by the flagellum
Authors: Hellenbrand, C. N.; Hershey, D. M.
Abstract: Bacteria colonize surfaces and form biofilms to survive in stressful environmental conditions. Many bacteria use an appendage called the flagellum to sense surface contact, and responding to these mechanical cues triggers rapid physiological changes to promote downstream attachment. Bacteria are known to secrete adhesins and alter their motility behavior to facilitate surface colonization, but these changes alone are insufficient to explain the breadth of adaptations observed in surface-attached cells. Disrupting flagellar assembly in the bacterium Caulobacter crescentus constitutively activates the surface sensing pathway, and this gain-of-function phenotype was previously used to identify a suite of flagellar signaling suppressor (fss) genes that promotes surface adhesion downstream of the flagellum. We show herein that a subset of fss genes also regulates the C. crescentus developmental program. Live-cell microscopy analysis of fss mutants identified independent sub-pathways that target stalked cell morphogenesis and cell cycle progression. We identify the predicted chemotaxis genes fssD and fssE as novel regulators of stalked cell morphogenesis and show that these genes act to stimulate the diguanylate cyclase PleD in flagellar assembly mutants. A separate pathway that includes the stator protein MotB and the recently characterized dNTPase FssC regulates entry into S phase downstream of the flagellum. We show that motB regulates cell cycle progression specifically in response to surface cues, and that stator-dependent cell cycle control occurs independently of c-di-GMP and CtrA. This work clarifies the downstream targets of the surface sensing network and establishes a comprehensive model for how surface sensing influences the C. crescentus developmental program.

Title: Cholinergic modulation engages a CHRM1-IL-17 neuroimmune axis to promote diabetic wound repair
Authors: Li, Z.; Theocharidis, G.; Lee, S.; Kalavros, N.; Nagalakshmi, S. U.; Contreras, M.; Valsami, E.-A.; Nam, H.; Guan, M.; Chu, G.; Mezghani, I.; Wang, E.; Sumpio, B. J.; Hou, J.; Gennari-Felipe, M.; Gilman, J.; Lafuente-Gomez, N.; Maeso Aragon, L.; Dimitrakakis, N.; Arruda de Amaral, A.; Wang, S.; Vlachos, I. S.; Mooney, D. J.; Veves, A.
Abstract: Chronic non-healing wounds are a major complication of diabetes, where persistent inflammation fails to transition into effective tissue repair (1-3). Here we identify cholinergic modulation as a mechanism that promotes productive inflammation and diabetic wound healing. Using a healing-associated fibroblast signature derived from single-cell profiling of human diabetic foot ulcers (3), we identified the acetylcholinesterase (AChE) inhibitor metrifonate as a candidate inducer of reparative wound programs. Topical delivery accelerated healing in diabetic mice and increased acetylcholine availability within the wound. Complementary receptor pharmacology identified muscarinic acetylcholine receptor 1 (CHRM1) as the principal receptor mediating the reparative response. Transcriptomic and cellular analyses revealed early induction of IL-17-associated inflammatory programs and enrichment of CHRM1NK1.1 innate lymphocytes. Depletion of NK1.1 cells or neutralization of IL-17A abolished the pro-healing effect, whereas spatial transcriptomics revealed treatment-associated organization of NK cells within vascular niches. Localized treatment further promoted repair in diabetic porcine wounds and human skin models. Together, these findings identify a CHRM1-IL-17 neuroimmune axis linking cholinergic modulation to diabetic wound repair and establish local AChE inhibition as a potential therapeutic strategy for chronic wounds.

Title: Deep phenomics of African green monkey and Baboon PBMCs using a 30-marker spectral flow cytometry panel
Authors: Barman, S.; Patel, A.; Buonopane, M. J.; Janoschek, B.; Hingorani, R.; Dowling, D. J.
Abstract: Vaccines are the best way to prevent and combat diseases. Non-human primate (NHP) models have proven to be the gold standard model for studying the efficacy of certain vaccine candidates prior to human trials. Cell-mediated immunity serves as a surrogate marker for predicting vaccine efficacy. Despite the availability of deep-immunophenotyping panels for T cells in the peripheral blood of humans, their application to NHPs, particularly African Green Monkeys (AGMs) and baboons, remains limited. Notably, AGMs are valuable for HIV and COVID-19 research, while baboons are utilized for pertussis research as a natural infection model and vaccine trial. To overcome such limitation, using spectral flow cytometry, we developed a 30-parameter panel to profile major immune cell subsets (B cells, NK cells, DCs, monocytes) either in AGM or baboon PBMCs. We also profiled T cells, memory phenotypes, functional cytokines by tracking established Th1 markers IFN{gamma}, TNF and IL-2; Th2 markers IL-4/5/13 and the Th17 marker, IL-17, activation-induced markers (AIMs) and FoxP3+ Tregs in both AGM and baboon PBMCs in steady state as well as in mitogen stimulated conditions. For AIMs, CD69, CD134 (OX40) and CD137 (4-1BB) are included and validated in both NHP species. This panel holds potential for exploratory analysis of the impact of these functional cytokines, AIMs, or Tregs on host immunity following infection or vaccination. The panels high level of customization empowers researchers to tailor it to their specific research needs.

Title: 41% of Gram-negative bacteria encode a Type Six Secretion System
Authors: Zhang, C.; Hassler, H.; Ratcliff, W.; Speare, L.; Hammer, B. K.
Abstract: The type six secretion system (T6SS) is a highly studied, versatile bacterial nanoweapon that is important in bacterial pathogenesis and evolution. Despite extensive study, its prevalence remains poorly quantified. Analyzing 35,467 representative genomes, we find that approximately 41% of genomes in the average well-sampled Gram-negative genus (more than 30 sampled genomes) encode a T6SS. Further, we show that the distribution of the T6SS is patchy at all taxonomic levels. The uneven distribution we found is consistent with context-dependent selection, repeated evolutionary loss, or greater evolutionary lability. Our dataset provides a foundation for studying the drivers of T6SS distribution, and our pipeline enables similar surveys of other secretion systems, gene clusters, and multi-protein complexes across bacteria.

Title: Reversible decrease in swimming motility accompanies emergent β-lactam antibiotic resistance in Escherichia coli
Authors: Stabryla, L.; Ackerman, W.; Dootz, J. N.; Servetas, S. L.; Jackson, S. A.; Kralj, J. G.
Abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) threatens global health, food security, and development; however, the evolutionary and molecular pathways that drive AMR remain poorly understood, limiting our ability to advance diagnostics and rapidly detect newly emerging resistance. In this report, we employed laboratory evolution of an environmental Escherichia coli strain (NIST 0056) under B-lactam antibiotic pressure (ampicillin and cephalexin) to specifically investigate the relationship between resistance genotype and motility phenotype. Within 10 passages, populations evolved varying levels of B-lactam resistance (including high-level resistance > 32 ug/mL) and showed consistent, dose-dependent reductions in swimming motility. Whole-population genome sequencing revealed large deletions in marR, SNPs in efflux pump gene acrB and fumarate reductase gene frdD, and mutations with evidence of amplification in the chromosomal class C B-lactamase gene ampC, collectively linking these efflux-mediated, B-lactam resistance mechanisms to loss of motility. Notably, motility reductions were more pronounced in individual clones than in the mixed populations (p < 0.005, Mann-Whitney; two-tailed test). Following removal of antibiotic pressure, motility was restored and AMR-associated mutations decreased in frequency, suggesting fitness costs associated with resistance. In aggregate, our results demonstrate that reduced swimming motility accompanies specific efflux-driven, B-lactam resistance mechanisms. Further work will investigate if the behavior is generalizable across flagellated Enterobacteriaceae. Because these rapid changes are amenable to high-throughput measurement, swimming motility may offer a tractable physiological metric for AMR detection in environmental surveillance.

Title: Receptor-guided engineering of oncolytic vaccinia creates a synthetic support niche for off-the-shelf NK cell therapy
Authors: Rezaei, R.; Gan, Z.; Akeem Akilimali, N.; Reff, J.; Lin, M.; Xiao, Y.; Parikh, K.; Vithlani, D.; Valentic, B.; Shestov, A. A.; Uslu, U.; Azad, T.; OConnor, R. S.; June, C. H.; Sheppard, N. C.
Abstract: Combining adoptive cell therapy with oncolytic viruses offers a means to provide localized support within solid tumors, yet viral chassis and therapeutic payloads are often selected independently of the biological state of the manufactured cell product. Here, we establish an engineering framework that uses the phenotypic and functional features of an adoptive cell product as design inputs for a complementary oncolytic niche. Using off-the-shelf expanded, frozen, and thawed (EFT) natural killer (NK) cells as a model system, we identified manufacturing-associated reductions in chemokine responsiveness, dependence on extrinsic cytokine support, and loss of sustained function at limiting effector-to-target ratios. In a head-to-head evaluation under human NK-cell antiviral pressure, oncolytic vaccinia virus (VV) retained replication and spread, whereas HSV-1 was rapidly restricted, establishing VV as a compatible viral chassis. Mapping endogenous receptor expression and applying sequential functional screening under increasingly limiting effector densities then prioritized a five-factor program comprising CXCL11, IL-15, IL-27, IL-2, and IL-1{beta} that supported NK-cell migration, survival, cytotoxicity, and metabolic fitness at effector-to-target ratios as low as 1:10. Consolidating these signals into a single viral chassis increased antitumor activity but revealed a systemic inflammatory liability associated with constitutive IL-1{beta} expression. We therefore placed the IL-2/IL-1{beta} module under chemically inducible control, retaining in vivo antitumor activity while limiting systemic toxicity. Together, these findings establish a framework in which the post-manufacturing state of an adoptive cell product guides viral chassis selection, payload prioritization, and programmable control of a complementary oncolytic support niche.

Title: Tissue-like Viscoelasticity Drives Muscle Stem Cell Expansion Through Mechanical Memory Formation
Authors: Hu, H.; Kwon, T. Y.; Gao, Z.; Zhou, P.; Madl, C. M.
Abstract: Mechanical cues are potent regulators of stem cell fate, with even transient exposure to substrates with varied elastic stiffness driving persistent changes in cell fate. Such elastic mechanical memory contributes to the loss of regenerative potential in skeletal muscle stem cells (MuSCs) when cultured on rigid substrates, hampering the translation of myogenic cell replacement therapies. Beyond elastic mechanical properties, cells also respond to time-dependent, viscoelastic mechanical properties, such as stress relaxation. However, whether tissue-like viscoelasticity can impart a mechanical memory that directs stem cell fate remains an open question. Accordingly, dual-network hydrogel biomaterials with decoupled control of stiffness, stress relaxation, and adhesive ligand presentation were engineered to recapitulate the viscoelastic mechanical properties of native muscle. Muscle-like viscoelastic substrates promote in vitro MuSC activation and accelerate stem cell expansion, matching in vivo activation timescales. Mechanistically, physiological viscoelasticity promotes focal adhesion stabilization and enhances Rac-Akt signaling, establishing a viscoelastic mechanical memory that supports progenitor expansion and persistent maintenance of a stem-like phenotype. These findings identify matrix viscoelasticity as a potent and persistent regulator of MuSC fate and provide a framework for engineering biomaterials that preserve MuSC stemness and expansion ex vivo.

Title: PRISM: probabilistic cell-type resolution with integrated spatial modelling for simultaneous ambient RNA decontamination and doublet correction in spatial transcriptomics
Authors: Cupaioli, F.; Merelli, I.
Abstract: Spatial transcriptomics count matrices are confounded by ambient RNA contamination and cell-segmentation doublets, two artifacts that co-occur but are rarely modelled jointly. We present PRISM, an Expectation-Maximization framework that simultaneously (i) assigns each cell a probabilistic cell-type identity, (ii) detects doublets via log-likelihood ratio testing of two-component mixtures, and (iii) estimates a per-cell contamination fraction  anchored to a spatially resolved ambient profile. In an in silico benchmark of 40,800 simulated cells, PRISM recovers  with Pearson r=1.000 across all contamination levels (0.05 to 0.50) and UMI depths (500 to 5,000), with zero doublet false positives and 100% singlet accuracy. Applied to a Visium HD mouse cerebellum dataset (four samples, 125,289 cells, 17 reference types) from a metachromatic leukodystrophy (MLD) model, PRISM identifies a median =0.60, flags 67.4% doublets (driven by the densely packed cerebellar granule layer), eliminates spurious myelin signal from microglia (0.82% to 0.00%), and doubles oligodendrocyte myelin purity (2.8% to 5.6%). PRISM runs on commodity CPUs in under 15 minutes and returns decontaminated integer count matrices for every measured gene.

Title: A Three-View System for CRISPR-Cas12a crRNA Activity Ranking: When to Ensemble, When Context Matters More
Authors: Deng, T.; Lin, Z.; Lam, H.; Xu, S.
Abstract: CRISPR-Cas12a assays require effective crRNA selection, but experimentally screening all possible candidates is costly. We developed TriCasRank, a ranking model that combines sequence features with EasyDesign reference mapping and activity summaries from related training records. Historical summaries were calculated within each training fold to avoid information leakage. In five-fold target-grouped cross-validation using out-of-fold predictions, TriCasRank improved the Spearman correlation from 0.741 for the sequence-only ensemble to 0.821 (paired difference, 0.080; 95% target-group bootstrap interval, 0.072 to 0.090). However, its performance was comparable to that of a strong sequence-plus-mapping XGBoost model (SCC, 0.822; paired difference, -0.001; 95% interval, -0.007 to 0.005). Separate perturbation analyses supported the predictive value of mapping and historical features, although their effect sizes were not directly comparable because they were evaluated using different model configurations. Prediction errors remained larger at the extremes of the activity distribution. Performance also became less stable when template identities were separated between training and evaluation. TriCasRank may therefore be useful for ranking candidates represented within the EasyDesign-derived domain, but evaluation on an independent experimental cohort is still needed.

Title: Integrated genotyping, annotation and epigenetic characterization of transposable elements with GraffiTE
Authors: Goubert, C.; Laflamme, R.; Eveleigh, R.; Ragoussis, I.; Wheeler, T.; Lettre, G.; Bourque, G.; Groza, C.
Abstract: Genotyping, annotating and characterizing TE variation leaped forward with long-read sequencing (LRS) and de novo assembly. LRS techniques also reveal CpG methylation, which enables measuring the impact of TEs on epigenomes and sheds light on the role of TEs as regulatory sequences. Yet, TE genotyping tools discard the valuable allele-specific epigenetic information. We introduce GraffiTE v1.1, the first Nextflow pipeline that genotypes SVs, annotates polymorphic mobile elements (MEI), and maps epigenetic data to TEs using pangenome graphs in one command. GraffiTE v1.1 is designed to map any epigenetic information that is based on LRS stencils, including Fiber-seq. We demonstrate the capabilities of GraffiTE v1.1 by analyzing genomes and methylomes obtained from 20 Quebec residents of French-Canadian descent. In these genomes, TE annotation yields 4,908 Alu, 704 LINE1, 112 SVA and 21 HERVK (HML-2) distinct polymorphic mobile elements (MEIs). We also identify 10 fixed HERVK insertions that vary between solo LTR and provirus, or in proviral copy number. We determine that these MEIs contribute 144,748 additional CpGs not present in the reference. From this, we identify 480 Alus, 67 LINE1s, 12 SVAs and 2 HERVKs in hypomethylated states. We note that Alus and SVAs are more methylated than other LINE1 and HERVK. Lastly, MEIs dating reported a mean of age 1.08 Mya (median: 640 kya) and beta regression identified a moderate demethylating effect of age on MEIs (effect: -0.069 log-odds per log10 years, P < 6.08 x 10-19). Our results show that the methylation level of a LINE1 MEI is expected to decrease from 86.4% to 80.8% in the first Mya. In conclusion, GraffiTE v1.1 genotypes SVs, annotates MEI, and characterizes their epigenetic state at the scale of populations by leveraging the full potential of LRS. While we showcase its application in human data, the pipeline can be deployed in any model for which a TE library is available.

Title: FACT frees Ubp10 from nucleosome sequestration after rapid H2B deubiquitination
Authors: Merino-Urteaga, R.; Zaehringer, J.; Nune, M.; Wolberger, C.; Ha, T.
Abstract: Chromatin-modifying enzymes must engage their substrate, act on it and release it, but which step limits their turnover is unclear. Using three-color single-molecule fluorescence, we directly visualized the yeast deubiquitinase Ubp10 removing ubiquitin from H2B on individual nucleosomes. Ubp10 cleaved the mark within seconds of binding, without detectable DNA unwrapping, yet it did not let go: ~80% of nucleosomes remained bound after 45 minutes, and unmodified nucleosomes formed similarly long-lived complexes. Ubp10 turnover is therefore limited by release rather than catalysis. The histone chaperone FACT relieved this bottleneck by accelerating Ubp10-nucleosome dissociation. In living yeast, nuclear depletion of the FACT subunit Spt16 increased the slowly diffusing, chromatin-bound fraction of nucleoplasmic Ubp10. These findings identify FACT-dependent release as a likely mechanism for recycling Ubp10 on chromatin. More broadly, a nucleosome can sequester the enzyme acting on it, making enzyme release a step at which chromatin modification can be controlled.

Title: Viral replication and host response in airway epithelial cells predicts coronavirus pathogenicity and identifies HCoV-229E as an atypical seasonal coronavirus
Authors: Gartner, M. J.; Hirankitti, A.; Mohenska, M.; Sanchez, S.; Sun, G.; Chen, J.; Tang, K.; Deshpande, N.; Suryadinata, R.; Wilcox, S.; Rawlinson, D. P.; Londrigan, S. L.; Steinfort, D.; Robinson, P.; Polo, J. M.; Fox, A.; Neil, J. A.; Subbarao, K.
Abstract: Human coronaviruses (HCoVs) range from mild seasonal strains to pathogenic viruses that cause severe pneumonia. The virological and host determinants that distinguish pathogenic coronaviruses (MERS-CoV, SARS-CoV-2) from seasonal strains (HCoV-229E, HCoV-NL63 and HCoV-OC43) remain poorly defined. To identify determinants of pathogenicity, we systematically compared replication, cellular tropism, innate responses and cytopathogenicity of pathogenic compared with seasonal HCoVs across nasal, bronchial, small airway and embryonic stem cell derived alveolar type II (AT2) epithelial cell cultures. All HCoVs preferentially infected ciliated cells in the upper airway, but only pathogenic viruses replicated to high titres in AT2 cells. Pathogenic HCoVs reprogrammed AT2 function and suppressed key innate immune signatures, consistent with distal lung epithelial dysfunction. In contrast, seasonal HCoVs were associated with limited alveolar replication and milder disruption of AT2 homeostasis. Strikingly, despite modest replication in all cell types, HCoV-229E induced pronounced epithelial injury, cilia loss and strong interferon stimulated gene expression, as well as induction of cellular stress/death programmes resembling those induced by MERS-CoV. These findings highlight the striking differences in cellular responses throughout the airways and between distinct HCoV strains and emphasizes the importance of assessing distal lung tropism and epithelial host responses to evaluate emergent coronaviruses to inform pandemic preparedness strategies.

Title: Chromosome-scale CRISPR screening reveals secretory pathway genes as drivers of aneuploidy-mediated antifungal tolerance
Authors: Gervais, N. C.; Esquivel, B. D.; Wensing, L. F.; Chhina, M.; Fogal, M.; Despres, P. C.; Hoyer, L. L.; White, T. C.; Gerstein, A. C.; Shapiro, R. S.
Abstract: The gain or loss of chromosomes in eukaryotes often drives aberrant phenotypes by altering the expression levels of hundreds or thousands of genes. In the case of beneficial aneuploidies, the genetic basis of fitness improvement has rarely been pinpointed, and identifying the causal genes remains a major challenge in engineering biology. The leading cause of human fungal infections, Candida albicans, frequently acquires extra copies of chromosome R (ChrR) following exposure to azole antifungal drugs, resulting in heightened antifungal tolerance. Despite this, why this aneuploidy frequently emerges following azole exposure and how it promotes antifungal tolerance remain unknown. Here, we combine RNA-seq with parallel chromosome-wide CRISPR activation (CRISPRa) and CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) screens to systematically profile the ChrR genes contributing to azole tolerance. Using multiplexed CRISPR-dCas12a tools, we further characterize the combinatorial effects of candidate genes and uncover a central role for post-Golgi secretory trafficking in antifungal tolerance. Specifically, we demonstrate that the secretory pathway regulators SEC4 and YPT31 are both necessary and sufficient for ChrR-mediated azole tolerance, and drive increased ergosterol content in the cell membrane. By leveraging a large-scale CRISPRa screen in a fungal pathogen, our work functionally dissects one of the most common aneuploidies observed in C. albicans, provides mechanistic insight into the molecular basis of antifungal tolerance, and establishes a generalizable framework for studying aneuploidy-mediated phenotypes across eukaryotic organisms.

Title: Nuclear retention and RNA editing safeguard self-tolerance to immunogenic intron lariats
Authors: Lee, K.; Ku, J.; Park, S. Y.; Widowati, T. A.; Jeon, M.; Kim, N.; Chung, H.; Kim, M. J.; Kim, D. S.; Kim, H. Y.; Chung, H.; Jang, W. D.; Ryu, H. S.; Kim, Y.
Abstract: Introns are excised as lariats and rapidly degraded upon linearization, leaving their post-splicing role unclear. Here, we investigate their immunoregulatory potential by analyzing the intron lariat landscape upon inhibition of the debranching enzyme DBR1. We find that lariats harboring transposable elements (TEs), especially inverted Alu repeats (IRAlus), elicit cell cycle-dependent activation of protein kinase R (PKR), but only in cells harboring a high burden, such as breast cancer. These immunogenic lariats are initially retained in the nucleus, but upon cytosolic release, they drive PKR activation and apoptosis. Exploiting this, we combine DBR1 depletion with anti-mitotic chemotherapy to enhance lariat-PKR interactions and promote cancer cell death in vitro and in vivo. We further show that A-to-I editing of IRAlus-containing lariats weakens their interaction with PKR and suppresses PKR activation. Our findings highlight two parallel molecular mechanisms to sustain self-tolerance to repeat-rich introns, revealing a vulnerability exploitable for anti-tumor therapy.

Title: LOca-1: A minimal calcium-activated arginyl-specific orthocaspase from the Loki's Castle hydrothermal vent field
Authors: Arsın, H.; Hribovsek, P.; Urich, L.; Fedoy, A.-E.; Stokke, R.; Mak, P.; Kaczorowska, A.-K.; ODonoghue, A. J.; Kaczorowski, T.; Steen, I. H.
Abstract: Orthocaspases are prokaryotic homologs of metacaspases within the C14 family of cysteine proteases, yet their biochemical properties and cellular roles remain poorly understood. Here, we report the discovery and comprehensive characterization of LOca-1, a metagenome-derived orthocaspase from the Loki's Castle hydrothermal vent field. LOca-1 consists primarily of a single, conserved p20 catalytic domain and undergoes calcium-dependent activation through cleavage at a conserved arginine residue. Once activated, LOca-1 displays strict arginyl-specific proteolytic activity and strong selectivity for residues surrounding the cleavage site. The enzyme is both thermoactive and thermostable, exhibiting maximal activity at 65 {degrees}C and a melting temperature of approximately 72 {degrees}C. Structural modelling revealed conservation of the catalytic core relative to plant metacaspases despite substantial sequence divergence. To our knowledge, LOca-1 is only the second biochemically characterized orthocaspase and the first reported from a deep-sea hydrothermal vent environment. LOca-1 expands the known biochemical diversity of prokaryotic metacaspase homologs and provides insights into the properties of a minimal p20-domain orthocaspase. Together, our findings establish LOca-1 as a thermostable, calcium-activated arginyl-specific orthocaspase and provide a foundation for future studies of orthocaspase function in prokaryotes.

Title: A TMEM175 Mutation Disrupts the Lysosomal-Mitochondrial Axis Causing Short QT Syndrome and Sudden Cardiac Death
Authors: Cruz, F. M.; Ruiz-Robles, J. M.; Martinez-Carrascoso, I. m.; Macias, A.; Moreno-Manuel, A. I.; Sanchez-Perez, P.; Corver, M.; Socuellamos, P. G.; Talavera-Gutierrez, A.; Bermudez-Jimenez, F. J.; Cabrera Borrego, E.; Macias-Ruiz, R.; Martinez, F.; Ochoa, J. P.; Jurgens, S. J.; Bezzina, C. R.; Jimenez-Jaimez, J.; Jalife, J.
Abstract: Short QT Syndrome (SQTS) is a rare cardiac channelopathy characterized by abnormally short QTc intervals and increased sudden cardiac death (SCD) risk. Only 20-30% of SQTS cases have been linked to genetic mutations, typi-cally in surface membrane ion channels. We identified a novel lysosomal TMEM175 gene mutation (p.Arg377His) in 7 patients in a family with SQTS and SCD. Genetic analyses, including whole exome sequencing in the family and rare-variant burden testing in [~]118,000 UK Biobank participants, sug-gested an association between TMEM175 rare variants and QT interval short-ening. Functional studies in CRISPR-engineered mice and patient-specific induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes (iPSC-CMs) revealed that TMEM175R377H causes shortened QT intervals and hastened repolariza-tion, respectively, as well an increased arrhythmia susceptibility. Isolated TMEM175R377H cardiomyocytes showed action potential duration (APD) abbre-viation, confirmed in whole TMEM175R377H mouse hearts and patient-specific iPSC-CM monolayers. In silico and electron microscopy studies showed that TMEM175R377H disrupts lysosomal-mitochondrial interactions, leading to mito-chondrial dysfunction, as evidenced by the reduced maximal respiration and spare respiratory capacity, with reduced ATP production, IKATP activation, and APD shortening. This mutation represents the first non-sarcolemmal ion chan-nel defect associated with SQTS and high SCD risk, potentially expanding the genetic landscape of the disease.

Title: Deep Vein Thrombosis-primed neutrophils reshape the brain microenvironment to promote brain metastasis
Authors: Endo, S.; Rujchanarong, D.; Keeran, K.; Jeffries, K.; Zhang, W.; Bannister, M.; Saeki, K.; Wei, D.; Tran, A.; Ellison, K.; Lee Fong, A.; Lim, L.; Kruhlak, M.; Lake, R.; Combs, C. A.; Steeg, P.; Kelly, M.; Lipkowitz, S.; Kanthi, Y.; Fujii, T.
Abstract: Brain metastasis (BrM) is a devastating complication of triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), yet how host macroenvironmental conditions influence brain metastatic susceptibility remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated the impact of deep vein thrombosis (DVT), a common complication in patients with cancer, on TNBC brain metastasis. Analysis of a large clinical cohort identified DVT as an independent risk factor for BrM in patients with metastatic breast cancer. Using two syngeneic TNBC models, we demonstrated that DVT selectively enhanced brain metastasis without significantly affecting primary tumor growth or lung metastasis. Mechanistically, DVT increased neutrophil accumulation in the brain metastatic microenvironment, and neutrophil depletion completely abrogated the metastasis-promoting effect of DVT. Single-cell RNA sequencing of CD45+ cells in peripheral blood revealed that DVT reprogrammed circulating neutrophils toward migratory and inflammatory transcriptomic profiles characterized by neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation. DVT increased CXCR2 expression on circulating neutrophils and enhanced neutrophil recruitment in brain. Moreover, DVT significantly increased circulating NETs. Collectively, our findings identify DVT as a systemic driver of TNBC brain metastasis and reveal that DVT primes circulating neutrophils toward enhanced vascular recruitment and NET formation, providing a mechanistic link between cancer-associated thrombosis and brain metastatic susceptibility.

Title: A LOV-domain photoreceptor mediates phototaxis in brown algae
Authors: Duchene, C.; Coelho, S. M.
Abstract: Phototaxis enables motile cells to navigate light environments and plays a critical role in survival and reproduction across diverse eukaryotic lineages. This ability has evolved independently through distinct photoreceptor systems. Yet, the molecular mechanisms underlying phototaxis remain poorly understood in many major eukaryotic lineages, including stramenopiles. Here, combining functional genetics, cell biology and evolutionary analyses, we identify Helmchrome (HELM), a LOV-domain protein required for phototaxis in the brown alga Ectocarpus. HELM localizes to the posterior flagellum and is responsible for the characteristic flavin-associated fluorescence of brown algal gametes. Loss of HELM abolishes phototactic accumulation and directional orientation without affecting basal motility or fertilization, demonstrating its specific requirement for light-directed movement. Phylogenetic analyses reveal that HELM-like proteins are distributed across diverse stramenopile lineages and that their domain architecture evolved through repeated duplication of an ancestral RGS-LOV module. Our findings identify HELM as a key component of the light-sensing machinery in brown algae, provide a molecular explanation for the long-standing observation of flagellar flavin fluorescence, and reveal a distinct phototaxis system that expands the known diversity of eukaryotic light-sensing mechanisms.

Title: Multiplexed Targeted iprm-PASEF Assays for MALDI Mass Spectrometry Imaging of Lipids, NAD+ 2 , and Related Metabolites in CD38 Knockout Mice
Authors: Schurman, C. A.; Bons, J.; Kumaar, P. V.; Fang, J.; Hormazabal, G. V.; Roberts, A.; Riley, R. R.; Tao, N.; Verdin, E.; Schilling, B.
Abstract: Mass spectrometry imaging (MSI) maps the molecular landscape of tissues; however, confident in situ identification and accurate quantification of analytes by matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization (MALDI)-MSI remain challenging. We present a new targeted imaging methodology, imaging parallel reaction monitoring parallel accumulation-serial fragmentation (iprm-PASEF), which utilizes trapped ion mobility spectrometry (TIMS) and MALDI for assessment of metabolites and lipids on the fragment ion level in tissue. We investigated liver tissues from wild-type and CD38 knockout (CD38-/-) mice, as CD38 contributes to age-related nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) decline and direct detection of NAD+ within tissue remains challenging. The iprm-PASEF workflow enabled confident differentiation of lipid isomers, resolving phosphatidylinositols at m/z 857.52 and confirming the presence of PI 36:4(16:0/20:4) and absence of PI 36:4(14:0/22:4) at the fragment ion level. We confirmed a more than 2-fold increase in NAD+ in CD38-/- liver tissues of male and female animals (n = 3 per genotype and sex) and decreased adenosine diphosphate ribose (ADPR) through relative quantification of characteristic fragment ions, confirming alteration of NAD metabolism in these animals. This approach provided confident and specific MS2-based identification and relative quantification of fragment ions in MSI experiments, with consistent fold changes across multiple characteristic fragment ions and biological replicates.

Title: Replication stress links Geminin depletion to centrosome amplification
Authors: Santos, I. B.; Glover, D. M.
Abstract: The timing of DNA replication and centrosome duplication is tightly regulated with cell cycle progression to ensure the faithful duplication of the genome during cell division. Both DNA and centrosomes are licensed for replication in late telophase/early G1, replicated in S phase and segregated during mitosis; yet how defects in DNA replication licensing are coupled to centrosome homeostasis remains poorly understood. Here, we show that depletion of the replication licensing inhibitor Geminin in proliferating mouse embryonic fibroblasts induces robust centrosome amplification together with impaired primary cilium assembly. Rather than promoting whole-genome reduplication, knockdown of Geminin triggers a replication stress response, characterized by DNA damage accumulation throughout the cycle, and activation of an ATR-dependent DNA damage response. Mechanistically, Geminin depletion-induced replication stress activates the ATR-Chk1-Wee1 checkpoint axis prolonging G2 and leading to premature centriole disengagement and centrosome amplification. These findings identify replication stress as the signaling module that couples defective DNA replication licensing to centrosome amplification.

Title: Kinetochore-microtubule attachments are strengthened by Cnn1 stabilization of Stu2
Authors: Maitra, N.; Edwards, D. T.; Nelson, C. R.; Hu, C.; Asbury, C. L.; Biggins, S.
Abstract: Accurate chromosome segregation requires kinetochores to form robust, load-bearing attachments to dynamic spindle microtubules, mediated primarily by the Ndc80 complex. Two receptors, Dsn1 and Cnn1 (CENP-T), recruit multiple copies of Ndc80c to the kinetochore. We previously demonstrated that kinetochore components co-purifying with the yeast Dsn1 protein can maintain persistent load-bearing attachments that track with microtubule tip growth and shortening, but the properties of the Cnn1 receptor have not been explored. Using an optical trapping-based assay, we show here that Cnn1 purifications also sustain dynamic microtubule attachments under load. Mutation of a conserved region within the disordered N-terminal tail of Cnn1 weakened attachment strength in vitro and caused a growth defect when Dsn1 function was impaired. The Cnn1 mutation reduced Stu2 kinetochore levels without altering other kinetochore proteins. Restoring Stu2, either by direct addition in vitro or by tethering it to Ndc80c in vivo, rescued both attachment strength and cellular viability. These findings reveal a biophysical role for Cnn1 in enabling Stu2-dependent stabilization of kinetochore-microtubule attachments.

Title: High-content screening identifies FDA-approved activators of mitophagy
Authors: Viscomi, C.; Giacchin, G.; Balmaceda, V.; Giacomello, M.; Eastes, A.; Corra, S.; Fernandez-Del-Rio, L.; Scillitani, N.; Steffan, D.; Sandri, M.; Fernandez-Vizarra, E.; Shirihai, O. S.; Beninca, C.
Abstract: Mitochondrial diseases are highly heterogeneous disorders caused by defects in oxidative phosphorylation, for which only limited therapeutic options are available. The elimination of dysfunctional mitochondria via mitophagy activation is an attractive strategy to treat several mitochondrial diseases, irrespective of the underlying genetic defect. To identify pharmacological activators of this pathway, we performed a high-content screening of 1,971 FDA-approved compounds using cellular reporters of TFEB nuclear translocation and mitophagy. This screening identified 294 compounds that promoted TFEB translocation, nine of which increased the number of mitolysosomes without compromising cell viability or damaging mitochondria. Among the selected compounds, Meptazinol and Ponatinib emerged as the top-ranked mitophagy inducers in fibroblasts from patients with complex I and IV deficiency, respectively, and were prioritised for further characterisation. However, they did not rescue the bioenergetic defect, suggesting that the stimulation of mitophagy per se is not sufficient to ameliorate the OXPHOS defect in mitochondrial diseases. Overall, our findings establish a scalable platform for the identification of pharmacological activators of TFEB and identify candidate compounds for therapeutic modulation of mitophagy.

Title: Receptor-proximal phosphoform organization precedes β2 integrin activation
Authors: Hummell, N. A.; Jonnagaddala, H.; Kalocsay, M.; Moore, T. I.
Abstract: Receptor signaling is often framed as protein recruitment after stimulation, but whether receptor-proximal environments are organized in composition and phosphorylation state beforehand remains unclear. We used CD18-APEX2 proximity labeling and a spatial membrane reference to quantify proteins and phosphosites near leukocyte {beta}2 integrins. At rest, receptors, adaptors and Rap GTPases were preferentially represented relative to several catalytic classes. Parent-protein correction revealed spatial phosphoform organization, with 32% of 4,564 phosphosites deviating significantly from the distribution center and 56% of proteins with multiple quantified sites showing divergence beyond measurement error. Sustained activation altered 31% of phosphosites while 95.9% of proteins remained equivalent within {+/-}0.5 log2 and spatial phosphoform organization largely persisted. Most phosphorylation responses were shared across both labeling environments, whereas receptor-preferential changes were dominated by phosphosites. These findings suggest that receptor signaling can regulate pre-existing molecular states without extensive protein redistribution.

Title: A population-scale isoform atlas enables isoform-based trait association and regulatory analysis in lettuce
Authors: Luo, G.; Xiao, L.; Zhang, X.; Xu, X.; Lan, G.; Chen, J.; Kuang, H.; Wang, X.
Abstract: Genomic variation shapes phenotypic diversity, yet how genetic variation contributes to transcript isoform diversity remains poorly understood at the population scale. Here, we integrated transcriptomic data from 240 lettuce accessions with a lettuce pangenome to construct a comprehensive pan isoform atlas comprising 531,657 isoforms from 49,729 transcribed loci. Isoform presence absence variation (iPAV) captured extensive transcript diversification during domestication and horticultural differentiation, providing additional resolution beyond locus-level analyses, particularly within loci shared across the population. To facilitate the systematic analysis of isoform trait associations, we developed ISONET-GWAS, a computational framework that integrates isoform-based association mapping, functional annotation, and network-based candidate prioritization. ISONET-GWAS recovered the known chlorophyll regulator LsGLK, identified 455 metabolite isoform associations across 77 metabolites, and prioritized candidate regulators of chlorophyll metabolism supported by functional validation. Genome-wide splicing quantitative trait locus (sQTL) mapping identified 10,498 sQTL associations, revealing widespread distal genetic associations with alternative splicing and candidate trans-sQTL hotspots. Notably, we identified a trans-sQTL hotspot overlapping LsPPR, which encodes a pentatricopeptide repeat RNA-binding protein. Perturbation of LsPPR resulted in widespread changes in alternative splicing of floweing-related genes, accompanied by delayed bolting and flowering and altered splicing of flowering-related genes. Together, our study establishes a population-scale pan-isoform resource and a broadly applicable analytical strategy for isoform-level trait association, candidate prioritization, and complementary analysis of the genetic regulation of alternative splicing in crops.

Title: MitoScope: a comprehensive mitochondrial genome analysis workflow for long-read sequencing data
Authors: Zakarian, C.; Smith, J. D.; Wong, C. H.; Frazar, C. D.; Ryke, E.; McGee, S. R.; Richardson, M.; Weiss, J. M.; Munson, K. M.; Hoekzema, K.; Mack, T.; Kwon, Y.; Ou, J.; Neph, S. J.; Sohn, M.-H.; Minkina, A.; Bennett, J. T.; Stergachis, A. B.; Eichler, E. E.; Wei, C.-L.
Abstract: The mitochondrial genome (mtDNA), rich in repeats and prone to nuclear mitochondrial DNA segments (NUMTs), is implicated in cancer, metabolic syndromes, and neurodegeneration, yet short-read sequencing yields incomplete catalogs, mapping artifacts, and false heteroplasmies. We introduce MitoScope, a scalable end-to-end long-read mitochondrial analysis workflow that integrates mtDNA-read selection, heteroplasmic variant detection, assembly, copy number estimation, read-level haplotyping, and NUMT profiling. Applied to benchmarking data from the Somatic Mosaicism Across Human Tissues (SMaHT) Network, we reveal high sensitivity and precision compared to existing methods and successfully uncover known mitochondrial biology relevant for variant interpretation, aging, and human disease.

Title: Functional genomics reveals mediators of beta cell survival in ER stress and type 2 diabetes risk
Authors: Okino, M.-L.; Zhu, H.; Corban, S.; Benaglio, P.; Huang, L.; Djulamsah, J.; Tseng, R.; OMahony, B.; Vanderstel, K.; Elgamal, R.; Miller, M.; Wang, A.; Sander, M.; Gaulton, K. J.
Abstract: Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress in pancreatic beta cells contributes to impaired function and type 2 diabetes (T2D). In this study we performed genome-wide perturbation screens and genomic profiling in beta cells to identify novel mediators of ER stress responses and diabetes risk. We defined gene regulatory networks in beta cells and identified specific beta cell networks enriched for T2D risk variants with altered expression in ER stress. We performed a loss-of-function CRISPR screen for survival under ER stress in EndoC-bH1 cells, which identified 167 pro-survival and 47 pro-death genes involved in processes related to insulin secretion, mitochondrial transport and protein ubiquitination. Beta cell survival genes collectively had limited genomic change in stress yet showed significant, independent enrichment for T2D risk variants, including novel T2D candidate gene DTNB which we validated protects against beta cell death during stress. Overall, our results revealed mediators of ER stress responses in beta cells and identified novel therapeutic targets to preserve beta cells in diabetes pathogenesis.

Title: EngA adopts multiple distinct conformational states during ribosome assembly
Authors: Arora, A.; Aggarwal, J.; Agarwal, N.; Kaushal, P. S.
Abstract: Ribosome assembly, a highly coordinated and crucial cellular process, is assisted by various assembly factors, including GTPases. EngA, an essential P-loop GTPase, is involved in late-stage assembly of the 50S ribosomal subunit. The structures of 50S ribosome in complex with EngA-bound GMPPNP, and EngA-bound GDP alone, without 50S subunit, have been reported previously. However, the molecular mechanism of EngA GTP hydrolysis-assisted 50S maturation remains poorly understood, and structures of the 50S ribosome in complex with EngA-bound GDP have yet to be deciphered. We have reported cryo- EM structures of the Mycobacterium smegmatis 50S ribosome in complex with EngA-bound GTP{gamma}S or GDP at 2.8 - 3.5 [A] resolution. Structural analysis revealed that EngA and 50S subunit undergo a coordinated structural rearrangement, and an assembly intermediate is formed in which the stem-loop of H80 makes base-pair interactions with the junction of H89 and H90, forming a unique stem-loop-junction (SLJ) motif. EngA-bound GDP adopts distinctly different conformations in its ribosome-bound and unbound states. In summary, this study proposed a multi-state conformational model for EngA-assisted ribosome assembly.

Title: Disentangled generative modeling of single-cell perturbation responses across dynamic cellular states
Authors: Wang, Y.; Zhao, Y.; Li, S.; Yang, D.
Abstract: Single-cell perturbation studies are increasingly conducted across complex, multi-condition biolog-ical systems, offering a powerful lens into how interventions reshape cell states and molecular pro-grams. However, standard computational models compress single-cell profiles into unified repre-sentations where treatment effects are obscured by cell division, lineage progression, donor varia-tion, and cellular stress. Here, we present Disentangled Variational Inference for Perturbation Re-sponse (PertVI), a deep generative model that separates baseline mitotic phase, cellular state, and batch effects from treatment-induced shifts while isolating aberrant off-manifold responses in or-thogonal anomaly space. This structured design tackles two intertwined tasks: (1) quantifying treatment-induced changes in cell-state composition, and (2) inferring state-gated transcriptional changes in response to treatment. Across simulated benchmarks, PertVI accurately disentangles coupled biological axes and recovers weak treatment signatures. In conditional chemical and genet-ic screens of primary human CD8+ and CD4+ T cells, PertVI separates memory-precursor adju-vants from toxic phenocopies, resolves co-clustered regulators into directional kinetic trajectories and biphasic rebounders obscured by standard workflows, and reveals that treatment-induced phe-notypic shifting is decoupled from broad transcriptional perturbation responses and instead gov-erned by state-specific impulses. Altogether, PertVI brings unique mechanistic granularity to sin-gle-cell perturbation response modeling, serving as a proof of principle for biology-informed, struc-ture-guided variance disentanglement in dynamic cellular systems.

Title: KLONE: An Imbalance-Robust k-NN Ensemble for Cross-Modal Single-Cell Clone Assignment
Authors: Huang, X.; Ye, S.; Silva, A.; Nakhleh, L.
Abstract: Single-cell DNA sequencing (scDNA-seq) and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) enable the inference of copy number clones and transcriptional states in tumor studies. However, these two assays usually profile different cells of the same tumor, requiring computational assignment of unpaired scRNA-seq cells to clones identified by scDNA-seq to link clonal genotypes with transcriptional profiles. This task is challenging because the only connection between the two modalities is a weak, gene-dependent dosage effect, and the absence of clone labels for RNA cells precludes supervised learning of this relationship. Moreover, clonal distributions may differ between the two modalities because the cells are profiled independently, while the inherent clonal imbalance of real tumors can leave minority subclones underrepresented, further compromising assignment accuracy. To address these challenges, we present KLONE, a per-clone $k$-nearest-neighbor ($k$-NN) ensemble that assigns RNA cells directly to copy-number clones based on cross-modal Pearson similarity, without the need for a parametric model or clone labels for RNA cells. To ensure a fair assessment of each clone's compatibility with a given RNA cell, KLONE allocates an identical neighborhood budget to every clone, preventing majority clones from dominating the affinity assessment solely through their greater abundance. We compare KLONE with six existing methods on three colorectal cancer patients, using cells profiled in both modalities as ground truth. KLONE is the most accurate method and recalls minority clones at 100\%. Despite discrepancies in clonal distribution between the two modalities, KLONE recovers the clonal distribution of RNA cells almost perfectly ($\rho = 0.99$).

Title: ASD Neuro Agentic (ANA): An Agentic Framework for Feature Discovery and Cross Site Generalization in Autism fMRI Classification
Authors: Rahimian, K.; Mahmanzar, M.; Bahrayni, R.; Bayat, S.; Higa, L.; Kavousi, K.; Deng, Y.
Abstract: Classifiers of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) from resting state functional MRI rarely generalize across sites, and many reported accuracies are inflated by data leakage.We show that an agentic artificial intelligence framework, ASD Neuro Agentic (ANA), whose language model agents propose features from the literature and researcher input while fixed tools perform every calculation, can search auditably for site independent classifiers while controlling the leakage. In 1,028 participants from 17 ABIDE I centers, ANA tested 71 pipelines and selected a ComBat harmonized ensemble of tangent space connectivity models from six parcellations and 98 public connectivity derivatives. In leave one center out testing, the ensemble reached an area under the curve of 0.814 (95% CI, 0.773 to 0.841), outperforming ASD DiagNet and ASD SAENet. Predictive connectivity was mainly reduced in ASD. Agentic AI offers a systematic and efficient approach to exploring, evaluating, and identifying pipelines as model selection grows complex.

Title: Joint protein-DNA language modeling enables prediction and engineering of DNA recognition specificity
Authors: Xiong, Y.; Ren, J.; Wei, X.; Li, X.; Li, J.; Wei, W.
Abstract: Protein-DNA recognition specificity underlies transcriptional regulation, DNA replication, chromatin remodeling and genome editing. Protein-DNA recognition depends on both interacting sequences, yet language models that learn this cross-molecular dependence explicitly during pretraining remain limited. Here, we developed the Protein-DNA Language Models (PDLMs), interaction-aware language models that jointly represent protein and DNA sequences. PDLMs were built by continued pretraining from ESM2 with masked language modeling on paired protein-DNA sequences. A shared encoder places amino acids and nucleotides in the same molecular context, enabling conditional sequence scoring and transferable pair representations. We further introduced a domain-aware masking strategy that increased masking probability within DNA-binding domains to strengthen learning of interaction-relevant regions. Across downstream tasks, PDLMs improved protein-DNA pair classification relative to independent-encoder baselines and supported prediction of mutation-associated binding changes. Zero-shot scoring recovered known changes in DNA-recognition specificity and prioritized variants with higher editing activity. Learned representations also supported cross-study prediction of base editor activity. After fine-tuning on transcription factor binding data, PDLMs predicted DNA motifs directly from protein sequences. Together, PDLMs provide a framework for interaction-aware biomolecular language modeling, with potential applications in protein engineering and genome editing.

Title: pLM-bVAE: protein language model-enhanced binary representation improves quantum annealing-based protein sequence design
Authors: Ueda, H. H.; Tucs, A.; Tsuda, K.; Umetsu, M.; Saito, Y.
Abstract: Quantum annealing (QA) has been explored as an approach for protein design in vast combinatorial sequence spaces. Applying QA to protein sequence design requires amino acid sequences to be encoded as binary vectors, and optimized vectors to be decoded back into amino acid sequences. Thus, both the quality of binary encoding and sequence reconstruction accuracy are important for effective QA-based optimization. Binary variational autoencoder (bVAE) has been used to map protein sequences to binary representations in QA-based protein sequence design. However, bVAE was originally developed for natural language modeling, and its suitability for proteins has not been systematically evaluated. Here, we present pLM-bVAE, which incorporates protein representations derived from a pretrained protein language model (pLM) into the original bVAE model. In computational experiments on three public protein variant datasets, pLM-bVAE showed higher sequence reconstruction accuracy and binary encoding performance than bVAE. Moreover, we incorporated pLM-bVAE into a QA-based protein sequence design framework. Across all three datasets, pLM-bVAE generated more high-scoring sequences with greater sequence dissimilarity from the training and validation data than bVAE. Our results demonstrate that pLM-bVAE provides an effective binary representation for improving QA-based protein sequence design. Availability The source code used in this manuscript is available at https://github.com/hueda8/pLM-bVAE.

Title: Statistical significance testing for spatial domain detection in spatial transcriptomics
Authors: Wang, H.; Cao, F.; Shen, H.; Liu, Y.; Yan, G.
Abstract: In spatial transcriptomics, domain-detection methods group platform-specific spatial measurement units--cells, bins or multicellular spots--into spatial domains for comparing molecular programs, cellular composition and interactions among tissue regions. However, the number of candidate domains detected in the same tissue can vary with user-specified parameters or model-selection criteria. Whether candidate domains should be merged can be framed as a test of a single-domain null hypothesis, under which each gene has constant mean expression across all spatial units in the combined region. However, testing candidate domains on the same gene-expression data used to detect them may induce post-selection bias and yield anti-conservative p-values, increasing the risk of oversegmentation. To address these challenges, we introduce SigDoTS (statistical Significance testing for Domain deTection in Spatial transcriptomics), a hypothesis-testing framework for spatial domain detection. SigDoTS uses hierarchical testing to determine which candidate domains to retain or merge, with adjustment for family-wise error control. It accounts for gene-gene covariance and spatial dependence and computes p-values by rerunning the upstream domain-detection pipeline on datasets simulated under the fitted single-domain null. In simulations, SigDoTS controlled the type I error rate at the root node under the single-domain null and improved recovery of the true spatial domains when multiple domains were present. In human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, SigDoTS retained superficial and deep Layer 6 domains but merged Layer 3 candidate domains across different initial numbers of candidate domains. In ovarian and colorectal cancers, SigDoTS retained epithelial domains with different gene-expression programs and local immune environments, together with immune, stromal and vascular domains.

Title: Mechanical Fidelity of Fixed-Cell Traction Force Microscopy
Authors: Mortazavi, A.; Jiang, J.; Sabass, B.
Abstract: Cellular traction forces contribute to biological processes including cell migration and tissue morphogenesis. Traction force microscopy (TFM) is widely used to quantify these forces in living cells, but it remains unclear how well measurements after fixation reproduce the live-cell state. Here, we systematically evaluated fixation-induced changes by paired comparison of the same cells before and after fixation using different fixation protocols and substrate stiffnesses. Fixation largely preserved the spatial organization and direction of substrate displacements and reconstructed traction fields, whereas displacement, traction, and strain-energy magnitudes showed fixation-dependent changes. Among the protocols tested, glutaraldehyde (GA) provided the closest agreement with live-cell measurements, retaining up to 99% of displacement and traction magnitudes and strain energy. Paraformaldehyde-based protocols caused larger reductions in these quantities while largely preserving their spatial organization. These results show that fixed-cell TFM, particularly with GA fixation under the conditions tested here, can provide measurements close to the live-cell state and offers a practical approach for combining TFM with post-fixation fluorescence imaging in a multi-well workflow.

Title: Bacterial-Mimetic Membranes Reveal Hopanoid-Associated Domain-Like Lateral Heterogeneity
Authors: Rzycki, M.; Kucharski, M.; Szulc, N.; Drabik, D.
Abstract: Bacterial membranes are increasingly recognized as laterally heterogeneous assemblies whose local organization can regulate transport, stress adaptation, and interactions with membrane-active compounds. However, the physical principles by which bacterial lipid composition generates spatially distinct membrane environments remain poorly understood, partly because experimentally tractable models that reproducibly exhibit lateral segregation and permit quantitative characterization are limited. Here, we show that a multicomponent, hopanoid-containing bacterial-inspired membrane spontaneously self-organizes into laterally distinct physical environments that are consistently resolved in experiments and molecular simulations. Giant unilamellar vesicles prepared from a lipid mixture inspired by lipid classes found in hopanoid-producing bacteria, including Methylorubrum extorquens, exhibit stable micron-scale lateral segregation, which is independently reproduced in compositionally matched coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations. The resulting membrane environments differ in composition, packing, order, mobility, and mechanical properties. Hopanoid-associated domain-like regions are more condensed, more ordered, and less mobile, whereas PE-rich non-domain regions remain more laterally expanded and exhibit faster lipid diffusion. At the global level, the bacterial-inspired membrane displays greater bending rigidity than a fluid phosphatidylcholine reference, while ATR-FTIR measurements independently support increased lipid-chain ordering and denser membrane packing. Together, these findings establish that hopanoid-containing bacterial-inspired membranes can spontaneously generate coexisting physical environments whose distinct local properties collectively determine global membrane behavior. The resulting experimental-computational framework provides a quantitative basis for investigating bacterial-like membrane heterogeneity and how local composition, dynamics, and mechanics govern responses to membrane-targeting perturbations.

Title: Preclinical Evaluation of a Novel BOC-Modified Triazoloacridinone (TRA-01AR) in Combination with 5-Fluorouracil in Colorectal Cancer
Authors: Switalska, M.; Czechowicz, P.; Milczarek, M.; Bartoszewska, S.; Filip-Psurska, B.; Wierzbicka, K.; Psurski, M.; Szczesny, D.; Turlej, E.; Krzyminski, K.; Gawronska, M.; Gebert, M.; Kalinowski, L.; Crossman, D. K.; Baginski, M.; Markuszewski, M.; Collawn, J. F.; Schaefer, L.; Bartoszewski, R.; Wietrzyk, J.
Abstract: 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) remains a cornerstone of colorectal cancer (CRC) therapy, yet its clinical efficacy is limited by resistance, systemic toxicity, and unfavorable pharmacokinetics. Strategies that enhance tumor sensitivity while maintaining tolerability are therefore of considerable interest. Here, we evaluated 5-FU in combination with two triazoloacridinones, C-1305 and a novel BOC-modified derivative, TRA-01AR, using integrated cellular, transcriptomic, bioenergetic, and in vivo approaches. Both compounds induced cytotoxic effects across cancer cell models and produced overlapping but distinct transcriptional responses, primarily affecting DNA replication and cell cycle pathways. Bioenergetic profiling revealed a shift toward oxidative phosphorylation accompanied by reduced glycolysis, indicating modulation of cellular metabolism relevant to chemotherapy response. Interestingly, TRA-01AR exhibited delayed cytotoxicity relative to C-1305, although the underlying mechanism remains to be defined. In vivo, the combination of 5-FU with C-1305 significantly reduced tumor weight in HT-29 xenografts, whereas 5-FU combined with TRA-01AR did not result in a statistically significant reduction compared to 5-FU alone. TRA-01AR was associated with a more favorable systemic profile and increased intratumoral blood flow compared with C-1305. Collectively, these findings indicate that triazoloacridinones modulate transcriptional and metabolic programs relevant to the 5-FU response. While C-1305 demonstrated greater antitumor activity under the tested conditions, TRA-01AR exhibited distinct biological effects, including improved tolerability and vascular modulation. Further studies are required to clarify TRA-01AR's mechanism of action and assess its potential relevance in CRC-specific therapies.

Title: Deep CyTOF immune profiles of ex vivo granulomatous responses to Mycobacterium tuberculosis differ with European and African geographical origin
Authors: Schmidiger, S.; McCaffrey, E. F.; Schmidt, J. M.; Zaragoza-Infante, L.; Ross, A.; Mpina, M.; Tumbo, A.; Mfinanga, E.; Haraka, F.; Hella, J.; Carballido, J. M.; Reither, K.; Arbues, A.; Portevin, D.
Abstract: Genetic and environmental factors influence human immunity and modulate responses to infection. Accounting for immune heterogeneity across human populations is critical to the design of novel vaccines and host-directed interventions that would optimally benefit populations experiencing the highest disease burden. Tuberculosis (TB) burden is unevenly distributed across geographical regions and our understanding of the differential immune response to Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) across human populations remains limited. Here, we sought to evaluate the impact of geographical origin on ex vivo granulomatous responses to Mtbinfection. We found that peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from healthy African donors exhibited greater control of Mtbgrowth ex vivo than those isolated from European individuals. High-dimensional single-cell profiling of the granulomatous responses by cytometry by time-of-flight (CyTOF) revealed divergent profiles based on the specimens' geographical origin. Monocytes from European donors displayed a pro-inflammatory phenotype - correlating with Mtbgrowth -, whereas PBMCs of African individuals were enriched in activated, cytotoxic T cells - correlating with Mtbcontrol. Reduced inflammatory response in African monocytes following various microbial stimulations was confirmed. Taken together, our comprehensive immune profiling indicates that environmental and genetic factors shape a cytotoxic-regulatory response that promotes bacterial control. Against the current "one-treatment-fits-all" approach, our findings support the use of specimens from intervention-relevant settings to inform the targeted design of TB vaccines and host-directed interventions.

Title: Identification and localization of bone marrow ILC2s using Id2/Cxcr6 dual-reporter mice
Authors: Lepetit, C.; Hedde, P.; Jacquemin, G.; Gomez-Perdiguero, E.; Mancini, S. J.; GOLUB, R.
Abstract: Type 2 innate lymphoid cells (ILC2s) are present in the bone marrow, where their identification and spatial localization remain challenging because of their low abundance and the expression of shared markers by other lymphoid populations. Here, we evaluated the use of Id2YFP/+ Cxcr6GFP/+ dual-reporter mice to identify and visualize bone marrow ILC2s. Using spectral flow cytometry, we showed that both ST2- and ST2 ILC2s expressed high levels of ID2, whereas CXCR6 expression differed between these subsets. However, the ID2 expressing compartments also contained NK cells, NKT cells, conventional T cells and ILC progenitors. Surface marker profiling identified CD25 and ICOS as useful markers for enriching ILC2 populations, with ST2 enabling the segregation of the ST2- and ST2 subsets. Single-cell RNA sequencing further characterized the diversity of Id2 and Cxcr6 expressing lymphoid populations and supported the use of CD5 and NKp46 as exclusion markers. Combining these markers with the dual-reporter system, confocal microscopy revealed YFPGFPCD5-NKp46- cells compatible with an ILC2 phenotype, distributed throughout the bone marrow as isolated cells or within multicellular clusters. Complementary flow cytometric analyses demonstrated that ILC2s accounted for more than 90% of a phenotypically related reporter-positive population after exclusion of major T and NK cell populations, providing additional support for the identification of the cells visualized in situ as putative ILC2s. Together, these findings establish a strategy combining dual-reporter mice, flow cytometry, transcriptomic profiling and confocal imaging to investigate the localization and spatial organization of putative bone marrow ILC2s.

Title: IL13 critically contributes to the antitumor activity of polyfunctional CD4+ T cells driven by constitutively active Stat5
Authors: Okoko, O. D.; Kehinde-Ige, M.; Wang, X.; Ye, Y.; Bhasin, A.; Pei, L.; Brandle, C.; Gazi, M. Y.; Ding, Z.-c.; Pacholczyk, R.; Shi, H.; Zhou, G.
Abstract: The presence of polyfunctional T cells capable of concurrently producing multiple cytokines correlates with favorable clinical outcomes in patients with cancer. We previously reported that overexpression of constitutively active Stat5a (CASTAT5) confers polyfunctionality on tumor-specific CD4 T cells, enabling durable antitumor immunity following adoptive cell therapy. However, the mechanisms underlying the enhanced antitumor effects of CASTAT5-modified T cells remain unclear. Here, we identify interleukin-13 (IL13) as a critical effector cytokine contributing to the multifaceted antitumor activity of CASTAT5-conditioned polyfunctional CD4 T cells (C5-CD4). C5-CD4 T cells exhibit a prominent T helper 2 (Th2) cytokine profile, accompanied by extensive epigenomic remodeling at the Th2 cytokine loci, as revealed by Hi-C and histone-modification CUT&Tag assays. Neutralization of IL13 diminished the antitumor efficacy of C5-CD4 T cells. Furthermore, targeted Il13 disruption substantially impaired tumor control and was associated with reduced donor T cell expansion and persistence, diminished systemic cytokine and chemokine responses, and attenuated activation of endogenous tumor-reactive CD8 T cells. Nonetheless, IL13 overexpression alone in donor CD4 T cells failed to fully recapitulate the therapeutic activity of C5-CD4 T cells, indicating that IL13 is a critical contributor but is insufficient to account for the full antitumor activity conferred by CASTAT5. Single-cell RNA sequencing associated donor-derived IL13 with increased representation of tumor-infiltrating myeloid cells and IL13-signaling in monocytes and macrophages exhibiting tissue-repair-associated transcriptional programs. Moreover, Il13 disruption diminished the therapeutic efficacy of CASTAT5-expressing CD19-targeted CAR-T cells in a mouse B-cell lymphoma model. Reanalysis of a human CD19CAR-T infusion-product dataset further revealed an association between IL13 expression and type 2 cytokine signatures linked to prolonged clinical response, suggesting a potential contribution of IL13 to the efficacy of human CD19CAR-T therapy. Together, these findings uncover an unexpected antitumor role for IL13 and establish it as a critical node linking polyfunctional donor T cells with endogenous immune cells to promote sustained tumor immunity.

Title: KAT6 and KAT7 actively maintain mitotic chromatin composition and acetylation to preserve developmental competence
Authors: Laguillo-Diego, A.; Lee, U.; Liu, X.; Lidoski, A.; Kasliwal, K.; del Castillo, U.; Kang, J. J.; Stransky, S.; Kaufman, S.; Katch, B. J.; Giannakakou, P.; Sidoli, S.; Yu, H.; Stadtfeld, M.; Apostolou, E.
Abstract: Mitotic bookmarking enables transmission of regulatory information across cell division, yet how active chromatin states are molecularly preserved during mitosis and how they contribute to postmitotic cell fate decisions remain unresolved. Here, we demonstrate that the acetyltransferases KAT6 and KAT7 remain chromatin-bound and catalytically active throughout mitosis in mouse and human pluripotent stem cells. Acute KAT6/7 depletion disrupts mitotic histone acetylation and the retention of multiple chromatin regulators with minimal effects on chromatin accessibility. Mechanistically, KAT6/7 bookmark both self renewal and developmental gene loci, where they are required for post-mitotic transcriptional reactivation and priming of lineage-specific programs. Consistently, genes impaired during postmitotic reactivation also fail to activate during neuronal differentiation upon continuous KAT6/7 perturbation, compromising the establishment of the neuronal program and identity. Altogether, our findings identify KAT6 and KAT7 as a cooperative mitotic chromatin maintenance system that couples active histone acetylation to preservation of chromatin composition, transcriptional memory, and developmental competence across cell division, extending the bookmarking function beyond transcriptional memory. These findings also provide a new framework for understanding KAT6/7 function in neurodevelopmental disorders and cancer.

Title: The co-evolution of adhesion and F-actin gives rise to hierarchical cellular force generation
Authors: Guo, Y.; Ottolenghi, N.; Amer, M.; He, J.; Bouchbinder, E.; Wolfenson, H.
Abstract: Cells --- the basic units of life --- dynamically adhere to their micro-environment, build their F-actin cytoskeleton, and apply molecular-motor generated contractile forces to it in a remarkably broad range of biological processes and physiological functions, in both health and disease. Yet, how these processes are orchestrated over multiple spatiotemporal scales is not fully understood. Using several experimental approaches and a theoretical framework, we show that adhesion assembly, on-adhesion F-actin accumulation and the contractile force itself all follow the same time evolution over tens of minutes, the cellular force timescale, at well-defined adhesion sites. We also show that the F-actin distribution away from the adhesion site features a multiplicative space-time decomposition. Finally, we show that F-actin retrograde flow --- central in the so-called molecular motor-clutch models --- is markedly faster than force generation rates, that it does not slow down over maturing adhesions and that its density drops at adhesion sites. These findings suggest a hierarchical, multi- scale force generation process that is controlled by slow adhesion recruitment, which is accompanied by rapid, bursty linear actin polymerization. The linear F-actin slowly accumulates with adhesion recruitment to form an extended near-adhesion F-actin network to which molecular motors attach and apply elastic-like contraction.

Title: Sequestration-based Protein Neural Networks Tolerate the Effects of Shared Translational Resources
Authors: He, E.; Britto Bisso, F.; Cuba Samaniego, C.
Abstract: Biochemical neural networks offer a promising framework for implementing advanced computation in living cells, yet how competition for shared cellular resources shapes their behavior remains poorly characterized. In this work, we develop a resource-aware mathematical framework to analyze how competition for ribosomes affects protein neural networks implemented via molecular sequestration in bacterial systems. Focusing on classification tasks, we show that when all mRNA species share identical ribosome-binding affinities, competition induces a uniform rescaling of the network's effective weights, reducing the output magnitude while preserving the geometry of the decision boundary. When these affinities differ, competition introduces curvature in the decision boundary, transforming a linear classifier into a nonlinear one through resource coupling. This curvature is constrained to a well-defined region of the input space whose extent is determined by the degree of variability in the binding affinities, making the effect both predictable and, potentially, exploitable for design. Next, we numerically extend our analysis from a single perceptron to multi-layer architectures with two hidden-layer nodes and show that, for both closed and non-convex decision boundaries, resource competition preserves the boundary geometry in the homogeneous-affinity case, while in the heterogeneous case, curvature distortions from hidden-layer nodes propagate and compose at the output within a bounded uncertainty region. Finally, we incorporate growth-mediated feedback into the framework and show that the structural form of the activation function and decision boundary is preserved. Overall, our results provide a quantitative basis for understanding how translational resource competition shapes the behavior of protein-level molecular classifiers.

Title: Damaged motile cilia undergo phagolysosomal clearance during regeneration
Authors: Ren, M.; Heesom, K.; Melia, C.; Matsuda, S.; Nakano, K.; Mali, G. R.
Abstract: The remodelling and regeneration of motile cilia are widespread yet poorly understood cellular responses to stress. Whether components from damaged cilia are reutilised during regeneration remains unclear. Here, we apply acute, non-lethal stress to the multiciliated eukaryote Tetrahymena thermophila to investigate the fate of damaged motile cilia during regeneration. We find that damaged axonemes accumulate intracellularly as coiled structures, termed c-rings, which are sequestered within phagosome-associated membrane compartments and subsequently associate with acidic compartments for clearance. Imaging, quantitative proteomics and genetic perturbations reveal a phagolysosomal route for processing damaged axonemes, accompanied by recruitment of autophagy-associated machinery. Remarkably, ciliary regeneration proceeds without detectable c-ring accumulation, even when new protein synthesis is inhibited, indicating that reutilisation of internalised axonemal material is not essential for ciliogenesis. Our findings uncover an unexpected mechanism for clearing damaged motile cilia and reveal how ciliary degradation and regeneration can operate as distinct cellular processes.

Title: Harnessing catalytic knowledge to guide enzyme discovery and evolution with AlphaEnzyme
Authors: Liu, Y.; Liu, J.; Shi, Z.; Song, R.; Zhao, Z.; He, B.; Liu, X.; Liu, H.; Chen, J.; Li, K.; Wang, J.; Huang, Y.; Wang, J.; Dang, Y.; Chen, C.-T.; Zheng, S.
Abstract: Retrieving an enzyme for a target reaction provides a starting point for evolution, but predicting how to improve it remains difficult. This requires connecting evolutionary information with the structural and chemical context of catalysis. Here we present AlphaEnzyme, an enzyme foundation model built on a structure-grounded representation of an enzyme paired with its reaction, from which catalytic compatibility, kinetics and mutational response are read out together. On a time-separated benchmark, AlphaEnzyme achieves a top-1 catalyst retrieval success rate of 30.1%, against 17.2% for the strongest baseline. Michaelis constant predictions achieve the highest rank correlations among the compared methods, reaching 0.64 for enzymes sharing at most 40% identity with the kinetic training set. The model also enriches high-fitness TrpB variants at a budget of 16 candidates without target-specific fitness training. In prospective transaminase engineering, several prioritized variants exceed the parent, with the best design yielding a 30.4-fold increase in product signal in a lysate-based assay while retaining (R)-selectivity. Together, AlphaEnzyme provides a common molecular basis for selecting starting enzymes and prioritizing sequence changes for their improvement.

Title: Where single-cell foundation models help: a benchmark of annotation, perturbation and regulatory inference against simple baselines
Authors: Cupaioli, F. A.; Merelli, I.
Abstract: Single-cell foundation models (FMs) are proposed as general tools for cell-type annotation, in silico perturbation and gene-regulatory-network (GRN) inference. To identify where they add value, we benchmarked five FMs (scGPT, Geneformer V1 and V2, Nicheformer, scFoundation), CellOracle, supervised perturbation models including STATE, and task-matched simple baselines on the same data, from K562 Perturb-seq screens and primary cells to healthy-donor and isogenic leukodystrophy brain organoids, a public organoid CRISPR screen and lung cancer biopsies. FMs were most useful when labels had to be transferred across species: from human to mouse lung, Nicheformer reached 0.98 accuracy and Geneformer V2 and scFoundation about 0.90, against 0.68 for the best baseline. Zero-shot in silico perturbations captured the direction of real responses in K562, with up to 75% of perturbations shifted in the expected direction (scFoundation, p < 1e-8), and Geneformer V2 networks recovered patient-level tumour differential expression better than co-expression (fold enrichment 2.9 versus 2.0). Within a species, FM embeddings annotated cells as accurately as principal components. In organoids, predicted knockout effects were largely explained by where the target is expressed, and an expression-matched control test isolated the gene-specific part, 12 to 35% of the effects. Isogenic Canavan and Krabbe organoids and 4H patient organoids, with one library per line and time point, did not yet separate methods from differences between clones and donors, which defines the replication needed for future validation. Fine-tuning changed classification accuracy but not knockout rankings. We release the benchmark, baselines, pipeline checks and the isogenic reference task as the fmaudit package, so that new models can be evaluated on the tasks where FMs already help.

Title: Language-guided domain adaptation improves protein sequence representations for antimicrobial resistance analysis
Authors: Ye, R.; Li, L.; Geng, Z.; Song, S.
Abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR), particularly antibiotic resistance in bacterial pathogens, complicates infectious disease management. Because bacterial resistance is often mediated by protein functions, including antibiotic inactivation and efflux, protein sequence analysis provides a molecular basis for digital AMR surveillance and therapeutic intervention. We developed BacLLM, a language guided protein representation framework that integrates annotation-derived functional knowledge into protein language model representations for AMR analysis in WHO priority bacterial pathogens. Through sequence enhancement, semantic enrichment of UniProt annotations, and cross modal contrastive learning, BacLLM transfers LLM encoded annotation priors into the sequence encoder. Compared with baselines, BacLLM provided more informative representations for resistance-gene identification and mechanism prediction, captured resistance associated mutational signals at single-residue resolution, and preserved taxonomic relationships not reflected by phenotype based clinical groupings.
