Moreover, BacLLM recovered resistance associated functional organization within a TolC-centered protein association network, prioritizing proteins with low sequence identity to TolC but predicted structural similarity to TolC. Extending from AMR characterization to therapeutic prioritization, BacLLM also improved strain-level phage host matching for phage therapy candidate prioritization. Together, these findings establish BacLLM as a protein representation framework supporting AMR surveillance, functional characterization, and therapeutic candidate prioritization.

Title: spearfish: ultrafast Δ-mapping of long reads to redundant transcriptomes
Authors: Abdelgawad, H.; Martayan, I.; MARCHET, C.; Patro, R.
Abstract: In a transcriptome, isoforms share most of their sequence, and gene families add further near-copies. Yet most long-read mappers treat each isoform as a separate target and repeat seeding, chaining and alignment for each. We introduce spearfish, a long-read mapper built for this redundancy. Its delta mapping ({Delta}-mapping) computes each target's alignment-score difference from the best candidate. It skips sequence that all candidates share, which cannot change the difference, and aligns where they differ once per distinct sequence rather than once per target. Seeds come from locally consistent parsing (LCP), so every isoform that contains an exon receives the same seeds in its interior. Collapsing them gives a core graph, a de Bruijn-like graph whose size is bounded by the distinct exonic sequence plus a small term per splice junction, independent of the number of isoforms. Over this graph, spearfish computes the exact colinear chaining score of every candidate transcript, sharing dynamic-programming state among transcripts via a procedure which we prove is equivalent to chaining on each transcript separately. Across RNA-seq experiments, using 32 threads, spearfish maps reads 24-102x faster than minimap2 in under a quarter of the memory, and 2.5-11.5x faster than lr-kallisto's pseudoalignment. On simulated reads it ranks the true transcript first more often than minimap2 on HiFi reads and at least as often on ONT reads. When using spearfish's {Delta}-mapping with oarfish for abundance estimation, the abundance estimates match or improve on those that make use of minimap2's alignments on both simulated reads (with or without primers and poly(A) tails) and on seven SG-NEx runs with spike-ins, and quantification is 4.1-8.8x faster than lr-kallisto in going from reads to abundances.

Title: Peptide Sequence Determines the Efficacy of Single-Dose AAV-Vectorized GLP-1R Agonists in Diet-Induced Obese Mice
Authors: Lee, D.; Bokvist, K.; Nachtrab, G.; Mezo, A.; Brust, T.; Trefts, E.; Brusilovsky, J.; Suk, J.; Luczak, V.; Edwards, L.; Benedetto, B.; Onyia, J.; Woldbye, D.
Abstract: Background: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R) agonists such as semaglutide produce substantial weight loss and glycemic improvement, but their long-term efficacy depends on sustained adherence to chronic dosing. Adeno-associated virus (AAV) gene therapy could, in principle, provide durable GLP-1R agonist (GLP-1RA) exposure from a single administration, but the degree of peptide engineering required for a vectorized GLP-1RA transgene to be efficacious in vivo is unknown. Methods: We generated four self-complementary AAV (scAAV) constructs encoding: native human GLP-1(7-36) (GLP-1), a DPP-IV-resistant Gly8-GLP-1(7-36) variant (Gly8), Exendin-4 (Ex4), or an Exendin-4 human IgG4 Fc fusion protein (Ex4-Fc). All four constructs were validated to secrete functional GLP-1R agonists in vitro using a conditioned-media potency assay. Subsequently, these constructs were packaged into PHP.eB capsids and administered as a single intravenous dose (5x1012 vg/kg) to diet-induced obese (DIO) mice alongside a vehicle control. Body weight, body composition, food intake, fasting plasma insulin, and oral glucose tolerance were assessed over a 3-week period. At the end of the study, tissues were harvested for assessments of plasma/liver lipids, tissue transgene transcript and peptide levels. Results: HEK293 cells transfected with the four AAV constructs all secreted active peptides/proteins as assessed by a cell-based GLP-1R activation assay, although the effective concentration of the GLP-1 constructs in the media spanned nearly four orders of magnitude 72 hours after transfection. In diet-induced obese (DIO) mice, Ex4 and Ex4-Fc vectors, but not GLP-1 or Gly8 vectors, produced significant reductions in body weight of up to 22.6% of starting body weight out to 21 days after a single dose. In addition, reductions in food intake, fat mass, and fasting insulin relative to vehicle were also observed for Ex4 and Ex4-Fc. Furthermore, Ex4-Fc improved oral glucose tolerance while reducing plasma cholesterol and liver triglycerides relative to vehicle. Although transcript levels did not differ appreciably among the four constructs in either brain or liver, measurable peptide product in plasma and brain lysate tracked the rank order of the in vitro supernatant screen, with GLP-1 and Gly8 groups indistinguishable from endogenous background. Conclusions: PHP.eB scAAV Ex4 and Ex4-Fc showed robust efficacy on multiple metabolic endpoints including weight loss and glucose tolerance. In contrast, vectorized GLP-1 and Gly8 showed no in vivo efficacy despite comparable levels of viral transcript in the brain and the liver. Vectorized GLP-1 and Gly8 also performed poorly compared to exendin-4-based constructs in vitro, suggesting that conditioned-media potency screening is a valid early filter for construct selection in vectorized-peptide AAV development. Engineering peptides to improve translation and secretion efficiency, in addition to circulating plasma stability, could further optimize vectorized GLP-1RA therapeutics.

Title: Use of Antibody Structural Information in Disease Prediction Models Reveals Antigen Specific B Cell Receptor Sequences in Bulk Repertoire Data
Authors: Nwogu, O.; Gill, K. K.; Moore, C.; Kroner, J. W.; Chang, W.-C.; Burkle, J.; Stevens, M. L.; Baatyrbek kyzy, A.; Miraldi, E. R.; Biagini, J. M.; Devonshire, A. L.; Kottyan, L.; Schwartz, J. T.; Assa'ad, A. H.; Martin, L. J.; Andorf, S.; Hershey, G. K. K.; Roskin, K. M.
Abstract: Convergent antibodies are highly similar antibodies elicited in multiple individuals in response to the same antigen. Convergent antibodies provide insight into shared immunological responses and show great promise as diagnostic biomarkers. They have typically been identified using methods that consider the amino acid sequence of the third complementarity-determining region (CDR3) of immunoglobulin heavy chain (IgH). In this study, we extend this definition of convergent antibodies to use structural information about the three IgH CDR regions (CDR1-3) and antibody isotype. We measure the performance of both definitions of convergence by their ability to predict disease status from bulk IgH sequencing data for two different disease cohorts: HIV infection and food allergen sensitization. We show that using predicted structural information outperforms prior approaches for the prediction of food sensitization status and performs on par for HIV infection status. Additionally, the use of structural information and antibody isotype enables better model interpretation and more immunological insights. The structurally convergent antibody groups driving HIV prediction accuracy are from known HIV-binding antibodies expressing the appropriate isotype. Thus, the incorporation of structural information can enable the identification of antigen specific antibody groups from bulk IgH sequencing data.

Title: Repurposing clofarabine against enteric pathogens via metabolic starvation
Authors: Deans, N. D.; Naylor, K. L.; Srour, S.; Mallick, B.; Pham, T. K.; Edmunds, G. S.; Sheffield, J. W.; Ansell, O. F.; Edington-Siddon, C. D.; Burt, E. A.; Stafford, G.; Collins, M.; Humphreys, D.
Abstract: Enteropathogenic and enterohaemorrhagic Escherichia coli (EPEC/EHEC) cause severe global diarrhoeal disease, exacerbated by rising antimicrobial resistance. Pathogenesis relies on attaching and effacing lesions, where bacteria generate actin pedestals to adhere, replicate, and destroy intestinal microvilli. To identify novel anti-virulence candidates targeting this process, we conducted a high-throughput phenotypic screen quantifying pedestal formation via high-content fluorescence microscopy. We identified the anticancer nucleotide analogue clofarabine as a potent inhibitor of EPEC growth and pathogenesis. Distinct from its oncology mechanism - inducing DNA chain termination and apoptosis - clofarabine competes with bacterial ATP-dependent processes to impede gene transcription, protein synthesis, and Type III Secretion System (T3SS) function. Remarkably, EPEC counteracts this inhibition by cleaving clofarabine, enabling restored protein synthesis and resumed growth. Furthermore, we report for the first time that clofarabine suppresses protein translation in human monocytes, suggesting an uncharacterised translational impact on mammalian cells. These findings reveal host and bacterial translation as interconnected vulnerabilities to purine antimetabolites, offering a novel strategy to disarm enteric pathogens while uncovering a bacterial enzymatic mechanism for neutralizing host-targeted therapeutics.

Title: Genome-wide interrogation of genetic requirements for root colonization by CRISPRi-seq in Bacillus subtilis
Authors: Minhas, V.; Abidi, W.; Camara-Almiron, J.; Tsai, H.-H. M.; Tendon, V. D.; Synefiaridou, D.; Veening, J.-W.; Geldner, N.
Abstract: Bacillus subtilis is a known plant growth promoting rhizobacterium. Yet, the genetic basis for effective B. subtilis root colonization remains unclear. Here, we applied genome-wide CRISPR interference sequencing (CRISPRi-seq) to systematically identify bacterial genes required for early Arabidopsis thaliana root colonization by the undomesticated B. subtilis strain NCIB3610. Complementary bacterial RNA-seq experiments in the same conditions further revealed a distinct transcriptional state of root-associated cells. Together, we identified 249 B. subtilis genes impacting root colonization. We reveal a critical, biofilm-independent, role of cell envelope remodeling during early root association, specifically wall teichoic acid synthesis and D-alanylation. Moreover, we observed a metabolic shift toward TCA-cycle-driven aerobic growth and utilization of fructose, induction of secondary metabolite biosynthesis, as well as active repression of sporulation, competence and prophage programs. Our work establishes CRISPRi-seq as a powerful tool for dissecting bacterial-plant interactions relevant to sustainable agriculture.

Title: Effect of Lactobacillus postbiotic supplementation on intestinal permeability, nutrient digestibility, and gut microbial and metabolic profiles in aging cats
Authors: Andreu-Sanchez, S.; Tamasi, B.; Boucard, A.-S.; Pagani, E.; van den Berg, M. A.; Klein, B.; Bernstein, D. R.; Hekman, M.; Thomas, D. G.; Fraser, K.; Eckhardt, E.
Abstract: Aging in cats is associated with declining nutrient digestibility and increased intestinal permeability, but evidence supporting microbiome-targeted interventions in older cats remains limited. We investigated whether daily supplementation with the Lactobacillus-derived postbiotic LB fermentate HF (LBHF) affected intestinal permeability, apparent total tract digestibility, gut microbiome composition, and fecal and plasma metabolomic profiles in older cats. Twenty cats aged 7.7-13.8 years were enrolled in a blinded, placebo-controlled crossover trial comprising two 29-day treatment periods separated by a 28-day washout; 18 cats completed both periods. Intestinal permeability was the primary endpoint, while nutrient digestibility, microbiome composition, and metabolomic profiles were secondary endpoints. LBHF did not affect intestinal permeability or absorptive capacity relative to placebo, although intestinal permeability was positively associated with age. Overall nutrient digestibility was higher during LBHF treatment, with the clearest endpoint-specific evidence observed for protein digestibility. LBHF was associated with a non-significant overall increase in Shannon diversity and a reduction in the relative abundance of Streptococcus lutetiensis. The increase in Shannon diversity was significant only in cats receiving placebo followed by LBHF, indicating a treatment-sequence-dependent response. Thirty-three plasma and 29 fecal metabolites showed significantly different changes during LBHF treatment compared with placebo. Plasma metabolites generally showed more positive changes during LBHF treatment, whereas most associated fecal metabolites showed more negative changes. Sequence-stratified microbiome and metabolome responses differed substantially, suggesting possible period, treatment-order, or carryover effects. Overall, LBHF did not improve intestinal permeability but was well tolerated and improved nutrient digestibility, particularly protein digestibility, while producing modest and sequence-dependent microbiome and metabolome responses. These findings suggest that the effects of LBHF in healthy older cats may relate more strongly to digestive efficiency and host metabolic responses than to intestinal permeability.

Title: The staphylococcal type VII secretion system delays inflammatory cell death during macrophage infection
Authors: Allen, R. D.; Farzand, R.; Chandrasekharan, G.; Watkins, K. E.; Agarwal, P.; Unnikrishnan, M.
Abstract: The human pathogen Staphylococcus aureus is a facultatively intracellular bacterium that can replicate and survive within macrophages. While macrophage-mediated immune modulation is pivotal in S. aureus pathogenesis, bacterial manipulation of macrophage pathways remains poorly understood. The specialised type VII secretion system (T7SSb) is an important virulence-associated factor during staphylococcal infection, although, unlike its mycobacterial counterparts, its role in controlling staphylococcal-macrophage interactions remains unclear. Employing high-resolution time-lapse imaging, we demonstrated an induction of pore-induced cellular traps (PITs) during S. aureus infection of macrophages in vitro, with a higher number of PITs forming in macrophages infected with S. aureus lacking EssC ({Delta}essC), a central T7SS transporter. Interestingly, {Delta}essC-infected macrophages displayed increased bacterial escape compared to wild type (WT)-infected cells, implicating a role for T7SS in delaying macrophage cell death. Changes in cell death were accompanied by a reduction in efferocytosis of {Delta}essC-infected cells in vitro. Investigation of cell death signalling markers in WT and {Delta}essC-infected macrophages demonstrated that the T7SS delayed induction of key cell death pathways, necroptosis and pyroptosis, and a dual RNAseq analysis of WT- and {Delta}essC-infected macrophages indicated a T7SS-dependent modulation of bacterial oxidative stress and selected host chemokines. We also demonstrated that T7SS effectors, EsxA and EsxC individually delayed macrophage cell death. Interestingly, {Delta}esxC mutants demonstrated accelerated calcium fluxes, indicating that the T7SS-mediated suppression of cellular calcium signalling may cause the delay in cell death. Furthermore, in a murine skin infection model, we showed that effector and transporter mutants have distinct S. aureus infection outcomes. Our findings suggest for the first time a key role for T7SSb proteins in controlling macrophage cell death, which impacts staphylococcal survival within the host during infection.

Title: The nucleus spatially partitions mechanoprotection and mechanosensing
Authors: Bouzignac, R.; Palandri, A.; Fritsch, L.; Merle, T.; Zine el Aabidine, A.; Mangeat, T.; Gracia, M.; Andrieu, C.; Garcia Idieder, P.; Trullo, A.; Cazales, M.; Marques Prieto, S.; Pimmett, V.; Costes, M.; Rouviere, C.; Lagha, M. L.; Suzanne, M.
Abstract: Mechanical forces shape cell behavior, but how the nucleus integrates its roles as genome protector and mechanosensor remains unresolved. Here, we dissect the spatiotemporal control of transcriptional response to forces during epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT). By combining genome-wide approaches, in vivo nuclear micromanipulation, and quantitative live imaging, we uncover two key properties of nuclear mechanosensing. First, mechanically induced changes in chromatin accessibility and transcription are spatially patterned within the nucleus: genes closest to deformations appear protected, revealing a local shielding mechanism associated with chromatin closure. Second, relocating a gene between chromatin environments is sufficient to alter its mechanosensitivity, challenging the concept of inherently force-sensitive genes. These findings demonstrate unexpected spatial partition of nuclear response to forces.

Title: Promoter-responsiveness to distal regulatory elements is mediated by the promoter-proximal region
Authors: Majchrzycka, B. M.; Huseyin, M.; Aksu, E. D.; Hansen, A. S.; Mundlos, S.; Krebs, A.; Ibrahim, D. M.
Abstract: Gene promoters induce transcription in response to distal enhancers located in large gene regulatory domains. How this long-range regulation specifically activates the target promoter while bypassing other promoters located in the same regulatory domain remains unclear. Here, we find that the promoter-proximal region is critical for cell-type specific promoter responsiveness. Using high-throughput genome-engineering in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESC), we systematically replace the endogenous Sox9 promoter with different libraries of core and extended (i.e. full) promoters and assess their response to long-range regulatory elements in mESCs and neural progenitor cells. We find that only a subset of full promoters is activated by distal neuronal enhancers and that the promoter-proximal region is necessary for this promoter responsiveness. Core promoters alone are insufficient to respond to distal enhancers but modulate the transcriptional output of responsive promoters. Our results suggest that within multipartite regulatory domains, the promoter-proximal region fulfills a facilitator-like function that filters and transmits signal from distal enhancers, ultimately conferring promoter responsiveness to long-range regulatory elements.

Title: Integrating Long-Read Structural Variant Analysis with single-nucleus RNA-seq to Elucidate Gene Expression Effects in Disease
Authors: Kim, K.; Lin, Z.; Simmons, S. K.; Parker, J.; Kearney, M.; Liao, Z.; Haywood, N.; Zhang, J.; Cline, M. P.; Tuncali, I.; Sharma, M.; Serrano, G. E.; Beach, T. G.; Dong, X.; Popic, V.; Scherzer, C. R.; Levin, J. Z.
Abstract: Structural variants (SVs) are a major source of genetic diversity, yet how they impact cell types in complex brain diseases remains largely unexplored, partially due to limitations of short-read sequencing. Here, we addressed this fundamental question in Parkinson's disease (PD). generating long-read whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data for 100 post-mortem brain samples from a PD cohort, constructing a high-confidence catalog of 74,552 SVs. To resolve their functional impact, we integrated single-nucleus RNA-sequencing data from two brain regions from the same samples and focused functional analyses on SVs proximal to genes previously nominated as cis-regulated, potential causal targets of PD-associated GWAS loci. Using expression quantitative trait locus and allele-specific expression analyses, we uncovered SVs significantly associated with expression in specific cell types as well as effects shared across cell types. This study demonstrates the power of uniting long-read WGS with transcriptomics to uncover SVs underlying complex disease architecture with cell type resolution.

Title: Multimodal imaging links molecular identity with nanoscale-resolved 3D cell morphology in opossum cortical cultures
Authors: Ayar, Z.; Pongrac, M.; Mladinic, M.; Ban, J.; Fantner, G. E.
Abstract: In the mammalian central nervous system (CNS), the ability to regenerate after injury drops sharply in the first weeks after birth, but how this change is reflected in cell morphology and organization is still not fully understood. Here we cultivated cortical cell cultures from the gray short-tailed opossum (Monodelphis domestica) and compared cells derived from early postnatal pups (postnatal day 3-6, "Pyoung") with those from older pups (postnatal day 16-18, "Pold"), which differ in their capacity to regenerate after injury. For each culture, we assessed marker-defined cellular composition using fluorescently labeled markers for neurons, glia, and immature/progenitor cells, and characterized their nanoscale-resolved three-dimensional morphology using label-free scanning ion conductance microscopy (SICM). Pyoung cultures exhibited active change in shape over time, contained a higher proportion of immature SOX2 cells, and grew more neurites (TUJ1) into the lesion site after injury. Moreover, Pold cultures showed more stable soma size (e.g., thickness, area, volume), a larger astroglial (SOX9) population early in culture, and a glia-dominated lesion response. These early astroglia included more immature or reactive (vimentin) astrocytes. SICM further revealed cellular bridges across the lesion, ridges left in the substrate by the injury, and aligned neurite outgrowth. Across all measurements, changes in molecular markers were associated with corresponding changes in cell morphology. This multimodal combination of fluorescence labeling and SICM therefore relates marker-defined cellular composition to physical organization across micro- and nanoscale features during and after postnatal in vitro development.

Title: Functional Performance of Electrospun Tissue-Engineered Heart Valve Scaffolds Across Geometries Under Aortic Conditions
Authors: Dillinger, H.; Saberi, A.; Manenti, M.; Gussenhoven, S.; Burgh-Vrees, I. v. d.; Bouten, C.
Abstract: Electrospun, bioresorbable polymer scaffolds are a promising platform for tissue-engineered heart valves (TEHVs) owing to their fibrous microstructure, tunable mechanics and capacity to support host-cell infiltration and remodeling. Recent in-vitro parametric studies of bioprosthetic heart valve (BHV) geometry have used silicone cast valves to link design parameters to hemodynamic performance and leaflet strain, but the functional behavior of electrospun whole-valve TEHV scaffolds across distinct leaflet geometries and clinically relevant aortic conditions remains poorly characterized. Here, we present an end-to-end workflow in which polycaprolactone (PCL) is electrospun directly onto parametrized, 3D-printed mandrels derived from two established analytical leaflet geometry models, yielding 21 whole-valve scaffolds across four geometries without cutting and assembling flat fiber sheets or suturing of flat fiber sheets. Fiber diameter, orientation and pore area were assessed by scanning electron microscopy and found to be consistent across scaffolds and geometries. Two scaffolds of each of four geometries were tested in a pulse duplicator under hypotensive, normotensive and hypertensive aortic conditions. All scaffolds opened and closed physiologically under all conditions, with a mean maximum geometric orifice area (GOA) of 44.5% of the valve area and a mean peak transvalvular pressure gradient of 10mmHg. Leaflet geometry had no apparent systematic effect on flow and pressure waveforms or on GOA. The mean regurgitant fraction was 82%, most likely due to leakage through the porous fiber network rather than incomplete leaflet closure. Electrospun whole-valve scaffolds thus achieve favorable leaflet kinematics at clinically relevant aortic conditions and the presented workflow provides a reproducible, parametric framework for their fabrication and translation toward regenerative heart valve replacement.

Title: A reformulation of the t-test in single-cell transcriptomics dramatically reduces false positives
Authors: Kviman, O.; Ferreira, P. F.; Jun, S.-H.; Toosi, H.; Lagergren, J.
Abstract: The default differential expression tests in single-cell analysis software provide fast and simple approaches that help practitioners annotate cell populations identified through clustering algorithms. Here, we use theoretical arguments and empirical studies to show that these tests suffer from inflated false positive rates that affect the resulting annotations. We introduce LN's t-test, which tests a novel, asymptotically unbiased log-fold change estimator and avoids these false positives, without compromising speed.

Title: Integrated transcriptomic and proteomic analyses identify novel biomarkers of bladder outlet obstruction
Authors: Bigger-Allen, A. A.; Das, B.; Tang, Y.; Costa, K.; Ocampo, G.-L.; Hashemi Gheinani, A.; DiMartino, S.; Kaull, J.; Froehlich, J.; Lee, R. S.; Adam, R.
Abstract: Bladder outlet obstruction leads to pathological remodeling and emergence of lower urinary tract symptoms. Although relief of obstruction is associated with symptomatic improvement, it is not universally successful, reflecting persistent alterations in the bladder. Reliable surrogate biomarkers of obstruction are lacking, particularly early in the disease course before irreversible damage to the bladder may have occurred. In this study, re-analysis of publicly available transcriptomic datasets from diverse rodent models of obstruction identified tissue transcripts including Cthrc1, Grem1, Ltbp2, Acta1 and Msn that were induced in response to injury. Candidate markers were validated experimentally in an independent model of neurogenic obstruction demonstrating time-dependent changes, and a subset (GREM1, LTBP2, ACTA1, MSN) was increased in bladder tissue from pediatric patients with neurogenic bladder. Several candidates including CTHRC1, ACTA1 and MSN were also differentially abundant in independent proteomic datasets from a rat model of partial bladder outlet obstruction. Candidate markers were also attenuated in datasets from rats with either surgical removal of obstruction or treatment with anticholinergic medication or inosine. Integrated analysis of tissue transcriptomics data and tissue and urine proteomics data from a model of neurogenic obstruction revealed modest but statistically significant concordance between markers observed in tissue and urine. These findings identify tissue and urine biomarkers of both non-neurogenic and neurogenic obstruction that may reflect early changes in obstructive uropathy that could be monitored in a non-invasive manner.

Title: Zebrafish lack canonical necroptosis despite retaining functional RIPK3
Authors: Furtado Milao, J.; Ramakrishnan, L.; Yamaguchi, N.
Abstract: Organismal development, homeostasis and immunity are facilitated by distinct forms of regulated cell death (RCD). These include conserved apoptosis and necroptosis, a proposed backup antimicrobial defence that requires RIPK3-mediated activation of MLKL and is predicted to be absent in several species lacking MLKL. Zebrafish studies have identified a RIPK3-dependent regulated necrosis that is distinct from necroptosis and is pathogenic in tuberculosis. Here, we experimentally confirm the bioinformatics-based prediction that zebrafish lack canonical necroptosis because they lack MLKL, despite retaining functional RIPK3. We take advantage of the finding that Caspase-8 promotes apoptosis while restraining necroptosis; its deficiency is embryonic lethal in mice unless RIPK3 or MLKL is also inhibited. In contrast, we found that Caspase-8-deficient zebrafish are viable through adulthood without obvious morphological defects. Inhibition of related caspases did not compromise viability, arguing against functional redundancy. Finally, Ripk3 overexpression failed to induce death in Caspase-8-deficient embryos. Our work highlights the zebrafish as a model for exploring RIPK3 and extrinsic apoptosis biology in disease contexts in the natural absence of canonical necroptotic execution.

Title: ACE-engineered human iPSC-derived neutrophils enhance host defense against multidrug-resistant bacterial infections
Authors: Shibata, T.; Bhat, S. A.; Saito, S.; Dar, T. B.; GC, B.; Bernstein, E. A.; Khan, N.; Sareen, D.; Goodridge, H. S.; Tourtellotte, W. G.; Bernstein, K. E.; Khan, Z.
Abstract: Severe neutropenia predisposes patients to life-threatening infections, while donor-dependent granulocyte transfusions are limited by availability and variable cell quality. Here, we engineered human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) to constitutively or inducibly express angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) and differentiated them into functional ACE-engineered neutrophils (ACE-iNeu). ACE expression enhanced granulocytic maturation, reactive oxygen species generation, inflammatory cytokine production, and antimicrobial signaling. ACE-iNeu exhibited enhanced bactericidal activity against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and multidrug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Following adoptive transfer into neutropenic mice, ACE-iNeu significantly reduced circulating and tissue bacterial burdens. Integrated metabolomic and transcriptomic analyses revealed ACE-associated alterations in adenine nucleotide abundance and developmental and inflammatory pathways. Together, these findings establish ACE engineering as a strategy to enhance the production and antimicrobial function of human iPSC-derived neutrophils and support further preclinical development of engineered granulocyte therapies for severe drug-resistant infections.

Title: Development of a core genome Multilocus Sequence Typing (cgMLST) and Life Identification Number (LIN) code schema for the Burkholderia cepacia complex
Authors: Parfitt, K. M.; Jolley, K. A.; Peeters, C.; Krisna, M. A.; Mahenthiralingam, E.; Maiden, M. C. J.
Abstract: Background The Burkholderia cepacia complex (Bcc) currently comprises over 20 closely related species; however, understanding Bcc population biology is complicated due to the continual advances in taxonomy and diversity driven by extensive horizontal gene transfer (HGT). Whilst there are conventional typing schemes for the Bcc, including Multilocus Sequence Typing (MLST), there remains a gap for fine-scale resolution typing of the species complex. Here, we present a 1,925 loci core genome MLST (cgMLST) and 14-digit Life Identification Number (LIN) barcoding scheme for the Bcc, that is embedded in the PubMLST database (https://PubMLST.org/organisms/burkholderia-cepacia-complex). Methods A dataset of 142 complete Bcc genomes spanning 19 species were downloaded from NCBI to develop the draft cgMLST scheme (Dataset 1). Two pangenome tools (PIRATE and PEPPAN) were then combined to give a consensus core gene list from Dataset 1. The 'core genes' from these outputs were then screened against the PubMLST loci, using a sequence tag scan, to identify their presence and curate new alleles. The core genes were then validated using a larger Bcc dataset (n = 934 genomes; 22 species) on PubMLST, which had been filtered for high-quality ([≤]200 contigs and 100% ribosomal MLST confidence). This refined the core gene list, ensuring a robust and reliable scheme using a threshold of 99% to classify the gene as 'core'. The population structure of the Bcc was subsequently analysed using the validation dataset to identify genetic clusters using ReporTree. Combined with statistical analysis, 14 allelic mismatch thresholds were identified for the LIN codes. Results The Bcc cgMLST scheme consists of 1,925 loci, which have been designated an arbitrary 'BCC' identifier. The cgMLST scheme and 14-threshold LIN code has been implemented in PubMLST and are publicly available for use. The Bcc genomes in the PubMLST database have been assigned cgSTs and LIN codes. Use cases of the LIN codes were validated using three previously published datasets, which spanned both outbreak investigation and phylogenomic lineage structures. Conclusions This stable, hierarchical LIN code nomenclature enhanced the ability to cluster isolates at multiple levels of resolution with examples overlayed on published datasets provided. The LIN code system is also backwards compatible with previous MLST and clonal complex (CC) nomenclature. Overall, the updated typing scheme will facilitate improve global public health through surveillance of the Bcc epidemiology including source tracing and outbreak investigation

Title: Moderately acid-tolerant Nitrospira strains obtained by single-colony isolation on plates
Authors: Zhu, Y.; Peng, Y.; Zheng, Y.; Lin, W.; Luo, J.
Abstract: Nitrospira are difficult to cultivate, and pure cultures are mainly obtained by dilution-to-extinction combined with other methods, a process that usually takes years to over a decade. Here, we isolated three Nitrospira strains from activated sludge and sediment within one year using conventional single-colony isolation. Pure cultures of two strains could grow and reform single colonies within 25-60 days on all three types of plates prepared with agar, agarose, and gellan gum. Phylogenetic and phylogenomic analyses placed them within lineage I and indicated that they represent potential novel species, with the provisional names Nitrospira monocolonialis for strain Z02 and Nitrospira limosa for strains Z47 and Z70. All three strains were moderately acid-tolerant, with a minimum tolerable pH of 5.0; strain Z02 showed the highest acid tolerance, retaining 74% of its activity at pH 5.5. Strain Z02 was also highly adaptable to oxygen concentrations of 1-21%, retaining 78% and 85% of its maximum growth rate at 1% and 21% O2, respectively. Compared with the representative lineage I strain Nitrospira defluvii, all three strains contain superoxide dismutase encoding genes and some unique genes. Comparative transcriptomic analysis suggested that strain Z02 upregulated genes involved in stress responses, cell envelope modification, and putative type IVa pilus systems under acidic condition. Overall, this study provides the first demonstration that Nitrospira can grow on plates prepared with common gelling agents and form single colonies within a short period, and that Nitrospira can also tolerate moderately acid conditions.

Title: An architectural RNA builds a reaction crucible through molecular concentration and activated enzyme selection
Authors: Ueno, T.; Adachi, S.; Yamazaki, T.; Ninomiya, K.; Hirose, T.
Abstract: Architectural RNAs (arcRNAs) scaffold membraneless organelles (MLOs), yet how they organize functional proteins remains unclear. Nuclear stress bodies (nSBs), MLOs scaffolded by HSATIII arcRNAs, incorporate SRSFs during stress. During stress recovery, nSBs function as reaction crucibles that recruit the kinase CLK1 to accelerate SRSF rephosphorylation and normalize stress-induced splicing. Here, we identify the ASAP complex as a recruitment factor that recognizes Ser341-phosphorylated, catalytically activated CLK1. HSATIII-bound SRSFs recruit ASAP, assembling a platform for CLK1 recruitment. Biochemical reconstitution reveals that this platform enhances SRSF phosphorylation by concentrating SRSFs and CLK1 while selectively recruiting activated CLK1, establishing nSB reaction crucibles as molecular concentrators and selectors. The SRSF-ASAP-CLK1 interaction network is conserved between humans and mice, suggesting that primate-specific HSATIII arcRNAs co-opted this pre-existing network to establish reaction-crucible function in nSBs. Our findings reveal how arcRNAs organize functional proteins through quantitative enrichment and qualitative selection to build biochemically active MLOs.

Title: Integrated exome-transcriptome analysis of a schizophrenia case with an exceptionally low polygenic risk score
Authors: Kondratyev, N. V.; Artyuhov, A. S.; Guven, V. A.; Lezheiko, T. V.; Efimova, O. I.; Ulianov, K. A.; Ebrahim, N.; Morozova, A. Y.; Kostyuk, G. P.; Khrameeva, E. E.; Dashinimaev, E. B.; Golimbet, V. E.
Abstract: Schizophrenia liability reflects both common polygenic variation and rarer variants of larger effect. We investigated a post-mortem schizophrenia case (SZ07) with a schizophrenia polygenic risk score below the first percentile among ancestry-matched cases, asking whether individual-level genomic and transcriptomic analyses could help identify potentially novel schizophrenia-relevant variants. We used exome analysis with multiple variant-prediction tools to generate a panel of variants and corresponding candidate genes potentially implicated in the pathological process in SZ07. The prioritised variants were then assessed using RNA sequencing of three cortical regions. Of these, only an IZUMO4 splice-acceptor variant showed direct RNA-level support. Beyond variant-specific analyses, we characterised broader transcriptomic abnormalities in the SZ07 brain. Pathway analysis of gene-level expression deviations implicated innate immune processes, calcium signalling, synaptic biology, and axon remodelling. Notably, compared with conventional single-sample biological pathway analysis, the analysis we used showed only a weak association with neuronal specificity, suggesting their reduced sensitivity to the main axis of variation related to cellular composition in bulk brain tissue gene expression data. Although the candidate genes showed no significant pathway-level convergence, the broader transcriptomic profile revealed coherent biological alterations largely compatible with the documented history of cerebrovascular disease in SZ07. These results demonstrate how the integration of exome and transcriptome data at the individual level enables the formulation and constraint of hypotheses regarding patient-specific genetic features and their molecular consequences, while highlighting important limitations related to tissue composition, comorbidity, and the choice of reference cohort.

Title: Non-coding RNA controls long-range enhancer-promoter interactions
Authors: Sagropoulou, S.; Velychko, T.; Laparra Cuervo, L.; Stitzinger, S.; Nicol, J.; Walshe, J.; Yan, Y.; Ramasamy, S.; tom Dieck, L.; Bahr, F.; Dybkov, O.; Urlaub, H.; Zumer, K.; Lidschreiber, M.; Oudelaar, A. M.
Abstract: Transcription regulation depends on interactions between enhancers and gene promoters, which often occur over large genomic distances. The molecular drivers of long-range enhancer-promoter interactions remain poorly understood. Enhancers themselves are known to be transcribed into non-coding RNAs, but the function of these transcripts is unclear. Here, we use acute genetic and chemical perturbations of transcription elongation and termination to study the role of non-coding RNA in enhancer-promoter interactions. By integrating high-resolution 3D genome mapping, transcriptomics, proteomics, biochemistry and live-cell super-resolution imaging in these perturbation contexts, we demonstrate that a strong increase in RNA molecules at enhancers disrupts their long-range interactions with gene promoters, whereas decreased RNA levels lead to stabilization of these interactions. Using separation-of-function perturbations, we show that this regulatory function of RNA is independent from the process of transcription and the proteins recruited to initiate transcription. Functionally, we show that RNA-mediated disruption of enhancer-promoter interactions is associated with reduced transcription of target genes, indicating a regulatory feedback mechanism. Together, our results uncover an additional regulatory principle of enhancer-promoter interactions mediated by non-coding RNA.

Title: Investigating the causal and consequential role of the nuclear encoded mitochondrial genome in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis
Authors: Ali, A. T.; Al Kheifat, A.; Al-Chalabi, A.; Hodgkinson, A.; Iacoangeli, A.
Abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction is implicated in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), but which mitochondrial pathways are involved, and whether their involvement is a cause or a consequence of disease remains unclear. We investigated whether nuclear-encoded mitochondrial gene (NEMG) pathways are enriched for ALS genetic risk, which are dysregulated in ALS tissue, whether pathway activity defines patient subgroups that differ in survival, and whether co-expression between the nuclear and mitochondrial genomes is altered. We tested MitoCarta3.0 pathways for enrichment of ALS genetic risk using MAGMA and the largest European ALS GWAS to date (27,205 cases and 110,881 controls), using hierarchical testing across pathway tiers, and annotated the direction of gene-level effects using published TWAS and SMR results. In >1,500 bulk RNA-seq samples from post-mortem motor cortex and spinal cord (KCL Brain Bank, NYGC ALS Consortium) and iPSC-derived motor neurones (Answer ALS), we performed cell type adjusted gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA), gene set variation analysis (GSVA)-based clustering with exploratory survival analysis, and nuclear-mitochondrial co-expression analysis. Of seven broad mitochondrial categories, only the mitochondrial central dogma was enriched for ALS risk after correction (Padj = 0.044). Hierarchical testing within this pathway localised the signal to translation (Padj = 0.008) and the mitoribosome (Padj = 0.014). Genetically predicted expression pointed in opposite directions for different mitoribosomal genes (lower MRPS33 and higher MRPL28 expression with increased risk), and did not agree in direction with differential expression in ALS tissue more often than expected by chance. A nominal enrichment in ROS and glutathione metabolism was largely attributable to SOD1. In tissue, mitochondrial genes were broadly more highly expressed in ALS motor cortex in both cohorts, largely as a global shift across mitochondrial genes. OXPHOS subunits and the mitoribosome were enriched beyond this shift in ALS Consortium motor cortex (both PFDR = 0.027), as were OXPHOS subunits in iPSC-derived motor neurones (PFDR = 2.4 x 10-), whereas spinal cord showed no genome-wide enrichment. GSVA based clusters were associated with diagnosis in motor cortex, and nominally with survival in lumbar spinal cord (adjusted HR 0.69, Punadj = 0.013), where cluster structure was weakest. No individual pathway was associated with survival after correction in adjusted models. In all four post-mortem tissues, nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes were more negatively co-expressed with mtDNA-encoded genes in ALS than in controls, most strongly in lumbar spinal cord, whereas iPSC-derived motor neurones showed the opposite pattern. In conclusion, inherited ALS risk shows a modest enrichment centred on mitochondrial translation, with gene specific rather than uniform directions of effect. The same pathway, alongside OXPHOS, is more highly expressed in end-stage ALS motor cortex, which may reflect a response to disease, residual differences in cell composition, or both. At the gene level, genetically predicted and observed expression changes did not agree in direction, so whether inherited risk and these tissue changes are linked remains unresolved.

Title: RNA Small-Molecule Binding-Site Prediction by Integrating RNA Language Models and Structural Geometry
Authors: Sharma, N.; Mitra, P.
Abstract: RNAs are emerging as promising therapeutic targets, and small-molecule binding can modulate their structure and function, creating opportunities for therapeutic development. Accurate identification of RNA small-molecule binding sites is therefore important for understanding RNA-ligand interactions and facilitating RNA-targeted drug discovery. However, the structural complexity of RNA and the limited availability of experimentally characterized RNA-ligand complexes pose challenges for computational binding-site prediction. In this study, we propose RSMBind, a graph attention-based deep learning framework for nucleotide-level prediction of RNA-small molecule binding sites. The model integrates geometric descriptors of the local three-dimensional environment with pretrained RNA language model embeddings to capture complementary structural and sequence information. We investigate three pretrained RNA language models RNA-BERT, ERNIE-RNA and RNA-FM and assess the contributions of sequence representations and geometric features through feature-level ablation experiments. The model is developed using the TR60 and HARIBOSS datasets and evaluated on four independent benchmark datasets: RB9, TE18, TL12 and JL10. RSMBind achieves the highest MCC among the compared methods on three of the four benchmarks, with relative improvements of 17.1% on RB9, 7.2% on TL12 and 16.0% on JL10 over the best previously reported results, while achieving competitive performance on TE18. Furthermore, RSMBind retains predictive capability when using only pretrained RNA language model embeddings, highlighting their potential utility when explicit tertiary structural features are unavailable. Structural analysis indicates differences in prediction performance across RNA structural regions, with loop-associated binding sites generally being captured more effectively than those embedded within stem regions. Additionally, 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations of selected RNA-ligand complexes provide insights into the relationship between predicted binding probabilities and dynamic ligand proximity, further highlighting the role of conformational dynamics in evaluating structure-based predictions. The source code is available at [ https://github.com/sharma-nandita/RSMBind].

Title: scDeepSim: Deep Generative Simulation for Controlled Benchmarking of Single-Cell Methods
Authors: Ma, L.; Li, J. J.; Sankaran, K.
Abstract: Benchmarking single-cell computational methods requires both realistic data and reliable ground truth. However, annotating real datasets is costly and, even when available, may not fully represent the diverse settings where methods are used. Simulators address this gap by generating synthetic data that has fully specified ground truth and whose structure can be tailored to challenge competing methods. Existing single-cell simulators can broadly be divided into statistical and deep generative classes. Statistical simulators offer interpretable parameters for controlling simulated data, but their modeling assumptions may not accurately represent real data. Deep generative models can learn complex expression patterns, but it remains unclear how to transparently control individual biological or technical factors without introducing unintended effects. We introduce scDeepSim, a simulator that combines a structured variational autoencoder with latent diffusion to generate synthetic single-cell expression profiles. It allows users to intervene on selected biological or technical factors at user-specified strengths, producing realistic datasets with benchmark ground truth. We demonstrate this capability by benchmarking batch correction and trajectory inference methods, showing how batch-effect strength affects batch mixing and cell-type preservation, and how trajectory geometry and noise affect pseudotime recovery. scDeepSim therefore enables researchers to vary selected biological and technical factors in realistic simulated data and assess how these changes affect the performance of single-cell analysis methods, helping understand when such methods may be appropriately applied. Code for the scDeepSim simulator and experiments is available at https://github.com/LangtianM/scDeepSim.

Title: Leveraging state-of-the-art AI structure predictors to generate atomic resolution ensembles of intrinsically disordered proteins
Authors: Schnapka, V.; Portal, N.; Bonomi, M.
Abstract: Intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) are central to many biological processes, but their function depends on dynamic conformational ensembles rather than a single structure. Despite the impact of artificial intelligence on protein structure prediction, determining these ensembles at atomistic resolution remains challenging. Recently, we introduced bAIes, a framework that leverages the structural information encoded in AlphaFold2 distograms to generate conformational ensembles of IDPs at atomistic resolution. Here, we extend this framework to six state-of-the-art structure prediction tools (AlphaFold2, AlphaFold3, Boltz-1, Boltz-2, ESMFold, and ESMFold2) and systematically compare the structural information encoded in their predicted inter-residue distance distributions. Despite differences between predictors, we show that bAIes generates ensembles with comparable accuracy against experimental NMR and SAXS data, and competitive performance relative to state-of-the-art all-atom simulations and alternative IDP ensemble generation methods. These results demonstrate that bAIes is robust to the choice of structure predictor and that the distance distributions generated by different deep learning architectures contain valuable information about the conformational preferences of disordered proteins. More broadly, our work highlights the potential of combining AI-derived structural information with physics-based modeling to generate atomistic ensembles of intrinsically disordered proteins and regions.

Title: Structural relationships between the SLC12 cotransporter C-terminal domain, universal stress proteins and adenylating enzymes
Authors: Rosta, E.; Dürr, K. L.
Abstract: Several SLC12 cotransporters bind ATP in a cytoplasmic C-terminal domain (CTD). We analysed 16,192 CTD-containing SLC12 sequences and compared 42,845 representative structures to examine the relationship between this nucleotide site, universal stress proteins (USPs) and adenylating enzymes. In phosphorylated NKCC1, D891 and D927 lie near the ATP phosphate chain, while R801 and K889 form a basic phosphate-binding clamp. NKCC1 retains this arrangement, whereas KCC paralogs replace or lose several corresponding groups. In structural comparisons with USP and adenylating-enzyme references, both CTD lobes score between universal stress proteins and EC-annotated domains, and the two lobes form separate lineages that include bacterial transporters. Lobe-specific and nucleotide-frame comparisons place ATP in the corresponding structural region used for -phosphate chemistry by catalytic members of this fold. Published work on UspG provides a precedent for protein-bound AMP in a natural USP. In the examined SLC12 structures and USP models, candidate protein hydroxyls lack an in-line geometry for attack at ATP P. Protein adenylation would require a change in protein or nucleotide geometry, or a different acceptor. These results define a structural basis for testing conditional protein adenylation at SLC12 nucleotide sites. The required evidence is a covalent protein-AMP adduct, identification of its acceptor and measurement of the expected pyrophosphate coproduct, with soluble nucleotide analysis to distinguish accompanying ATP reactions.

Title: Mechanical and chemical macrophage activation differ by arm, not by amplitude
Authors: Zhong, C.; Chen, W.; Zeng, T.; Zhang, S.; zhu, J.; Cong, Z.
Abstract: Mechanical cues are widely reported to polarize macrophages toward an M1-like state, but the claim rests on nuclear factor kappa B/activator protein 1 (NF-{kappa}B/AP-1) effector markers read without a common scale, and the literature does not agree on the sign of the stiffness effect. We asked a quantitative question instead: by what fraction of the chemical M1 response does mechanical perturbation move the interferon-stimulated gene factor 3 (ISGF3)-dependent interferon-stimulated gene module? Scoring ten independent studies of substrate stiffness and applied force against lipopolysaccharide (LPS) + interferon-gamma (IFN-{gamma}) anchors, processed through an identical pipeline, we find a pooled shift of -0.9% of the chemical response (95% confidence interval -6.2% to +4.5%), equivalent to zero at a {+/-}10% margin (p = 0.0019) with a minimum detectable effect of 8.8%. The result is unchanged across three independent ISG definitions. Nor is it a sensitivity failure: the most transcriptionally responsive mechanical contrast rewires thousands of genes while leaving the module inside a size-matched random distribution. Extending to ten further mechanical modalities shows mechanics is not inert toward these genes; shifts run in both directions, but no contrast supported by within-study inference exceeds 15% of the chemical anchor. Rescoring the same contrasts against an NF-{kappa}B effector module anchored on human LPS kinetics separates the two arms: across 21 modality contrasts the effector arm sits 17.7 percentage points above the interferon arm (paired p = 0.032), and in the four designs whose permutation space can reach p < 0.05 the separation is 34 points. Compression moves the effector arm +36% of the LPS anchor (p = 0.002) and the interferon arm -9% (p = 0.004). The separation is absent under static stiffness, where neither arm moves, and its sign is not fixed. A three-arm in-vivo magnetomechanical dataset assigns the effect to the rotating field rather than the internalized particle, raising the effector arm while lowering the interferon arm. Mechanically induced "M1-like" states are not the chemical M1 program rescaled. Where mechanical loading registers at all, it moves the effector arm and not the interferon arm: interferon-stimulated genes are the wrong readout for mechanical perturbation of macrophages.

Title: Longitudinal CCR2 PET Imaging Tracks Early Inflammatory Monocyte and Macrophage Infiltration in Experimental Arthritis
Authors: Menendez Montes, M. I.; Venkatesan, R.; Lenz, K.; Luehmann, H.; Heo, G. S.; Springer, L.; Yan, H.; Sultan, D.; Tao, J.; Gao, V.; Liu, Y.; Pham, C.; Guilak, F.
Abstract: Objective. Recruitment of C-C motif chemokine receptor 2 (CCR2+) inflammatory monocytes and macrophages represent an early event in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) pathogenesis that cannot be tracked noninvasively with existing imaging modalities. We evaluated longitudinal Ga-DOTA-ECL1i positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) to track and quantify CCR2 cell recruitment in experimental inflammatory arthritis. Methods. Longitudinal Ga-DOTA-ECL1i PET/CT imaging was performed in K/BXN serum transfer arthritis (STA) mice. Imaging findings were validated using biodistribution, autoradiography, histopathology, immunofluorescence, microCT, cytokine profiling, clinical assessment, and pain-related behavioral testing. Results. Joint Ga-DOTA-ECL1i uptake increased during the acute arthritis and declined with disease resolution. Increased tracer signal localized to inflamed joints, coinciding with CCR2 monocyte and macrophage infiltration, synovial inflammation, cartilage damage, local CCL2 elevation, and mechanical allodynia. PET uptake correlated with ankle swelling, clinical disease severity, pain, and paw CCL2 levels, with peak tracer signal preceding progressive structural bone remodeling. Conclusion. Longitudinal Ga-DOTA-ECL1i PET/CT enables noninvasive visualization and quantification of early CCR2 monocyte and macrophage recruitment, establishing CCR2 PET imaging as a mechanism-based molecular platform for early detection, risk stratification, and therapeutic monitoring in inflammatory arthritis.

Title: A proteomics screen of HIV-1 ASP interactors reveals multifaceted effects on host cell homeostasis
Authors: Iqbal, M. S.; Lee, T.-H.; Li, C. L.; Wang, Y.; Ji, X.; Li, R.; Liu, X.; Caico, I.; Oberdoerffer, P.; Romerio, F.
Abstract: Nearly four decades after the identification of the HIV-1 antisense gene asp, the function of its protein product remains unclear. Evidence of ASP expression in vivo and the high degree of conservation of the asp gene among pandemic HIV-1 strains suggest a beneficial role for the virus. Using a mass spectrometry (MS)-based proteomics screen for ASP interactors, we identified nuclear, cytosolic, and mitochondrial host factors, congruent with variable sub-cellular ASP localization. A majority of the host factors identified in the MS screen are involved in pathways essential for host cell homeostasis, including DNA damage repair, intracellular protein transport, mitochondrial function and protein translation. Validating the biological relevance of these findings, we demonstrate that ASP shuttles to the nucleus to promote DNA damage repair and cell viability in response to genotoxic stress. We also finds that ASP promotes translation of mitochondrially encoded host proteins involved in cellular respiration and contributes to maintain mitochondrial membrane potential. Together, these studies identify ASP as a modulator of two major pathways of cellular homeostasis in infected cells, which has direct implications for HIV-1 persistence, spread, and the long-term survival of the viral reservoir.

Title: Fast Pangenome Matching Statistics in Compressed Space with Move Structures
Authors: Brown, N. K.; Sanaullah, A.; Shakya, P.; Zhang, S.; Langmead, B.
Abstract: Matching statistics and supermaximal exact matches (SMEMs) are key inputs for sequence homology search and classification. Methods such as MONI, PHONI, and ropebwt3 compute these statistics using compressed pangenome indexes, but are substantially slower than methods that compute approximations of matching statistics, such as pseudo-matching lengths (PMLs). PMLs can be computed quickly in a single pass, but SMEM computation can require overlapping forward or backward passes over the query. We present ms2, a suite of algorithms that use "move structures" to compute matching statistics and SMEMs efficiently in compressed space. Our four algorithms compose move structures for the LF, {Psi}, {varphi}, and {varphi}-1 permutations with additional longest common prefix (LCP) array summaries and samples. The algorithms offer different tradeoffs among speed, index size, and support for reporting SMEM offsets. They inherit the move structure's fast, constant-time operations and achieve high throughput by leveraging the move structure's locality of reference. Thanks to recent advances, move structures can be constructed in optimal time and compressed space, including the LCP information needed for "match recovery" during SMEM computation. On 100 haplotypes of human chromosome 22, ms2's fastest algorithm computes matching statistics 35 to 48 times as fast as PHONI's online approach, while using an index of similar size. On the 472-haplotype HPRC2 pangenome and human reads, three ms2 modes achieve speedups of at least 22, 19, and 15 times over ropebwt3, whose index is about 15% the size of ms2's fastest mode. When additionally reporting SMEMs and their offsets, ms2 achieves speedups of 25 to 34 times over ropebwt3. Together, these advances enable online computation of matching statistics and SMEMs at a throughput that supports real-time processing of approximately 21 PromethION nanopore flow cells on a single thread. The ms2 software is open source and available at https://github.com/langmead-lab/ms2. It builds on the open-source TeraTools suite (https://github.com/ucfcbb/TeraTools) and Orbit library (https://github.com/drnatebrown/orbit). Experimental scripts and other details are described in: https://github.com/langmead-lab/ms2-experiments.

Title: SubCellSeg: A generalist model for subcellular structure segmentation in 3D fluorescence microscopy
Authors: Mishra, S.; Samudre, A.; Khan, A.; Hookway, C.; Borensztejn, A.; Thirstrup, D.; Chen, J.; Rafelski, S.; Viana, M. P.
Abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) segmentation of subcellular structures from fluorescence microscopy images is the foundation of many analyses in quantitative cell biology. The prevailing approach addresses 3D segmentation one structure at a time, with a separate model trained for each structure type. By developing SubCellSeg, we demonstrate that a single model, trained jointly across a diverse range of structures, substantially and consistently outperforms structure-specific specialist models. SubCellSeg is a 3D segmentation model trained on expert-curated fluorescence images and their computationally generated reference masks, of 13 morphologically distinct subcellular structures in human induced pluripotent stem (hiPS) cell lines from the Allen Cell Collection, spanning compact puncta, planar junctions, reticular networks, and tubular structures. Without any structure-specific input, SubCellSeg achieves a mean Dice score of 0.909 across the 13 structures and outperforms each of the 13 specialist models on the structure it was trained for (specialist mean Dice 0.773). SubCellSeg also achieves zero-shot generalization, segmenting subcellular structures with morphologies not represented in the training data. This generalization extends to images acquired on different microscopes and with different imaging configurations, to cells under drug perturbation, and to a morphologically distinct cell type, hiPS cell-derived cardiomyocytes. Where zero-shot results are insufficient for a specific application, SubCellSeg can be fine-tuned: starting from its pretrained weights, 10% of the labeled images (16 images) gave better results than training a new model from scratch on all of them. SubCellSeg is distributed through the napari plugin allencell-segmenter-ml[1] with pretrained checkpoints, so it can be run on new data without any training; the training and evaluation code is available at https://github.com/AllenCell/SubCellSeg.

Title: The Confessions of a Protein Language Model: Steering, Activations, and What Predicted Confidence Cannot Certify
Authors: Shah, P.; Panchali, R.; Mody, P.; Sanghvi, M.; Narvekar, M.; Karani, R.
Abstract: Protein generate-and-screen pipelines use interventions and readouts to select candidates, but rarely test whether these track their intended targets. We audit published repetition steering, ESMFold confidence, and an activation readout. Steering preserves confidence at its operating point, but a fitted cliff follows at alpha_50 = 1.240x (sweep's own control: 64.0%). Direction matters at moderate matched-norm push, but not at saturation. Unsteered generator activations predict the confidence gate (ROC-AUC 0.786 +/- 0.004), supporting cost-aware, model-specific triage. We also replicate established length sensitivity, through which shortening can manufacture false nulls. Yet on composition- and length-matched design--scramble pairs, no balanced-accuracy interval excludes chance for experimental stability. Predicting the gate does not establish foldability. We should test what a readout measures before using it to select. Code and data: https://github.com/paninishah/plm-steering-audit

Title: REVEAL: RNA Ensemble Validation and Exploration with AI-guided Landscapes
Authors: Bhakat, S.; Vats, S.
Abstract: Capturing the sparsely populated but functionally important, excited states of RNA remains a central challenge for molecular simulation, because the underlying transitions are rare events that unbiased molecular dynamics cannot reach from a single starting structure. Here we introduce REVEAL (RNA Ensemble Validation and Exploration with AI-guided Landscapes), a workflow that couples generative secondary structure sampling, secondary structure conditioned tertiary structure prediction with trRosettaRNA2, unbiased molecular dynamics and Markov state modeling. Using only the sequence of the engineered HIV-1 TAR mutant, in which the excited state ES2 is the dominant conformation, we show that REVEAL captures the reversible ES2 to GS register shift from 6.8 s of aggregate unbiased sampling across 34 seeds, recovering both basins, the intermediate states, and correctly identifies ES2 as the dominant state, consistent with the design of the construct. In contrast, molecular dynamics seeded from the ES2-dominant HIV-1 TAR mutant NMR ensemble remains trapped in ES2 despite substantially longer aggregate simulation time, and sequence-only ensemble predictors (AlphaFold3, Boltz-2, ESMFold2, OpenFold3 and Protenix-v2) place every structure near the ground state and invert the experimentally observed population ordering. The information content of the seed ensemble, rather than the total simulation time, determines whether the transition is sampled. We further introduce ''population-weighted consensus score'' (PWCS) that ranks conformers by how representative they are of the equilibrium ensemble directly from the simulation data, without experimental restraints and independent of the choice of collective variables. PWCS identifies the dominant state even when low-dimensional representations fail to separate the states. Built entirely from open-source tools, REVEAL provides a transparent and extensible route to RNA conformational ensembles beyond the single-structure paradigm.

Title: Inferring chromatin looping interactions from microscopy-based measurements: opportunities and pitfalls
Authors: Jusuf, J. M.; Hansen, A. S.; Zechner, C.
Abstract: Chromatin looping plays essential roles in several nuclear processes and live-cell microscopy has become a key method for studying how chromatin loops behave in time. Extracting dynamical parameters including looping probability, lifetime, and search time from live-imaging data requires inferring looping events from noisy 3D distance trajectories. By analyzing polymer simulation data with known ground truth, we show that with realistic localization precision, the common method of simple thresholding on 3D distance measurements can result in severe misestimation of looping probability, lifetime, and search time. We use simple statistical considerations to show that inference from simple thresholding becomes infeasible when localization error is comparable to the size of the interaction to be studied. Finally, we demonstrate how noise-aware methods can be used to estimate looping parameters more accurately in these regimes.

Title: Theory of large-bead AFM compression of pressurized rod-shaped bacteria
Authors: Albarran Arriagada, O. E.; Garces Perez, R. C.; Po, G.; Schmidt, C. F.; Eldredge, J. D.
Abstract: Motivated by our atomic force microscopy (AFM) experiments measuring turgor pressure in living bacteria, we develop a theoretical description of pressurized spherocylindrical cells compressed by spherical probes whose radius greatly exceeds the cell radius. In this global-loading regime, the mechanical response is governed primarily by cell geometry and turgor pressure, while the elastic properties of the cell envelope enter as higher-order corrections. The strong confinement imposed by the probe drives water efflux from the cytoplasm, thereby increasing the turgor pressure. We present a theoretical framework for determining bacterial turgor pressure from AFM force--displacement curves, accounting for cell geometry and probe dimensions. Combining numerical simulations with analytical theory, we show that the mechanical response can be approximated in terms of cylindrical and hemispherical contributions. The leading-order force--displacement dependency is captured by an analytical description derived in the large-aspect-ratio limit, where the mechanics reduce to a tension-dominated cross-sectional problem. Finite cell aspect ratio and probe curvature are incorporated through geometric renormalizations. The resulting framework provides a quantitative basis for extracting bacterial turgor pressure from AFM measurements while simultaneously predicting cell deformation geometry.

Title: HIV broadly neutralizing antibody precursor maturation induced by mRNA vaccination in nonhuman primates
Authors: Phung, I.; Freeman, B. L.; Liguori, A.; Seymour, A.; Xie, Z.; Phulera, S.; Kalyuzhniy, O.; Madden, P. J.; Marina-Zarate, E.; Willis, J. R.; Cottrell, C. A.; Ma, K. M.; Baboo, S.; Flynn, C. T.; Kifude, C.; Lu, D.; Phelps, N.; Goodwin, D.; Adachi, Y.; Tingle, R.; Georgeson, E.; Tran, J.; Kalyuzhniy, A.; Hu, X.; Lewis, V. R.; Ngo, J. T.; Liu, X.; Diedrich, J. K.; Nair, U.; Himansu, S.; Schiffner, T.; Lusso, P.; Paulson, J. C.; Yates, J. R.; Carnathan, D. G.; Burton, D. R.; Irvine, D. J.; Silvestri, G.; Ward, A. B.; Ozorowski, G.; Batista, F. D.; Ramezani-Rad, P.; Steichen, J. M.; Crotty, S.; Schi
Abstract: The induction of broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) is a principal goal of prophylactic HIV vaccines. For many bnAbs, priming ultrarare precursors from the naive B cell repertoire is the first major immunological hurdle. Previous studies have shown that the germline-targeting (GT) priming immunogen N332-GT5 delivered as adjuvanted protein to non-human primates (NHPs) activates bnAb precursor B cells for the human bnAb BG18 targeting the V3-glycan supersite on the HIV envelope (Env) glycoprotein. Here, we engineered N332-GT6 to improve binding affinity to diverse BG18-class precursor naive B cells by 9-fold. mRNA-LNP vaccines expressing N332-GT5 or N332-GT6 as membrane-bound (gp151) trimers were evaluated for their ability to prime BG18-class precursor B cells in NHPs across three related studies. Although N332-GT5 gp151 mRNA-LNP priming induced BG18-class precursor B cells in most animals after two vaccinations, the higher-affinity N332-GT6 gp151 induced responses more consistently after only one immunization. Sequential vaccination with two heterologous mRNA-LNP booster immunizations drove affinity maturation and induced BG18-class memory B cells capable of binding wildtype HIV Env. Together, these findings demonstrate that mRNA immunization can achieve GT priming, boosting, and early maturation of ultrarare bnAb-class B cells in NHPs.

Title: Herbivore and carnivore microbial signatures indicate diet and health variation in human gut microbiota
Authors: Miura, H.; Takagi, T.; Ujihara, D.; Konno, A.; Oda, M.; Ishikawa, S.; Ikeda, H.; Nagaoka, K.; Kitae, H.; Matoba, S.; Tsukahara, T.; Naito, Y.; Inoue, R.
Abstract: Diet is a key factor shaping gut microbiota in mammals, with herbivores and carnivores harboring distinct microbial communities. However, despite humans being highly omnivorous, it remains unclear whether their gut microbiota more closely resembles that of herbivores or carnivores or how individual-level variations along this spectrum are associated with human health status. We compared gut microbiota profiles of 858 samples from 109 mammalian species and constructed a Herbivore-Carnivore (HC) index based on bacterial groups characteristic of each diet. The HC-index positioned humans between herbivores and carnivores and showed that traditional hunter-gatherers and nonhuman apes retained herbivore-leaning profiles, whereas urbanized humans exhibited a shift toward a carnivore-leaning state. By applying the HC-index to >72,000 participants across multiple cohorts worldwide, we found that elevated HC-index values were associated with plant-based and fiber-rich diets, greater microbial diversity, enhanced potential to degrade plant-derived carbohydrates, favorable clinical measures, and lower prevalence of self-reported disease. We demonstrated that the HC balance of gut microbiota captures a conserved diet-related gradient across mammals and provides an interpretable framework linking human diet, microbial function, and health.

Title: Saturation barcoding of ribosomal DNA resolves the nucleolar organizer regions of the human genome
Authors: Zhao, S.; Wallentin, J.; Potapova, T.; Zheng, S.; Liu, X.; Daza, R. M.; Gerton, J. L.; Shendure, J.; Li, X.
Abstract: The nucleolus is the hub for ribosome biogenesis in eukaryotic cells. It is assembled on nucleolar organizer regions (NORs), tandem arrays of ribosomal DNA (rDNA) units. In humans, each rDNA unit is ~45 kb and encodes the 47S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) precursor. Hundreds of rDNA units are present per germline genome, spread across 10 NORs positioned on the short arms of the five acrocentric chromosomes. However, their precise count and structure are unknown. In fact, twenty-five years after the first draft of the human genome, NORs are the only regions of the human genome that remain incompletely resolved, represented in telomere-to-telomere (T2T) reference genomes as gaps or modeled sequences rather than bona fide assemblies. Here we use prime editing to insert degenerate 6-bp DNA barcodes to 99% of taggable rDNA units in a clonal derivative of the leukemia-derived K562 cell line. Following ultra-long-read sequencing, these barcodes serve as molecular identifiers that guide the end-to-end assembly of all 18 NORs of K562s pseudotriploid genome. The assembly yields: (i) a precise rDNA copy number for each NOR (range 5-43; total 290); (ii) the cis- and trans- architecture of intragenomic variation in rDNA sequence, both structural and fine-scale; and (iii) patterns of divergence and homogenization within and across NORs that may have arisen during cancer evolution and the subsequent passaging of this line. Finally, by reading the same tags from RNA, we define the relationship between DNA methylation and Pol I transcription at the resolution of individual rDNA units. Together, our study demonstrates how the final tangles of the human genome can at last be resolved, and opens the door to more extensive investigations of how genetic, epigenetic and functional rDNA variation contributes to health and disease.

Title: Rise and Fall of a Superbug: Analyzing the epidemic success of a distinct clone of vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium ST117/CT71 in Germany, 2017 - 2024.
Authors: Weber, R. E.; Werner, G.; Bender, J. K.; Haldemann, B.; Drechsel, O.; Fischer, M. A.
Abstract: Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium (VREfm) is a major cause of healthcare-associated infections, yet outbreak analysis remains challenging, particularly for prevalent lineages. One of the most striking examples is the Sequence Type (ST) 117/Complex Type (CT) 71/vanB lineage, whose rapid expansion across Germany coincided with a sharp rise in VRE prevalence observed around 2019. Defining reliable genomic thresholds remains particularly difficult, as current core-genome Multi-Locus Sequence Typing (cgMLST) cutoffs are based largely on expert consensus or limited case series. Here, we evaluate the discriminatory performance of cgMLST and split k-mer analysis (SKA) for resolving relatedness within ST117/CT71 and investigate whether low core-genome diversity represents a lineage-specific trait or a population-wide property of E. faecium. While cgMLST captures the overall population structure of ST117/CT71, SKA provided higher resolution, distinguishing isolates identical by cgMLST. Analysis of 2,505 genomes showed that ST117/CT71 does not exhibit reduced allelic variability compared with other hospital-adapted lineages, suggesting that limited core-genome diversity is a broader population characteristic. Complementary transposon analyses further identified two temporally distinct ST117/CT71 sublineages carrying different Tn1549-like structures. To assess allelic variation within confirmed transmission events, we analyzed 138 outbreak clusters from 96 hospitals. Outbreak-associated isolates showed sharply compressed allelic differences (median = 1), with 90% of pairwise comparisons falling within [≤]9 alleles. Thus, the commonly applied [≤]20-allele threshold risks overestimating genomic relatedness and grouping unrelated isolates. Based on these data, we propose lowering the cgMLST alert threshold to [≤]9 alleles for initial cluster detection of local outbreaks, followed by confirmatory high-resolution analyses such as SKA.

Title: PAMP: Continuous-to-Discrete Mutation Projection for Enzyme Engineering
Authors: wang, h.; yu, z.; ren, y.; yuan, r.
Abstract: Efficient enzyme engineering requires translating quantitative turnover predictions into specific mutations that im- prove catalytic activity while reducing experimental search. Here we introduce Proximal Adversarial Mutation Projection (PAMP), a gradient-guided framework that maps a differentiable turnover objective directly to single-amino-acid substitutions by combining multi-point gradient averaging with distance-penalized projection in protein embedding space. Using a substrate-conditioned Resid- ual Predictor trained on CataPro-derived data, PAMP achieved a mean first-round predicted gain of 0.1795 log2 units across 2,754 enzyme substrate pairs, with positive changes in 84.64% of cases; among the top five ranked substitutions, 99.49% of records contained at least one positive candidate. Five sequential rounds increased the mean cumulative predicted gain to 0.5631 log2 units, and re-scoring with an independent, non-differentiable predictor left the ordering of the methods intact while attenuating the absolute gain. PAMP provides a computationally efficient strategy for prioritizing experimentally testable enzyme mutations under small candidate budgets.

Title: OligoFragger: spectrum graph-guided analysis of modified RNA oligonucleotides by mass spectrometry
Authors: Shen, J.; Polasky, D. A.; Yu, F.; Simcox, K. M.; Zhu, B.; Koutmou, K. S.; Nesvizhskii, A. I.
Abstract: RNA modifications are widespread modulators of RNA function, but comprehensive identification remains technically challenging. This is especially true for densely modified RNAs such as tRNAs, where multiple modified residues and many possible chemistries occur within short sequence contexts. Tandem mass spectrometry provides direct chemical and positional evidence for modified oligonucleotides, but current database-search strategies struggle when dozens of candidate modifications must be considered simultaneously. Here, we present OligoFragger, a spectrum graph-guided computational tool that uses fragment evidence to constrain modified-oligonucleotide searches before full database scoring, enabling rapid and robust oligonucleotide identification. Using controlled RNA samples and tRNA datasets from E. coli and human cells, we demonstrate that OligoFragger increases identifications under stringent FDR control while recovering known modification patterns and supporting label-free quantification. This strategy enables sensitive, FDR-controlled identification and label-free quantification of modified RNA oligonucleotides in complex epitranscriptomic search spaces.

Title: Differential regulation of myeloid Scavenger Receptor A (CD204) expression in humans versus mice in response to sepsis
Authors: Ozment, T. R.; McGlothlin, M.; Schweitzer, J.; Adkins, J.; Hopkins, N.; Williams, D. L.
Abstract: Sepsis is the number one cause of mortality in the critically ill patient. The underlying pathophysiology of sepsis is not fully understood. Scavenger Receptor A (SR-A) is a promiscuous receptor of myeloid cells that binds multiple pathogen associated molecular patterns (PAMPs). We have demonstrated that SR-A promotes mortality in murine sepsis. The present study sought to examine the effect of sepsis on myeloid SR-A expression in septic mice and compare it to sepsis patients. Leukocytes were isolated from mice after cecal ligation and puncture. Blood leukocytes were isolated from sepsis patients. Myeloid cells were isolated from healthy mice or human subjects and were treated with PAMPs. Leukocyte phenotype and SR-A expression were determined by flow cytometry. CLP increased SR-A expression when compared to sham operated animals on both neutrophils and monocytes/macrophages. In contrast, SR-A expression was not changed on either neutrophils or monocytes from sepsis patients when compared to healthy control subjects. Treatment of murine neutrophils and macrophages with Pam3CSK4 and treatment of macrophages with LPS increased SR-A expression. Human neutrophil SR-A expression was not altered by any PAMPs, and only treatment with C. albicans glucan increased SR-A expression on human monocytes.
