Myeloid SR-A expression is increased in septic mice, and this increase plays a detrimental role in the response to sepsis, while SR-A expression is not changed in leukocytes from septic patients and does not correlate with SOFA II scores. Thus, myeloid SR-A expression does not appear to play significant a role in the pathophysiology of human sepsis.

Title: Necroptosis is a targetable driver of severe coronavirus pathogenesis
Authors: Hou, Y.; Shi, J.; Zhou, M.; Sui, B.; Zhang, H.; Hu, Y.; Li, H.; He, Y.; Sun, Z.; Chen, Z.; DeAntoneo, C.; Liu, H.; Li, J.; Gautam, A.; Luo, C.; Wen, L.; Yoon, C.; Chen, Y.; Wang, Y.; Zhu, T.; Liu, Y.; Hu, B.; Yuen, T. T.-T.; Zhang, X.; Cai, J.; Shuai, H.; Li, C.; Zhao, X.; Liu, M.; Ma, X.; Yuan, S.; Zhou, J.; Zhang, B.-Z.; Lee, K. F. L.; Wang, Z.; Kok, K.-H.; Huang, J.-D.; Jin, D.-Y.; Chan, J. F.-W.; Cao, B.; Chan, F. K.-M.; Balachandran, S.; Yuen, K.-Y.; Chu, H.
Abstract: Human-pathogenic coronaviruses differ dramatically in pathogenicity but the underlying mechanisms are incompletely understood. Here, we demonstrate that highly pathogenic coronaviruses trigger necroptosis in the infected cells and lung tissues, whereas necroptosis is not detected in cells infected by seasonal coronavirus. Mechanistically, highly pathogenic coronaviruses produce Z-RNA, activate ZBP1 and initiates necroptotic cell death signaling, triggering necroinflammation and lung injury. In contrast, seasonal coronaviruses produce little to no Z-RNA, and do not activate necroptosis. Importantly, small-molecule inhibition of necroptosis attenuates inflammatory cytokine expression and markedly ameliorates lung damage in mice infected with all three highly pathogenic coronaviruses, independent of virus clearance. Overall, our study identifies necroptosis as a dominant mediator of coronavirus pathogenesis, and positions necroptosis blockade as a new therapeutic target against severe coronavirus diseases.

Title: A ribosome-dependent small-ORF switch controls flagellar gene expression and virulence
Authors: Lastovka, F.; Bryant, O. J.; Meggers, D.; Alexeeva, E.; Knorr, M.; Narberhaus, F.; Chung, B. Y.
Abstract: RNA structures are active regulators of bacterial translation. Here, we identified a naturally occurring translation-enhancing small open reading frame (tesORF) that controls the expression of the flagellar operon fliFGHIJK in Salmonella enterica and other motile Enterobacterales. Nucleotide-resolution ribosome profiling revealed this previously unannotated 54-nucleotide ORF immediately upstream of fliF. Genetic, transcriptomic, and biochemical analyses support a model in which tesORF translation counteracts an inhibitory RNA structure, exposing the fliF ribosome-binding site and promoting translation initiation independently of the encoded peptide sequence. Disruption of tesORF translation reduced expression of the downstream operon and impaired motility and virulence-associated phenotypes in Escherichia coli, Salmonella, and Yersinia. Together, our findings reveal how translation of a conserved small ORF regulates an entire flagellar operon through RNA structural remodelling, with consequences expending to the wider flagellar regulon, linking RNA structural dynamics to bacterial motility and virulence.

Title: Distinct binding modes shape exploitable asymmetries between echinocandin and triterpenoid resistance landscapes in Fks1
Authors: Carolus, H.; Wang, N.; Jacobs, S.; Dube, A. K.; Sofras, D.; Lobo Romero, C.; Durand, R.; Spruijtenburg, B.; Meijer, E. F. J.; Van Dijck, P.; Lague, P.; Landry, C. R.
Abstract: Echinocandins are the first-line treatment for invasive fungal infections and work by inhibiting the fungal {beta}-1,3-glucan synthase Fks1. Recently, a first-in-class triterpenoid Fks1 inhibitor, ibrexafungerp, was approved for clinical use. The extent to which the difference between these drug classes alters the landscape of resistance mutations in Fks1 is unknown. We used deep mutational scanning (DMS) to quantify the effects of all single-amino-acid variants spanning 159 residues across the three canonical Fks1 resistance hotspots and flanking regions in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Drug selections revealed widespread position-specific cross-resistance and differential resistance, including an ibrexafungerp-specific resistance cluster downstream of hotspot 2 that defines a novel triterpenoid-specific resistance hotspot. We defined this as hotspot 4 and redefined the boundaries of the remaining three canonical echinocandin hotspots, based on the mutational landscape of our DMS analyses. Susceptibility testing of individual FKS1 variants of S. cerevisiae and Candidozyma auris strains confirmed conserved class-specific and cross-resistance patterns. Structure-guided ligand placement, molecular dynamics-based simulated annealing, and DMS-informed pose selection linked drug-specific phenotypes to distinct interaction networks, providing a molecular rationale for the observed differential resistance patterns. These data provide a framework for predicting antifungal resistance, informing treatment strategies and future drug design.

Title: Elevational variation in gut microbial community composition and predicted functional potential across three Himalayan redstart species
Authors: Chhetri, P.; Dahal, N.; Kumar, A.; Rai, S.; Bhattacharjee, S.; Kumar, R.; Lamichhaney, S.
Abstract: Environmental gradients and seasonal migration may influence host-associated microbial communities, yet their contributions to gut microbiome variation in montane birds remain poorly understood. We investigated gut microbial communities across 1,300 to 4,200 m in three Himalayan redstarts (Phoenicurus fuliginosus, P. leucocephalus, and P. frontalis) exhibiting contrasting seasonal movement strategies. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing of 46 fecal samples, we characterized microbial diversity, community composition, distance decay relationships, co-occurrence networks, and predicted functional potential. Elevation was significantly associated with microbial community composition, explaining approximately 3% of variation, whereas host species showed no significant association after accounting for elevation. P. fuliginosus exhibited significant compositional differences among most sampled elevations, whereas P. leucocephalus showed significant positive distance decay relationships. Alpha diversity showed no consistent elevational trend, while core microbial taxa and co-occurrence networks varied among elevational groups. PICRUSt2 analyses identified 28 predicted KEGG Level 3 pathways differing significantly among elevations, including pathways associated with amino acid, lipid, glycan, carbohydrate, and bile acid metabolism. Together, these findings highlight elevation as a significant correlate of gut microbial community composition and predicted functional potential, with distinct patterns of microbial turnover among closely related Himalayan redstarts.

Title: Desiccation stress enhances virulence potential of group B Streptococcus
Authors: Jafar, T.; da Conceicao Mendonca, J.; Boland, N.; Burcham, L. R.
Abstract: Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B Streptococcus, GBS) asymptomatically inhabits the gastrointestinal and female reproductive tracts but can also cause invasive diseases in susceptible individuals. Despite its clinical importance, relatively little is known about its ability to survive outside the host and whether environmental persistence contributes to transmission and infection. Here we investigate the GBS survival under nutrient starvation and desiccation, characterizing phenotypic and genomic adaptations associated with environmental persistence. GBS remained viable for 30 days during starvation at room temperature and for more than 80 days under desiccated conditions, with GBS grown to stationary-phase bacteria exhibiting greater survival than actively growing bacteria. Survival under desiccation was conserved among several clinically relevant GBS serotypes. Following rehydration desiccated GBS exhibited enhanced biofilm formation compared to control non-desiccated strains. Whole-genome sequencing identified mutations in genes involved in capsule biosynthesis, cell-envelope homeostasis, nutrient transport, and carbohydrate metabolism, suggesting that multiple adaptive pathways may contribute to environmental persistence. Importantly, desiccated GBS retained the capacity to colonize the vaginal mucosa and displayed increased invasion of reproductive tissues in a murine vaginal colonization model. In a systemic infection model, desiccated GBS exhibited enhanced virulence compared to control non-desiccated GBS, demonstrating that environmental survival does not diminish pathogenic potential. This environmental persistence may represent an underappreciated factor contributing to GBS transmission and the epidemiology of late-onset neonatal disease.

Title: Hepadnavirus tropism determined by diversified NTCP functionality in Feline species
Authors: Mifune, J.; Ekimoto, T.; Takeuchi, J. S.; Kobayashi, C.; Kurata, M.; Shionoya, K.; Kawano, M. X.; Saito, A.; Sureau, C.; Ikeguchi, M.; Watashi, K.
Abstract: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) exhibits a narrow host range, largely determined by sodium taurocholate cotransporting polypeptides (NTCP), a hepatic bile acid transporter acting as the HBV receptor. NTCP among animals appears to have evolved following trade-off mutations to lose its viral receptor activity while preserving its transporter function. Here, through profiling of the NTCP homologs from 23 mammalian species, we uncover unexpected functional heterogeneity of feline NTCPs. NTCPs derived from cat, tiger, and leopard supported viral preS1 binding and HBV infection, whereas lion-NTCP was deficient for preS1 binding and, notably, exhibited markedly reduced bile acid transport. Cat-NTCP was further demonstrated to have viral receptor function by productive infection in primary cat hepatocytes. Experimental mutagenesis identified double substitution at positions 191 and 268 as key determinants: introducing lion-type substitutions into cat-NTCP (G191R and T268A) abolished preS1 binding, whereas reciprocal substitutions in lion-NTCP restored receptor function. Molecular dynamics simulations suggested that lion-NTCP adopts conformation in which a transmembrane helix bending enlarges the whole bile acid tunnel and disrupts preS1 compatibility. Such differences also determined host susceptibility to another feline-infected domestic cat HBV. These findings reveal diversified NTCP functionality with evolutionary plasticity that acquires resistance to hepadnavirus infection at the expense of physiological transporter function.

Title: Differential properties of gp120 from HIV-1 group M subtypes A and B
Authors: Tamazawa, Y. C.; Suzuki, D. I.; Suzuki, Y. J.; Shults, N. V.
Abstract: HIV-1 group M subtypes A and B differ substantially in their gp120 sequence. To determine whether these differences contribute to subtype-specific complications, particularly pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), rats were injected with gp120 from subtype A or B. Pulmonary artery (PA) remodeling was assessed after four weeks using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining and the Vessel Morphometry Analysis tool by Autona (autona.org). Subtype A gp120 potently increased PA wall thickness and right ventricular hypertrophy. The CD4-binding region of subtype A lacks a stretch of 16 amino acids (V1 N-glycosylation site), and experiments showed stronger binding of subtype B to CD4. Subtype B gp120 contains an RGKV sequence, which resembles the RGKR sequence of the rabies virus glycoprotein G that binds to the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChR). Subtype A gp120 possesses a KDKK sequence instead. Molecular dynamics simulations indicated that both sites are surface-exposed. Although nAChR is expressed in PA cells and could potentially drive the pronounced effects of subtype A, MD simulations estimated that subtype B gp120 binds more strongly to nAChR. We also noted a single amino acid difference immediately preceding the REKR furin cleavage sequence: glutamate in subtype A versus glutamine in subtype B gp120. Simulations predicted that subtype A gp120 interacts more effectively with furin, and enzyme assays demonstrated that subtype A promotes a positive feedback loop more strongly than subtype B. Thus, HIV-1 gp120 subtype A is more potent in promoting PAH, and the mechanism may involve enhancing furin activity to elevate gp120 levels.

Title: Uncovering Features of ProteinMPNN with Sparse Autoencoders
Authors: Mukkavilli, N.; Ivanov, K.; Beck, D. A. C.; Akbari, H.; McCully, M.
Abstract: Customization and modification of machine learning derived sequences can be achieved by understanding the mechanics behind state-of-the-art protein design models such as ProteinMPNN. Uninterpretability is hypothesized to be due largely to polysemanticity where neural networks store more features than they have dimensions. Here, we introduce sparse autoencoders (SAEs) into ProteinMPNN which expand its latent space and uncovers correlations between the activations in sparse dimensions and the presence of protein features such as secondary structure, residue volume, residue shape, disulfide bridges, and coordination to ligands. Additionally, we show that sparse activations can be manipulated to produce a variant of the short chain variable fragment Brolucizumab that is more thermostable than variants produced by traditional machine learning methods based on high temperature molecular dynamics simulations. Thus, SAEs provide both mechanistic understanding of protein design models and allow customizable manipulation of sequence prediction.

Title: RawMod: Modification-Agnostic Detection of DNA Base Modifications from Nanopore Signal Pileups
Authors: Srinivasan, B.; Nazar, S.; Gandhi, V.; Zhang, E.; Bachvaroff, T.; Kolmogorov, M.; Place, A.; Firtina, C.
Abstract: Summary: Identifying epigenetically modified bases (e.g., methylation) is crucial for many important applications such as discovering mechanisms of cancer development, cell differentiation, and bacterial defense. Nanopore sequencing generates electrical signals that can differentiate canonical bases from modified ones. To detect base modifications from signals, machine learning (ML) methods and statistical approaches are commonly used. These methods can either detect a specific modification type or require an additional unmodified copy of the same DNA as a control group. However, no released model detects modification types beyond those it was trained for, which makes it difficult to detect rare modification types without an unmodified control. Our goal is to accurately identify the presence of modified sites regardless of their modification type, which we define as modification-agnostic detection. To this end, we propose RawMod, a transformer-based modification-agnostic and control-free method for detecting epigenetically modified genomic positions. The key idea of RawMod is to compare the raw signals of many reads at each site with the unmodified reference sequence, using a small model that learns many modification types as a single modified class. Based on our extensive evaluations on the detection of various modification types (5mC, 5hmC, 4mC, 6mA, and 5hmU) using various genomes, RawMod achieves the highest mean AUROC across modifications compared to control-based methods and control-free modification models. A single RawMod model with 0.23M parameters detects five modification types with a mean AUROC of 0.964, against 0.799 for the best released model. When a modification type is withheld from training, RawMod still detects it (AUROC 0.91--0.98), provided another modification of the same base was seen in training. We use RawMod to map 5hmU without a control across a 7.7 Mb contig of the Amphidinium carterae genome, consistent with two published trends. Further, we show that the modification-aware embeddings from RawMod can be used to differentiate read origin (e.g., cell types, tumor/normal origin, and native/PCR-amplified DNA). We discuss how RawMod can enable further work on label-free classification of cell types using these modification-aware embeddings. Availability and Implementation: RawMod is available at https://github.com/STORMgroup/RawMod and at https://huggingface.co/STORMResearch/RawMod. We also provide the scripts to fully reproduce our results on our GitHub page and release our datasets on SquiDBase.

Title: Paired-unit activation steering for context-aware protein design
Authors: Zhou, Y.; Qian, X.; Yoon, B.-J.
Abstract: Activation steering in protein language models enables controllable sequence generation without changing the model weights. However, existing methods typically construct steering vectors from global differences between property-positive and property-negative protein populations, overlooking how property-improving directions vary across different protein sequence backgrounds. To address this, we propose \textit{Paired-Unit local steering of embeddings (PULSE)}, which matches positive- and negative-property proteins by maximizing their representation cosine similarity and constructs steering vectors by aggregating similarity-weighted, unit-normalized differences between matched pairs. Across three protein optimization objectives--solubility, immunogenicity, and toxicity--PULSE consistently outperforms global population-centroid steering in both final predicted property scores and optimization success rates. Further analysis reveals that conventional static steering-vector diagnostics cannot adequately explain optimization performance. To characterize steering reliability during iterative sequence editing, we introduce \textit{Local Directional Support (LDS)}, which measures how well successive representation changes align with property-improving directions from similar protein backgrounds. We show that LDS captures differences in trajectory reliability and enables predictor-free candidate prioritization, enriching successful protein designs without requiring property predictions during candidate selection. Together, these findings demonstrate the importance of context-aware steering and trajectory-level evaluation for controllable protein sequence optimization.

Title: A High-Efficiency Geranylation Platform Enabled by Rational Tuning of a Single-Residue-Coded Chemo- and Regioselective Switch in Aromatic Prenyltransferases
Authors: Qiu, R.; Zhang, H.; Li, M.; Hu, Z.; He, Z.; Ding, S.; Gao, L.; Liu, Y.; Chen, B.; Huang, M.; Zhang, Z.-M.; Wang, J.-b.
Abstract: Geranylation is an efficient post-modification strategy for enhancing or introducing new properties to molecules; however, achieving both high efficiency and precision remains challenging. Aromatic prenyltransferases (PTs) provide a mild and sustainable approach, yet their practical application is often limited by the trade-off between broad substrate scope and low selectivity, and successfully balancing these properties is rare. Here, using the pharmaceutically relevant cannabigerol framework as a model, we identify a single-residue switch in a prenyltransferase from Aspergillus terreus (AtaPT) that governs both chemo- and regioselectivity. Rational tuning of this switch preserves broad substrate scope while enhancing selectivity, enabling the selective formation of each of the three possible mono-geranylated products in the model reaction. Structural analysis reveals that this residue modulates the selectivity and activity through coupled steric and electrostatic effects. Notably, transplantation of this site into three homologous PTs similarly reprogrammed selectivity, establishing a conserved and generalizable control mechanism. Leveraging these insights, we achieved selective geranylation across 36 aromatic substrates, affording 41 products. Integration with an efficient geranyl donor regeneration system enabled preparative-scale synthesis, reaching titers up to 324 mg/L. This work defines a unifying mechanism for selectivity control in PTs and provides a high-efficiency platform for geranylation.

Title: Avian reovirus triggered ferroptosis, modulated lipid metabolism, and induced lipid droplet formation in infected cells, which was mediated in part by the p10/FAST protein
Authors: Liu, M.; Kehlbeck, D.; Egana-Labrin, S.; Brodrick, A.; Sun, L.; Jones, J.; Sunny, N.; Broadbent, A. J.
Abstract: In this study, we evaluated how avian reovirus (ARV) affected lipid metabolism and lipid droplets (LDs) in cell culture. ARV infection of chicken LMH cells significantly increased the size and number of LDs, however, LDs did not co-localize with virus factories, and neither overexpression by treatment with fatty acids (FAs), nor inhibition by treatment with TOFA or DGAT inhibitors significantly affected ARV replication. Lipidomic analysis revealed that following infection, total cellular lipid content increased approximately 25-fold, phosphatidylcholine (PC) content increased from 23.5 to 57.9%, and the polyunsaturated FA:monounsaturated FA ratio (PUFA:MUFA) decreased in membrane phospholipids but increased in triglycerides. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that there was also a reduction in the expression of genes involved in PUFA synthesis. As membrane PUFAs are susceptible to peroxidation, we investigated whether ARV induced ferroptosis. Consistent with this, ARV led to an increase in oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation that was partially iron dependent, and we found evidence that ferroptosis was proviral. Moreover, as ARV is known to form syncytia, we hypothesized that our observations were also the result of plasma membrane remodeling. Consistent with this, cells transfected with the ARV fusogenic p10/FAST protein formed syncytia, had a significantly upregulated number of LDs, and displayed hallmarks of ferroptosis. Taken together, we hypothesize that ARV induces syncytium formation and ferroptosis to facilitate viral spread to neighboring cells, but to prevent premature cell death due to these processes, lipid metabolism is modulated by infection, leading to an increase in LDs.

Title: Ksp37 is a rapidly mobilized NK cell secretory protein that engages FGF2
Authors: Hermans, C. K.; Chudasama, K. K.; Berg-Larsen, A.; Haugsten, E. M.; Thune Wiiger, M.; Sanchez, A.; Zandstra Krokeide, S.; Graczyk-Bartnik, A.; Klopotowska, M.; Firczuk, M.; Wesche, J.; Malmberg, K.-J.; Pfefferle, A.
Abstract: A key feature of natural killer (NK) cells is their preloaded arsenal of effector molecules, allowing them to rapidly respond upon activation. In this study, we characterized a previously unexplored secretory protein, termed killer-specific secretory protein of 37 kDa (Ksp37), which is highly abundant in differentiated CD56dim NK cells. Ksp37 is rapidly secreted in a dose-dependent and JAK-1 dependent manner upon low levels of cytokine stimulation, making it a sensitive readout for NK cell activation. Following secretion, intracellular levels were rapidly replenished, preserving responsiveness to subsequent cytokine stimulation. We found that Ksp37 is stored in polarized intracellular compartments distinct from those containing canonical cytotoxic effector molecules, including granzyme B and perforin, which require stronger stimulation for release. Lastly, we identified Ksp37 as a novel binding partner of fibroblast growth factor 2 (FGF2). This opens new avenues of exploration for the role of NK cells in remodeling their extracellular environment by modulating the FGF2-FGFR1 axis, which plays a key role in tumor growth, angiogenesis and tissue repair.

Title: Reverse Transcription Loop-Mediated Isothermal Amplification Combined with Lateral Flow Assay (RT-LAMP-LFA) for Rapid Detection of the 2026 Bundibugyo Virus (BDBV) Outbreak Strain
Authors: Sato, L. S.; Ihara, M.; Hidano, A.; Takamatsu, Y.
Abstract: Making accurate diagnosis is a critical first step in patient management and control for emerging and re-emerging disease outbreaks. Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) is a filovirus that causes Ebola disease, and the 2026 outbreak highlights the need for rapid diagnostic approaches that can be deployed in settings with limited laboratory infrastructure. Here, we developed a reverse transcription loop-mediated isothermal amplification-lateral flow assay (RT-LAMP-LFA) for rapid detection of the 2026 BDBV outbreak strain. LAMP primers were designed based on the genome sequence of the 2026 outbreak strain, and the conservation of the primer binding sites among all available 2026 outbreak genomes was confirmed in silico. LAMP primers were evaluated for analytical specificity and sensitivity using in vitro-transcribed RNA (ivtRNA) from BDBV and other filoviruses, as well as RNA derived from arboviruses and mammalian cells. Amplification products were detected using a Chromatography-Printed Array Strip (C-PAS) lateral flow platform. The newly designed primers specifically detected the presence of BDBV RNA without nonspecific amplification of the other viral or cellular RNA samples tested. Consistent amplification was observed down to 103 copies per reaction. In addition, BDBV viral RNA was successfully amplified, and the amplification products were detected using C-PAS, with the total workflow being completed within 25 min. These findings demonstrate the analytical specificity and sensitivity of the developed RT-LAMP-LFA assay and its compatibility with rapid visual lateral flow detection, supporting its potential application as a point-of-care approach for BDBV detection.

Title: Higher-order metabolic interactions among oral commensals gate pathobiont expansion through succinate-driven pH modulation
Authors: Soh, D.; Bhat, A.; Li, L.; Smardz, M.; Parker, C.; Tiede, E.; Nelson, B.; Frerichs, V.; Wood, T.; Ikonomou, L.; Ton-That, H.; Diaz, P. I.
Abstract: Despite advances in defining microbiome shifts associated with inflammatory mucosal diseases, the ecological interactions that constrain or facilitate pathobiont expansion remain poorly understood. Using a six-species synthetic oral microbial community and factorial interaction screening, we identified a higher-order interaction governing the growth of the periodontal pathobiont Porphyromonas gingivalis. The core community member Veillonella parvula was the strongest positive determinant of P. gingivalis growth, but this effect was substantially reduced by the health-associated commensal Actinomyces oris. A. oris-mediated antagonism resulted from extracellular acidification and was enhanced under anaerobic conditions. Genetic dissection of A. oris fermentation revealed that lactate dehydrogenase (ldh1) contributes to anaerobic lactate production, but ldh1 deletion only partially relieved P. gingivalis inhibition. Instead, succinate, produced through a succinate dehydrogenase/fumarate reductase pathway (sdh2), emerged as the principal driver of acidification and P. gingivalis suppression. At high cell densities, however, V. parvula consumed both lactate and succinate, reversing acidification and restoring conditions permissive for P. gingivalis growth. To assess the relevance of these interactions in vivo, we analyzed subgingival microbiome from 1,355 adults, including 555 with detectable P. gingivalis. Among these individuals, P. gingivalis abundance was negatively associated with Actinomyces abundance after adjustment for periodontitis severity, whereas this association was attenuated at high V. parvula abundance, consistent with the interaction observed in vitro. Together, these findings identify succinate as a previously unrecognized mediator of interbacterial antagonism and reveal how higher-order metabolic interactions among oral commensals regulate pathobiont expansion through pH modulation, with protective effects shaped by oxygen availability and metabolic cross-feeding.

Title: Divergent methane production and microbial community responses to carbon enrichment in freshwater wetland sediments
Authors: Ghantous, J.; Azaizah, H.; Levintal, E.; Golan, R.; Rosenberg, Y. O.; Antler, G.; Yanuka-Golub, K.
Abstract: Methane (CH4) accumulation in wetland sediments reflects interactions among organic matter, sediment chemistry, and microbial communities. We combined depth-resolved field characterization across four wetland habitats in northern Israel with complementary incubations to examine methane accumulation and responses to labile-carbon enrichment. Sediment cores were characterized using Rock-Eval analysis, porewater chemistry, oxygen profiling at three sites, and mcrA amplicon sequencing. High CH4 concentrations occurred under contrasting conditions: Ein Nimfit (EN) contained approximately 12% total organic carbon and reached 2.1 mM CH4, whereas Ein Afek site EA2 contained approximately 5% carbon and accumulated 0.7-1.7 mM CH4. Both showed sulfate depletion, but EN exhibited pronounced sulfide accumulation, whereas EA2 showed greater dissolved iron and nutrient enrichment. Their classified methanogenic assemblages also differed. EA1 remained methane poor despite increasing carbon content with depth, while EA3 combined low carbon content and CH4 accumulation with detectable methanogens and lower methanogenic diversity. In a 36-day bottle experiments using sediments from two of the four wetland habitats, sucrose-amended EA3 exhibited a transient maximum of 18.8 mmol collected CH4 kg-1 wet sediment during Days 22-29, whereas EN reached its highest collected amount during Days 29-36. Methane proportions increased before the large output increase in EA3 but remained comparatively stable and high in EN. Soluble chemical oxygen demand trajectories and microbial community changes also differed. These findings identify distinct biogeochemical settings supporting methane accumulation and demonstrate methanogenic potential in low-CH4 sediment, emphasizing the complementary information provided by field profiles, microbial characterization, and exploratory enrichment experiments.

Title: The absence of microbiome in germ-free mice exacerbates the pathogenicity of mouse-adapted SARS-CoV-2 MA10
Authors: Griffin, E. P.; Feldman, S. H.; Jain, R.; Le, S. T.; Conaway, M. R.; Li, S.; Robinson, S. R.; Larner, J. M.; Mandell, J. W.; Everitt, J. I.; andarawewa, k. L.
Abstract: Germ-free mice, which are devoid of microbiota, provide a powerful system to define the contribution of the microbiome to host responses during infection. Severe COVID-19 outcomes are associated with multiple comorbidities that are themselves characterized by microbiome dysbiosis; however, the causal role of the microbiota in SARS-CoV-2 pathogenesis remains poorly understood. Here, we use germ-free mouse models to evaluate the impact of the microbiome on disease severity following infection with mouse-adapted SARS-CoV-2 MA10. Comparison with conventionally housed mice revealed that the absence of the microbiome markedly exacerbates SARS-CoV-2-induced disease in both C57BL/6 and Swiss Webster backgrounds. Germ-free mice exhibited greater weight loss, impaired lung function, worsened pulmonary pathology, and pronounced alterations in circulating cytokine and chemokine profiles compared with conventional controls. These findings show that resident microbiota limit SARS-CoV-2 pathogenicity and establish germ-free COVID-19 models as a powerful platform to identify protective microbial taxa and microbiota-based interventions to reduce severe disease.

Title: Varied forms of mutant tRNA mistranslation produce distinct phenotypes across multiple model organisms
Authors: Charles, B. S.; Moehring, A. J.
Abstract: Mutant tRNA mistranslation is a phenomenon in which specific tRNA gene mutations cause translational errors wherein amino acids incorporated during translation differ from those coded by mRNA sequences. The biological consequences of mutant tRNA mistranslation are highly complex and contextual, but are often deleterious. Importantly, many variables exist that are likely to affect the outcomes of any one mutant mistranslating tRNA; biochemical characteristics of the exchanged amino acids, frequency of use, identity of mistranslated products, and so on. Here, we generate a carefully curated array of tRNA mutants to assess which characteristics of mistranslating tRNA variants are most predictive of deleterious phenotypes. We find that toxicity often arises from mutant tRNAs that induce dramatic changes in biochemical properties between exchanged amino acids, as well as mistranslation that occurs more frequently. Importantly, exceptions are also observed to each of these general rules, implying instead that some deliriousness may arise from more granular, product-specific mechanisms. Additionally, quantification of mistranslation via mass spectrometry demonstrates a weak relationship between quantity of mistranslated products and severity of toxic phenotypes. Lastly, despite previous establishment of mutant mistranslating tRNA models in Drosophila melanogaster, incorporation of higher frequency mistranslating tRNA variants was largely unsuccessful, and incorporation of lower frequency mistranslating tRNA variants produces no detectable developmental phenotypes. These experiments support the notion that although general rules may be capable of reasonably predicting their consequences, each mistranslating tRNA variant warrants individual consideration and investigation for thorough understanding of its biological outcomes and precise mechanisms of toxicity.

Title: Pangenome Discoveries from Clinical Long-Read Genomes in Underrepresented Populations with Neurodevelopmental Disorders
Authors: Hashmi, M. A.; Nassir, N.; Balan, B.; Hanif, S.; Jamalalail, B.; Eldesouky, M.; Tambi, R.; BinEshaq, S.; Perera, K. D. H.; Elsokary, H.; Shiyas, S.; Zehra, B.; Advani, D.; Sabeel, S.; Bashir, O.; Khalifa, A.; Ibrahim, A.; Al Obathani, M.; Alsuwaidi, S.; Yousuff, M.; Mohamed, N.; Giddey, A.; Alshamsi, N.; Liao, W.-W.; Hebbar, P.; A. Audano, P.; Islam, A.; S AlKhnbashi, O.; Akter, H.; Sarker, S.; K. Jan, R.; Murtaza, M.; Berdiev, B.; C. Soares, N.; Cisse, B.; Faniran, S.; Chencheri, N.; Elbashir, H.; Bokhari, S. A.; Buhumaid, R.; Alsuwaidi, H.; Miga, K.; Jarvis, E.; Almarri, M.; Human Pangenome
Abstract: Genetic diagnoses remain elusive for many individuals with neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs), and the gap is wider in populations poorly represented in genomic reference resources. To demonstrate the equitable advantage of long-read whole genome sequencing (LR-WGS) and pangenomes in terms of clinical utility, we analyzed 211 NDD cases and 107 unaffected relatives from 24 populations, integrating their assemblies, resulting in a total of 1204 haplotypes with the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium Release 2 (HPRC_r2) and the Arab Pangenome Reference (APR) datasets. Clinical interpretation of small variants and structural variants (SVs) revealed pathogenic or likely pathogenic findings in 38.9% of the cases (82/211), and our workflow further detected pathogenic repeat expansions in 3.8% of the cases and runs of homozygosity (ROHs) exceeding 300 Mb in 4.7% of the cases, revealing substantial autozygosity suggestive of strong inbreeding. Beyond these clinical assessments, pangenome analysis revealed 3.9 million population-level novel small variants, 39,782 SVs and an average of 2.17 Mb of novel sequence per individual absent from linear references and global pangenomes. We identified 85.9 kb of case-unique nonreference sequences in exonic segments overlapping with curated NDD gene sets. Graph-based tertiary analysis further identified rare exonic complex homozygous rearrangements in the NDD associated genes for 2.4% of the cases. Together, these findings emphasize how diverse genome assemblies extend variant discovery beyond established linear reference-based clinical interpretation.

Title: Structure of human hephaestin reveals a homodimer anchored to the cell membrane
Authors: Liang, C.; Zhou, M.; Pan, Y.
Abstract: Hephaestin (Heph) is a membrane-bound ferroxidase that oxidizes ferrous ion (Fe2+) exported by ferroportin (Fpn) to ferric ion (Fe3+), enabling iron loading onto transferrin for systemic delivery. Loss-of-function mutations in Heph cause iron accumulation in intestinal enterocytes and systemic iron deficiency in animal models, underscoring its role in iron export. Heph has a large extracellular domain anchored to the cell membrane by a single transmembrane helix. However, full-length Heph has not previously been purified, and our understanding of its structure and function remains incomplete. Here, we report the expression and purification of functional fulllength human Heph and determination of its structure by cryo-electron microscopy at an overall resolution of approximately 2.3 [A]. The structure reveals a stable homodimer with well-resolved extracellular domains. Although the transmembrane helices are less well resolved, their positions can be defined. The substrate-binding site is connected to an electronegative funnel that may facilitate Fe2+ capture. These findings establish the structural organization of full-length human Heph and provide structural constraints for understanding its interaction with Fpn.

Title: Volumetric Cross-Amplitude Modulation (VxAM) for Transcranial Gas Vesicle Imaging
Authors: Weitz, A. S.; Belgharbi, H.; Sode, M.; Jones-Sinnott, R. M.; Nayak, R.; Fochtman, T.; Shapiro, M. G.; Dayton, P. A.; Pinton, G. F.
Abstract: Cross-amplitude modulation (xAM) is a commonly used pulse sequence for non-destructive, quasi-artifact-free detection of gas-vesicle (GV) contrast agents, but it has so far been limited to two-dimensional cross-sections acquired with one-dimensional linear arrays. We present the first implementation of xAM on a fully sampled two-dimensional matrix array, extending the half-aperture split of conventional xAM to a family of 2D sub-aperture partitions on a 32x32-element Vermon probe (7.81 MHz, 300 m element pitch). Angular spectrum simulations compared three primary bisections (X-axis, Y-axis, and diagonal (D1,D2)), and the selected Y-split was tested experimentally in GV-loaded tissue-mimicking phantoms. We also simulated an electronic asymmetric-angle sweep as an alternative to the robotic translation used in the experiments, and measured contrast through an ex vivo mouse skull. The non-emissive regions between the elevation panels of the Vermon probe accounted for most of the simulated differences among partitions, through both the continuity of the aperture parallel to the bisector plane and the side-lobe structure. At a 6 degree steering angle, the Y-split gave a contrast-to-tissue ratio (CTR) of ~29 dB for single frames and ~49 dB with 100-frame averaging without the skull, and a contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) of ~8 dB for single frames and ~12 dB with 100-frame averaging through the skull, where the inclusion remained resolvable. These results give design rules for xAM on matrix arrays. The through-skull result comes from a single ex vivo specimen, and in vivo work is the next step toward non-invasive, longitudinal, three-dimensional monitoring of GV-labeled glioblastoma and other targets of nonlinear contrast agents.

Title: Material context and TGF-β blockade timing determine matrix retained after withdrawal in patient-derived GelMA-bioprinted keratoconus stroma
Authors: Jiang, H.; Zhou, C.; Gao, F.; Pang, Y.; Li, Y.; Jie, Y.; Yang, H.; Jiang, Y.
Abstract: Keratoconus (KC) repair depends on host matrix, yet cultured KC cells produce less matrix. This has been interpreted as impaired synthesis, whereas tissue analyses point to the state of a thinned stroma. TGF-{beta} induces matrix alongside myofibroblast transformation (scarring). Scarless repair separates the two in vivo, but two-dimensional (2D) culture does not. Donor-matched, patient-derived three-dimensional (3D) gelatin methacryloyl (GelMA) bioprints from six KC and six normal donors preserved the KC tissue expression state and restored this separation. KC matrix secretion per unit DNA matched that of normal cells, and lower total output arose only from fewer cells. A single TGF-{beta} pulse induced matrix synthesis with less scarring, increasing programs low in KC tissue and the collagen genes COL5A1 and COL1A1, whose risk alleles thin and soften the cornea. Delayed receptor blockade for a finite course left more native collagen and less scarring than vehicle in 9 of 12 donors after withdrawal. Surrogate readouts used to select courses disagreed with retained host matrix. Continuous blockade suppressed scarring most deeply during treatment and produced the lowest matrix-gene expression. The course preferred in 2D produced less matrix and more scarring in 3D. Selection by retained matrix instead of readouts during treatment left 22.2% more native collagen. TGF-{beta}-pathway courses should therefore be evaluated by the host matrix and scarring remaining after withdrawal.

Title: DeePEn - A Depth sensitive benchmark for Protein Engineering
Authors: Schmirler, R.; Brenner, M.; Franz, S.; Heinzinger, M.; Rost, B.
Abstract: Recent progress in modeling techniques and high-throughput screening has significantly enhanced the accessibility of protein engineering. Nevertheless, further progress gets hindered by the lack of robust benchmarks that capture the practical challenges for real-world protein engineering. Here, we introduced DeePEn, a Depth-sensitive benchmark for Protein Engineering that quantifies model generalization to held-out variants at increasing mutational distance from the wild type. We defined distance as the number of simultaneous point mutations, i.e., single amino acid variants (SAVs), moving from wild-type to mutant (edit distance in computer science jargon). DeePEn retrospectively evaluates prediction and prioritization using experimentally labelled variants from deep mutational scanning (DMS) datasets; it does not benchmark prospective sequence generation or goal-directed optimization. Specifically selecting four DMS datasets with sufficient multi-mutation data points from ProteinGym, we assessed recent predictive models, including general and biophysics-informed protein Language Models (pLMs), and a non-transformer neural network. Our results highlight how the performance of all models deteriorates with increasing mutational distance and that no single metric sufficiently captures the diverse requirements of protein engineering. To overcome these shortcomings, DeePEn provides a readily available resource for multi-metric benchmarking that focuses on variant-effect prediction of variants distant from the wild type.

Title: AntiSite: Unified paratope prediction for antibodies and nanobodies with or without structure
Authors: Papadopoulos, A. M.; Alvarez, F.; Daras, P.
Abstract: Accurate paratope prediction provides insights into antibody--antigen recognition while supporting antibody discovery and engineering. Existing predictors are fixed to a single input setting: sequence-based methods cannot use an antibody structure, structure-based methods require coordinates, and methods covering both combine separately trained predictors. We present AntiSite, an antigen-agnostic predictor whose sequence encoder, fusion block and prediction head are shared across both settings; structure-aware inference adds molecular-surface features from our previously developed ParaSurf model, used here as a frozen, separately trained structural encoder. Structural-modality dropout enables both inference settings without retraining. Across five antibody--antigen benchmarks, structure-aware AntiSite achieved the highest mean PR-AUC among all evaluated methods, while sequence-only PR AUC was generally lower than that of the strongest dedicated antigen-agnostic sequence baseline. AntiSite also demonstrated zero-shot generalization to nanobodies without additional training. We further evaluated structures from recent antibody-specific and general protein folding methods, including Ibex, Protenix-v1, Boltz-2 and Chai-1, in antibody-only or antigen-aware co-folding settings. Their benefit was associated with structural accuracy, with the most accurate inputs yielding performance close to that obtained with experimental structures. AntiSite thus provides a shared predictor for antibody and nanobody binding sites, usable from sequence alone and refined when reliable structural information is available. Code and trained checkpoints are openly available.

Title: DemuxHMM: Large-Scale Single-Cell Embryo Profiling via Recombination Barcoding
Authors: Afanassiev, A. I.; Wei, K.; Yachie, N.; Sugioka, K.; Schiebinger, G.
Abstract: High-resolution developmental time-courses with single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) increasingly target trajectory inference and other analyses in the study of development and disease. Researchers can efficiently generate these datasets by pooling individuals and inferring cell-to-individual mappings after sequencing, in a process called demultiplexing. Existing demultiplexing methods face limitations in the number of timepoints they can support, due to either the need for individual-by-individual processing or reduced accuracy at large numbers of individuals. To address these limitations, we introduce a computational framework for demultiplexing large-scale, individual-resolved datasets. Our framework includes a recombination-aware demultiplexing method, DemuxHMM, which uses a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) to explicitly model contiguous SNP patterns that arise from simple breeding schemes. We demonstrate substantial performance and scalability gains from this recombination-aware approach on both a real Diversity Outbred (DO) mouse data and a simulated Drosophila dataset. This performance demonstrates the value of the method when used for common applications on model organisms such as time series, crossover position inference, and eQTLS, among others.

Title: Panmap: Scalable phylogeny-guided alignment, genotyping, and placement on pangenomes
Authors: Kramer, A. M.; Zhang, A.; Ayala, N.; de Sanctis, B.; Karim, L. M.; Hinrichs, A. S.; Walia, S.; Turakhia, Y.; Corbett-Detig, R.
Abstract: Pangenomes capture population-level variation but remain computationally challenging at scale. We present Panmap, a tool that leverages evolutionary structure to place, align, and genotype sequencing reads against mutation-annotated pangenomes containing up to millions of genomes. Panmap introduces a phylogenetically compressed k-mer index that stores only sequence differences along branches, enabling efficient comparison of reads to both sampled genomes and inferred ancestors. This approach reduces index size by up to 600-fold and construction time by over three orders of magnitude relative to existing tools. Panmap places a 100x coverage SARS-CoV-2 sample onto 20,000 genomes in 0.4 seconds and onto 8 million genomes in under two minutes. Furthermore, it enables accurate haplotype identification and abundance estimation in metagenomic samples and sensitive placement of ancient environmental DNA without prior alignment. Our approach makes large-scale pangenomes directly amenable to read mapping, genome assembly, alignment-free phylogenetic placement, and metagenomic analysis.

Title: Macroscopic Vibronic Coherence and Non-Dispersive Soliton Propagation Across a Protein-Solvent Interface
Authors: Woods, K.
Abstract: A foundational tenet of modern biophysics dictates that protein-solvent interactions and charge-transport dynamics operate strictly within microscopic, sub-nanometer boundaries where long-range coordination is natively suppressed by rapid room-temperature thermal dephasing. Here, we report an unexpected phenomenon that fundamentally challenges this paradigm: the long-distance, quantum-coherent communication between isolated protein samples in aqueous solution across macroscopic spatial separations. By mapping the distance-dependence of a weak, protein-emitted electromagnetic field on the response dynamics of an adjacent complex, we demonstrate that this inter-protein communication establishes a stable, intermolecular vibronic coupling operating across millimeter-scale distances up to at least 40 mm. This field interference induces a robust quantum coherence that lowers the local potential energy surface, transforming the coupled protein-solvent network into an un-attenuated, low-barrier energy transfer conduit. This stabilized pathway launches a topologically protected, non-dispersive soliton that exhibits exceptional phase stability against room-temperature thermal dephasing. These findings provide definitive empirical evidence of a sophisticated, field-driven quantum infrastructure embedded within a biological macromolecule. More explicitly, they reveal that a protein can possess an inherent capacity to preserve coherent wave propagation over macroscopic scales previously deemed impossible in room-temperature aqueous environments.

Title: Comparative cryo-EM structures of CGMMV and ToMMV reveal divergent coat protein packing and electrostatics indicating Tobamovirus host specificity
Authors: Chatterjee, A.; Venkatasubramanian, A.; Jailani, A. A. K.; Mazumder, P.; Singh, S.; Basu, S.; Das, U.; Roy, A.; Mandal, B.; Datta, P. P.
Abstract: Tobamoviruses are a group of economically important plant viruses exhibiting extreme stability and persistence. Despite high morphological similarity, they show extensive host-family specificity, induce a wide range of symptoms, and inflict significant global yield losses in fruit and vegetable crops. Composed of a rod-shaped helical assembly of identical coat proteins encasing a single-stranded RNA, tobamoviruses have long served as fundamental models for understanding helical assemblies. Here we report the cryo-EM structures of two viruses from this genus, cucumber green mottle mosaic virus (CGMMV) and tomato mottle mosaic virus (ToMMV), at 2.86 [A] and 2.71 [A] resolution, respectively, revealing divergent packing strategies within the virion assembly. Whereas the solanaceous-infecting ToMMV closely mirrors genetically-similar canonical tobacco mosaic virus (TMV), CGMMV employs a specialized hydrophobic packing strategy based at the solvent-exposed inner loop lining the solvent-exposed central canal. Comparative biophysical and molecular dynamics analyses from the reconstructed structures reveal more stable and compact protein packing for CGMMV at both the subunit and assembly levels. Furthermore, we identify a conserved electrostatic pentapeptide motif (residues 113 to117) on the lower radial alpha helix that serves as an additional RNA-stabilizing region, harbouring a clade-defining Lys113 synapomorphy in cucurbit-infecting tobamoviruses. Together, our findings elucidate how subtle electrostatic tuning and divergent hydrophobic packing strategies drive differential virion stability and host-family adaptation within a strictly conserved helical scaffold.

Title: Digital molecular kinetics enabled by large-scale nanopore arrays for multidimensional biophysical profiling
Authors: Li, K.; Wang, Y.; Cheng, Y.; Zheng, T.; Long, S.; Zhong, L.; Wu, M.; Zou, Y.
Abstract: While widely used, traditional technologies like surface plasmon resonance (SPR) are limited by narrow temporal windows (transient capture and baseline drift), dynamic heterogeneity, and poor physiological temperature performance. Meanwhile, early nanopore approaches are often constrained by limited throughput and heavy reliance on customized modification schemes. Here, we present a digital molecular kinetics (DMK) platform based on large-scale nanopore arrays. By introducing a universal coupling and probe reporting system, DMK achieves broad versatility across diverse molecular pairs, including proteins, peptides, small molecules, DNA, and polymerase complexes. In addition to accurately recovering classical SPR association and dissociation rate constants, by harnessing massive single-molecule event analysis, DMK breaks traditional performance boundaries: it facilitates robust thermodynamic-kinetic profiling across a wide temperature range, resolves distinct conformations in heterogeneous samples, enables ultra-low dissociation rate quantification via maximum likelihood estimation, and reveals energy wells via voltage gradients for binding analysis against environmental perturbations. Furthermore, DMK enables the capture of rapid binding events missed by SPR, offering a new perspective on molecular interaction complexity. This platform offers an effective alternative and upgrade to SPR, opening a digital paradigm for complex molecular analysis and drug discovery.

Title: HERC1-mediated orphan subunit quality control maintains proteasome homeostasis and is disrupted in HERC1-associated neurodevelopmental disease
Authors: Garcia-Diez, M.; Costa-Sastre, L.; Sala-Gaston, J.; Lopez-Hernandez, T.; Ramirez, J.; Osinalde, N.; Valer, J.; Arnedo-Pac, C.; Mayor, U.; Ventura, F.; Rosa, J. L.
Abstract: Biallelic hypomorphic variants in the E3 ubiquitin ligase HERC1 cause a neurological disorder clinically characterized by macrocephaly, dysmorphic facies, and psychomotor delay. Identifying the substrates of HERC1 is essential for understanding its biological functions and the mechanisms underlying disease-associated variants. To address this, we performed a quantitative proteomic analysis using biotinylated ubiquitin to identify HERC1 targets and examine their regulation in cells expressing HERC1 with or without ubiquitin ligase activity. This approach revealed a broad set of HERC1-dependent ubiquitylation substrates, including proteins from major multiprotein complexes such as the proteasome, the translation initiation machinery, and pathways involved in cell metabolism. Focusing on the proteasome, the most prominently represented complex, we identified several regulatory particle subunits, including PSMC6, PSME1, and PSME2. Specifically, within the 19S regulatory particle, we demonstrated that ubiquitylation of the PSMC6 subunit involves the formation of K48-linked polyubiquitin chains and depends on HERC1 activity. Other 19S subunits, such as PSMC2, PSMC4, and PSMC5, undergo a similar modification. Mechanistically, we show that HERC1 selectively recognizes unassembled subunits, promotes their ubiquitylation, and targets them for proteasomal degradation. Notably, in HERC1-deficient cells, disruption of this mechanism impaired proteasomal activity. At the disease level, quantitative proteomic analysis of the pathogenic HERC1 variant c.1448G>A (p.Gly483Glu) likewise identified altered ubiquitylation of proteasome subunits and components of the translation initiation machinery. Biochemical analyses further revealed impaired ubiquitylation of PSMC6 by the mutant HERC1 protein, associated with a loss of interaction between HERC1 and PSMC6. Together, these findings establish a link between HERC1-associated neurological disorders and defective ubiquitylation pathways. They elucidate the molecular mechanisms by which HERC1 regulates proteostasis and demonstrate how disruption of these processes contributes to disease pathogenesis, thereby highlighting potential avenues for therapeutic intervention.

Title: Expansion of human hematopoietic stem cells by inhibiting translation
Authors: Li, C.; Shin, H.; Bhavanasi, D.; Liu, M.; Briones, M. I.; Yu, X.; Liu, X.; Herbst, F.; Said, H.; Alameh, M.-G.; Breda, L.; Kovuru, N.; Kwa, Y.; Sam Ravi, N.; Schultz, D. C.; Cherry, S. R.; Rivella, S.; Alvarez--Dominguez, J. R.; Blobel, G. A.; Gregory, B. D.; Peslak, S. A.; Huang, J.; Klein, P. S.
Abstract: Hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) transplantation using umbilical cord blood (UCB) is a potentially life-saving treatment for leukemia and bone marrow failure but is limited by the low number of HSCs in UCB. The loss of HSCs after ex vivo manipulation is also a major obstacle to gene editing for inherited blood disorders. HSCs require a low rate of translation to maintain their capacity for self-renewal, but hematopoietic cytokines used to expand HSCs stimulate protein synthesis and impair long-term self-renewal. We previously described cytokine-free conditions that maintain but do not expand human and mouse HSCs ex vivo. Here we performed a high-throughput screen and identified translation inhibitors that allow ex vivo expansion of human HSCs while minimizing cytokine exposure. Transplantation assays show a ~4.3-fold expansion of long-term HSCs from UCB after one week of culture in low cytokine conditions that include the translation initiation inhibitor 4E1RCat. Single cell transcriptomic analysis demonstrates maintenance of the HSC/MPP transcriptional signature and reduced expression of stress markers under culture conditions that maintain or expand functional long-term HSCs. Addition of 4E1RCat induces a dose-dependent increase in autophagic vacuoles and reduces expression of oxidative phosphorylation and cell cycle gene expression programs. These culture conditions maintain adult HSCs after CRISPR/Cas9 editing of the BCL11A+58 enhancer, overcoming a major obstacle to ex vivo gene correction for human hemoglobinopathies.

Title: Ex vivo autologous immune cell assay to study modulation of type 2 Inflammation by processed- or novel food extracts in peanut allergy
Authors: Janssen, R.; Berends, A. J.; Zuurveld, M.; Terlouw, S.; de Jong, G. A. H.; Somhorst, D. B. P. M.; Boudewijn, A.; Veenbergen, S.; Wichers, H. J.; Garssen, J.; Bastiaan-Net, S.; Masereeuw, R.; de Jong, N. W.; Willemsen, L. E.
Abstract: Peanut allergy represents a major food-allergy burden, raising concerns about food processing and novel dietary products. Current diagnostics assess primarily allergic endpoints rather than immune mechanisms initiating and maintaining type 2 inflammation, particularly DC2-mediated Th2 polarization. Here, an ex vivo autologous type 2 inflammatory monocyte-derived dendritic cell (moDC) DC2/T cell and B cell assay has been introduced enabling to study immunomodulatory effects induced by unprocessed (P-D) versus processed (P-DH (heated) or P-DHG (heated and glycated)) peanut proteins. Separately, different emerging food samples were assessed (protein concentrates or whole biomass) enabling to study their capacities to modify inflammatory DC2/T cell responses. CD14+ monocytes, CD4+ T cells and CD19+ B cells were isolated from six peanut-allergic patients' PBMCs. MoDCs generated with IL4/GM-CSF were exposed (48h) to type 2 polarizing cytokine (DC2) mix, or DC2 mix combined with the food samples. Next, DC2s were co-cultured with T cells (5d), followed by B cells incubation with DC2/T cell supernatant and food samples (10d). Supernatants and cells were analyzed for Th1/Th2/Th-regulatory (Treg) cells, IgE and IgG profiles. DC2 induced a strong Th2 phenotype and activity, P-D DC2 further enhanced IL13 secretion and %Tregs. P-DH DC2 favored Th2, whereas P-DHG DC2 increased IFN{gamma}, with neither increasing %Treg. P-D and P-DH DC2 increased CD40L+CD25+ memory Th2, and P-DHG showed the same tendency. Wheat, whey and seaweed biomass had little effect on DC2/Th2 driven type 2 inflammation at the dose studied, whereas algae showed distinct immunomodulatory, adjuvant-like activity upon co-exposure during inflammatory DC2 maturation. In conclusion, this autologous in vitro assay captures modification of type 2 inflammatory response in DC2-Th2 interaction, which can compile both allergen-specific and generic reactivity to food samples, supporting the potential future use of this assay as an additional tool to assess type 2-driving potential and possible allergenicity of emerging foods and processing methods in peanut-allergic patients.

Title: One high-order ion-coupling mechanism generates multiple SLC1A stoichiometries
Authors: Wu, Q.; Jiang, Y.; Briot, C.; Fakharzadeh, A.; Dooley, M. M.; Pant, S.; Venugopal, H.; Reddy, K. D.; Tajkhorshid, E.; Ryan, R. M.
Abstract: Human excitatory amino acid transporter 2 (hEAAT2) is a glial transporter that clears glutamate and aspartate from the extracellular space to terminate neurotransmission. When this essential role is disrupted, excess extracellular glutamate causes excitotoxicity and neurological disease. hEAAT2 transports amino acids into cells against their concentration gradients by coupling uptake to the co-transport of Na+ and H+, and counter-transport of K+. Substrate transport also activates a thermodynamically uncoupled Cl- conductance, whose significance is unknown. Here, to dissect the molecular mechanisms underlying coupled and uncoupled ion transport by EAATs, we leverage the tractable Drosophila melanogaster homologue dEAAT2, which transports taurine as well as glutamate and aspartate. By functionally characterising dEAAT2, we confirmed it has features of a canonical EAAT transport cycle, including an uncoupled Cl- conductance. However, it functions an ion-independent electroneutral exchanger, in stark contrast to its ion-coupled electrogenic human counterpart. Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) and computational simulations confirmed the inability of dEAAT2 to transport cations, but just two point mutations conferred Na+, H+, and K+ dependence, reconstituting the complex ion coupling profile of human transporters in the Drosophila exchanger. We also showed that dEAAT2 transports taurine in a complex with Cl-, bestowing a unique Cl--dependence on taurine transport, independent of uncoupled Cl- flux. Our findings show that ancestral exchangers in the EAAT family preserve the machinery to achieve complex ion-coupled transport, revealing the molecular basis of high-order ion coupling in hEAATs.

Title: Cerebrospinal Fluid Inflammation in Prodromal Parkinson's Disease
Authors: Yasumizu, Y.; Deerhake, M. E.; Corbin-Stein, N. J.; Neish, K. J.; Moon, J.; Buitrago-Pocasangre, N.; Renkl, E.; Esposito, S.; Russo, A.; Wang, H.; Zhu, B.; Seibyl, J. P.; Reddy, V.; Cheon, M.; Wang, Q.; Spillantini, M. G.; Posner, D. A.; Sumida, T. S.; Longbrake, E. E.; Clatworthy, M.; Cedarbaum, J. M.; Zhang, L.; Hafler, D. A.
Abstract: We hypothesized that prodromal Parkinson's disease (PD), characterized by rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder (RBD) and/or hyposmia, begins with inflammation in the central nervous system that evolves into neurodegeneration. We combined clinical phenotyping and proteomics with single-cell RNA sequencing of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and blood from individuals with RBD, PD, and healthy controls, with multiple sclerosis as a comparator. CSF immune cell numbers were increased in RBD, particularly in those with lower prodromal PD probability scores, a composite score associated with time to phenoconversion. In these participants, CSF macrophages showed enhanced TNF, IL-6/JAK/STAT3, and interferon-{gamma} signaling and predicted crosstalk with CD4+ T cells involving TNF, antigen presentation, and costimulatory pathways. CSF Macrophages resembled mouse dural macrophages and shared TNF signaling with gut immune cells from -synuclein mouse models. These findings uncover a stage-specific TNF-associated inflammation involving crosstalk between CSF Macrophages and CD4+ T cells in prodromal PD.

Title: Vermeer: Autoregressive generative modeling of microscopy predicts protein localization
Authors: Kambhampati, S.; Zimmermann, E.; Hayir, E.; Yang, K. K.; Chen, F.; Lu, A. X.
Abstract: Fluorescent microscopy provides a rich view into how proteins localize within cells, but it remains experimentally infeasible to image human proteins across all of the different factors that can impact localization. We introduce Vermeer, a channel-adaptive autoregressive generative model for in silico generation of microscopy images of protein localization. Vermeer conditions generations on protein sequences and landmark stains showing the morphology of cells, which enables it to generalize to unseen proteins and cell lines. We show that Vermeer, trained on the Human Protein Atlas, can generate images with substantially improved perceptual quality and biological fidelity over previous proposals. Additionally, Vermeer's autoregressive framework enables flexible generation using varying channel subsets and orderings, enabling zero-shot transfer to data collected under different imaging conditions and channel configurations than those used for training. These results position Vermeer to enable scalable modeling of protein localization and is a step towards generative foundation models that can operate over distinct microscopy datasets. Code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/microsoft/vermeer.git.

Title: Detection of zoonotic Cryptosporidium parvum in invasive beavers from southern Tierra del Fuego, Chile
Authors: Aguilar, P. A. L.; Contreras, G.; Cabrera, G.; Arredondo, C.; Dougnac, C.; Federici, F.; Briceno, C.
Abstract: Since their introduction to Tierra del Fuego in 1946, invasive beavers have expanded their population and caused extensive environmental degradation across the subantarctic region. Beaver dams have profoundly impacted peatlands, mature sub-Antarctic forests, and watercourses. Here, we report a pathogen in invasive beavers in Patagonia and discuss their potential role as a reservoir of waterborne zoonotic pathogens. We detected Cryptosporidium through microscopy using the Ziehl-Neelsen staining technique in beaver collected from southern Tierra del Fuego. Out of the 105 beavers examined, three tested positive to optical microscopy, which were then identified molecularly as Cryptosporidium parvum by sequence analysis of the 18S ribosomal DNA (rDNA). Given the potential impacts of Cryptosporidium parvum upon native species, wildlife, and human health, this finding highlights the potential risks associated with the ongoing expansion of beavers into other areas of the sub-Antarctic region. A potential role of invasive beavers as reservoirs of zoonotic Cryptosporidium spp. in Patagonia emphasizes the unknown consequences of human-introduced exotic species on pristine ecosystems.

Title: PolyFold: Homology Filtering Approach Alters Apparent Structure Prediction Model Performances
Authors: Stephenson, H.; Voicu, D.; Novakov, V.; Levy, M.; Marsilio, J.; Kottke, C.; Sarparast, S.; Ebert, M.
Abstract: As structure prediction models become increasingly central to biological research and drug discovery, rigorous and reproducible benchmarking is critical to assess model performance and generalization. PolyFold is an end-to-end workflow automation and benchmarking framework that streamlines input file creation, batch automation, and a more conservative evaluation of model performances. We conduct a head-to-head comparison of Boltz-2 and OpenFold 3 - leading open-source alternatives to AlphaFold 3. We first curate an evaluation set of several thousand high-quality PDB structures, homology-filtered against both models' training sets, then automate inference and evaluation using PolyFold. Using a cluster analysis, we directly connect features of the underlying structures to model performance profiles, demonstrating the nonrandom nature of failure and success modes. While initial analyses using conventional homology filtering techniques show performance differences favouring Boltz-2, we show that using minimum chain fractional identity for novelty filtering can cause residual training-data leakage in multichain complexes, inflating apparent performances. To address this, we introduce a length-weighted average fractional identity (WAFI) for whole-complex homology filtering. This provides a more conservative evaluation by reducing residual leakage. While Boltz-2 maintains higher aggregate metric averages for categories such as nucleic acid-containing structures, membrane-bound proteins, and antibody-antigen complexes, the performance gap significantly narrows or disappears for effectively all partitions after implementing WAFI filtering, demonstrating the need for more stringent conventions in homology filtering. Both models still struggle with homomultimers, small molecule realism, and structures with non-canonical amino acids, demonstrating persisting limitations in the field. In summary, PolyFold enables practitioners to rapidly compare models on a variety of inference tasks and supports the broader adoption of accessible computational tools to facilitate biomolecular science.

Title: SOX7 and ERG reprograms neuroectoderm into microenvironmentally attuned brain endothelial cells that possess forebrain regional bias
Authors: Lu, T. M.; Akcan, U.; Rhee, A. J.; Cui, A.; Wang, J.; Houghton, S.; Geng, F.; Martinez, V. A.; Shahriar, S.; Xiang, J. Z.; Rozenwaks, Z.; Rafii, S.; Pedersen, I. M.; Gorman, J.; Wadgaonkar, R.; Barone, F. C.; Galie, P.; Agalliu, D.; Lis, R.
Abstract: Reliable human blood brain barrier (BBB) models are limited by a persistent problem of cellular identity: many protocols select cells for barrier or transporter properties rather than authentic, regionally specified brain endothelium. Here we show that constitutive expression of the transcription factors SOX7 and ERG converts human pluripotent stem cell derived epithelial barrier-forming cells into bona-fide vascular endothelial cells (SE rECs) whose transcriptome and proteome converge on primary human brain endothelium. Benchmarked against a human adult-brain endothelial atlas, SEr ECs acquire a forebrain-biased regional program stronger than that of permissively (ETS-)reprogrammed or umbilical-vein endothelial cells, reproducibly across biological replicates, although it does not reach the absolute regional identity of in-vivo brain endothelium. At the transcript level, epithelial-derived barrier forming cells (iBFCs) cells score highly on select barrier and transporters genes yet lack endothelial lineage identity, showing that transporter benchmarks alone do not establish endothelial fate. Coculture of SE rECs with astrocytes and pericytes in a two-dimensional neurovascular-unit model as well as a perfused microfluidic device induces mature BBB features and reduces paracellular permeability. SE rECs thus provide a lineage-faithful, organotypically informed platform for modelling the human BBB.

Title: A short nucleophosmin isoform couples nucleolar remodeling to DNA damage repair during meiosis
Authors: Potgieter, S.; Nayyab, S.; Uccello, M.; Snyder, E. M.
Abstract: Nucleoli are nuclear compartments wherein ribosome biogenesis occurs. Observations spanning over a century have demonstrated that meiotic male germ cell nucleoli have unusual morphology and a close association with a large DNA damage repair foci formed around the sex chromosomes termed the XY-body. A mechanistic understanding of this relationship and its impact on ribosome biogenesis has remained elusive. High-resolution microscopy revealed XY-body associated nucleoli have an unusual two-part morphology made up of an XY-body intercalated and an XY-body adjacent part, each marked by different isoforms of the nucleolar protein nucleophosmin. Additionally, the entire structure is transcriptionally inactive and likely derived from autosomal nucleoli. Further, proper formation and maintenance of the structure rely on an interaction between NPM1 and the DNA damage marker {gamma}H2AX. These findings provide mechanistic insight into the XY-body and nucleolus association and reveal unrecognized connections between nucleolar proteins, ribosome biogenesis, and DNA damage repair during meiosis.

Title: Proteomic analysis of early SASP-associated responses in doxorubicin-treated cardiac fibroblasts
Authors: Riojas, A. M.; Gharraee, N.; Hamid, Z.; Dragun, K. W.; Zimmerman, K. D.; Olivier, M.; Melendez, G. C.
Abstract: Anthracycline-induced cardiotoxicity is associated with progressive cardiac dysfunction and fibrotic remodeling, processes in which cardiac fibroblast senescence and the senescence-associated secretory phenotype have been implicated. However, the early secretory responses that precede established senescence following doxorubicin (DOX) exposure remain poorly defined. Primary cardiac fibroblasts isolated from healthy rat hearts were treated with varying concentrations of DOX (0-3 M) for 24 hours. Media collected at Day 1 were analyzed by untargeted proteomics, while cell viability, proliferation, and senescence-associated {beta}-galactosidase activity were assessed at Days 1 and 7. Acute DOX exposure reduced cell viability and proliferation at Day 1 without significantly increasing senescence-associated {beta}-galactosidase activity. At Day 7, we observed persistent proliferative arrest and increased {beta}-galactosidase activity with DOX exposure, consistent with delayed senescence. Proteomic analysis of Day 1 conditioned media identified 35 proteins significantly associated with DOX treatment after false discovery rate correction (22 positive and 13 negative associations; P-FDR < 0.05). Functional annotation identified proteins related to extracellular matrix (ECM) regulation, mitochondrial function, cellular stress, cytoskeletal organization, calcium signaling, protease activity, and cell-cycle regulation. Network analysis identified a collagen-centered network (COL1A1, COL1A2, and COL3A1) associated with reduced abundance of ECM proteins and a second network centered on GAPDH, HSPA8, and HSPA9 that included proteins associated with mitochondrial proteostasis, oxidative stress, metabolic adaptation, and structural remodeling.

Title: Rab7 activation ameliorates impaired lysosome dynamics and mitophagic flux during chronic iron overload
Authors: Mansat, M.; Sung, H. K.; Tam, E.; Anwar, S.; Narciso, M. R.; Sweeney, G.; Botelho, R. J.
Abstract: Iron homeostasis is essential for cellular function, yet iron overload is linked to pathologies including cardiovascular disease and metabolic syndrome. Although excess iron has been associated with impaired autophagy and mitochondrial dysfunction, the effects of iron overload on lysosomal dynamics and mitophagy remain poorly defined. In this study, we demonstrate that iron overload disrupts mitochondrial morphology and lysosomal homeostasis, accompanied by iron accumulation in both organelles. While mitophagy is triggered upon iron overload, mitophagic flux is impaired, suggesting a defect in mitophagosome maturation and incomplete clearance. Notably, lysosomes in iron loaded cells were hyper-acidic and degradative, but became enlarged, perinuclear, and less motile, suggesting that altered lysosomal dynamics may contribute to defective mitophagic clearance. Interestingly, pharmacological activation of Rab7 restores lysosomal motility and mitophagic flux under iron overload conditions. It also improves mitochondrial function and cell viability. Together, these findings indicate that iron overload disrupts organelle homeostasis by impairing lysosomal and mitochondrial dynamics, ultimately arresting mitophagic flux due to altered lysosome dynamics and promoting cell death. Targeted activation of Rab7 mitigates these iron-induced effects, providing a potential therapeutic target for iron overload-induced cell death and tissue damage.

Title: DM4ISL: high-fidelity and uncertainty-aware in silico labeling of fluorescence images via diffusion models
Authors: Rotem, O.; Kliper-Gross, O.; Zaritsky, A.
Abstract: In silico labeling predicts organelle-specific localizations from label-free images, potentially enabling longitudinal and multiplexed live-cell imaging. Here we present DM4ISL (Diffusion Model for In Silico Labeling), a high-fidelity and uncertainty-aware model that overcomes current limitations, such as blurry or structurally inaccurate predictions, by resolving the intrinsic entanglement of biological signal and noise that characterizes fluorescence imaging. DM4ISL leverages the iterative nature of diffusion through a step-wise self-ensemble averaging approach that marginalizes these stochastic fluctuations, preventing the overfitting to noise that typically degrades standard final-step predictions. Benchmarking across six organelles demonstrates that DM4ISL systematically outperforms state-of-the-art architectures in structural fidelity, as confirmed through both pixel-based and application-specific metrics. Furthermore, calculating the standard deviation across intermediate denoising steps generates localized uncertainty maps that automatically detect erroneous predictions at inference time. Providing high-fidelity predictions alongside built-in reliability metrics, DM4ISL offers a robust method for trustworthy, data-driven discovery in cell biology.

Title: Mapping genome-wide RNA-RNA and RNA-DNA interactions in nuclear hubs of male and female Drosophila cells
Authors: Gunasekera, S.; Carlson, M.; Ray, M.; Larschan, E.
Abstract: Nuclear bodies are nucleoprotein complexes with established functions that target chromatin at specific locations and regulate specific RNA processing functions, thereby influencing gene expression. However, the mechanisms that define how nuclear bodies are targeted to specific locations within the genome where they function remain poorly understood. One significant challenge is capturing and understanding the multiple cell-specific interactions occurring in these complexes, arising from RNA components interacting with each other and with DNA and nucleic acid-binding proteins within the context of the nucleus's three-dimensional organization. Mapping these interactions is critical for elucidating mechanisms such as RNA splicing, a key driver of cell-specific transcript diversity. Here, we use RNA-DNA Split Pool Recognition of Interactions by Tag Extension (RD-SPRITE) to characterize, for the first time, sex-specific RNA-RNA and RNA-DNA interactions in Drosophila S2 (male) and Kc (female) cells. We determined the sex-specific RNA-RNA interaction map within the nucleus and, using RNA-DNA interaction data, pinpointed the target loci of various RNA molecules, including small nuclear RNAs (snRNAs), which are core components of the spliceosome, ribonucleoprotein complex involved in RNA splicing. Based on RNA-RNA interaction data, we also identified novel long non-coding RNAs that may regulate splicing. Furthermore, we investigated the role of transcription factor (TF) CLAMP in sex-specific targeting of the spliceosome. We generated RD-SPRITE datasets in the presence and absence of CLAMP, a key TF involved in dosage compensation, sex-specific RNA splicing, and chromatin organization. We determined that CLAMP regulates global changes in spliceosomal interactions with chromatin, inhibits aberrant snRNA interactions, and regulates sex-specific interactions of RNAs involved in splicing function. Additionally, our dataset provides a valuable resource for investigating additional processes, such as miRNA-mediated silencing, nucleolar functions of snoRNAs, and Cajal body functions of scaRNAs, among others. To facilitate broad community use, we have developed a computational platform, "FlySprite," that enables Drosophila researchers to explore sex-specific RNA-RNA interactions, as well as DNA targets of RNA clusters, through a user-friendly interface.

Title: Within-colony color variation in a chalice coral is associated with region-specific pigment expression and higher photoconvertible pigment transcripts
Authors: Baumgarte, O.; Moore, Z. J.
Abstract: A single colony of colonial coral often demonstrates conspicuous color variation. However, the molecular basis of this variation within a single, clonal individual is poorly understood. While coral tissues within a single colony have distinct colors, they share the same genetic background, suggesting differences between them are regulatory rather than genetic. This pilot study aims to characterize the transcriptional mechanisms of color regions in a green-and-orange chalice coral colony through an end-to-end transcriptomic analysis.
