First, we sampled the green body, an orange oral region, and a transition region between them. Then, a holobiont transcriptome was assembled de novo from paired-end RNA-seq of each color region. In the holobiont transcriptome, coral host transcripts were separated from dinoflagellate symbiont transcripts. Green fluorescent protein (GFP)-like pigment genes were classified phylogenetically. Their expression was then quantified using host-only normalization, which corrects for a large regional difference in symbiont read fraction, and compared across color regions. Relative to the green body, the orange oral region showed higher expression of two sets of host pigment genes: distinct orange fluorescent-protein and chromoprotein transcripts, and green-to-red photoconvertible EosFP-family proteins whose unconverted state is green, implicating photoconversion as a contributing mechanism. This study reveals that distinct color regions within a single colony are associated with region-specific up-regulation of different pigment transcripts, including both directly colored proteins and photoconvertible proteins. Further research is needed to confirm spectrally that photoconversion contributes to the coloration and test whether the pattern holds across multiple colonies.

Title: Freebie: A Multi-Camera System for Real-Time Markerless Hand Tracking in Non-Human Primates
Authors: Joseph, J. C.; Ceradini, M.; Liu, L.; Kelberman, M.; Mender, M. J.; DeMatteo, J.; Lee, O.; Temmar, H.; Copenhaver, M.; Ward, A.; Kung, T.; Chestek, C. A.; Draelos, A.
Abstract: Objective. Neural decoders for dexterous finger movements are limited by the accuracy with which ground truth movement is measured. In non-human primates (NHPs), hand kinematics are typically recorded with instrumentation that constrains movement dimensionality. We evaluated whether a markerless camera system could replace conventional methods for tracking movements in real time. Approach. We developed Freebie, a real-time markerless system for tracking NHP finger movements. Keypoints detected online were used in place of manipulandum bend sensor signals. Two NHPs performed tasks by flexing fingers to move a virtual hand into target zones. The virtual hand was directly controlled using bend sensors or Freebie-derived kinematics, or indirectly controlled through a Kalman filter (KF) decoding kinematics from forearm electromyographic (EMG) activity. We quantified Freebie's accuracy relative to manual labels, agreement with bend sensor measurements, and latencies. We assessed online performance under Freebie control and compared EMG KFs trained using Freebie-derived labels with those trained using bend-sensor-derived labels. Main Results. We observed a median end-to-end latency of 15.8 ms at a 30 FPS camera acquisition rate, and 16.2 ms at 60 FPS. Freebie labels closely tracked bend sensor positions (median |r|=0.96). Median keypoint errors were 1.7 to 6.5 pixels, below the 20-pixel width of the smallest tracked finger. Direct Freebie control did not differ from bend sensor control on five of six online metrics; path efficiency was higher with Freebie. EMG KFs trained on Freebie-derived labels performed similarly to those trained on bend sensor labels online. When evaluated offline, models trained with Freebie had lower error. Significance. These findings indicate that bend sensors are not required to obtain finger labels for training a decoder: markerless keypoints alone provided effective labels. This is an important first step towards real-time tracking of more complex movements, beyond what could be easily measured with a manipulandum.

Title: Engineered endocrine objects tolerate hypoxia in macroencapsulation devices and enable subcutaneous engraftment in diabetic mice
Authors: Wang, K.; Okada, K.; Jin, M.; Deng, J.; Wang, B.; Flanders, J. A.; Tran, P. L.; Lee, M.; Ma, M.
Abstract: Islet encapsulation has been pursued for decades as a potential immunosuppression-free transplantation strategy to treat type 1 diabetes (T1D). The encapsulation device protects islets from immune cell-contact mediated killing, but it also prevents vascular penetration and intra-islet vascularization, leading to poor mass transfer and islet central necrosis. In healthy pancreas, islets with sizes > ~40 m are vascularized while non-islet endocrine cell clusters below ~40 m exist without internal capillaries. Here, we developed scalable and reproducible engineered endocrine objects (EEOs) as small as ~47 m by mesh-induced fragmentation of native islets, followed by a recovery culture. Under hypoxic culture condition (1% O2 for 24 hours), EEOs showed enhanced viability of >90%, compared to 49% for the native islet control. With a flat, thin (0.5-mm-thick) alginate-based macroencapsulation device, rat EEOs at a marginal dose of 300 islet equivalents (IEQ) achieved glycemic control for over 5 weeks in the challenging, hypoxic subcutaneous space of immunocompetent diabetic mice. The engrafted mice displayed near-physiological glycemic profiles upon glucose challenge, and the retrieved EEOs showed enhanced viability with significantly reduced central necrosis compared with native islets. Overall, engineering hypoxia-resistance into cellular products mitigates intrinsic constraints of encapsulation devices, offering a promising strategy for convenient, immunosuppression-free subcutaneous islet transplantation.

Title: Versatile and Cross-Species Alveolar Type II Cell Isolation Using Humanized Monoclonal Antibody Upifitamab
Authors: Forrester, M. T.; Liu, S.; Tsuge, K.; Lee-Ferris, R.; Rangarajan, K.; Cumming, R. I.; Enkhbayar, K.; Morowitz, J. M.; Whitlow, T. J.; Tata, A.; Li, B.; Eyler, C. E.; Tighe, R. M.; Tata, P. R.
Abstract: Alveolar type 2 (AT2) cells are primary adult alveolar stem cells that maintain healthy alveoli. AT2 cell dysfunction is broadly linked to many lung pathologies from emphysema to fibrosis. Isolation of AT2 cells with high purity is therefore central to diagnostic studies, proteomics, transcriptomics and ex vivo experiments that can lead to future AT2 cellular therapies. Current markers for AT2 isolation exhibit various limitations from species-restrictions (e.g., mouse vs human) to limited AT2 specificity, which creates challenges for flow cytometric gating/sorting and application to magnetic-activated cell isolation. While underrepresented in the literature, these bottlenecks have made AT2 cell isolation inherently difficult and slowed AT2 cell research. Here we leverage surface protein-restricted transcriptomics to identify the sodium phosphate transporter NaPi2b (SLC34A2) as a highly specific AT2 cell marker optimally detected with the humanized monoclonal antibody upifitamab. Upifitamab-based labeling of AT2 cells is compatible with flow cytometric or magnetic-activated AT2 isolation and applies to both mouse and human AT2 cells, thus streamlining protocols and circumventing species-specific nuances. AT2 cells obtained with upifitamab can be cultured as organoids, in monolayers or differentiated to AT1 cells. This simplified AT2 isolation approach should overcome several current barriers while facilitating ex vivo studies on alveolar biology and related therapeutic developments.

Title: HPV Oncogenes rewire DNA crosslink repair to create a PRIMPOL-dependent therapeutic vulnerability
Authors: Dessapt, J.; Berube, M.-A.; Le Doeuff, O.; Soucy, N.; Balistaire, L.; Morin, B.; Valeh Sheida, s.; Blondeau, A.; Coulombe, Y.; G. Lavoie, E.; Masson, J.-Y. M. I.; Hussein, S. M. I.; Fradet-Turcotte, A.
Abstract: Cisplatin-based chemoradiation is the standard of care for both HPV-negative (HPV-) and HPV-positive (HPV+) head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), even though patients with HPV+ tumors have better treatment responses and a better prognosis. Understanding how HPV status shapes this response could guide alternative strategies that lower long-term toxicity. Using genome-wide CRISPR screens, we show that the genetic requirements for surviving chemoradiation diverge between HPV- and HPV+ HNSCC cells. HPV+ cells tolerate cisplatin-induced interstrand crosslinks independently of the Fanconi anemia pathway, a phenotype recapitulated by expressing HPV16 E6 and E7 in an HPV-negative background. In these cells, DNA damage tolerance depends instead on PRIMPOL-mediated repriming and post-replicative gap filling by translesion synthesis polymerases. Although they recruit BRCA1 normally to double-strand breaks, BRCA1 accumulation at cisplatin-stalled forks is markedly reduced, indicating that BRCA1 function is uncoupled between these two substrates. This tolerance pathway leaves cells dependent on dynamic RAD51 turnover at single-stranded DNA gaps. Depletion of the RAD51 unloading factor FIRRM, or chemical stabilization of RAD51 filaments, selectively kills HPV+ and HPV oncogene-expressing cells treated with cisplatin, and PRIMPOL depletion rescues this lethality. Our findings show that HPV oncogenes rewire the response to crosslink-induced replication stress and identify RAD51 filament dynamics as a therapeutic vulnerability in HPV+ HNSCC.

Title: Lipid-Driven NRF2 Preconditioning Links Estrogen Deprivation to Hepatic Resilience Against Acetaminophen Injury
Authors: Garcia Consuegra, J.; Goikoetxea Usandizaga, N.; Gil Martin, A. Q.; Sagrera, A.; Lanza Arnaiz, J. M.; Gonzalez Recio, I.; Conter, C.; Andrade, R. J.; Lucena, M. I.; Grumati, P.; Ramos Molina, B.; Area-Gomez, E.; Dear, J. W.; Humphries, C.; Formentini, L.; Martinez Chantar, M. L.; Cogliati, S.
Abstract: Background & Aims: Menopause is associated with a sustained decline in estrogen signaling that profoundly alters hepatic lipid metabolism; however, its impact on the liver response to xenobiotic stress remains poorly understood. Given that acetaminophen (APAP) overdose is a leading cause of drug-induced acute liver failure (DILI) and that sex and age influence susceptibility to hepatotoxicity, we investigated how long-term estrogen deprivation affects the development of APAP-induced liver injury (AP-ILI). Methods: Clinical data from a multicenter cohort of patients admitted following APAP overdose were analyzed to assess susceptibility to AP-ILI. To model the postmenopausal state, 12-week-old female C57BL/6JOlaHsd mice underwent bilateral ovariectomy (OVX) or sham surgery and, six months later, were challenged with acetaminophen (360 or 600 mg/kg). Mechanistic studies included NRF2 silencing, estradiol replacement, and dietary lipid modulation using a high-fat diet. Comprehensive lipidomic profiling was performed to characterize hepatic lipid remodeling, while human liver biopsies were analyzed to validate the expression of key molecular targets. Results: Women [≥]50 years of age showed a lower risk of severe AP-ILI, a phenotype recapitulated in OVX mice. Long-term estrogen deprivation induced hepatic lipid remodeling characterized by larger lipid droplets and enrichment in saturated neutral lipids, leading to sustained NRF2 activation. Enhancement of lipid remodeling with high-fat diet increased NRF2 signaling and hepatoprotection, whereas estradiol replacement reversed these effects. Consistent with these findings, women over 50 years of age exhibited increased hepatic expression of NRF2 and its target genes. Conclusions: Long-term estrogen deprivation confers protection against AP-ILI through extensive hepatic lipid remodeling, characterized by lipid droplet expansion and altered neutral lipid composition, which promotes sustained NRF2 activation.

Title: Volumetric building blocks: A simple and modular approach to create perfusable models via assembly of volumetrically printed subunits
Authors: Bartolf-Kopp, M.; Geroneit, I.; Gergely, C.; Moser, F.; Galaba, L.; Chicaiza-Cabezas, N.; Priebe, V.; Beaumont, M.; Jungst, T.
Abstract: Tomographic volumetric additive manufacturing (tVAM) enables rapid 3D printing of constructs with intricate, freestanding geometries. Besides demonstrating very promising applications in tissue engineering and biofabrication, a limitation of the technology has been the relatively high material consumption and limited maximal model size due to optical and technical constraints. Here we demonstrate the fabrication and use of highly modular hollow structures created with tVAM to produce large scale tubular systems that allow the formation of complex, hollow networks beyond the build space of commercial tVAM devices. In many cases, it can reduce the overall dead volume used for printing by more than 50% compared to printing the whole structure at once. As proof of concept, we made a channel system recapitulating the physiological complexity of human vasculature in vitro. The system was tested with liquid flow dynamic and stent placement into stenosed segments to show that leaktight models could be created. Further, by using gelatin methacryloyl, a large-scale system out of seven single units could be created and effectively endothelialized, showing the potential of the approach for fabrication of physiological stent placement phantoms or vascular tissue models.

Title: Effective utilization of xylose-rich substrates for butyric acid production by Clostridium tyrobutyricum ATCC 25755 despite carbon catabolite repression
Authors: Kim, K.-Y.; Oh, H. J.; Ahn, J. H.; Ko, J. K.; Gong, G.; Um, Y.
Abstract: Carbon catabolite repression (CCR) can restrict xylose utilization during butyric acid production from lignocellulosic hydrolysates by Clostridium tyrobutyricum ATCC 25755. This study evaluated CCR behavior using 2-deoxy-D-glucose (2-DG), a glucose analog, and examined the effects of glucose-xylose composition on mixed-sugar fermentation. 2-DG caused concentration-dependent growth inhibition in xylose-containing medium, indicating CCR-like behavior. However, xylose was partially co-consumed in the presence of glucose or 2-DG, suggesting incomplete inhibition. In batch fermentations with 80 g/L total sugars, the overall xylose consumption rate declined from 2.68 to 0.53 g/L/h as the initial glucose concentration increased from 20 to 60 g/L. Nevertheless, a xylose-rich mixture (20 g/L glucose and 60 g/L xylose) achieved an overall total sugar consumption rate of 3.54 g/L/h and a butyric acid productivity of 1.22 g/L/h, comparable to those with 80 g/L glucose alone (3.64 and 1.26 g/L/h, respectively). Detectable xylose isomerase activity during glucose-xylose co-utilization further supported incomplete repression of xylose metabolism. In xylose-rich rice straw hydrolysate (5.0 g/L glucose and 15.1 g/L xylose), both sugars were completely consumed, producing 7.68 g/L butyric acid. These findings suggest that xylose-rich mixtures can support effective sugar utilization and butyric acid production by C. tyrobutyricum despite its CCR-like behavior.

Title: Torque generation and regulation in the flagellar motor of Campylobacter jejuni differ from those of model organisms
Authors: Hoffmann, W. H.; Leturcq, S.; Giannetti, A.; Cohen, E. J.; Beeby, M.; Pedaci, F.; Nord, A. L.
Abstract: The bacterial flagellar motor is a rotary nanomachine that powers motility by driving the rotation of a helical filament. Most of our mechanistic understanding of this motor derives from studies of model organisms, particularly Escherichia coli and Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium, yet recent structural work has revealed substantial architectural diversity, raising questions about the universality of established biophysical models. Here, we present the first single-motor measurements of torque output and stator dynamics in Campylobacter jejuni, a species with a structurally elaborate motor adapted for motility in high-viscosity environments. The C.~jejuni motor generates an exceptionally high stall torque (~3600~pN{middle dot}nm) and, rather than the biphasic torque--speed relationship characteristic of model systems, exhibits an approximately linear decline in torque with increasing speed over the measured range. Time-resolved measurements reveal discrete speed changes, indicating that the stator output remains dynamic despite the presence of a scaffolded stator ring. The inferred number of active stator units averaged 11{+/-}4, below the 17-unit complement observed structurally, and showed no clear dependence on viscous load despite substantial motor-to-motor heterogeneity. Following transient collapse of the proton motive force, motor activity recovers rapidly, consistent with reversible activation of pre-associated stator units. Together, these findings reveal a distinct mode of flagellar motor operation, consistent with dynamic regulation of a preassembled stator ring rather than regulation through physical stator exchange, and show that the canonical behavior defined in model organisms is not universal.

Title: A quantitative molecular model of the lymphocyte death timer
Authors: Ruhle, M.; Thomas, E.; Dann, E.; Gottscheber, N.; Teh, C. E.; Gray, D. H.; Dowling, M. R.; Heinzel, S.; Hodgkin, P. D.
Abstract: When stimulated, individual lymphocytes program times for division and death that are inherited within families, revealing a common timing mechanism transmitted over generations. Here we describe a threshold-based mechanism for the time to die. By comparing protein levels in control and apoptosis disabled B and T lymphocytes, we show that death can be predicted by a cooperating ensemble of BCL-2 family proteins falling below a critical threshold. Single cell measurements predict the time of death with a simple formula, where additional inhibition factors explain accelerated death induced by BH3 mimetic compounds. Thus, we identify the death timer as a protein-threshold device that underlies signal integration machinery. Together these results reveal that predicting lymphocyte behavior at single cell level, in complex environments, is possible with modular models that incorporate independent timers and heritability features of critical proteins.

Title: Comparative transcriptomic response of bank vole kidney and respiratory epithelial cells to distinct orthohantaviruses
Authors: Badonnel, K.; Cokelaer, T.; Turc, E.; Monot, M.; Manuguerra, J.-C.; Ermonval, M.; Gallo, G.
Abstract: Orthohantaviruses are rodent-borne viruses distributed worldwide that can cause diseases of varying severity in humans following occasional aerosol transmission. While infections remain asymptomatic in their natural small-mammal reservoirs, hantaviral pathogenesis in humans is associated with an exacerbated immune response. The increasing number of outbreaks in endemic regions caused by the modification of rodent habitats due to human activities and the risks of reassortments in areas where multiple orthohantaviruses co-circulate with their animal reservoirs, are of public health concern. These challenges highlight the need to better understand how these viruses interact with host cells to spread within and between organisms, and how antiviral responses are regulated, particularly in their natural hosts. We previously showed that cellular susceptibility to orthohantaviruses depends on both cell type and virus species and correlates with cellular restrictions acting at different stages of the viral cycle. Here, we performed a comparative RNA-sequencing study and transcriptomic analysis of the cellular responses induced by three different orthohantaviruses in kidneys and respiratory tract cells derived from bank voles, the natural host of an orthohantavirus pathogenic to humans. Transcriptomic analyses revealed common as well as virus- and tissue-specific regulatory pathways that may underlie distinct infection outcomes. It highlighted the complexity of viral interactions with bank vole at a cellular level, including innate immune responses and antiviral signaling pathways.

Title: Chemical warfare in the rice plant rhizosphere: Diverse Pseudomonas antagonize the green alga Chlamydomonas
Authors: Yang, X.; Shetty, P.; Vajrangi, B.; Ul Haq, I.; Mittag, M.
Abstract: Algae and bacteria form dynamic partnerships that shape diverse ecosystems. The model green microalga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii is often found in paddy rice fields, where the diversity and functional characteristics of its bacterial partners remain largely unexplored. Here, we isolated 12 bacterial strains from the rice rhizosphere and its surrounding soil. Phylogenetic analysis based on 16S rRNA gene sequences revealed that eight isolates belong to the genus Pseudomonas. Three Pseudomonas rhizosphere strains exhibited antagonistic effects against C. reinhardtii, negatively impacting its growth, pigmentation and cell morphology. Close physical associations between the three antagonistic Pseudomonas strains and C. reinhardtii were observed in liquid cultures. Whole genome sequencing identified the antagonistic strains as Pseudomonas alloputida, Pseudomonas tohonis, and Pseudomonas asiatica. The three bacterial genomes encode several factors well-known for mediating chemical warfare. Notably, P. tohonis bears a gene cluster encoding the phenolic toxin, 2,4-diacetylphloroglucinol (DAPG). DAPG inhibits the growth and alters the cell morphology of C. reinhardtii. These findings expand our understanding of the diversity of bacterial partners associated with C. reinhardtii and highlight the role of Pseudomonas rice rhizosphere-associated bacteria as potent green algal antagonists. They harbor a reservoir of common functional traits that negatively influence green algal population dynamics.

Title: GradeBins: quality control of bins from synthetic and real metagenomes
Authors: Bushnell, B.; Bowers, R. M.; Villada, J. C.
Abstract: Genomes reconstructed from metagenomes support studies of microbial diversity and function, but their interpretation depends on how much DNA is recovered and whether foreign sequence is included. Quality can be measured in benchmarks, where contig origins are known, but must be estimated in routine analyses. Here we present GradeBins, which assesses individual bins (contigs assigned to one candidate genome) and summarizes the complete bin set from an assembly. For 6,374 simulated bins, its measurements agreed with AMBER and independent calculations within rounding. In control bins built from 20 kb fragments of reference genomes, GradeBins had lower observed completeness error than CheckM1 and CheckM2 and the highest observed F1 (the harmonic mean of precision and recall) for bin selection. With 2 kb fragments, GradeBins overestimated the completeness of incomplete bins, and its error increased from 3.1 to 17.6 percentage points. Contamination estimates differed among GradeBins, CheckM1, CheckM2 and GUNC, which define contamination differently. In sequenced metagenomes, the choice of estimator changed which bins passed quality cutoffs. GradeBins estimated quality faster than CheckM1, CheckM2 and GUNC on the same hardware. GradeBins thus provides fast quality assessment of prokaryotic bins and bin sets, with completeness estimates that are most accurate for long contigs.

Title: Structural basis for site-specific histone H3 acetylation-dependent regulation of RNAPII transcription through nucleosomes
Authors: Oishi, T.; Hatazawa, S.; Kujirai, T.; Suzuki, S.; Nakatsu, K.; Hayashi, G.; Kato, J.; Kobayashi, Y.; Ogasawara, M.; Ehara, H.; Sekine, S.-i.; Takizawa, Y.; Kurumizaka, H.
Abstract: Acetylation of histone H3 regulates chromatin dynamics and transcription, but how specific acetylation sites affect RNA polymerase II (RNAPII) transcription through nucleosomes remains unclear. Here, we found that H3 acetylation at Lys56 and Lys122 markedly enhances RNAPII transcription through nucleosomes, whereas acetylation at Lys64 has little effect. To elucidate the structural basis for these functional differences, we determined cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of nucleosomes bearing site-specific acetylation at H3K56, H3K64, or H3K122. The cryo-EM structures revealed that H3K56ac and H3K122ac locally weaken histone-DNA interactions at the DNA entry/exit region and near the dyad, respectively, while H3K64ac induces no detectable structural changes. These structural differences correlate with the observed transcriptional outcomes, indicating that acetylation at H3K56 and H3K122, but not H3K64, alleviates the nucleosomal barrier to RNAPII progression. Our findings provide direct structural evidence that specific acetylations within the histone fold domain of H3 fine-tune nucleosome dynamics to facilitate RNAPII transcription.

Title: Conjugative pilus tip structure reveals convergence in secretion systems
Authors: Paillard, P.; Rouger, Q.; Thomet, M.; Legros, J.; Georgeault, S.; Chat, S.; Giudice, E.; Mace, K.
Abstract: Bacteria deploy specialised secretion systems to transfer proteins and DNA into other cells, driving microbial evolution, virulence and the spread of antibiotic resistance1. Among these, type IV secretion systems (T4SSs) are unique in mediating both effector delivery and conjugative DNA transfer via extracellular pili that establish contact with recipient cells2. How these molecular machines couple recipient-cell engagement to the opening of a secretion channel is a central unresolved question across direct-contact secretion systems. Here we present the first high-resolution structure of a conjugative pilus tip from the R388 T4SS. The tip comprises the major pilin VirB2 and the minor pilin VirB5 together with two unexpected components: VirB6, repositioned from the inner-membrane stalk to the pilus apex where it forms a dynamic gate, and KikA, a modular distal adhesin likely involved in recipient-cell engagement. These findings unify pilus biogenesis, entry exclusion and recipient-cell engagement into a single structural mechanism in which VirB6 acts as a gatekeeper that couples tip contact to channel opening, while KikA shapes a pointed adhesin at the apex. By comparing this architecture to the type III and type VI secretion systems, we reveal convergent gating and penetration principles to contact-dependent bacterial secretion.

Title: A role for TRIP12 in regulating the E3 ligase network under proteotoxic stress
Authors: Trinh, H.; Kaschani, F.; Kaiser, M.; Lueong, S. S.; Siveke, J.; Paschen, A.; Hellerschmied, D.; Ehrmann, M.
Abstract: Cellular proteostasis relies on the coordinated action of molecular chaperones and protein degradation pathways to maintain protein folding and turnover. While the roles of chaperones and the proteasome are well established, how ubiquitin E3 ligases contribute to the proteostasis network remains incompletely understood. Here, we analyzed proteostasis in melanoma cells using quantitative proteomics under mild protein folding stress induced by HSP90 and proteasome inhibition. We identified the HECT-type E3 ligase TRIP12 as a proteostasis-responsive factor that was upregulated upon proteasome inhibition. Depletion of TRIP12 led to protein accumulation of a distinct group of epigenetic and transcriptional regulators, suggesting that these proteins may constitute a novel class of TRIP12 targets. Notably, the loss of TRIP12 led to a widespread reduction in the abundance of many other proteins, including components of the proteostasis network, particularly ubiquitin E3 ligases. These changes occurred largely without corresponding mRNA alterations, indicating post-transcriptional regulation. HSP90 inhibition similarly reduced protein abundance and acted in an additive manner with TRIP12 depletion to further destabilize the proteome. Together, our findings suggest that TRIP12 functions as a regulator of the E3 ligase network and proteostasis capacity, and that its loss, particularly under folding stress, causes a reduction of global protein content. These results reveal an unexpected role for TRIP12 in maintaining proteome stability and support the functional interplay between ubiquitin ligases and molecular chaperones in buffering proteotoxic stress.

Title: Extending Mendelian randomisation to founder-haplotype data in Diversity Outbred mice
Authors: Dai, X.; Hemani, G.; Mesner, L.; Calabrese, G.; Farber, C.; Churchill, G. A.; Davey Smith, G.
Abstract: Observational associations can reflect confounding or reverse causation, which Mendelian randomisation (MR) avoids by using genetic variation to estimate causal effects. In Diversity Outbred (DO) mice such estimates can be tested experimentally, but applying human summary-data MR, with one scalar association per variant, ignores the differing effects of their eight founder haplotypes. We introduce Founder GLS-IVW, which uses each locus's founder-effect pattern for causal estimation and diagnosis. At Qsox1, it recovered the direction of effect seen in knockout mice, which one scalar coding failed to detect. Across 4,596 trait pairs, scalar and founder analyses disagreed for 29.7%; in seven of eight, only the founder analysis found an effect, using information scalar coding discards. Because exposure and outcome may be measured in different or partly overlapping animals, the method supports two-sample MR across separate experiments. Our R package qtl2mr, built on the widely used R/qtl2, helps prioritise mechanistic experiments.

Title: Sedimentary ancient DNA expands bioarchaeological evidence and interpretation at Roman Harelbeke
Authors: Özdogan, K. T.; Furni, F.; Nota, K.; Erven, J.; Aal, J.; Reurings, S.; den Boef, L.; van Mousch, R.; de Groot, G. A.; Plets, G.
Abstract: Sedimentary ancient DNA (sedaDNA) can expand archaeological research by recovering broad biological signals from small amounts of sediment. Here, we apply shotgun sedaDNA metagenomics and target capture (also known as hybridization capture) to disused Roman wells from the vicus of Harelbeke, Belgium, dated to ca. 160-300 CE, and integrate the results with existing bioarchaeological datasets. Moving beyond individual introduced taxa as proxies for Roman influence, we reconstruct community-level profiles spanning consumption-related, synanthropic, and environmental organisms. SedaDNA reproduced most established bioarchaeological signals, including cultivated plants and domestic animals, while also recovering additional environmental taxa that established methods underrepresented. Mitochondrial target capture strengthened selected faunal detections and enabled phylogenetic placement of a pig (Sus scrofa) within the European mitochondrial lineage. The predominance of previously established consumption-related taxa is consistent with subsistence continuity and selective adoption of Roman-introduced resources, although taxon counts alone cannot establish their relative importance. Analytical-effort modeling further indicates that batch-based sedaDNA workflows can provide broad biological profiles at lower cost and time investment than established archaeological methods. Overall, sedaDNA complements conventional bioarchaeology by broadening taxonomic recovery, supporting scalable sampling, and providing a broad-spectrum approach to reconstructing settlement ecology, subsistence, and human-environment interaction.

Title: Designed Minibinders Rewire Receptor Signaling to Enable Functional Human Myogenic Reprogramming
Authors: Keshri, R.; Jessop, A.; Robinson, A. J.; Foreman, Z.; Barrett, P.; Reyes, G.; Krishnakumar, A.; Kumar, S.; Phal, A. A.; Narog, E.; Chiu, M.; Jain, S.; Wang, X.; Lee, D.; Exposit, M.; Abedi, M.; Smith, A. S. T.; Srivatsan, S. R.; Shendure, J.; Mathieu, J.; Mack, D. L.; Baker, D.; Ruohola-Baker, H.
Abstract: Sarcopenia, loss of muscle mass is a considerable health burden that demands immediate societal attention. Direct myogenic somatic cell reprogramming, a potential muscle regeneration method is constrained by an inability to control the signaling logic that governs cell fate. Here, we show that this barrier can be overcome using AI-designed receptor modulators. Screening de novo minibinders, we identify a synthetic protein cocktail, C6-DPC, that drives efficient human fibroblast-to-muscle transdifferentiation with robust structural and metabolic maturation. C6-DPC reprograms extracellular signaling by activating pro-myogenic FGFR1/2c pathways while suppressing anti-myogenic inputs through ALK1 and TGFBR2; targeted depletion of ALK1 is sufficient to lower the reprogramming barrier. Inflammatory signaling via gp130 emerges as a dominant checkpoint, and its inhibition further enhances conversion. Engineered tissues generate high twitch and tetanic forces in both wild-type and dystrophindeficient human cells. These findings demonstrate that programmable synthetic ligands can rewrite receptor-level signaling to direct cell fate and enable functional tissue regeneration.

Title: Genetic ancestry influences the relative expression of ancestral haplotypes within admixed individuals
Authors: vazquez-hidalgo, e.; Mews, M. A.; Gomez, L.; Gu, t.; Griswold, A. J.; Bush, W.
Abstract: Allele-specific expression (ASE) reflects differences between the two haplotypes a person carries, but most ASE studies have been done in European-descent samples. Admixed individuals carry haplotypes from different ancestral backgrounds within the same cell, which allows ancestry effects on regulation to be measured directly. We integrated phased whole-blood RNA-seq with local ancestry inference in 779 participants from the MAGENTA cohort, including non-Hispanic White, African American, Caribbean Hispanic, and Peruvian individuals. Higher West African (YRI) ancestry proportion was associated with more ASE-positive genes per person, and the association remained after adjusting for age, sex, Alzheimer's disease status, APOE genotype, and the number of heterozygous genes. Peruvian ancestry showed no significant association. A gene-level test of imbalance across population groups found 2,053 of 15,008 genes with significant differences, including the major histocompatibility complex in all four groups. A genome-wide scan of 2,213 1 Mb windows compared people carrying two haplotypes of different ancestries with those carrying two of the same ancestry. It identified 52 non-redundant loci that replicated across all four population groups, containing 201, 60, and 110 ancestry-associated genes under the CEU, YRI, and PEL reference baselines. A haplotype-resolved directional analysis showed no genome-wide advantage for either ancestry. It found locus-specific dominance at 11 loci, and only chr8:2-3 Mb (CSMD1) showed the same direction in more than one population group. Genetic ancestry therefore shapes allelic regulation at global, gene, and locus scales.

Title: MicroDUET: a dual-headed genomic foundation model for pathogen surveillance
Authors: Barber, M.; Suster, C. J. E.; Lei, J.; Getchell, M.; Wulandari, S.; Sintchenko, V.; Pronyk, P. M.
Abstract: Pathogen genomic surveillance works from raw reads, assembled genomes and alignments, representations that are slow and costly to compare at scale. Compact embeddings from genomic language models offer an alternative, but surveillance requires resolving both evolutionary ancestry (phylogeny) and phenotypic capability (function) - which need not co-vary. Here we present MicroDUET, which adapts a 26.6-million-parameter ProkBERT backbone with two 3.5-million-parameter adapter heads: a phylogeny head trained contrastively on genome windows from the same microbes, and a function head trained to identify genes across taxa. On held-out retrieval benchmarks, the phylogeny head returned the correct species for 80.3% and 66.6% of cellular and viral queries, and the function head the correct gene family for 97.3% and 97.2%, reaching 74.4% accuracy on an independent antimicrobial resistance-class benchmark. Across all three benchmarks MicroDUET outranked 17 other genomic encoders. Without training on lineage, clade or drug-susceptibility tasks, MicroDUET identified Mycobacterium tuberculosis and mpox virus lineages and clades (0.965, 0.975 accuracy), discriminated rifampicin resistance without lineage adjustment (AUROC 0.985), and retrospectively identified an emerging mpox lineage as anomalous (AUROC 0.974). MicroDUET operates 10^3 - 10^4 times faster than single-threaded sequence-based alignments. MicroDUET therefore provides a compact, reusable representation for scalable pathogen surveillance and sequence triage.

Title: Proteomic Evaluation of the Progression from Acute Kidney Injury to Chronic Kidney Disease
Authors: Sims-Lucas, S.; Bons, J.; Pfister, K. E.; Silva-Barbosa, A.; Uhlean, R.; Goetzman, E. S.; Schilling, B.
Abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) and chronic kidney disease (CKD) are interconnected syndromes with substantial global burden, yet the molecular mechanisms driving the transition from acute injury to chronic fibrosis remain incompletely understood. We performed quantitative data-independent acquisition mass spectrometry (DIA-MS) proteomics on mouse models of AKI (ischemia-reperfusion injury) and CKD (unilateral ureteral obstruction), quantifying 5,985 protein groups. A conserved core injury response of 1,475 shared proteins (46%) was dominated by mitochondrial dysfunction, loss of solute transporters, and immune and extracellular matrix remodeling. AKI was marked by chromatin reorganization, DNA damage response, and acute inflammation, whereas CKD showed sustained fibrosis, complement activation, and coagulation. Peroxisomal proteins, including the {beta}-oxidation enzymes Acox1 and Ehhadh, were consistently down-regulated in both AKI and CKD, with no peroxisomal protein up-regulated. Both models also displayed a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP)-like signature, including Havcr1, Spp1, Igfbp7, Plau, and lysosomal cathepsins. We further identified 95 candidate progression markers, including Brat1 and Col3a1, 93 proteins with greater loss in CKD, 14 proteins changing in opposite directions, and seven disease-associated co-expression modules. These findings provide a proteomics resource for biomarker discovery and therapeutic targeting, including peroxisomal restoration and senolytic strategies, in AKI and CKD.

Title: Spatiotemporal multiplexing on subretinal prosthesis increases selectivity of the network-mediated stimulation
Authors: Jensen, N.; Ly, K.; Pham-Howard, D.; Bhuckory, M. B.; Palanker, D.
Abstract: Subretinal photovoltaic implants (PRIMA) provide form vision in patients blinded by age-related macular degeneration. The success of this approach is attributed in part to the network-mediated stimulation, which preserves many features of the natural retinal signal encoding. For efficient stimulation of bipolar cells (BC) with smaller pixels, electric field confinement should be relaxed, yet direct activation of the retinal ganglion cells (RGC) should be avoided. Here we present a new method for selective stimulation of bipolar cells using image multiplexing - sequential presentation of the image's components in several subframes. With sizes of the subframe islands optimized by computational modelling, the selectivity of network (BC) mediated retinal stimulation increased over 5 times in rats. Using this approach, electric field confinement can be relaxed, allowing pixels as small as 20 m to efficiently stimulate bipolar cells, while avoiding direct stimulation of RGCs and preserving high contrast of the pattern. This software-based improvement enables higher visual acuity of prosthetic vision without a change in implanted hardware.

Title: Machine learning assisted multi-level differentiation of blood cells using multi-frequency electro-mechanical impedance cytometry
Authors: Bansal, I.; Suresh, S. K.; Sagar, N.; Sen, P.
Abstract: We report a multi-frequency microfluidic impedance cytometer with multimodal measurement of electrical and mechanical cell properties. Using the large feature set from the multimodality, we implemented machine learning assisted differentiation of cells. We have demonstrated a constriction-equipped channel to study the mechanical cell properties, and integrated multiple microelectrodes that capture electric field information pertaining to various stages of cell transit. Our system works over a wide frequency range from 800 kHz to 8 MHz. We developed a machine learning workflow to classify cells using our multi-modal data. Using this platform to show blood cell differentiation, our system shows minimum F1 score to be 0.92, minimizing both false negatives and false positives, which is important for medical diagnosis. Furthermore, we also identified the presence of two populations in the mixed sample of neutrophils and PBMCs. Our workflow allows classification of cells in a new sample along with identification of top 5 distinguishing parameters out of 70+ features extracted from the raw impedance signal.

Title: Affinity-guided design of PDZ-binding peptides in a shared latent space
Authors: Yamahata, I.; Shimamura, T.; Hayashi, S.
Abstract: PDZ-binding motifs (PBMs) are short C-terminal sequences that bind PDZ domains and contribute to protein localization and complex assembly. Designing PBMs could modulate these interactions while leaving most of the original protein sequence unchanged. Because PDZ recognition preferences overlap, modulating intended interactions requires considering off-target binding alongside target affinity. Computational PBM design methods generally use sequence-based affinity prediction and structure-based evaluation, but it remains challenging to guide sequence searches toward different binding objectives with a single trained model. Here, we propose a deep learning-based method to design PBMs by analytically formulating single-target, off-target-aware, and dual-target design objectives as directions in a PDZ-PBM shared latent space learned through quantitative PDZ-PBM affinity prediction. In single-target PBM redesign for DLG4-PDZ3, our method identified 100 top-ranked candidates, 84 of which were in the top 1% for experimentally measured interaction fitness in a published mutant library, compared with 64 using an existing method. In single-target de novo design of 10-residue PBMs, our method achieved the highest median in silico binding scores among the compared methods for three of the four PDZ domains tested. In off-target-aware and dual-target PBM design for PTPN3 and SCRIB-PDZ3, off-target-aware design increased between-group score differences within each domain at the cost of lower target-domain scores, whereas dual-target design yielded scores close to those of the respective single-target designs for both domains. Together, these results show that shared latent representations learned from quantitative affinities allow a single trained model to guide PBM design across different binding objectives without retraining.

Title: Evaluating speech-like distortion product otoacoustic emissions: a comparison of time- and frequency-domain metrics across three datasets
Authors: Steinebach, J.; Reichenbach, T.
Abstract: Speech-like distortion-product otoacoustic emissions (DPOAEs) allow cochlear activity to be measured during the perception of natural, continuous speech and have been used to study attentional effects in the cochlea. The technique is still young, however, and existing studies differ in stimulus design and in the metric used to quantify the emissions, which makes their results difficult to compare. Here, we reanalysed three existing datasets (106 participants, 14 stimulus types) with a common pipeline. We compared six metrics: the band power of the recording, the magnitude-squared coherence (MSC) between the recording and a DPOAE template, and four metrics derived from their complex cross-correlation, namely peak magnitude, signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), peak area and peak width. A separability index quantified how well each metric separated in-ear recordings from out-of-ear control recordings without emissions. Band power, MSC and SNR separated best, with mean separability indices of about 0.9, whereas the peak magnitude performed worst and was inverted for half of the stimulus types. Since band power does not require a DPOAE template, it serves as a sanity check of the setup rather than as evidence for an emission. The MSC was insensitive to the latency of the emission but well suited for comparisons across stimuli, whereas the cross-correlation additionally provided the latency. The emissions differed significantly between the stimulus types of the three datasets, and those below about 700 Hz were measured least reliably. We derive practical recommendations for the analysis and stimulus design of future experiments.

Title: DNA Sequence Differentially Modulates Histone Core and Tail Interactions in Canonical and Centromeric Nucleosomes
Authors: Ghosh Moulick, A.; Erhardt, S.; Kozlowska, M.
Abstract: Human centromeric chromatin is a specialized chromatin domain characterized by CENP-A-containing nucleosomes interspersed with canonical histone H3 nucleosomes. It is assembled on tandem repeats of -satellite DNA and defines centromere identity. How histone variant identity and DNA sequence jointly shape nucleosome structure and histone-DNA interactions that underpin centromeric chromatin formation remains incompletely understood. Here, we investigate the structural plasticity of the histone core and nucleosomal DNA, histone tail dynamics and DNA-sequence dependent changes for canonical (H3) and centromeric (CENP-A) nucleosomes using the SIRAH coarse-grained molecular dynamics (CG-MD) simulations. Nucleosomes containing -satellite positioning sequence (ASP) and Widom 601 DNA sequence are systematically analyzed and compared. Our simulations reveal that the centromeric nucleosome exhibits a more stable histone core with lower structural plasticity and the histone tails engage DNA differently with an overall reduction in the histone-DNA contacts compared to the canonical nucleosome. Further investigation of CENP-N binding to the CENP-A nucleosome demonstrates substantial modulation of nucleosomal DNA dynamics and histone-DNA interactions. Replacing the ASP DNA sequence with the Widom 601 sequence preserves the stability of both types of the histone core while markedly altering histone-tail dynamics. The conformational dynamics of canonical nucleosomes is more strongly affected by the Widom 601 DNA sequence than those of their centromeric counterparts. However, CENP-N binding induces more spatially extensive changes in DNA geometry in Widom 601 than in ASP DNA. Our findings suggest that DNA sequence and histone composition have residue-level differences translating into distinct nucleosome dynamics, which could be among the determinants governing the structural and dynamic properties of centromeric chromatin and its biological function.

Title: Advancing AOPs for genotoxicity through quantifying KERs linking DNA alkylation to increase in mutations and chromosome aberrations
Authors: Winkelman, L. M. T.; Demuynck, E.; Bryce, S. M.; Stepnik, M.; Thienpont, A. I.; Van Goethem, F.; Majid, S.; Pronk, T. E.; Audebert, M.; Mertens, B.; Beltman, J. B.
Abstract: Quantitative Adverse Outcome Pathways (qAOPs) help translate mechanistic knowledge into quantitative toxicity predictions; however, their development is constrained by the limited availability and heterogeneity of quantitative data. Here, we investigated the feasibility of developing a qAOP for genotoxicity by modeling quantitative relationships linking DNA alkylation to increased mutations and structural chromosome aberrations through intermediate biological key events (KEs). We compiled and harmonized published concentration-response data from human lymphoblastoid TK6 cells exposed to ethyl methanesulfonate, methyl methanesulfonate, or N-ethyl-N-nitrosourea, covering eight genotoxicity assays representing five KEs with well-established dependencies. We evaluated sources of variability, compared points of departure (PoDs), and quantified relationships between successive events using response-response modeling. Substantial between-study variability could to a limited extent be explained through differences in experimental design while batch effects for individual studies and researchers were substantial. PoD estimates that were calculated from combined results of independent studies with similar experimental design, were often uncertain due to insufficient concentration-response characterization or conflicting results between studies. Nevertheless, response-response modeling suggested a threshold effect for certain key-event relationships (KERs). Specifically, DNA adducts seemed to be triggered at lower concentrations of alkylating agents compared to the subsequent KEs of DNA strand breaks and chromosome aberrations. Furthermore, these fitted response-response models can be used for prediction of downstream KEs from earlier ones. The general approach we developed for BMC analysis followed by response-response modeling is applicable to other AOPs as well. These findings highlight both the feasibility and limitations of using existing data for qAOP development.

Title: Chromosome-level genomics and cross-species enzyme screening enable high-titer bakuchiol production in Yarrowia lipolytica
Authors: Li, j.; Chang, H.; Liu, C.; Li, S.; Zhang, J.; Bai, J.; Wang, H.; Liu, X.; Fan, Z.; Jiang, H.
Abstract: The diversity of enzymes supporting bakuchiol biosynthesis remains incompletely characterized, limiting the repertoire available for microbial pathway engineering. Here, we combined chromosome-level genomics, cross-species enzyme screening and metabolic engineering to establish high-titer bakuchiol production in Yarrowia lipolytica. We assembled a 471.76-Mb Psoralea corylifolia genome anchored to 11 pseudochromosomes, with a contig N50 of 40.33 Mb. Genome-guided screening and functional validation identified four prenyltransferases from P. corylifolia and Vigna radiata whose N-terminally truncated variants supported bakuchiol production in yeast. These results extend experimental evidence for bakuchiol-producing activity across legume prenyltransferase sequences and species. For PcPT6, corresponding to the previously reported PcPT07, removing 40 N-terminal amino acids increased bakuchiol production by 53% relative to the full-length enzyme. We reconstructed bakuchiol biosynthesis in Y. lipolytica and reinforced aromatic precursor synthesis to increase p-coumaric acid supply. Coordinating mevalonate pathway reinforcement with increased t40PcPT6 gene dosage further improved bakuchiol production. Following fermentation optimization, titers reached 108.29 mg/L in shake flasks and 6.03 g/L in a 7.5-L fed-batch bioreactor. These findings connect an expanded set of functional prenyltransferases with coordinated pathway engineering, enabling gram-per-liter microbial bakuchiol production.

Title: A Mathematical Model Connecting Appetite-Driven Food Intake to Metabolic Changes across Diet and GLP-1RA Treatments in Mice
Authors: Silfvergren, O.; Simonsson, C.; Sundqvist, M.; Nordell, P.; Gennemark, P.; Cedersund, G.
Abstract: Mouse models are widely used to study obesity and the effects of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) on appetite-driven meal responses and eating behaviours. However, connecting these behavioural changes to disease prevention remains limited. One reason is that eating behaviour is often summarised as daily or weekly energy intake, obscuring meal-level dynamics. Here we present a mathematical model of mouse appetite-driven food intake across diets and treatment with the GLP-1RAs semaglutide and exenatide. The model jointly described three studies and passed both qualitative assessments and a statistical {chi}2 test (disagreement<threshold, 348<1111). Predictive performance was subsequently validated using four pre-existing studies and one new study. Finally, the model was used to simulate mouse populations under dietary and GLP-1RA interventions, with predictions showing qualitative agreement with the literature. This work aids preclinical drug discovery, supports mouse study design, and improves understanding of how individual meals accumulate into long-term physiological changes.

Title: Large language models complement established workflows for mechanistic model construction and refinement in systems biology
Authors: Doresic, D.; Liu, Y.; Wieland, V.; Jost, P. J.; Huth, M.; Merkt, S.; Alvarez-Garavito, C.; Moore Dillems, P. R.; Thiele, C.; Seep, L.; Pathirana, D.; Hasenauer, J.
Abstract: Mechanistic models provide a framework for describing, understanding, and predicting biological processes, but their development requires an interdisciplinary team with expertise in biology, mathematics, and computation. Here we present Octomod, a multi-agent workflow based on large language models (LLMs) that integrates biological knowledge retrieval, model construction, parameter estimation, and hypothesis testing. Built on established software tools, including AMICI and pyPESTO, and community standards, including SBML and PEtab, Octomod supports model development and refinement through natural-language interaction with a user. The agents' proposals must pass defined checks and the user's decision before they are used. Every input, model, check, and decision is recorded, so that model building remains transparent and reproducible. We applied Octomod to four problems. Three used published data and differ in model size and in how much the user guided the run: Octomod constructed a model that matched a published model without user guidance, supported the interactive refinement of a gene-regulatory model, and built models of cell-cell communication that explained the responses of five immune cell types to different stimuli. In the fourth application, on newly generated and unpublished lipidomics data, Octomod helped to determine which processes the measurements could inform, identify unresolved label fluxes, and reduce a supplied model to those processes. Together, these results show how LLMs can strengthen and complement established workflows for constructing and refining biologically informed models.

Title: Ciliated keratinocytes define a spatially restricted pro-inflammatory state in psoriasis and atopic dermatitis
Authors: Ike, M.; Hayashi, Y.; Nakamura, M.; He, H.; Nakaoku, A.; Ishii, K. J.; Fujita, F.; Motooka, D.; Toriyama, M.; Morita, A.
Abstract: Abstract Background: Psoriasis vulgaris (Pso) and atopic dermatitis (AD) are characterized by recurrent flares and incomplete disease resolution. Primary cilia are antenna-like sensory organelles that project from the cell surface and coordinate extracellular signaling. Although epidermal ciliated cells are rarely detected in healthy skin and are selectively increased in AD and Pso, their molecular identity, functional properties, and clinical relevance remain unclear. Objective: To characterize epidermal ciliated cells in Pso and AD and determine their molecular identity, functional properties, and clinical relevance. Methods: We integrated single-cell-resolved spatial transcriptomics with primary cilia immunostaining in healthy skin (n=6), AD lesions (n=10), and paired psoriatic skin before and after phototherapy (n=7 each). Functional analyses using HaCaT cells with increased primary cilia formation included MAPK/NFkB signaling assays, ATAC-seq, and pathway inhibition assays. Results: Ciliated cells were largely restricted to AD and both pre and post treatment psoriatic skin, with KCs accounting for more than 70% of all ciliated cells. Ciliated KCs were predominantly localized to the basal and spinous layers. These cells exhibited disease and stage specific inflammatory programs and formed spatially organized communication networks with surrounding cells, including non ciliated KCs, fibroblasts, endothelial cells, and myeloid cells, suggesting a ciliated KC centered inflammation niche. Mechanistically, increased primary cilia formation enhanced MAPK and NFkB signaling and increased chromatin accessibility at inflammatory gene loci enriched for AP1 motifs, even in the absence of stimulation, consistent with a chromatin primed state. Higher residual ciliated KC abundance after phototherapy was associated with subsequent treatment escalation. ERK1/2 inhibition reduced cytokine induced primary cilia formation. Conclusions: Ciliated KCs represent an inflammatory epithelial cell state associated with residual disease activity in AD and Pso. The suppression of cytokine-induced primary cilia formation by ERK1/2 inhibition suggests that inflammation associated primary cilia formation may be modifiable process in persistent skin inflammation.

Title: Peripheral Immune Cell Shifts Associated With Alzheimer's Disease Vary in Multi-Ancestry Cohorts
Authors: Mustafa, Y.; Yang, Y.; Mews, M. A.; Gu, T.; Gomez, L.; Adams, L. D.; Starks, T. D.; Silva, C.; McInerney, K. F.; Vance, J. M.; Cuccaro, M. L.; Illanes-Manrique, M.; Cornejo-Olivas, M. R.; Feliciano-Astacio, B. E.; Goldie, B. S.; Pericak-Vance, M. A.; Haines, J. L.; Griswold, A. J.; Bush, W.
Abstract: Background: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is heavily influenced by immune system dysregulation, yet the role of peripheral immune processes--and how these vary across ethnicities--remains understudied. Objective: To investigate ancestry-specific immune alterations in AD by profiling peripheral immune cell proportions using high-resolution deconvolution of whole blood RNA-sequencing data, characterizing disease associated cell types, and identifying enriched biological pathways. Methods: We analyzed whole blood RNA-seq data from non-Hispanic White (NHW), African American (AA), Caribbean Hispanic (CariHISP), and Peruvian (PERU) individuals, balanced between AD cases and cognitively normal controls. Immune cell proportions were estimated using CIBERSORTx and compared using linear models (propeller R package) adjusted for age, sex, and APOE genotypes in case-control models. Cell-type-specific differential expression was performed using CARseq, and pathway enrichment analyses performed using MSigDB gene sets. Results: Baseline immune composition differed substantially across cohorts for multiple innate and adaptive cell types. In a multi-ethnic AD versus control analysis, eight cell types reached FDR significance: AD was associated with decreased proportions naive B cells, CD56dim NK cells, B cells, intermediate monocyte I, and double-negative T cells, alongside significant expansion in neutrophils and non-classical monocytes. Interaction analyses revealed heterogeneous group-specific effects, with the broadest shifts in AA and CariHISP. Pathway enrichment indicated shared heme metabolism, interferon, and oxidative phosphorylation programs across groups, with distinct emphases: broad, strong heme metabolism enrichment and the highest oxidative phosphorylation signal (in myeloid populations) in AA; MYC targets in naive B cells and eosinophils in CariHISP; dendritic cell - and T follicular helper cell - centered interferon, inflammatory, and proliferative programs in NHW; and TGF-{beta} and apoptosis signatures, unique to PERU, alongside the broadest cell-type coverage. Conclusions: Peripheral immune dysregulation in AD is characterized by depletion of lymphoid and intermediate monocyte populations with concurrent neutrophil and non-classical monocyte expansion, and these patterns vary meaningfully by ancestry. These findings underscore the need for population-informed biomarkers and therapeutic strategies in AD.

Title: MAFB and MAF cooperatively orchestrate human anti-inflammatory macrophage identity via autocrine Interleukin-10
Authors: del Castillo-Buey, A.; Rios, I.; Simon-Fuentes, M.; Capel-Jorquera, A.; Herrero, C.; Maldonado, A.; Zapico, I.; Clemente, F.; Angelina, A.; Palomares, O.; Vega, M. A.; Corbi, A. L.
Abstract: Macrophage lineage identity is governed by intricate transcriptional networks. Although the large MAF basic region-leucine zipper (bZIP) transcription factors MAFB and MAF are critical regulators of anti-inflammatory programs, their molecular coordination and non-redundant contributions within human macrophages remain poorly defined. Here, utilizing integrated proteomic, transcriptomic, and epigenomic profiling, we demonstrate that endogenous MAFB and MAF physically associate to form a stable heterodimeric complex on chromatin in human M-CSF-dependent monocyte-derived macrophages (M-Mac). Genome-wide CUT&Tag mapping reveals a hierarchical epigenomic architecture in which MAFB acts as the primary global anchor of M-Mac identity, whereas MAF provides localized transcriptional tuning. Mechanistically, both factors directly bind the IL10 locus, but functional IL-10 expression is primarily driven by MAFB. Neutralizing antibody assays reveal that endogenously produced IL-10 establishes an obligate autocrine feedback loop mandatory for both the initial acquisition and the maintenance of the M-Mac anti-inflammatory profile. Functionally, MAFB and MAF exert non-redundant control over core macrophage effectors: MAFB dictates apoptotic cell efferocytosis amd T cell activation, whereas MAF modulates phagocytosis, and acts as a brake suppressing acute pro-inflammatory cytokine/chemokine hyper-induction. Together, these findings establish a comprehensive molecular blueprint of how MAFB and MAF cooperatively fine-tune human monocyte-derived macrophage identity and functional plasticity.

Title: Strain-specific early, host-shaped late: the rhizobial transcriptome across symbiosis
Authors: Acosta-Jurado, S.; Fuentes-Romero, F.; Navarro-Gomez, P.; Ayala-Garcia, P.; Ollero, F. J.; Jimenez-Zurdo, J. I.; Perez-Montano, F.; Lopez-Baena, F. J.; Vinardell, J. M.
Abstract: The two ends of the rhizobial symbiotic trajectory have only been described separately. Here we report strand-specific RNA-seq of bacteroids of two strains, each against free-living cells of the same strain and alongside its flavonoid response: Sinorhizobium fredii HH103 from soybean (Glycine max), Glycyrrhiza uralensis and Lotus burttii, and Rhizobium tropici CIAT 899 from common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris) and L. burttii, the one legume both strains nodulate. Between 1877 and 2284 genes respond per strain-host combination, and most of that response is host-common: 1171 of 2855 genes respond in all three hosts of HH103 and 1664 of 2703 in both hosts of CIAT 899. What distinguishes the remainder is host identity rather than nodule type, since HH103 bacteroids from the indeterminate-nodule G. uralensis resemble those from L. burttii more than either resembles those from soybean, its natural host. Nitrogen fixation and the stress response are over-represented in every bacteroid and motility is almost entirely repressed, yet the shared core of CIAT 899 is the only repression-dominated gene set here and its translational machinery is induced where that of HH103 is repressed. Dismantling of the early programme is selective: in HH103 the type III apparatus is switched off, the Nod factor operons are attenuated but retained, and the fixABCX operon under a nod box is amplified, so a nod box does not by itself mark a gene as early. CIAT 899, lacking a type III system and placing no nif/fix gene under flavonoid control, keeps that block flat until the nodule, then engages 26 of its 30 genes. Across genera, 26% of responding orthologue pairs are shared in the bacteroid against 5% in the flavonoid response: each bacterium negotiates entry in a dialect of its own and converges on a shared end state whose amplitude, rather than content, the host modulates.

Title: Protein-peptide binding pathways revealed by two-dimensional replica-exchange molecular dynamics
Authors: Wu, Y.; Zhang, Y.; Shinobu, A.
Abstract: Protein kinases recognize their substrates through specific short peptide motifs, and this specificity has motivated broad interest in developing peptide-based kinase inhibitors. Traditional studies have focused mainly on this specific, bound-pose interaction, whereas the nonspecific interactions that precede specific binding have received comparatively little attention. Such nonspecific interactions are transient, making them difficult to capture using either experimental techniques or conventional molecular dynamics simulations, and consequently their biological significance and functional role remain poorly understood. Here, we used two-dimensional replica exchange (gREST/REUS) to study the binding process between Abl kinase and its optimal synthetic substrate, Abltide. The simulations revealed that, in addition to the specific bound pose, the surface of Abl kinase harbors multiple nonspecific binding sites that constitute distinct encounter states, mediated primarily by electrostatic interactions. Abltide proceeds toward the binding pocket from encounter states at three of these sites. As Abltide enters the pocket, the EF/G/{beta}11 patch plays a central role in stabilizing the resulting intermediate states, primarily through hydrophobic interactions. Within the substrate-binding site, the Abltide backbone also shifts progressively out of the register of the specific bound pose, forming backbone hydrogen bonds with the kinase that are absent from the bound pose. These findings indicate that substrate recognition by Abl kinase is encoded not only at the specific binding site but also across the surrounding kinase surface, and that peptide-based inhibitor design should consider both the specific and nonspecific binding behavior of the peptide.

Title: Lipid Scrambling Amplifies Plasma Membrane Undulations via Anti-Registered Domains Stabilized by Long-Chain Sphingomyelin
Authors: Yamada, T.; Shinoda, W.
Abstract: Lipid scrambling, which dissipates the transbilayer lipid asymmetry of plasma membranes (PMs), plays an essential role in various large-scale membrane remodeling processes. Although lipid domains have been implicated in these processes, the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood, owing to the lack of a molecular-level picture of how lipid scrambling reorganizes these domains. Here, using coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations of asymmetric and fully scrambled PM models, we show that lipid scrambling markedly enhances membrane undulations. We identify two key features of the domain organization underlying this enhancement in the scrambled PM: domain anti-registration, which couples to membrane curvature through a mismatch in preferred curvature between the two leaflets, and scrambling-induced domain enlargement, which permits this curvature to extend over large length scales. Simulations with different sphingomyelin (SM) compositions demonstrate that long-chain SMs stabilize anti-registered domains and the associated membrane curvature. Together, these results suggest a physical mechanism by which lipid scrambling primes the PM for remodeling through the reorganization of lipid domains, with long-chain SMs playing a key role. We also find that the interleaflet domain organization of the scrambled PM model depends strongly on system size, shifting from anti-registration to registration as the simulation box is reduced, and we discuss the origin of this finite-size effect.

Title: 6S RNA tunes virulence, surface immunogenicity, and phenotypic heterogeneity in tissue-invading Yersinia
Authors: Sarigoz, O.; Valeriano, V. D.; Avican, U.; Suer, S. G.; Ntokaki, A.; Doruk, T.; Wang, H.; Nilsson, K.; Hasanzade, N.; Mahmood, F.; Fahlgren, A.; Bauer, S.; griffie, J.; Fallman, M.; Avican, K.
Abstract: Enteric pathogens must reprogram transcription as they leave the gut lumen and enter tissue, yet this reprogramming has been studied almost entirely in in vitro culture systems. Using Yersinia pseudotuberculosis mouse infection for in vivo RNA-seq, we recovered near-complete transcriptomes from bacteria in the mouse cecal lumen and the associated lymphoid tissue they invade. Tissue-localized bacteria induced the type III secretion system, raised virulence plasmid copy number, and shifted transcription toward alternative sigma factor regulons. The most strongly induced transcript was 6S RNA, among the most conserved noncoding regulators, which sequesters RpoD-containing RNA polymerase but has so far lacked an infection phenotype. Our study shows that 6S RNA acts as a tuner, not a switch: its absence causes T3SS overexpression, increased display of TLR-activating envelope components elevating host expression of proinflammatory mediators, reduced phenotypic heterogeneity in tissue, and delayed colonization. T3SS and 6S RNA transcripts are concentrated in bacteria facing infiltrating neutrophils, defining a local program that couples virulence timing to immune evasion.

Title: CpG islands are topological sinks for transcription-induced DNA supercoiling
Authors: Naughton, C.; Bonato, A.; Chiang, M.; Corless, S.; Stocks, J.; Forsyth, E.; Grimes, G. R.; Halliday, D.; Bentivoglio, A.; Brackley, C. A.; Marenduzzo, D.; Gilbert, N.
Abstract: Transcription-induced DNA supercoiling is relaxed by topoisomerases, yet negative supercoiling accumulates at active gene promoters. How promoter sequences and chromatin architecture organise and regulate this torsional stress remains poorly understood. Using Twist-seq, a genome-wide assay for DNA supercoiling, we show that highly transcribed CpG island (CGI) promoters accumulate elevated levels of negative supercoiling compared to highly transcribed non-CGI promoters. Coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations predict that the capacity of CGI promoters to accommodate elevated negative supercoiling arises from the intrinsic physical properties of CGI DNA. CGI sequence and local chromatin architecture favour localised melting at AT-rich pockets and DNA writhe within promoter-proximal nucleosome-free regions, providing an energetically favourable mechanism to dissipate torsional stress. Consistently, CGI promoters show a depletion in Top1 and increased ssDNA in vivo. We propose that CGIs function as sequence-encoded topological sinks that buffer transcription-induced torsional stress, with increased somatic mutation rates at highly expressed CGI promoters suggesting a potential genome-stability cost.

Title: Impact of Driving Dynamic Fluctuations of 6DOF-SVC Model Predictions Across Five Real-World Driving Studies
Authors: Buchheit, B.; Robin, Y.; Schneider, E. N.; Alayan, M.; Strauss, D. J.
Abstract: Despite the use of technological countermeasures for motion sickness (MS), studies show that the sensory conflict, and thus symptoms of MS such as nausea, cannot be completely prevented while traveling as a car passenger. Accordingly, reliable prediction of MS will represent a possible solution for intelligent vehicles to avoid the abortion of the drive, e.g., through adapted driving strategies or route planning. Although the modeling of individual subjective well-being is becoming increasingly important, the prediction of overall motion sickness incidence (MSI) in groups along a route remains a complementary assessment metric. In the present study, application-oriented parameter sets for the popular 6DOF-SVC model to estimate MSI were validated using five previously conducted real-world driving experiments. The results demonstrate that the MSI of unknown routes can be successfully predicted in an application-oriented manner; however, inaccuracies in the predicted MSI trajectories remain. In addition, for the first time, it is shown that the natural MSI fluctuations, based on the driving dynamic profile, route characteristics, or driving style, is approximately 10%. Moreover, findings indicate that individual MSI thresholds lie in a range of 16.65% to 36.73% and slightly correlate with MS susceptibility. However, their high variability across driving scenarios limits their applicability.

Title: Asymmetry and Allostery: Insights into the Mechanism of Directional Peptide Translocation in AAA+ Unfoldases
Authors: Southam, T. G.; Breslin, J.; Oh, M.; Haque, I.; Todd, L.; Glynn, S. E.; Swanson, J. M.
Abstract: Molecular motors convert stochastic ATP chemistry into directional motion. Modern nonequilibrium theories explain this through kinetic asymmetry, yet the molecular mechanisms remain unresolved. Cryo-EM of asymmetric helical staircases has inspired the processive hand-over-hand mechanism, while biochemical and single-molecule studies have reported variable step sizes indicative of stochastic behavior. Reconciling these observations and explaining how directional motion emerges from stochastic ATP hydrolysis remain central questions. Here we use all-atom simulations and biochemical assays of AAA+ unfoldases Yme1 and Vps4 to explore structural changes induced by hydrolysis, ADP release, and ATP association. The simulations reveal pre- and post-hydrolysis conformations consistent with cryo-EM densities and interconnected allosteric communication networks. One network links the Walker B glutamate to the proximal subunits nucleotide binding pocket (NBP), providing a mechanism for backward propagation of hydrolysis competence around the hexamer. Another couples NBP and salt bridge rearrangements to pore-loop dynamics, connecting subunit position rather than ATP hydrolysis to substrate release. Mutational analysis demonstrates that disruption of the second network inhibits substrate degradation more than ATP hydrolysis, supporting its role in mechanochemical coupling. A second mutant points to interactions between N424 and the Walker B glutamate in ATP hydrolysis. Simulations of nucleotide exchange intermediates show that ATP binding before ADP and/or Mg2+ release can induce strain leading to alternative hydrolysis-competent configurations while preserving the directional bias of the staircase. Together, these findings suggest that structural asymmetry creates position-dependent allosteric interactions that generate kinetic asymmetry, biasing a fundamentally stochastic ATPase cycle toward directional substrate translocation while still permitting variations in stepping behavior.

Title: SureCLIP and DrCLIP: Genetic manipulation-free, sub-hour protein interaction mapping in cells and zebrafish
Authors: Cline, B. T.; Torrice, C. D.; Fan, W. B.; Addish, S. A.; Hazelbaker, M.; Lee, H.; Bear, J. E.; Cho, U. H.
Abstract: Proximity labeling has made interactome profiling broadly accessible, but it requires transgenic cell lines and animals. In primary or sensitive cells, deriving lines risks clonal drift and overexpression artifacts. In zebrafish, transgenesis imposes at least six months of lead time, and overnight labeling cannot resolve events on the timescale of embryogenesis. Here, we present SureCLIP and DrCLIP, protein interaction mapping methods that achieve sub-hour temporal resolution in cultured cells and zebrafish, respectively, without genetic manipulation. Central to these methods are the reversible crosslinkers DSP and DTBP. SureCLIP analysis of Hic-5 and lamin B1 compared favorably with published proximity labeling datasets in coverage and enrichment and identified new interactors. DrCLIP enabled stage-resolved endogenous interactome profiling in wild-type zebrafish and revealed that kindlin-2 is required for ECM assembly at somite boundaries and for myotendinous junction formation. Together, SureCLIP and DrCLIP circumvent the logistical, biological, and temporal limitations of transgene-based protein interaction mapping.

Title: Using Oyster Genomics to Understand Human Health
Authors: Bargmann, W.; Chen, Z.; Wang, S.; Cawood, M. L.; Parulekar, A.; Martucci, C.; Hoh, J.
Abstract: As sessile filter feeders that experience continuous environmental exposure, oysters, particularly Crassostrea virginica, offer a unique opportunity to understand how environmental exposure alters the genome and influence health. Furthermore, oysters must be sorted by size for market value for premium size and taste. However, it requires intensive labor, specialized equipment (tumblers), and is susceptible to environmental risks like pollution. Therefore, it is desirable to produce uniform oysters without machines. However, limitations in the previous reference genome [2] have constrained our understanding of how genes are organized and maintained in oyster populations. To this end, we harvested 240 adult oysters in same location, 120 extremely large size and 120 extremely small, controlled with all confounding factors such as age and water temperature. We perform a genome wide associate study (GWAS) using next generation whole genome sequencing, aiming to discover genomic regions associated with oyster size. Using PacBio HiFi, Illumina, and Hi-C technologies, we generated a 99.7% complete chromosome-level genome assembly for C. virginica (NCBI RefSeq GCF_053477285.1) [75]. We identified a ~13 Mb region on chromosome 1 uniquely expanded in C. virginica and enriched for innate immune and stress-response genes. To evaluate whether these structural features are reflected at the population level, we then conducted a k-mer analysis. This revealed differential sequence patterns by size, including enrichment of bacterial DNA in smaller individuals and host variation at the RNF213 locus within this region. By highlighting genome structure as a mediator of immune resilience, this work supports the use of oysters as sentinels to advance out understanding of how the dynamic reassembly of the genome due to environmental exposures influence health in human populations.

Title: Systematic Analysis of GARP- and EARP-Mediated Trafficking Pathways Using Lysosomal Proteomics
Authors: Sivalingam, B.; Altuzar, J.; Walter, S.; Holthuis, J.; Esch, B. M.; Fröhlich, F.
Abstract: Eukaryotic cells utilize tethering complexes for sorting of proteins within the endo-lysosomal system. The Golgi-associated retrograde protein (GARP) complex and the endosome-associated recycling protein (EARP) are two tethering complexes involved in endosomal recycling pathways. Both complexes share three common subunits (VPS51, VPS52, and VPS53), with each relying on one specific subunit: VPS54 for GARP and VPS50 for EARP. Mutations in both complexes are linked to various neurodegenerative disorders, such as progressive cerebello-cerebral atrophy. While model cargoes have been described, the cargo spectrum of both complexes remains largely elusive. Here, we combined lysosomal proteomics with knockdowns of GARP and EARP to analyze their cargo spectra. We first generated a deep lysosomal reference proteome. Using the lysosome as a terminal reference point for mis-sorted proteins, we show that GARP depletion causes a loss in lysosomal hydrolases and accumulation of non-lysosomal cargo. EARP depletion results in lysosomal accumulation of secreted proteins. Our findings serve as a reference to study GARP and EARP complexes and provide a comprehensive overview of the lysosomal proteome. We demonstrate that a systematic phenotypic analysis of trafficking mutants is necessary to understand the pathological consequences of their dysfunction

Title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Protein Language Models Reveals Encoded Structural and Functional Properties of Intrinsically Disordered Proteins
Authors: Naworski, L. E.; Good, L. L.; Scrutton, R.; Knowles, T. P. J.
Abstract: Protein language models (PLMs) such as ESM-2 encode protein sequences as embeddings for downstream tasks. PLMs are trained on a masked learning objective that leverages evolutionary constraints. While interpretability studies of ESM-2 have focused on folded proteins, their behavior on intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs), which constitute a substantial fraction of the human proteome and are implicated in numerous diseases, remains understudied. Because IDPs experience different types of evolutionary constraints on their amino acid sequences, we hypothesized that PLMs would behave differently on disordered versus folded regions.
