Here we show that ESM-2 exhibits reduced attention on disordered regions, yet still encodes meaningful biological signals. The model assigns heightened attention to disease-relevant residues even at high levels of disorder. Moreover, we show that both the radius of gyration and individual dynamic contact maps, key characteristics of IDPs, can be obtained from the model logits and embeddings. These findings suggest PLMs capture valuable information relevant to IDP biology despite their bias toward structured residues.

Title: Motor Occupancy Drives Emergent Mechanical States in Cardiac Myosin Ensembles
Authors: Alazzam, O. Y.; Chowdhury, M. A. H.; Stevens, H. M.; Reinemann, D. N.
Abstract: Myosin II generates force through the collective action of mechanically coupled motor ensembles, yet the mechanisms by which these ensembles sense changes in motor occupancy and coordinate force generation remain poorly understood. Ensemble force production may be governed by an optimal balance between effective motor occupancy and mechanical coordination rather than by motor number alone. We reconstituted cardiac myosin ensembles and systematically perturbed effective motor occupancy using the small-molecule drugs omecamtiv mecarbil (OM), which prolongs actomyosin interactions, and mavacamten (MAVA), which reduces the number of available force-generating myosin heads. Optical trapping measurements of full-length and S1 cardiac myosin ensembles revealed that force generation depended on both myosin concentration and pharmacological perturbation. Reducing myosin concentration increased force generation in the absence of drug, while OM and MAVA produced responses that varied with the initial occupancy state of the ensemble. Low concentrations of MAVA enhanced force generation under high motor occupancy but reduced force under low motor occupancy, whereas OM produced occupancy-dependent changes in both endpoint force and force dynamics. Force traces further revealed changes in the persistence and temporal coordination of force generation. These findings support a model in which cardiac myosin ensembles operate along an occupancy-coordination landscape, where productive force generation is achieved at an intermediate level of effective motor occupancy. Our results highlight the importance of effective motor occupancy in shaping emergent ensemble mechanics and suggest that force generation reflects a balance between motor availability and mechanical coordination.

Title: A rigid anchor and a flexible blade: calcium activates gelsolin through an asymmetric conformational ensemble
Authors: Stegani, B.; Girois, L.; Ballabio, F.; Giorgino, T.; Capelli, R.; Gerbaud, G.; Bollati, M.; Milani, M.; Bonucci, A.; Camilloni, C.; de Rosa, M.
Abstract: Gelsolin is the founding member of a superfamily of multidomain proteins that remodel the actin cytoskeleton in response to calcium. How the full-length protein is activated remains unclear because its active form has escaped structural characterization. Here, we combine small-angle X-ray scattering, pulsed EPR spectroscopy and molecular simulations to follow its transition from the compact inactive state to the active form. Activation proceeds through sequential, domain-specific rearrangements and culminates not in a single structure but in a heterogeneous ensemble, in which a comparatively rigid half implicated in filament capping coexists with a highly dynamic half implicated in severing. These states are populated progressively across the nanomolar-to-millimolar calcium concentrations that gelsolin encounters inside and outside cells, linking local calcium availability to the protein's functional repertoire. Gelsolin activation thus emerges as a graded population shift rather than a switch between discrete conformations, providing a structural framework for its diverse functions and, more generally, for the regulation of dynamic multidomain proteins.

Title: deepTools4: Faster, Scalable, and Modernized Genomic Data Analysis
Authors: Deboutte, W.; Salatino, A.; Maier, W.; Videm, P.; Navandar, M.; Erikson, G.; Momin, S.; Caballero-Perez, J.; Rabbani, L.; Lopez-Delisle, L.; Grüning, B.; Manke, T.
Abstract: The deepTools suite is widely used for quality control, summarization, and visualization of high-throughput sequencing data. However, as genomic datasets grow in scale and depth, existing tools often become computational bottlenecks. We present deepTools4, a modernized framework designed for high performance, scalability, and enhanced usability, while maintaining seamless integration with the Galaxy platform. Core functionality has been rewritten and thoroughly benchmarked, achieving substantial computational speed-ups. Visualization tools have been modernized to provide more intuitive, high-quality graphical outputs. In addition, our testing framework has been expanded to facilitate continuous development and ensure robustness. We demonstrate the utility of deepTools4 across diverse epigenomics and transcriptomics datasets, highlighting its ability to summarize genome-wide signals, apply a wide range of common normalization methods, and visualize enrichment patterns. The enhanced deepTools4 framework delivers a faster, more scalable solution for reproducible genome-wide analysis and interpretation across many sequencing modalities. Availability: https://github.com/deeptools/deepTools/

Title: Overlap of competing voices may mask attentional effects on speech-like distortion product otoacoustic emissions
Authors: Steinebach, J.; Reichenbach, T.
Abstract: Whether selective auditory attention modulates the cochlear amplifier through the medial olivocochlear system remains debated. Using speech-like distortion-product otoacoustic emissions (DPOAEs), elicited by waveforms that follow the harmonics of natural speech, we previously found that selectively attending one of two competing talkers reduced the emissions related to the resolved harmonics of the female voice. Here, we attempted to reproduce this effect in a design that separated different frequency regimes and harmonic resolvability. Forty-four participants attended one of two competing talkers, a female and a male voice, presented to one ear, while speech-like DPOAEs related to both voices were recorded from the other ear. Stimuli were derived from resolved and unresolved harmonics in a low-frequency (up to 1.5 kHz) and a transitional (1.5 to 4 kHz) regime, which required pitch-shifting both voices so that their fundamental frequencies were much closer to each other than in the original study. Speech-like DPOAEs emerged for most stimulus types, although they were weak for some and absent for one. Their amplitude, however, did not depend on attention for any stimulus type. Further time-domain metrics showed only isolated attentional effects of opposite direction for two stimulus types, and a frequency-domain metric showed none. A cochlear excitation model suggests that, due to the closely spaced fundamental frequencies of the two voices, the emissions most comparable to the original study presumably arose at cochlear locations shared by both voices, where attention would modulate both voices alike.

Title: Exploring taxonomic diversity in the genus Suberites Nardo, 1833: Insights from microbial, phylogenetic, and morphological analyses
Authors: Llorente-Vaquero, V.; Gracia-Sancha, C.; Baldo, F.; Turon, M.; Minarro, M.; Corral-Lou, A.; Cassidy, R.; Cristobo, J.; Taboada, S.; Riesgo, A.
Abstract: Marine sponges (phylum Porifera) are a highly diverse and polymorphic group of marine invertebrates whose taxonomic delimitation is often challenging due to high intraspecific variability and the scarcity of diagnostic morphological characters. Their close association with microbial symbionts also makes them an important source of secondary metabolites, some of which may contribute to sponge colouration. Here, we use morphological characters, molecular phylogenetic markers, and 16S metabarcoding of the symbiont community to understand speciation in a common Mediterranean sponge lineage. We collected 43 specimens of the genus Suberites from the Mediterranean Sea and the North and South Atlantic Oceans, between 55-150 m depths, and sequenced two barcoding genes, cytochrome c oxidase I and 28S rDNA, as well as studied their spicular complements. We identified five closely-related species: S. domuncula, S. ficus/pagurorum, S. dandelenae, S. ambulodomus, and a new species of Suberites from the Balearic Islands, Suberites sp. nov. The latter represents a potential new pseudo-cryptic species closely related to S. domuncula, because of their strong morphological and molecular affinities. The potential new Mediterranean species exhibits six colour morphotypes (yellow, gray, orange, brown, red, and blue), and the microbiome analyses of the symbiotic communities revealed significant differences in bacterial community composition among colour morphotypes, specially of bacteria that produce different pigments which potentially give the sponge is colouration. These results provide valuable insights into species boundaries and evolutionary relationships within the genus Suberites and support a role for the microbiome in sponge colouration.

Title: bofasa enables high-quality orthology inference across diverse multi-species bacterial genome sets
Authors: Salamzade, R. A.; Yaffe, E.; Kottapalli, A.; Kalan, L. R.; Relman, D. A.
Abstract: Bacterial species can be separated by billions of years of evolution. However, studies of such ancient relationships often rely on methods developed for eukaryotes, which are less diverse. Such methods can regard instances of horizontal gene transfer as contamination, rely heavily on a species phylogeny when partitioning paralogs, and fail to account for the multi-domain architectures of some genes. Here, we introduce, showcase, and benchmark bofasa, a software for high-quality and automated inference of ortholog groups across distantly related bacterial species. bofasa employs a recursive algorithm to split coarse homolog groups into paralogous subsets and first establishes domain-level ortholog groups prior to assessing evolutionary relationships between entire proteins. In comparison to other methods commonly used for multi-species bacterial comparative genomics, bofasa is substantially more conservative in predicting orthology yet can often recover the largest single-copy core genome. Beyond orthology inference, the software also features several additional utility functionalities, including assessment of which ortholog groups are commonly found on mobile genetic elements or possess variable genomic contexts.

Title: Multivalent BBSome-IFT proximities support IFT-A-IFT-B coordination in vivo
Authors: Shen, Z.; Chen, G.; Li, M.; Chai, Y.; Li, W.; Ou, G.
Abstract: Intraflagellar transport (IFT) depends on coordinated movement of IFT-A and IFT-B, yet how these assemblies remain coupled within dynamic ciliary trains is unclear. Here, we combine endogenous fluorescent knock-in tagging, quantitative in vivo FLIM-FRET, structural modeling, and targeted mutagenesis to define IFT organization in C. elegans and mammalian cells. FLIM-FRET mapping identifies proximity networks within IFT-B and places IFT144 near IFT172 and IFT88 in intact cilia. Loss of BBSome function is associated with weaker IFT-A-IFT-B proximity signals and divergent subcomplex transport dynamics, consistent with a contribution of the BBSome to IFT coordination in vivo. Split-GFP complementation places BBSome components near IFT-A and IFT-B, while structural modeling nominates complementary charged surfaces on the IFT46-IFT52 dimer and BBS7/BBS9. Charge-reversal mutations targeting these surfaces impair BBSome recruitment and functional rescue. Together, these findings support a model in which multivalent BBSome-IFT proximities contribute to IFT-A-IFT-B coordination during ciliary transport.

Title: Longitudinal miRNA-mRNA Profiling Reveals Network Reorganization in Preeclampsia
Authors: Mirzakhani, H.; Jung, C.; Lu, Z.; Handy, D. E.; Loscalzo, J.; Weiss, S. T.
Abstract: Background: Preeclampsia (PE) is a leading cause of maternal and perinatal morbidity. Temporal dynamics of molecular dysregulation across pregnancy remain poorly understood. We performed longitudinal RNA sequencing of maternal whole blood to characterize miRNA-mRNA regulatory network evolution in PE. Methods: Whole-blood samples from early (M1: 10-18 weeks) and late pregnancy (M2: 32-38 weeks) were analyzed from 43 PE cases and 106 normotensive controls, including 109 paired samples (36 PE cases, 73 controls). Differential expression, temporal classification, pathway enrichment, and miRNA-mRNA network integration were performed. Placental expression support was assessed using internal RNA-seq and public databases. Key miRNA-mRNA interactions were experimentally validated in HTR-8/SVneo trophoblast cells. Results: PE exhibited marked temporal reorganization of miRNA-mRNA networks, with strongly opposing temporal effect sizes across overlapping miRNA and mRNA features (Spearman {rho} = -0.82, P < 0.0001). PI3K/AKT/mTORC1 signaling showed biphasic reversal (NES = +1.46, FDR = 0.028 at M1; NES = -1.64, FDR = 0.025 at M2), and heme-metabolism programs showed progressive suppression (2.1-fold NES intensification; FDR < 0.05 at both timepoints). Network analysis identified 29 high-confidence biphasic miRNA-mRNA pairs, including convergent targeting of ADGRA2 by three miRNAs and HSD17B1 by three miRNAs. miR-101-3p overexpression reduced DEPP1 mRNA (~40%) and protein (~26%) in trophoblast cells (P < 0.01), supporting a FOXO-DEPP1 axis. Blood-derived pairs showed pathway convergence with placental VGLL3-centered programs (PI3K/AKT, FOXO, TGF-{beta}, trophoblast differentiation). Conclusions: PE is associated with predominantly stage-specific or biphasic miRNA-mRNA network reorganization, with PI3K/AKT/mTORC1 dynamic remodeling and progressive heme-metabolism suppression. These findings support gestational-age-specific biomarker development and identify regulatory axes, including miR-101-3p [->] DEPP1, for mechanistic investigation.

Title: An oxidative mutational signature in normal tissues of a monoallelic  MUTYH  carrier
Authors: Grochowski, C. M.; Zhang, Y.; Venner, E.; Gingras, M.-C.; Bhamidipati, S.; Khan, Z.; Farek, J.; Paulin, L. F.; Fu, Y.; Zong, C.; Sedlazeck, F. J.; Doddapaneni, H.; The SMaHT Consortium,  ; Gibbs, R. A.
Abstract: Biallelic loss of MUTYH causes MUTYH-associated polyposis (OMIM: 608456), characterized by the oxidative base-excision-repair mutational signature SBS18, but whether the roughly 1 in 100 individuals who carry a single pathogenic MUTYH allele acquire a mutational phenotype in normal tissue is unknown. Analysis of multi-tissue sequencing of 25 donors from the Somatic Mosaicism across Human Tissues (SMaHT) Network identified three heterozygous carriers of MUTYH p.Gly396Asp. One carrier showed SBS18 across multiple normal tissues, ranking first of 25 donors with three independent methods and remaining significant after adjustment for tissue, without a somatic, epigenetic or transcriptional second hit at the MUTYH locus. A single hypomorphic MUTYH allele can therefore leave a measurable oxidative mutational mark in healthy tissues, supporting tissue-level mutational readouts as an approach to cancer risk stratification within this common carrier state.

Title: DeepRNAi: Predicting on- and off-target siRNA activity and establishing a benchmark
Authors: Masse, N. Y.; Lau, T. T. Y.; Wintersinger, J.; Slobodyanyuk, M.; Li, R.; Chu, V. S.; Zhu, H.; Kanuparthi, B.; La, J.; Fischbacher, B.; Arseneault, K.; Johnson, S.; Lu, W.-T.; Lorincz-Comi, N.; Bohn, E.; Cole, C. B.; Hoffman, G. R.; Lazar, N. H.; Findlay, S. D.; Celaj, A.; Frey, B. J.
Abstract: Small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) silence target genes through RISC-mediated hybridization and cleavage, but can silence unintended transcripts and cause toxicity or complicate regulatory approval. In drug development, empirical assessment by qPCR and RNA-seq is slow, forces early candidate prioritization, and is limited by available species- and genome-appropriate cell models. While extensive empirical screening remains standard practice, there is a significant opportunity for modern AI methods to change this paradigm. We introduce DeepRNAi, a deep learning model that accurately predicts on- and off-target knockdown from siRNA and mRNA sequence. Trained on 16 million siRNA-transcript pairs from 2,031 siRNAs designed to interrogate known siRNA failure modes, and incorporating transcript context from biological foundation models, DeepRNAi is the first in silico method that approaches experimental accuracy. It generalizes across cell models, transcripts, genomes and species, and in a small study distinguishes approved therapeutics from hepatotoxic candidates. The value of DeepRNAi for prioritizing better candidates up front improving likelihood of success later in development is evidenced by a genome-wide survey of 24.4 million siRNAs targeting 7,946 genes, which indicates that 90.1% of the 100 most potent siRNAs have at least some off-target concerns. To support the community, we are publishing a training and benchmark dataset containing 1.84 million siRNA-transcript pairs from 240 siRNAs.

Title: HieraPTM: From PTM Site Recognition to Functional Phosphosite Prediction through Hierarchical Context and Protein Mechanics
Authors: Yuan, Y.; Wang, D.; Chen, P.; Niu, Y.; Yang, Z.; Zhang, H.; He, X.; Li, H.; Su, Z.; Lin, C.; Chen, T.; Lin, C.; LU, T.
Abstract: Protein post-translational modifications (PTMs) regulate cellular signaling and protein function, making accurate site identification essential for understanding protein regulation. However, PTM site recognition and functional phosphosite prediction are largely modeled independently, limiting the transfer of large-scale recognition knowledge to functional prioritization. Here, we introduce HieraPTM-HieraFuncPhos, a cross-task hierarchical framework that separately models and conditionally integrates transferable PTM recognition representations and function-specific mechanical evidence. HieraPTM integrates local sequence patterns, protein language model representations, and three-dimensional structural information to recognize multiple PTM types. HieraFuncPhos transfers these representations through parameter-efficient adaptation and adaptively retrieves local and distal mechanical evidence conditioned on functional representations. At HSP90AA1 T36 and T115, the model reveals distinct mechanical response patterns consistent with published nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) observations, suggesting that the framework not only prioritizes functional phosphosites but also provides biophysically grounded, testable hypotheses regarding site-specific regulation. HieraPTM achieved macro-averaged AUROC and AUPRC values of 0.9237 and 0.8425 across eight PTM tasks, while maintaining competitive performance on severely imbalanced external benchmarks. HieraFuncPhos achieved an AUROC of 0.8274 and an AUPRC of 0.8188, outperforming existing comparison methods. Together, this framework connects PTM site recognition, functional prioritization, and structure-informed hypotheses regarding potential regulatory processes.

Title: Unsupervised Deep Learning for Cryo-EM/ET Particle Classification
Authors: Uddin, M. R.; Min, S.; Wu, Q.; Zhan, X.; Chen, M.; Xu, M.
Abstract: Cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) is widely used to determine protein structures from purified samples. With cryogenic electron tomography (cryo-ET), it is possible to image thin sections of cells and directly visualize diverse proteins in their native environment. However, separating the massive mixture of different types of proteins inside cells remains challenging, especially without human intervention. In this work, we present an unsupervised deep learning framework for classifying cryo-EM/ET particle images that jointly optimizes for pose and structure through an autoencoder-based multi-stage pipeline. On single-particle cryo-EM datasets, our framework can capture the continuous variation in particle views and separate images of real particles from contamination. Using in silico mixtures of multiple types of proteins, we demonstrated our method's capability of separating the protein classes without supervision. Finally in a real cryo-ET dataset of algal chloroplast, our deep learning model successfully detected the four main protein complexes of photosynthesis on native thylakoid membranes. Taken together, these results demonstrate that our framework offers a scalable, annotation-free solution for robust structural discovery across diverse cryo-EM and cryo-ET applications.

Title: ECMExplainer: a functional matrisome framework for decoding cellular stress states and aging trajectories
Authors: Sheekey, E.; Avelar, R. A.; Fujiwara, H.
Abstract: The extracellular matrix (ECM) is increasingly recognized as both a hallmark of aging and a durable record of the cellular stress states that shape age-related tissue dysfunction. Despite its apparent role in aging and disease, translating matrisome gene expression into interpretable biological meaning remains an unresolved challenge. Here we introduce ECMExplainer, a framework that uses 180 matrisome gene-pair ratios, partitioned into 76 Assembly/Destruction and 104 Signaling/Signaling pairs to position fibroblast transcriptomes within a functional matrisome phenotype space defined by six reference fibroblast states spanning physiological and stress-associated conditions: Proliferating, Quiescence, Senescence, Fibrosis, Inflammation, and Hypoxia. Because each ratio records only which of the two genes is more highly expressed, it is largely insensitive to sequencing depth and batch offsets, allowing ECMExplainer to outperform magnitude-based classifiers on unseen data. Rather than assigning only a single phenotype label, ECMExplainer measures a sample's coordinate distance to each reference state, enabling quantitative mapping of matrisome state trajectories while giving biological meaning even to conditions that fall between or outside the training phenotypes. Across 20 independent fibroblast datasets, ECMExplainer uncovered conserved ECM signatures underlying diverse fibroblast states and showed that they capture multiple aging-related processes. Specifically, it identified FST/ITGA1 as a rapamycin-sensitive senescence-associated ratio, revealed a fibrosis-biased ECM trajectory in Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome distinct from chronological aging, and distinguished successful from failed OSKM reprogramming using an ECM Aging Score without retraining. Together, these findings establish the matrisome as a compact and biologically interpretable carrier of cellular state information, and ECMExplainer as a quantitative foundation for interpreting aging, fibrosis and rejuvenation through the lens of the ECM.

Title: Deoxycholic Acid (DCA) a Secondary Bile Acid, Mitigates Ovariectomy-Induced Bone Loss and promotes Bone Healing: A Novel Candidate for Orthopaedic Applications
Authors: Yadav, S.; Rajput, S.; Ahlawat, P.; Saini, C.; Sharma, M.; Sharma, H. P.; Garg, B.; Manhas, V.; Batra, S.; Sharma, N.; Maras, J. S.; Mishra, P. K.; SIngh, D.; Srivastava, R. K.
Abstract: Introduction Postmenopausal osteoporosis (PMO) is a metabolic disorder, characterized by accelerated bone loss, gut microbiota (GM) dysbiosis and altered microbial metabolites. Deoxycholic acid (DCA) is a secondary bile acid with an FDA-approved drug status for submental fat treatment in adults; however its effect on bone health remains underexplored. Materials and Methods This study investigated the effects of DCA on bone health using both preclinical animal model of PMO and clinical samples from PMO women. DCA (20 mg/kg) was administered to ovariectomised (OVX) mice for 45 days, and its effects on bone microarchitecture and serum cytokines were analysed. Osteoclastogenesis and osteoblastogenesis were evaluated using murine and human samples. Untargeted and targeted metabolomics analyses were performed using an ultra-high-performance liquid chromatographic system coupled with high-resolution Orbitrap mass spectrometry (HRMS). Secondary analysis of 16S rRNA sequencing data was performed using R programming. Results GM analysis and plasma metabolomics revealed an alteration in bacterial taxa associated with secondary BA synthesis and reduced circulating DCA levels. DCA administration improved impaired trabecular and cortical bone microarchitecture in the OVX mice by inhibiting osteoclastogenesis and enhancing osteoblastogenesis. Moreover, DCA altered circulating osteoclastogenic (IL-6, Il-9, IL-17A, IFN-{gamma}, RANKL) and osteoblastogenic (OPG, TGF-{beta}, IL-10) factors. Mechanically, DCA suppressed osteoclast differentiation and the expression of genes associated with osteoclast formation (NFATC1, NFKB, TRAF6, TREM2, SYNB), fusion (CSF1R, DC-STAMP, CD47), and resorption (CTSK, ATP6VOD1, ATP6VOD2, CAR2, SPP1) in human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs), while promoting osteogenic differentiation and matrix mineralization in bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) from PMO women. Additionally, DCA enhanced the nascent calcium deposition at the fracture site and improved bone healing via inhibiting osteoclastogenesis. Conclusion Overall, reduced DCA availability was associated with PMO, while DCA treatment mitigated OVX-induced bone loss and improved bone healing. This study highlights the therapeutic potential of DCA for maintaining both bone homeostasis in PMO and fracture healing with immense orthopaedic applications.

Title: Multivalent mRNA tuberculosis vaccines protect against mycobacterial infection in zebrafish, mice and guinea pigs
Authors: Saralahti, A. K.; Isotalo, T. A.; Niskanen, M. T.; Kummola, L.; Mäkinen, L.; Nguyen, D.; Ackart, D. F.; Hunstad, L.; Miller, O. R.; Elkashif, A.; Easton, R. J.; Gonzalez-Rodriguez, M.; Junno, M.; Valanne, S.; Junttila, I. S.; Podell, B. K.; Saunders, B. M.; Rämet, M.
Abstract: Despite a century of BCG use, tuberculosis remains a leading cause of death from infectious diseases and more effective vaccines are urgently needed. Here we combined antigen discovery in zebrafish with mRNA vaccine technology to generate multivalent vaccine candidates, TUmRNA4, TUmRNA6 and TUmRNA9, encoding four, six, or nine Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens, respectively. The vaccines were well tolerated, and induced robust antigen-specific cellular immune responses, including IFN{gamma} production and expansion of memory T-cell populations. In mice, TUmRNA4 and TUmRNA6 reduced pulmonary M. tuberculosis burden and lung pathology to levels comparable to BCG vaccination and TUmRNA6 enhanced BCG-mediated protection when used as a booster vaccine. In guinea pigs, TUmRNA9 reduced bacterial burden in the lungs, spleen, and lymph nodes and decreased pulmonary lesions. These findings demonstrate that protective antigens identified in zebrafish can be translated into effective multivalent mRNA vaccines and establish a framework for tuberculosis vaccine development across multiple preclinical models.

Title: Multi-specific nanobody-Fc fusions against TcdB protect in vivo from diverse Clostridioides difficile strains
Authors: Ehni, A. G.; Lanca, B. B. C.; Kroh, H. K.; Smith, A. J.; Thomas, A. K.; Washington, M. K.; Spiller, B. W.; Lacy, D. B.
Abstract: Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI) is an urgent antibiotic-associated threat and the leading cause of nosocomial diarrhea in the United States, with a high rate of recurrence. Antibiotics are the standard of care for treating CDI but can prolong microbial dysbiosis in the gut. The only FDA-approved monoclonal antibody (mAb) for the prevention of recurrent CDI, Zinplava (bezlotoxumab), was discontinued in January 2025. The target of bezlotoxumab is the dominant virulence factor of C. difficile, the exotoxin B (TcdB). However, TcdB sequences vary across strains and encompass twelve distinct subtypes. Consequently, sequence variation between subtypes presents a challenge for the identification of pan-neutralizing mAb therapeutics. Here, we describe the generation of three bi-specific and one tri-specific nanobody-Fc fusions targeting TcdB. Each fusion neutralizes TcdB in vitro across clinically relevant subtypes with greater potency than bezlotoxumab. In a mouse model of CDI, using three diverse C. difficile strains, several of the fusion proteins improve infection outcomes over bezlotoxumab when administered prophylactically. We also highlight one fusion that improves survival in a therapeutic mouse model of CDI. These data demonstrate multi-specific nanobody-Fc fusions as a strategy to improve potency and mitigate the impact of sequence variation within the toxin. Our fusions outperform the standards established by bezlotoxumab and represent strong candidates for translation.

Title: Phage peptide promotes bacterial cell death via inner and outer membrane targets
Authors: Debrah, M. A.; Carrillo, L. A.; Baral, B. K.; Schnarre, M.; Wardrip, L.; Lorigan, G. A.; Schromm, A. B.; Ramsey, J. R.
Abstract: ABSTRACT Cationic antimicrobial peptides (CAMPs) play a major role in mammalian innate immunity by preferentially targeting bacterial membranes through charge-dependent interactions. While CAMPs are extensively studied in eukaryotic systems, less is known about phage-encoded CAMPs and their role in bacterial lysis. Here, we characterize gp28, a 56-aa cationic peptide encoded by the T7-like coliphage phiKT to define its mechanism of membrane disruption and bacteriostatic activity. Biochemical fractionation reveals that gp28 is asymmetrically distributed across bacterial membranes. Supporting its direct role in causing cell death, gp28 induces permeability changes at the inner membrane. Using synthetic gp28 peptide, we also show that gp28 activity is blocked by lipopolysaccharide and divalent cation competition. This led us to discover that gp28 is also active against Gram-positive bacteria in a surface charge-dependent manner. Finally, we demonstrate gp28 has broad bacteriostatic activity against multiple Gram-negative species, including clinical Uropathogenic E. coli (UPEC) isolates. Together, our results support a model in which gp28 exploits charge-based interactions with bacterial surface molecules to gain access to membranes, then destabilizes the envelope to promote host cell death. These findings expand our understanding of phage lysis strategies and highlight phage-derived peptides as potential scaffolds for antimicrobial development. SIGNIFICANCE STATEMENT Cationic antimicrobial peptides produced by eukaryotes target and disrupt bacterial membranes. These peptides are integral members of the innate immune system and potential antibacterials. Due to their cellular origin, the genetics to understand their mechanisms of action are cumbersome. Here, we demonstrate functional similarity between a bacteriophage peptide called gp28 and cationic antimicrobial peptides. Gp28 partitions between both membranes of Gram-negative bacteria and reduces their integrity. We show that gp28 employs charge-based interactions to associate with and disrupt membranes, suggesting that gp28 targets charged polymers on the membrane surface. Additionally, gp28 inhibits the growth of Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, and renders them more susceptible to antibiotics. Our studies provide a foundation for future genetics and development of phage peptide-based antimicrobials.

Title: Chromatin accessibility predictions reveal lineage-structured effects of noncoding variants across hematopoiesis
Authors: Kazemi, M.; Morris, J. A.
Abstract: Background. Noncoding variants account for over 90% of genome-wide association study (GWAS) findings, but their mechanisms are often unclear. Sequence-to-function models provide one approach to variant interpretation by predicting the effects of genetic variation on molecular phenotypes. ChromBPNet predicts variant effects on chromatin accessibility, but how these predictions are organized across differentiation hierarchies and relate to orthogonal predictions remains unclear. Results. We trained ChromBPNet models for 17 hematopoietic cell types and scored 302,830 variants. Of 242,307 variants accessible in at least one cell type, 5.6% were predicted to alter chromatin accessibility. Variants active in more cell types had larger predicted effects. Predicted effects also reflected hematopoietic lineage structure, with sharing declining with lineage distance while effect direction was preserved in 99.6% of parent-child comparisons. ChromBPNet predictions agreed with GWAS fine-mapping but largely identified distinct variants. Fine-mapping-only variants were enriched for coding and transcript-associated variation, whereas ChromBPNet-only variants were enriched for regulatory elements, accessible chromatin, and trait-relevant activity. In K562 CRISPRi datasets, predicted accessibility gain showed limited association with target-gene validation. Regulatory elements containing CTCF motifs were less likely to have validated target genes, consistent with a role in chromatin organization rather than gene activation. Conclusions. ChromBPNet and fine-mapping provide complementary information about variant function. Predicted accessibility effects identify the cell types in which noncoding variants are likely to act and capture relationships across the hematopoietic hierarchy, but provide limited information about the genes they regulate. All predictions are available at: https://bloodnnet.ccbr.utoronto.ca/.

Title: The P-body component Edc3 is required for yeast proliferation in the phyllosphere
Authors: Sekioka, F.; Shiraishi, K.; Akagi, M.; Habata, A.; Arima, Y.; Sakai, Y.; Yurimoto, H.
Abstract: Processing bodies (P-bodies) are major cytosolic ribonucleoprotein granules involved in post-transcriptional regulation. Yeast has been an invaluable model for elucidating the functions of P-bodies under laboratory conditions. However, the physiological significance of P-bodies in natural environments remains unclear. Here, we demonstrate that the P-body component Edc3 is required for yeast proliferation in the phyllosphere, the aerial parts of plants. Deletion of EDC3, a gene critical for P-body formation, impaired proliferation of the methanol-utilizing yeast Candida boidinii on Arabidopsis thaliana leaves where the yeast assimilates methanol as the carbon source while adapting to changes in environmental conditions. In vitro experiments showed that Edc3 contributes to the spatiotemporal regulation of methanol-induced mRNAs (mimRNAs). These mimRNAs form cytosolic dot structures (termed mimRNA granules) that harbor multiple kinds of mimRNAs. In the edc3{Delta} strain, the formation of mimRNA granules was reduced along with a decrease in mimRNA abundance. Under oxidative stress, colocalization of P-bodies with mimRNA granules markedly increased and growth of the edc3{Delta} strain on methanol was suppressed, suggesting that Edc3 contributes to stress tolerance, possibly through enhanced sequestration of mimRNAs into P-bodies. Time-lapse microscopy revealed dynamic interactions between P-bodies and mimRNA granules with transient colocalization. Together, our findings indicate that Edc3-dependent functions of P-bodies participate in the regulation of mimRNAs and contribute to yeast adaptation to the phyllosphere.

Title: Multicellular signaling in reverse cardiac remodeling revealed by integrated bulk and single-nucleus transcriptomics
Authors: Steier, M.; Rivero-Garcia, I.; Flores, R. O. R.; Deshpande, A.; Aijaz, I.; Poetzsch, J.; Nazir, S.; Talamini, M.; Ast, V.; Mossinger, K.; Dewenter, M.; Meder, B.; Leuschner, F.; Kumari, M.; Backs, J.; Rangrez, A. Y.; Saez-Rodriguez, J.; Frey, N.
Abstract: Heart failure results from maladaptive multicellular remodeling triggered by sustained biomechanical stress. Although mechanical unloading can promote reverse remodeling, recovery is frequently incomplete and its mechanistic basis remains unclear. Using a reversible murine pressure-overload model combined with bulk and single-nucleus transcriptomics, we demonstrate that reverse remodeling represents an actively maintained yet constrained multicellular state. Unloading improved cardiac function and partially restored extracellular matrix and metabolic programs, whereas inflammatory and mitochondrial dysfunction signatures persisted. Cardiomyocytes and endothelial cells largely re-established homeostatic transcriptional states, while fibroblasts retained activated programs that dominated residual pathology. Multicellular factor analysis delineated a reversible metabolic stress program and a persistent inflammatory-mitochondrial program coordinated across cardiac cell types. Cell-cell communication analysis identified lymphatic endothelial cells as key instructive regulators of recovery. Notably, lymphatic-derived Reelin (RELN) directly suppressed pathological fetal gene activation in murine and human cardiomyocytes, uncovering a previously unrecognized lymphoangiocrine mechanism that constrains myocardial recovery in chronic heart failure.

Title: Network modeling identifies vitamin B2 control of AIFM2 deficit-driven hepatocyte death in MASLD
Authors: Weihs, J.; Baldo, F.; Cardinali, A.; Youssef, G.; Ludwik, K.; Haep, N.; Tang, P.; Kumar, P.; Engelmann, C.; Quach, S.; Meindl, M.; Kucklick, M.; Engelmann, S.; Chilian, B.; Rothe, M.; Lurje, I.; Hammerich, L.; Romeike, M.; Ramachandran, P.; Kendall, T. J.; Fallowfield, J. A.; Vallier, L.; Stachelscheid, H.; Sauer, I.; Tacke, F.; Bufler, P.; Hudert, C.; Han, N.; Rezvani, M.; Takebe, T.
Abstract: Drug discovery for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) remains difficult due to network effects. We developed MetaLiver, a public resource to identify druggable nodes within complex interactomes. It incorporates a MASLD-specific knowledge graph that improves bioactive compound contextualization while reducing computing time 18.8-fold. Layering progression-resolved bulk and hepatocyte-specific single-cell MASLD data onto this graph identified the vitamin B2-dependent flavoproteome (FlavProt) as an injury-sensitive network. Induced pluripotent stem cell-derived and primary human hepatocytes validated that flavin-cofactor replenishment mitigates FlavProt-dependent dysregulation, augmenting metabolic functions under cellular stress. Saturating flavin-cofactor availability blunted human immune cell activation. Clinically, a FlavProt expression score significantly correlated with poor outcomes in retrospectively stratified MASLD patients. We identified the oxidoreductase AIFM2 from this score and established experimentally that its injury-associated deficit causes hepatocyte death yet is controllable by flavin-cofactor availability. This study reveals the FlavProt as critical yet modifiable in MASLD and establishes MetaLiver for network discovery.

Title: A dynamic displacement mechanism drives protein import into mitochondria
Authors: Sucec, I.; Guillerm, U.; Schneider, J.; Ganesan, I.; Webling, N.; Kapitonova, A.; Steiert, C.; Schmelter, F.; Feignier, A.; Singh, R.; Fielden, L. F.; Dung, J.; Rapaport, D.; Bersch, B.; Busch, K. B.; Dehez, F.; Wiedemann, N.; Schanda, P.
Abstract: Most mitochondrial proteins are produced in the cytosol and imported through the translocase of the outer mitochondrial membrane (TOM) to reach their final destination. Although this protein entry gate has been structurally characterized, it remains unclear how precursor proteins are handed off from the cytosolic receptor domains to the translocation pore. Here we show that the cytosolic domain of Tom22 - traditionally viewed as the central TOM receptor - acts not as a structured scaffold but as a largely disordered, flexible segment that plays an active role in precursor transfer. Atomic-level structural techniques and in vivo experiments identified a conserved short linear motif that forms a transient -helical element within this disordered domain. By binding to the canonical precursor protein binding sites of the receptors Tom20 and Tom70, this critical -helical segment acts as a precursor protein displacement element (PPDE). This competitive interaction facilitates the release of preproteins directly above the import pore, and thereby drives translocation across the outer mitochondrial membrane. These findings reveal that flexibility, rather than rigid structure, underlies the central transfer step of mitochondrial outer-membrane protein translocation. Our results point to a versatile mechanism for ligand displacement in chaperone, receptor, and transport systems that must balance selective binding with efficient release.

Title: Planar, organoid-independent iPSC-derived small intestinal epithelium from celiac disease patient for studying cytokine-induced changes
Authors: Kukkoaho, P.; Annala, M.; Kosunen, M.; Kaunisto, H.; Tanner, K.; Siddique, F.; Soltin, E.; Kandikanti, N.; Kaksonen, S.; Leskinen, K.; Saavalainen, P.; Kesseli, J.; Nykter, M.; Aalto-Setälä, K.; Kaukinen, K.; Lindfors, K.; Juuti-Uusitalo, K.
Abstract: Background and aims: Celiac disease is a wheat-induced immune-mediated enteropathy characterized by cytokine, especially IFNg upregulation. Intestinal organoid models for adult stem cell based celiac disease exist, but planar iPSC based small intestinal epithelial models derived from celiac disease patients that would allow direct assessment from both sides of the epithelium have been lacking. We aimed to bridge this gap by setting up a two-dimensional in vitro model based on small intestinal epithelial cells derived from iPSC from celiac disease patient. Methods: IPSCs from celiac disease patient and control patient were directly differentiated into small intestinal epithelium on Transwell inserts without intermediate organoid phase or replating. Model maturity and celiac disease specific cytokine responses were analysed using immunofluorescence, transcriptomic profiling, and LDH cytotoxicity assay. Results: Two-dimensionally cultured celiac disease derived line and control patient derived iPSCs matured similarly towards intestinal epithelium which expressed enterocyte specific PEPT1 and EpCAM. To the cytokine stimuli, celiac and healthy iPSC-SIECs responded by increasing the expression IRF1, ICAM1 and IDO1, and several other known cytokine responsive genes. Conclusions: These findings suggest that the 2D iPSC celiac disease small intestinal epithelium model represent an appropriate platform for studying inflammation-associated enteropathies, such as celiac disease.

Title: From Network Topology to Parameterization: An Optimized Model of Endothelial Mechanobiology
Authors: Gueldner, P. H.; Irons, L.; Warren, J. L.; Li, D. S.; Humphrey, J.
Abstract: Endothelial cells integrate biomechanical and biochemical cues to regulate vascular function, which can be modeled using signaling networks. Yet, the extent to which their signaling behavior is determined by network topology versus reaction-specific parameterization remains unclear. We developed a continuous logic-based ordinary differential equation model of endothelial signaling containing 70 species and 123 regulatory reactions assembled from the literature. Model predictions were evaluated against 79 literature-defined responses to imposed wall stress, wall shear stress, hypoxia, or TNF. We first tested whether a single global parameter triplet (describing reaction weight, Hill coefficient, and half-maximal activation) could reproduce these observations. Investigator-selected global parameters reproduced 62/79 responses (78.48%). Monte Carlo sampling of 100,000 globally constant parameter sets improved agreement to 69/79 responses (87.34%), indicating that network topology alone captured most qualitative signaling behavior but remained sensitive to parameter choice. Allowing reaction-specific parameters, also by Monte Carlo sampling within 100,000 additional parameter sets, increased the best agreement to 75/79 responses (94.94%). We then used a genetic algorithm to identify the smallest subset of reactions requiring reaction-specific specification while retaining a common constant-parameter spine for the remainder of the network. Near complete agreement with literature-defined responses (78/79, or 98.73%) was achieved with reaction-specific parameterization of only 18 of 123 reactions. The optimized model was subsequently used to simulate responses to continuous changes in wall shear stress, revealing pathway-dependent nonlinear responses including monotonic increases in nitric oxide and pSmad1/5, nonmonotonic responses in endothelin-1 and NF-{kappa}B, and a biphasic pSmad2/3 response. These findings show that most observed endothelial signaling behavior can be reproduced by a fixed network topology and broadly shared reaction parameters with only a limited subset of interactions requiring quantitative specialization. This framework provides a compact endothelial signaling model for investigating mechanobiological regulation and for future integration with multiscale models of vascular adaptation and disease.

Title: Dynamic Hierarchical Interleaved Bloom Filter: An Updatable Index for Large-Scale Fast Sequence Search
Authors: Seiler, E.; Willemsen, M.; Piro, V. C.; Reinert, K.
Abstract: Motivation: A continued decrease in sequencing costs has facilitated the exponential increase in available sequencing data, with public databases like the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA) and Sequence Read Archive (SRA) reaching well in the order of petabases. This has been the incentive to develop more scalable tools for common bioinformatics tasks. One such task is the approximate searching of short sequence patterns like genes or reads in reference data sets. In recent years, a variety of indexing data structures have been proposed for searching large sequencing databases. The state-of-the-art index, the Hierarchical Interleaved Bloom Filter (HIBF), was first-in-class to index one million samples. However, its static design necessitates costly full reconstructions as repositories grow, motivating an extension to support dynamic updates. Results: In this paper, we introduce a scalable and updatable sequence-search index by extending the HIBF with partial rebuilding to support efficient updates. We demonstrate the Dynamic HIBF's capacity for large-scale data by iteratively creating an index from over 100 TB of compressed reads across more than 39,000 full human RNA-Seq samples, updated in consecutive batches of 100. To benchmark against state-of-the-art tools, we evaluated incremental performance on a subset of 5,000 samples sub-sampled to 1% of their original read depth. In this comparative setting, the dynamic HIBF completed the sequential insertion of all 5,000 samples in 5.3 hours--23 to 42 times faster than competing methods and twice as fast as the static HIBF.

Title: The role of nonspecific binding in kinase-peptide recognition revealed by molecular dynamics simulations
Authors: Wu, Y.; Zhang, Y.; Shinobu, A.
Abstract: Protein kinases recognize their substrates through specific short peptide motifs, and this specificity has motivated broad interest in developing peptide-based kinase inhibitors. Traditional studies have focused mainly on this specific, bound-pose interaction, whereas the nonspecific interactions that precede specific binding have received comparatively little attention. Such nonspecific interactions are transient, making them difficult to capture using either experimental techniques or conventional molecular dynamics simulations, and consequently their biological significance and functional role remain poorly understood. Here, we used two-dimensional replica exchange (gREST/REUS) to study the binding process between Abl kinase and its optimal synthetic substrate, Abltide. The simulations revealed that, in addition to the specific bound pose, the surface of Abl kinase harbors multiple nonspecific binding sites that constitute distinct encounter states, mediated primarily by electrostatic interactions. Abltide proceeds toward the binding pocket from encounter states at three of these sites. As Abltide enters the pocket, the EF/G/{beta}11 patch plays a central role in stabilizing the resulting intermediate states, primarily through hydrophobic interactions. Within the substrate-binding site, the Abltide backbone also shifts progressively out of the register of the specific bound pose, forming backbone hydrogen bonds with the kinase that are absent from the bound pose. These findings indicate that substrate recognition by Abl kinase is encoded not only at the specific binding site but also across the surrounding kinase surface, and that peptide-based inhibitor design should consider both the specific and nonspecific binding behavior of the peptide.

Title: Peripheral detection of viruses shapes brain immunity and behavior in zebrafish
Authors: Kraus, A.; Garcia, B.; Ma, J.; Herrera, K. J.; Zwaka, H.; Harpaz, R.; Wong, R.; Engert, F.; Salinas, I.
Abstract: Olfactory sensory neurons (OSNs) are constantly exposed to pathogens, including viruses. However, serious brain infection via the olfactory route rarely occurs. When OSNs detect a virus, they coordinate local antiviral immune responses to stop virus progression to the brain. Despite effective immune control in the olfactory periphery, pathogen-triggered neuronal signals reach the CNS via the olfactory bulb (OB). We hypothesized that neuronal detection of a virus by OSNs initiates neuroimmune responses in the OB that prevent pathogen invasion. Using zebrafish (Danio rerio) as a model, we demonstrate viral-specific neuronal activation of OSNs projecting into the OB, indicating that OSNs are electrically activated by viruses. Further, behavioral changes are seen in both adult and larval zebrafish after viral exposure. By profiling the transcription of single cells in the OB after OSNs are exposed to virus, we found that both microglia and neurons enter a protective state. Microglia and macrophage populations in the OB respond within minutes of nasal viral delivery followed decreased expression of neuronal differentiation factors and enrichment of genes in the neuropeptide signaling pathway in neuronal clusters. Pituitary adenylate-cyclase-activating polypeptide (pacap), a known antimicrobial, was especially enriched in a neuronal cluster. We confirm that PACAP is antiviral in vitro and that PACAP expression increases in the OB 1 day post-viral treatment. Our work reveals how encounters with viruses in the olfactory periphery shape the vertebrate brain by inducing antimicrobial programs in neurons and by altering host behavior.

Title: The bile acid receptor TGR5 is a modulator of the bone marrow microenvironment
Authors: Alonso-Calleja, A.; Perino, A.; Schyrr, F.; Ferreira Lopes, S.; Delitsikou, V.; Jalil, A.; Kettenberger, U.; Galavotti, M. C.; Martins, A.; Bataclan, C.; Pioletti, D. P.; Schoonjans, K.; Naveiras, O.
Abstract: The gut is an emerging regulator of bone marrow (BM) hematopoiesis, with several molecules involved in this communication. Among them, bile acids (BAs) act as a relay between the microbiota and the rest of the body by activating specific receptors, including Takeda G protein-coupled receptor 5 (TGR5). Although TGR5 has potent regulatory effects in immune cells, its role in the BM remains unclear. Here, we show that TGR5 is expressed across hematopoietic populations, including hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells. While TGR5 deficiency did not affect steady-state hematopoiesis, it mildly impaired cell-autonomous short-term hematopoietic reconstitution. In contrast, TGR5 deletion altered the BM microenvironment. Young male, but not female, Tgr5-/- mice showed reduced bone marrow adipose tissue (BMAT) alongside an accumulation of BM adipocyte progenitors, consistent with impaired progenitor differentiation. TGR5 deficiency also blunted BMAT expansion during obesity and aging, with reduced myeloid-lymphoid progenitor ratios in male mice. Together, our results indicate that TGR5 contributes to sex-dependent regulation of BM adiposity and identify it as a potential target for modulating the BM niche.

Title: Identification of a somatic H3K23me3 methyltransferase SET-19 in C. elegans
Authors: Xu, M.; Fan, Z.; Yan, C.; Chen, X.; Huang, X.; Zhu, C.; Hong, M.; Cheng, J.; Hou, X.; Li, S.; Li, M.; Zhao, Z.; Shi, Y.; Huang, M.; Guang, S.; Feng, X.
Abstract: Histone methylation plays essential roles in modulating chromatin organization and gene expression. H3K23 methylation is a conserved histone modification, yet its biological roles and the enzymes responsible for its deposition remain poorly understood. Here, we show that the loss of set-19 leads to a pronounced reduction in H3K23 methylation in C. elegans, as revealed by quantitative mass spectrometry, western blotting, and immunofluorescence staining. In vitro biochemical assays show that recombinant SET-19 proteins purified from E. coli directly catalyze H3K23 methylation. Genome-wide chromatin immunoprecipitation assays reveal that H3K23me3 is enriched at heterochromatic regions and that loss of set-19 alters H3K23me3 levels, accompanied by derepression of a subset of genes. Genetic analyses indicate that SET-19 is dispensable for both germline and somatic RNAi as well as transgenerational epigenetic inheritance of RNAi. SET-19 is predominantly expressed in somatic cells and specifically mediates H3K23me3 deposition in somatic tissues. The loss of set-19 causes a modest developmental delay. Together, our results identify SET-19 as a somatic H3K23 methyltransferase and link SET-19-dependent H3K23me3 to transcriptional repression in C. elegans.

Title: Can Folding Models Tell Binders from Bluffers? Evidence from POISK: The Patent-Derived Antibody Dataset
Authors: Tupikina, D.; Roncoli, A.; Bujotzek, A.; Abanades, B.
Abstract: Structure prediction models are increasingly deployed as zero-shot digital screens in antibody design, operating under the assumption that high folding confidence implies true binding. However, rigorous validation of this premise has been limited by small test sets, narrow target diversity, and the risk of data leakage from training-adjacent structures. Here we introduce POISK: Patent-extracted Organization of Immunoglobulin Sequence Knowledge, a large-scale dataset derived from the US patent literature, comprising 89074 antibody-antigen records extracted from 10110 patents using an LLM-based pipeline. From this resource, we curate a balanced benchmark set of 22494 complexes: 11247 patent-validated binders without a known resolved structure paired with putative non-binders constructed from sequence-similar human repertoire antibodies. Using this dataset, we benchmark six leading structure prediction models (AlphaFold-Multimer, Boltz-2, IntelliFold v2, OpenFold3, Protenix-v1, and Protenix-v2) on their ability to discriminate binders from decoys. The best-performing model, Protenix-v2, achieves 72% pairwise accuracy over all pairs and 87% on the most confident half of predictions, and correctly identifies the true binder from a pool of 50 candidates in 29% of trials; this represents a substantial enrichment over random selection, yet remains far from reliable single-candidate identification. Structural consensus across models also discriminates binders from decoys, with pairwise accuracy reaching 73.1% when three or more models converge on a pose (DockQ>0.23, covering around 54.2% of pairs). Epitope localization remains unreliable: the best model contacts annotated epitope residues in only 62.8% of cases, indicating that binding discrimination does not establish accurate epitope localization. Our results suggest that current folding models provide useful but limited signal for antibody screening and should be complemented by orthogonal methods. We release POISK as a community resource for future benchmarking and model training.

Title: CellChat Hotspot: A Targeted Approach to Cell Cell Communication Analysis With Spatial transcriptomics Validation.
Authors: Monaco, D.; Dioguardi, M.; Dipalma, M.; Mattioli, E.; Zito, F. A.; Giovannelli, F.; Ricco, A.; Brunetti, O.; Argentiero, A.; De Summa, S.
Abstract: Abstract. In recent years, single cell RNA sequencing (scRNA seq) has enabled the investigation of intercellular communication through Cell Cell Communication (CCC) tools such as CellChat. Despite their potential, these approaches remain challenging to interpret, particularly when global analyses generate complex interaction networks that may include biologically irrelevant signals. To address this limitation, we developed a framework termed CellChat Hotspot, designed to improve the biological interpretability of inferred communication networks. This approach integrates gene set enrichment analysis with a context driven filtering strategy, selecting both genes and cells based on their functional relevance prior to communication inference. Applied to stage II colon cancer data, CellChat Hotspot enabled the identification of condition-specific interaction patterns associated with recurrence. Non recurrent patients showed enrichment of immune related processes, whereas recurrent cases were characterized by pathways associated with invasion and metastasis. Notably, a loss of interaction in the HSPG pathway between CALB1+ and stromal cells was observed in recurrent patients, suggesting a potential disruption of cell matrix adhesion mechanisms. To verify the reliability of this finding, we applied the framework to spatial transcriptomics data, which confirmed the presence of the HSPG2 DAG1 interaction in non-recurrent tumors and its near absence in recurrent ones. Overall, this framework provides a biologically guided strategy for studying intercellular communication in complex systems such as the tumor microenvironment.

Title: Mathematical Modeling of the Canonical Aryl Hydrocarbon Receptor Pathway in murine bone-marrow-derived macrophages
Authors: Wieland, V.; Blum, T.; Iriady, I.; Reverte-Salisa, L.; Pathirana, D.; Foerster, I.; Weighardt, H.; Hasenauer, J.
Abstract: The aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) is a ligand-activated transcription factor involved in xenobiotic sensing, as well as development, immunity, and tissue homeostasis. AhR signaling proceeds through a canonical and a non-canonical branch. It remains unclear which biochemical steps of the canonical pathway are responsible for distinct ligand specific transcriptional responses. Here, we developed a mechanistic ordinary differential equation model of the canonical AhR pathway in murine bone-marrow-derived macrophages. We calibrated it to time-resolved qPCR measurements of Cyp1a1 and Ahrr mRNA in mouse bone-marrow-derived macrophages exposed to three structurally diverse, environmentally relevant ligands with known immunomodulatory activity: 3-methylcholanthrene, indolo[3,2-]carbazole and bisphenol A. Calibration used global optimization under a heteroskedastic likelihood. To dissect ligand specificity, we evaluated 528 distinct candidate models that allow one or two ligand-involving reaction rate constants to vary. Model selection revealed a dominant regime governed by faster promoter binding. Furthermore, it supported that ICZ requires no ligand-specific parameter relative to 3MC and most differences are visible in the expression levels of Ahrr mRNA. In addition, the model revealed that differences at the promoter binding and transcriptional levels were better supported than upstream signaling events. The resulting model is made available in SBML and PEtab formats for reproducibility, and to enable further research into whether ligand-specific effects are conserved or rewired across cell types.

Title: Loss of riboflavin biosynthesis leads to accumulation of select aromatic amino acids and loss of infectivity in Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Authors: Jaisinghani, N.; Arasappan, A.; Pradhan, A.; Kaur, R.; Li, K.; Aube, J.; Cross, J. R.; Jesus Faustino Ramos, R. J.; Hartman, T.; Previti, M. L.; Vorkas, C. K.; Seeliger, J. C.
Abstract: Riboflavin biosynthesis is required for in vitro survival of the human pathogen Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb). However, despite the lack of a known transporter, growth can be rescued by exogenous riboflavin. The riboflavin biosynthesis pathway is also predicted essential in vivo, but whether riboflavin levels available in the host can support survival has not been directly tested. Here we constructed a set of inducible CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) knockdown and targeted gene deletion strains for known riboflavin biosynthesis genes (ribA2, ribG, ribH, ribC) as tools to characterize riboflavin requirements, uptake, and metabolite changes and to assess in vivo essentiality. We found that riboflavin, but not flavin adenine dinucleotide or flavin mononucleotide, rescued auxotrophy for all strains tested. Further, riboflavin uptake was not affected by disruption of proton motive force or ATP synthesis, suggesting that uptake is not via an active mechanism. Targeted metabolite profiling after removal of riboflavin from growth medium confirmed reduced riboflavin levels. While other riboflavin intermediates were not detected, significant accumulation of aromatic amino acids (Phe, Tyr) was observed across all assayed strains, as well as alteration in a vitamin B9 metabolite. Selecting the ribC knockout as a representative strain, we found that riboflavin depletion had a bacteriostatic effect as late as 3 weeks after removal. Unexpectedly, {Delta}ribC lacked infectivity in an aerosol mouse infection, suggesting that the potential to scavenge riboflavin from the host is not sufficient to survive in vivo. Overall, our results show that altered metabolism upon loss of riboflavin biosynthesis leads to compromised Mtb infectivity.

Title: Measuring satellite arrays of the human Y chromosome from sequencing reads
Authors: Ortigas-Vasquez, A.; Guarracino, A.
Abstract: Human Y chromosome satellites vary widely but remain difficult to measure in large cohorts. We developed Yruler, which uses pangenome assemblies to measure satellite lengths, composition and Y dosage from sequencing reads without alignment. Across cohorts, we find lineage-associated differences in centromere and non-centromeric array length, and show that heterochromatin components vary unequally within lineages. Yruler enables population-scale studies of how Y satellite variation relates to health and disease.

Title: CNVSIM: an interpretable cross-study copy-number reference atlas for cancer subtyping
Authors: YU, J.; Bardet-Trouilloud, J.; Jaeger, S.; Baudis, M.
Abstract: Genome-wide copy-number variation (CNV) profiles provide a representation of structural changes in cancer genomes, but interpreting new profiles with respect to their underlying biology remains challenging. We developed CNVSIM, which organizes CNV profiles into root-specific reference spaces and defines subtypes with chromosome-scale and gene-level signatures. Applied to the Progenetix dataset, CNVSIM established 112 CNV-defined subtypes across 19 cancer roots, supported by 155,881 neoplastic analyses from diverse studies and assay platforms. In the context of diagnostic concepts, these subtypes distinguish genomic architectures and reveal associated differences in somatic mutation patterns, with selected associations supported across cohorts. In practice, CNVSIM enables new profiles to be projected onto the established reference and linked to corresponding reference analyses. Additionally, CNVSIM enables the identification of cancer cell lines with copy-number architectures similar to individual subtypes, while also revealing gaps in subtype and alteration coverage based on available data. Reference robustness was supported by subtype recovery after data reduction and assignment of 77.6% of held-out TCGA profiles using a reference reconstructed without TCGA.

Title: pH-driven dynamics and mechanisms of LNP-mediated siRNA delivery
Authors: Hossain, K. A.; Valerio, M.; Medina, P.; Souza, P. C. T.; Orozco, M.
Abstract: We present a comprehensive analysis of a clinically relevant DLin-MC3-DMA (MC3)-based lipid nanoparticle (LNP) formulation that exhibits strong short interfering RNA (siRNA, ~21 nt) delivery and potent inhibition of targeted RNAs. Using a combination of coarse-grained and atomistic molecular dynamics simulations, we characterize the pH-dependent structure of both unloaded and siRNA-loaded LNPs, elucidate the mechanism of siRNA encapsulation, and use these models to propose a plausible mechanism of endosomal escape. Consistent with prior experimental and computational studies, our simulations reproduce an inverted-hexagonal-type morphology in a ~70 nm siRNA-loaded LNPs. For the smaller LNPs mimetics, with only one siRNA sequence, we observe a similar hydrated core as observed in the larger 70 nm LNP model. Such hydrated channel provides a polar environment suitable for accommodating RNA, whose charge is neutralized mainly by the MC3 ionizable lipids that remain protonated near the RNA even at high pH, thereby bridging the RNA with the surrounding lipid environment. This structural picture is also consistently observed across our multiscale simulations, with smaller self-assembled LNP mimetics reproducing the same local organization at both coarse-grained and atomistic resolution. A potential mechanism of endosomal escape, emerges spontaneously from the simulations, involving stalk formation between the LNP and the endosomal membrane, followed by the opening of a water-filled pore that permits slow siRNA diffusion, in line with the low efficiency and slow kinetics reported for endosomal escape. The rate-limiting step of endosomal escape arises from persistent electrostatic coupling between RNA and protonated MC3 ionizable lipids maintained by the immediate RNA-lipid environment, hindering cargo disengagement even after pore formation. This delayed release is consistent with the experimentally observed time-dependent inhibitory activity of the loaded LNP. Together, these results highlight the importance of local pKa; and protonation effects near the RNA, which are not captured by global apparent pKa; measurements.

Title: GradeBins: quality control of bins from synthetic and real metagenomes
Authors: Bushnell, B.; Bowers, R. M.; Villada, J. C.
Abstract: Genomes reconstructed from metagenomes support studies of microbial diversity and function, but their interpretation depends on how much DNA is recovered and whether foreign sequence is included. Quality can be measured in benchmarks, where contig origins are known, but must be estimated in routine analyses. Here we present GradeBins, which assesses individual bins (contigs assigned to one candidate genome) and summarizes the complete bin set from an assembly. For 6,374 simulated bins, its measurements agreed with AMBER and independent calculations within rounding. In control bins built from 20 kb fragments of reference genomes, GradeBins had lower observed completeness error than CheckM1 and CheckM2 and the highest observed F1 (the harmonic mean of precision and recall) for bin selection. With 2 kb fragments, GradeBins overestimated the completeness of incomplete bins, and its error increased from 3.1 to 17.6 percentage points. Contamination estimates differed among GradeBins, CheckM1, CheckM2 and GUNC, which define contamination differently. In sequenced metagenomes, the choice of estimator changed which bins passed quality cutoffs. GradeBins estimated quality faster than CheckM1, CheckM2 and GUNC on the same hardware. GradeBins thus provides fast quality assessment of prokaryotic bins and bin sets, with completeness estimates that are most accurate for long contigs.

Title: Unravelling the hidden diversity of the monkfish Lophius gastrophysus using integrative taxonomy
Authors: D'Elia, A. K. P.; Soares, L. M. M.; Henning, F.; Sole-Cava, A. M.
Abstract: The monkfish Lophius gastrophysus is a commercially exploited demersal species distributed along the continental shelf and slope of the western Atlantic Ocean. Like other anglerfish species, L. gastrophysus has a pelagic larval stage that can facilitate dispersal by oceanic currents (Farina et al., 2008). It is considered the most widely distributed species in the genus, spanning more than 10,000 km of the western Atlantic Coast, from North Carolina to Argentina. Previous morphological analyses based on a limited set of traits suggested that L. gastrophysus may comprise two distinct species. We tested this hypothesis by combining molecular and morphometric data. Sequence data were obtained from 38 L. gastrophysus individuals collected from Northern and Southern American populations. We also used a subset of 13 specimens for geometric morphometrics. Phylogenetic analyses and automatic species delimitation methods consistently distinguished Northern and Southern Atlantic L. gastrophysus as separate clades, and geometric morphometrics supported the same split. The congruence among geographic, molecular, and morphometric data indicates that L. gastrophysus harbours two distinct lineages, highlighting the need for a formal taxonomic revision and separate fisheries management of northern and southern Atlantic populations.

Title: Centromere divergence and allopolyploidy reshape carnivorous sundew genomes
Authors: Avila Robledillo, L.; Fukushima, K.; Salojarvi, J.; Marques, A.; Albert, V. A.
Abstract: Centromeres are essential for chromosome function, yet how contrasting centromere architectures shape polyploid genome evolution and plant diversification remains unresolved. In monocentric chromosomes, centromeric activity is restricted to one chromosomal region; in holocentric chromosomes, it is distributed along the chromosome length. Hybridization followed by genome doubling can place chromosome sets with different centromeres, repeat complements, and rearrangement histories in the same nucleus. We examined whether such genomic mergers are associated with later chromosome restructuring in carnivorous Caryophyllales, focusing on chromosome-scale assemblies of putatively holocentric Drosera regia and monocentric D. capensis. The two sundews retain broad syntenic continuity and related polyploid ancestry, but their present genomes differ sharply. D. regia preserves several ancestral chromosomal fusions and dispersed candidate centromere-associated satellite repeats, whereas D. capensis has stronger internal duplication, extensive rearrangement, and localized centromeres. Phylogenomic and structural analyses suggest a reticulate evolutionary history for D. regia, with part of its genome showing preferential structural affinity to the Venus flytrap lineage. Whereas D. regia exhibits threefold syntenic depth consistent with hexaploidy, D. capensis exhibits sixfold depth consistent with dodecaploidy, and structural comparisons do not support simple doubling of the extant D. regia-like architecture. Repeat profiling across a broad sample of Drosera also shows rapid turnover and species-level differences in centromere-associated DNA. These results place centromere organization alongside polyploid history and chromosome restructuring as a major axis of genome evolution in sundews.

Title: CLASSIFICATION OF PROKARYOTIC DNA METHYLTRANSFERASES BY CATALYTIC DOMAIN TOPOLOGY
Authors: Samokhina, M.
Abstract: Prokaryotic DNA methyltransferases (MTases) are essential enzymes that play a crucial role in restriction-modification systems, preventing the degradation of self DNA by restriction enzymes. In addition, they contribute to the regulation of gene expression, DNA repair, DNA replication, and other processes. Here, we propose a novel classification of prokaryotic MTases based on the 3D topology of the catalytic domain, which addresses the limitations of the previous scheme developed by Malone and Bujnicki. The latter, which grouped MTases into categories such as , {beta}, {gamma}, etc., has been in use for over 20 years. We identified seven structural classes (A-G) of MTases by analyzing 38 experimentally determined 3D structures and several AlphaFold-predicted models, and validated the classification against all reviewed DNA MTases from Swiss-Prot. The catalytic domains of each class exhibit homology not only in structure but also in conserved motifs. Our classification system provides a framework for understanding the diversity and evolution of prokaryotic DNA MTases, with applications in genomic annotation and evolutionary studies.
