These results place centromere organization alongside polyploid history and chromosome restructuring as a major axis of genome evolution in sundews.

Title: Restriction Enzyme activity under Force determined with autonomous DNA Origami Force Clamps via Gel Electrophoresis
Authors: Ermatov, A.; Matthies, M.; Sulc, P.; Liedl, T.
Abstract: Investigating force-depending behaviour in biological systems is a challenging task, with most techniques requiring complex experimental equipment while also often being limited in scalability. We designed a facile force spectroscopy technique using DNA origami-based force clamps that apply forces up to ~40 pN. We validated the approach by using type II endonucleases that have been previously studied quantitatively by single-molecule measurements. Using ensemble measurements based on ubiquitously used agarose gel electrophoresis, we qualitatively observed force-dependent behaviour for EcoRV and force-independent behaviour for BamHI, replicating previous data for these enzymes. Interestingly, we also observed force-dependent behaviour for EcoRI, whose restriction behaviour has been previously described as force-independent. Our experimental design opens a path to force spectroscopy based on bottom-up techniques and ensemble measurements, allowing to collect statistical data in large quantities with readily available techniques in many wet labs.

Title: Biomolecular design through latent reasoning with RFD4-Proteina
Authors: Corley, N.; Didi, K.; Kazman, M. W.; Brent, R. I.; Bauer, M. S.; Biswas, R.; Bonzanini, J. E.; Chazin-Gray, A. M.; Chen, J.; Favor, A.; Gantz, M.; Jones, H. A.; Kim, P.; Lunn-Halbert, M. C.; McNamara-Bordewick, N. K.; Salike, S.; See, D. L.; Sharma, S.; Sun, E.; Venkatesh, P.; Woodbury, S. M.; Wu, K.; Zhang, Y.; Allen, J. D.; Butcher, J.; Chang, L.; Cho, Y.; Courbet, A.; Coventry, B.; Dallago, C.; Delfosse, E. S.; Eisenach, H. E.; Garcia Sanchez, M.; Geffner, T.; Goreshnik, I.; Greisen, P.; Hunt, A. C.; Kim, D. E.; Kim, D.; King, B. R.; Krishna, R.; Li, Y.; Li, Z. M.; Muraishi, A.; Muratspahic
Abstract: Biomolecular design requires finding chemically and geometrically compatible arrangements of interacting atoms and molecules. The complexity of problems which can be tackled by deep learning design models is limited by both the molecular landscape they encompass and their ability to explore that landscape effectively. Here we introduce RFD4-Proteina, which addresses these limitations through intrinsic and extrinsic reasoning within a shared chemical and conformational latent space. The latent space encompasses standard and modified amino acids, sugars, DNA, and RNA, with force-field supervision favoring physically plausible atomic reconstructions. Within this space, intrinsic reasoning uses recurrent refinement to adaptively allocate computation, while extrinsic reasoning guides search with arbitrary constraints such as energetic or geometric criteria. Across in silico protein design benchmarks, RFD4-Proteina achieves higher design success rates at greater generation throughput than all previous methods evaluated, with further gains from conformational flexibility, recurrent refinement, and search. The same model performs equivalently to or better than state-of-the-art specialist methods for side-chain packing, sequence design, conformational sampling, and design refinement. We demonstrate the power and versatility of RFD4-Proteina experimentally by designing specific and cross-reactive binders to therapeutically relevant targets, recognizing phosphorylations, controlling glycosylation, and creating enzymes that catalyze both bond-breaking and bond-forming reactions, including a first proof-of-concept demonstration of a de novo designed enzyme for active pharmaceutical ingredient synthesis. By unifying diverse chemistry, conformational flexibility, and scalable reasoning in a single physically grounded latent space, RFD4-Proteina expands the frontier of biomolecular design.

Title: ISdetector: precise mapping of insertion sequences and associated structural variations from short-read sequencing data
Authors: Zhou, Y.; Lu, B.; Zhao, Y.
Abstract: Motivation. Repetitive insertion sequences (ISs) and adjacent structural variants (SVs) complicate precise mapping from bacte-rial short reads. Accurate insertion coordinates are important for studying genome evolution and tracking transmission. Results. ISdetector constructs IS-specific references with target copies removed and clusters soft-clipped reads to pinpoint insertion sites. On simulated genomes, it had higher recall and F1 score than ISMapper and MGEFinder. On 19 Mycobacterium tuberculosis genomes, it achieved the highest high-confidence F1 score (0.86). On five Shigella sonnei genomes, it performed comparably to ISMapper (F1 score 0.85). It detected 81 of 105 IS6110 copies with associated SVs or complex events, versus 41 (ISMapper) and 12 (MGEFinder). With four threads, it outpaced both comparators at any thread count. Availability and Implementation. ISdetector is implemented in Python and the archived release are available at https://github.com/carolynzy/ISdetector/releases/tag/v1.1.0 .

Title: Inferring single-cell gene expression profiles from multicellular spatial transcriptomics data with st2sc
Authors: Lee, Y. J.; Shah, S.; Mantrala, S.; Lugo-Martinez, J.
Abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) enables the quantitative measurement of gene expression within tissue sections but is currently limited in spatial resolution, as each spot aggregates signals from multiple cells. Recovering single-cell gene expression profiles from these multicellular measurements requires two steps: explicit identification of individual cells and accurate estimation of per-gene expression. While existing methods have demonstrated the feasibility of recovering single-cell expression profiles, accurately estimating gene-level expression for individual cells remains an important challenge. To address this challenge, we propose st2sc (Spatial Transcriptomics to Single-Cell), an end-to-end framework for inferring single-cell gene profiles from multicellular ST data. st2sc introduces a novel Attention Gradient Flow Tracking (AGFT) algorithm that extracts attention maps from a Vision-Gene Transformer to identify candidate cell instances without predefined background constraints. The detected instances are then used by a set of regressors trained under a multiple-instance, multiple-target regression setting to predict precise single-cell gene expression counts. Comprehensive evaluations on synthetic and Visium-like datasets demonstrate that st2sc significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in accurately segmenting cellular instances and predicting gene counts. The method can further resolve contested 2um bin in Visium HD. Application to human IPF lung showed the model can recover the subtype marker level analysis. This advancement further improves single-cell resolution analysis in spatial transcriptomics, facilitating more accurate downstream biological analyses.

Title: DNA methylation assigns sequencing reads to closely related bacterial strains when their sequence cannot
Authors: Kakabra, K.; Claesson, M. J.
Abstract: Clinical and public-health questions often concern strains rather than species, yet co-resident strains of one species can be so closely related that a single long read carries no sequence difference between them. We measured how often this happens in 639 pairs of isolates of Enterococcus faecium, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Listeria monocytogenes and Staphylococcus aureus sequenced on one nanopore platform. Among the 297 pairs above 99% average nucleotide identity (ANI), 40.37% of read placements (a read counted against one strain's genome) carried no sequence difference between the two strains, and above 99.9% ANI about three quarters did. Strains of one species also differ in the DNA motifs they methylate. Our method, Epilect, assigns single nanopore reads to strains from the basecaller's methylation calls, given a methylation profile for each strain, and declines to call when the evidence is weak. In the pairs above 99% ANI it correctly assigned 21.8% of the read placements that sequence could not place, at a precision of 0.959. In computational mixtures of 65 pairs of distinct strains at or above 99.5% ANI that were predicted to differ in methylation, its per-read F1 score exceeded that of the best of three sequence-based read-phasing tools by 0.25 (95% CI 0.08 to 0.37); where equally related strains were predicted to share a methylome, the comparison reversed. DNA methylation therefore supplies strain evidence on reads whose sequence carries none, and whether it will do so for a given pair of strains can be estimated before sequencing.

Title: Point mutations in the FimH lectin domain: predicted folding stability versus conformational dynamics for R60P, Q133K and Y137A
Authors: Navas Passos, J. A.; Pereira Tapia, A.; Velez Duncan, C.; Alviz Amador, A.
Abstract: Background. The adhesin FimH attaches uropathogenic Escherichia coli to the urinary epithelium through a force-regulated catch-bond that single lectin-domain substitutions can modulate. How such substitutions reshape the dynamics of the isolated lectin domain, and whether stability predictors anticipate them, is unclear. Methods. We compared the wild-type (WT) lectin domain (PDB 4XO8, apo) with R60P, Y137A and Q133K, using three 500 ns molecular dynamics (MD) replicates per system (6 microseconds total) and three folding-stability predictors (FoldX, a Cartesian-ddG-type Rosetta protocol, ERIS-2). The replicate was the unit of analysis (n = 3), with 95% confidence intervals and a WT replicate-to-replicate control. Results. FoldX and ERIS-2 ranked the variants consistently, R60P most destabilising and Q133K neutral; the Rosetta value for Q133K was anomalously high. All systems stayed folded. R60P gave the only reproduced local change, loss of beta-strand structure at residues 60-61 and of three local hydrogen bonds. Y137A did not bring Thr158 into the pocket, and the Q133K Gln133-Asp54 polar contact became a Lys133-Asp54 salt bridge. In the principal-component landscape, departures from the WT region came from individual replicates (Y137A replicate 1; Q133K replicates 2-3), not a systematic shift. Conclusions. A substitution perturbs local structure most clearly when it breaks a beta-strand (R60P), and the stability predictions and dynamics together give a consistent ranking of the variants, including the first dynamic characterisation of Q133K. The results characterise the apo lectin domain and give a reproducible basis for interpreting FimH mutations, not for inferring affinity. Keywords: FimH; lectin domain; point mutations; molecular dynamics; folding stability ({Delta}{Delta}G); protein stability prediction; principal component analysis; urinary tract infection.

Title: A Rare Constitutional Centromeric Expansion of Chromosome 1 in a Phenotypically Normal Individual: A Comprehensive Cytogenetic Study
Authors: Shirsath, K. B.; Desai, U. N.; Notnani, A.; Chaurasia, R. K.; Bhat, N. N.; Khan, A.
Abstract: Constitutional centromeric heteromorphisms are uncommon chromosomal variants that may complicate cytogenetic interpretation. We report a constitutional enlargement of the centromeric region of one chromosome 1 homologue identified incidentally during biological dose estimation in a suspected occupationally exposed individual. Conventional cytogenetics, pancentromeric fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), and multiplex FISH confirmed the variant and excluded cryptic chromosomal rearrangements. Analysis of 500 metaphases revealed no dicentric chromosomes. Quantitative assessment demonstrated a centromere to chromosome length ratio of 0.314 plus/minus 0.019 for the enlarged homologue compared with 0.169 plus/minus 0.019 for the unaffected homologue and 0.161 to 0.186 in controls, representing an approximately 1.86 fold increase (t = 28.4, p < 0.0001). The findings establish a benign constitutional centromeric heteromorphism of chromosome 1 and highlight the importance of distinguishing such variants from structural chromosomal abnormalities during routine cytogenetic evaluation.

Title: Fast and background-suppressed DNA-PAINT
Authors: Sun, T.; Liu, S.; Zhang, X.; Tang, H.; Hua, B.; Xia, X.-H.
Abstract: The speed and resolution of DNA-PAINT imaging is partly limited by the background fluorescence at high imager-strand concentrations. Here, we combine the photoactivatable fluorophore-quencher-DNA probes with the photoactivation, diffusion, and excitation strategy on a spinning disk confocal microscope, decoupling background fluorescence from the imager-strand concentration. This method yields >7-fold faster DNA-PAINT imaging in cells, a ~15 nm localization precision in hydrogels, without using specialized or speed-optimized imager strands.

Title: Tycholyzer: NanoTemper NT.6 Tycho Analysis Tool
Authors: Ghani, V. G.; Boudker, O.
Abstract: NanoTemper Tycho NT.6 is a nano differential scanning fluorimetry (nanoDSF) instrument that enables rapid measurement of apparent protein melting temperatures. Thermal shift assays are widely used to assess protein stability under different conditions, including screening for protein-ligand interactions. These experiments often involve multiple samples, conditions, and replicates collected across several instrument runs, generating datasets that can be cumbersome to organize, compare, and analyze quantitatively. Here, we introduce Tycholyzer, a user-friendly software application that streamlines processing and analysis of Tycho nanoDSF data. Tycholyzer allows users to combine data from multiple runs, inspect and select individual fluorescence traces, and normalize and group replicate profiles for comparison across experimental conditions. The software provides two complementary approaches for determining apparent melting temperatures: sigmoidal fitting of fluorescence ratio profiles and identification of extrema in their first derivatives. Automated fitting of individual replicates enables calculation of mean melting temperatures and standard deviations, facilitating quantitative assessment of experimental variability. By integrating these capabilities into a single graphical interface, Tycholyzer promotes consistent, efficient, and rigorous analysis of nanoDSF experiments. Tycholyzer is freely available and can be run in MATLAB or as a standalone application using MATLAB Runtime (https://github.com/VGhani/Tycholyzer.git).

Title: EcoToxFred: A knowledge-graph-grounded conversational agent for exploring ecotoxicological monitoring and hazard data
Authors: Scheibe, P.; Schmid, T. S.; Schor, J.
Abstract: Assessing chemical risks to aquatic ecosystems requires the joint interpretation of monitoring data, ecotoxicity data, and derived risk indicators, yet such integrated data are rarely accessible to users without database expertise. We present EcoToxFred, an open-source conversational agent that provides natural language access to a curated knowledge graph of chemical monitoring and hazard data for European surface waters. EcoToxFred couples a large language model (LLM) with a Neo4j graph database in a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) architecture. An agent interprets user questions, selects tools, translates questions into graph queries, and returns answers as text, tables, or interactive maps, together with the executed query for reproducibility. We evaluated EcoToxFred with GPT-4.1 and GPT-5 on a benchmark of 25 questions, including six questions derived from an expert workshop, each posed three times. Answers were scored for tool selection, execution accuracy against human-written reference queries, and goal accuracy using the RAGAS evaluation framework with an independent LLM judge. With both models, EcoToxFred selected an appropriate tool in at least 92% of runs and reproduced the reference result in 74% of runs with a reference query, including all lookup questions. Goal accuracy was 52% with GPT-4.1 and 63% with GPT-5. Failures concentrated on multi-step analytical questions, incomplete presentation of long results, and mismatches between user and database vocabulary. EcoToxFred shows how knowledge-graph-grounded LLM agents can lower the barrier to ecotoxicological data exploration while keeping answers traceable to the underlying data, and its architecture is transferable to other ecological data infrastructures.

Title: Ultrasensitive Regulation in the Tryptophan System in Escherichia coli Provides Effective Noise Mitigation
Authors: Bavdekar, V.; Bhartiya, S.; Venkatesh, K. V.
Abstract: The tryptophan system in Escherichia coli maintains intracellular concentration of tryptophan in a narrow band regardless of the nutritional status and uncertainty in its environment. The system is characterized by three distinct regulations namely, genetic regulation, mRNA attenuation and enzyme inhibition, that use the tryptophan concentration as a feedback signal. It has been shown previously, that the multiple feedback loop design is responsible for rapid synthesis of tryptophan when faced with starvation. It is well known that a design with rapid response to external signals also implies poorer noise mitigation properties. This work investigates the design elements that limit the adverse impact of the multiple feedback loop architecture on noise propagation in the tryptophan system using a frequency response analysis. Specifically, we use sinusoidal input describing functions to approximate the transfer characteristics of the ultrasensitive regulators and then obtain the frequency response of the closed-loop feedback system. The study suggests that the tryptophan system of E. coli has evolved to simultaneously satisfy the two properties of rapid response and noise mitigation. Particularly, the multiple feedback loop is responsible for the rapid response, while the nonlinear regulation provides effective noise mitigation.

Title: Combination of in vitro and ex vivo infection models highlights the role of NAD-dependent ADP-ribosylation in Influenza A virus infection.
Authors: Jacolin, F.; Aublin-Gex, A.; Vellet, M.; Decimo, D.; Lepetit, M.; Denecheau, T.; Canus, L.; OGIRE, E.; Cezard, A.; Jacquemin, C.; Potelet, G.; Croze, S.; Lachuer, J.; LOTTEAU, V.; Diaz, O.; Marcy, G.; Vidalain, P.-O.; Si-Tahar, M.; Mathieu, C.; Perrin-Cocon, L.
Abstract: Influenza A viruses (IAV) remain a major public health concern, causing an estimated 650 000 deaths annually. Although vaccines are available, vaccination coverage is limited and must be repeated annually due to the genetic variability of these viruses. Furthermore, although direct acting antivirals are available, they must be administered as early as possible after infection to be effective. In this context, understanding the metabolic alterations associated with the replication and pathogenesis of IAV could contribute to the development of treatments that promote virus clearance and patient recovery. In this study, we identified the intracellular level of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) as a key factor in the replication of IAV. The depletion of NAD using nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase (NAMPT) inhibitors or the administration of the antimetabolite 6-aminonicotinamide (6-AN) suppressed IAV replication both in vitro and ex vivo. Using a model of infected murine organotypic lung cultures (mOLCs) combined with untargeted metabolomic profiling and spatial transcriptomic analyses, our research also revealed that IAV-infection decreased NAD+ levels in mOLCs, while PARPs, a group of NAD+-consuming enzymes, were upregulated. Pharmacological inhibition of the mono-ADP-ribosyl transferase (mono-ART) activity of PARPs restricted IAV infection ex vivo, suggesting that NAD+ sustains the proviral activity of these enzymes. Overall, our study identifies NAD metabolism as a central regulator of IAV infection and highlights NAMPT and PARP mono-ART activities as promising antiviral targets.

Title: Azospirillum brasilense and cytidine as combination treatment to enhance drought resilience of peas
Authors: Ojha, B.; Tagoe, J.; Horne, S. M.; Pruess, B. M.
Abstract: Aims: This study tested the efficacy of two combination treatments on drought resilience of peas; Azospirillum brasilense Sp7 with the chemoattractant seedling exudate compound cytidine or pea seedling exudate. Methods and Results: Phenotypic characterization revealed that drought tolerance of peas treated with ACyt was 68.9% higher than that of peas treated with the inoculant alone (A). Dry shoot weight of ACyt Drought plants was 30.7% higher than that of plants from the untreated control group NB Drought, drought recovery of ACyt plants was 21.6% better. The treatment with seedling exudate (AEx) was less effective. 16S rDNA analysis revealed that increase in drought tolerance was accompanied by modulation of the rhizosphere. The abundance of Azospirillum sp. was 954% higher in ACyt Drought plants than in NB Drought ones. The ACyt treatment may contribute to protecting pea plants from drought by increasing the abundance of Azospirillum. Within the complete analysis of the 16S rDNA data set, both ACyt Drought and AEx Drought groups had similar increases in Shannon and Pielou alpha-diversity indices, relative to the NB Drought group. These two test groups also exhibited similar changes in the bacterial community structure. Conclusion: The ACyt treatment enhanced drought tolerance and recovery. Both treatments enhanced alpha-diversity and modulated the rhizosphere.

Title: Engineered Miniature ParTasR Enables Efficient PAMless Genome Editing
Authors: Zhu, Q.; Zhang, Z.; Cao, Q.; Ma, X.; Zeng, Y.; Shang, M.; Zhang, X.
Abstract: TIGR-Tas system holds great promise for genome-engineering applications owing to its compact size and PAMless targeting capability. However, its low editing efficiency in mammalian cells severely limits its broader utility. Here, we engineered a highly active variant of ParTasR, termed eTasR, through structure-guided rational design of ParTasR combined with fusion to the exonuclease TREX2. eTasR increased mammalian editing efficiency from the original 4.29% to 48.94% with an average 26.52-fold increase, significantly surpassing the efficiency of SpRY, a reported version of PAM-free nuclease. More importantly, single-AAV delivery enabled efficient Hpd disruption in vivo, resulting in robust phenotypic rescue. Thus, eTasR provides a compact, PAMless and highly efficient platform for genome editing and therapeutic applications.

Title: Highly multiplexed fluorescent imaging via fluidic-free, rapid sequential plasmonic heating activated signal exchange of DNA probes
Authors: Xu, E.; Chen, Y.; Harugeri, A. A.; Pabel, M. Y.; Moor, R. S. F.; Sayour, E.; Ghiaseddin, A. P.; Wei, W. D.; Hong, F.; Song, Q.; Wang, Q.
Abstract: Fluorescence microscopic methods are critical for spatial profiling of multiple biological targets in cells and tissues to study cell and tissue functions, but their multiplexity was limited to 3~5 targets under a conventional setup using different fluorescent channels because of spectra overlap. Here, we introduce a simple, rapid, wash-free multiplexed fluorescence imaging method in cells and tissues, termed DNA based plasmonic heating activated signal exchange reaction (PHASER). PHASER uses infrared light-induced plasmonic heating of gold bipyramid nanoparticles to sequentially activate thermodynamically calibrated DNA thermal probes in situ for rapid and multiplexed fluorescent imaging of biological targets. We showed that the signal exchange per round between biological targets in PHASER can be completed within 30 seconds, and that 5 irradiation pulses of photothermal heating can activate DNA thermal probes with 5 different signal temperatures in cells and tissues. To demonstrate its practical use, we applied PHASER to profile the subcellular spatial organization of different organelles in cultured cells and validated its performance in FFPE tissue. We further used PHASER to resolve up to 15 different protein spatial expression profiles in mouse brain tissue with dimensions of millimeters for single-cell proteomic analysis. PHASER is expected to have broad biotechnical applications with multiplexed fluorescence imaging for a wide variety of biological targets across diverse samples.

Title: Transcription factor activities as a shared representation for drug repurposing hypotheses in breast cancer
Authors: Fernandez-Lozano, C.; Ferreiro, D.; V.-del-Rio, P.
Abstract: Drug repurposing could expand the limited targeted options for triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). PRECISION trains a heterogeneous graph neural network (GNN) over prior-knowledge edges on the PRISM screen, describing cell lines mostly by transcription factor (TF) activities. On held-out cell lines the GNN fell below a drug-mean reference and a TF-based Random Forest. Integrated Gradients attributions define ten core TFs, shared by the drugs examined and partly stable across seeds. Per-drug Ridge models on the same TF activities carried predictions to unselected breast cancer cohorts, where predicted sensitivity was associated with overall survival for 623 of 1,447 drugs in SCAN-B and 74 in METABRIC, partly through a shared prognostic axis. An explicit rule selects seven kinase or histone deacetylase inhibitors whose associations are prognostic and persist only partly within TNBC. Neither TNBC cell lines nor a triple-negative cohort supported them. The shared TF representation yields repurposing hypotheses, not validated treatments.

Title: SroA links SigS-dependent stress signaling to metabolic remodeling in Staphylococcus aureus
Authors: Alqahtani, S. A.; Pasham, S.; Alsulami, J.; Al Ali, A.; Aubee, J. I.; Tomlinson, B. R.; Kennedy, S.; Felton, E. A.; Shaw, L. N.; Thompson, K. M.
Abstract: Staphylococcus aureus encounters diverse environmental conditions during colonization and infection, including fluctuations in nutrient availability, oxidative stress, and oxygen limitation. Adaptation to these environments requires regulatory systems that coordinate stress responses with metabolic physiology. The extracytoplasmic function sigma factor SigS contributes to stress adaptation and virulence in S. aureus and directly activates expression of the sroAB operon, which encodes the small proteins SroA and SroB. Previous work demonstrated that SroA participates in feedback regulation of sigS expression, but the broader physiological role of SroA has remained unclear. To further define the regulatory functions of SroA, we performed RNA sequencing following inducible overexpression of sroA in S. aureus. Transcriptome analysis identified altered expression of genes associated with nitrate respiration, nucleotide biosynthesis, stress responses, and nutrient acquisition. Northern blot and quantitative RT-PCR analysis confirmed repression of narG and narJ transcripts following SroA overexpression. Consistent with these transcriptional changes, SroA overexpression impaired nitrate reduction and produced a modest but significant growth disadvantage under anaerobic conditions in chemically defined medium supplemented with glucose and nitrate. In addition to repression of nitrate respiration genes, SroA overexpression reduced expression of genes involved in de novo purine and pyrimidine biosynthesis, while transcripts associated with stress responses and nutrient acquisition, including sosA and pstS, were increased. Together, these findings support a role for SroA in modulating nitrate respiration-associated pathways and growth under conditions supporting anaerobic respiration, linking SigS-dependent stress signaling to metabolic adaptation in S. aureus.
